3. CITES is legally binding on the States that have joined it, but this Convention does not take the place of national laws. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Environment
detail: IUCN, founded in 1948 at Fontainebleau, France, is a hybrid membership organisation. Its members include sovereign states, government agencies and NGOs. It is headquartered in Gland, Switzerland, and has Observer status at the UN General Assembly, but it is not a UN organ. It publishes the Red List of Threatened Species, and its field work spans thousands of projects worldwide. CITES was drafted following an IUCN resolution of 1963 and signed in Washington DC on 3 March 1973. It entered into force on 1 July 1975, and the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) administers its Secretariat. CITES is an international agreement between governments, and it is legally binding on the Parties. It does not replace national laws. Instead, it gives a framework that each Party must implement through its own domestic legislation. For India, the relevant law is the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. Species are listed in Appendices I, II and III according to the degree of protection they need. Elimination logic: statement 1 fails because IUCN is not a UN organ. That rules out options (a), (c) and (d), so (b) is the only remaining option.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it accepts statement 1, which is false: IUCN is not a UN organ. It also leaves out statements 2 and 3, which are correct.
(b) is correct because statement 2 (IUCN runs thousands of field projects) and statement 3 (CITES is binding but does not replace national laws) are both true. Statement 1 is false.
(c) is wrong because it includes statement 1, which is false, and omits statement 2, which is true.
(d) is wrong because it includes statement 1, which is false, since IUCN is not an organ of the United Nations.
keyfact: IUCN (1948, Gland) is a non-UN membership union that runs field projects; CITES (1973) is a binding treaty enforced through national laws.
option_notes: Option (a), statement 1 only: this would hold only if IUCN were a UN body. It is actually a hybrid membership union founded in 1948, with governments and NGOs as members. It is headquartered in Gland, Switzerland, and has UNGA Observer status. It publishes the Red List and has Species Survival and Protected Areas commissions. It is not part of the UN system, so this option is wrong.

Option (b), statements 2 and 3 only: this is the official answer. It reflects IUCN as a large implementer of conservation field projects. It also reflects CITES (1973, in force 1975) as a legally binding treaty that works through national legislation. CITES is administered by a Secretariat under UNEP, and the Appendices I-III classify the species it covers.

Option (c), statements 1 and 3 only: it correctly treats CITES as binding but not replacing national laws. It wrongly treats IUCN as a UN organ. IUCN is a non-UN union, and it was involved in drafting CITES after a 1963 resolution. Such traps, which turn an independent body into a UN organ, recur in UPSC questions.

Option (d), all three statements: it would require IUCN to be a UN organ, which is false. Remember that CITES has a UNEP-hosted Secretariat but is a treaty, whereas IUCN is an independent union with observer status at the UN. Mixing these up is the usual error, and the option fails on statement 1 alone.
related: IUCN was founded in 1948 and is headquartered in Gland, Switzerland.
CITES was signed in 1973 and came into force in 1975; the CITES Secretariat is hosted by UNEP in Geneva.
World Wildlife Day is celebrated on 3 March, the anniversary of CITES's adoption.
Appendix I of CITES covers species threatened with extinction, with commercial trade generally prohibited.
TRAFFIC is a wildlife trade monitoring network run by WWF and IUCN.
India joined CITES in 1976, and the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 is the main implementing law.
The IUCN Red List categories run from Extinct to Least Concern, including Critically Endangered, Endangered and Vulnerable.
IUCN has Observer status at the UN General Assembly but is not a UN organ.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: IUCN is not a UN organ; it is an independent membership union of states and NGOs. CITES is indeed an agreement between governments, but the first half of the statement makes it false. IUCN was founded in 1948 as the International Union for the Protection of Nature, with headquarters at Gland, Switzerland. It has over 1,400 members, including states, government agencies and civil society organisations. It holds Observer status at the UN General Assembly. It is best known for the Red List, and it also advises on the World Heritage Convention for natural sites.

2 — Correct: IUCN describes itself as running thousands of field projects worldwide to manage natural environments better. Its work covers species conservation, protected areas, ecosystem restoration and sustainable livelihoods. It is organised into six commissions, including the Species Survival Commission (SSC) and the World Commission on Protected Areas (WCPA). Its World Congress meets about every four years. It also helped create the Ramsar Convention, CITES and the World Heritage Convention, and it has a regional office in India.

3 — Correct: CITES is legally binding on the Parties, which are the states that have joined it, but it does not take the place of national laws. Parties must adopt domestic legislation to implement it. The Convention was signed in 1973, came into force in 1975, and has about 180+ Parties. India joined in 1976. The Conference of the Parties (CoP) meets every 2-3 years. Appendix I lists species threatened with extinction, and commercial trade in them is generally prohibited. Appendix II lists species where trade is regulated through permits. Appendix III lists species that a Party has asked others to help it protect.
summary: The answer is (b): statements 2 and 3 are correct and statement 1 is wrong. IUCN is not an organ of the United Nations; it is a membership union of governments and NGOs. It does run thousands of field projects, and CITES is legally binding on its Parties but works through their national laws.
topic_notes:
IUCN (International Union for Conservation of Nature) was founded on 5 October 1948 at Fontainebleau, France. It is headquartered in Gland, Switzerland. It is the world's largest and most diverse environmental network, with governments, NGOs and scientists as members. It issues the Red List of Threatened Species, which uses these categories: Extinct (EX), Extinct in the Wild (EW), Critically Endangered (CR), Endangered (EN), Vulnerable (VU), Near Threatened (NT), Least Concern (LC), Data Deficient (DD) and Not Evaluated (NE). The IUCN Green Status of Species assesses recovery. The IUCN also classifies protected areas into categories Ia to VI.

CITES was adopted on 3 March 1973 in Washington DC, so 3 March is World Wildlife Day. It came into force on 1 July 1975. The Secretariat is administered by UNEP and located in Geneva. Appendix I covers species threatened with extinction, with trade permitted only in exceptional circumstances. Appendix II covers species not necessarily threatened but whose trade must be controlled. Appendix III covers species protected in at least one country that has asked other Parties for help in controlling trade. CITES issues permits and certificates, and it works with a 'non-detriment finding' principle.

India is a Party to CITES (since 1976), and the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and the Wildlife Protection Amendment Act, 2022 give effect to it. TRAFFIC is the wildlife trade monitoring network run by WWF and IUCN. Other related conventions are Ramsar (1971), CMS (Bonn, 1979), the Convention on Biological Diversity (1992), the World Heritage Convention (1972) and the Nagoya Protocol. UPSC may also ask about Red List status of specific species, Appendices, and the bodies that administer each convention.

question: The Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) of sugarcane is approved by the
options: Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices
Directorate of Marketing and Inspection, Ministry of Agriculture
subject: Economy
detail: The Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) is the minimum price that sugar mills must pay to sugarcane growers. It replaced the Statutory Minimum Price (SMP) from the 2009-10 sugar season, under the Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1966, issued under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. The process has three steps. First, the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP) examines costs of production, returns from alternative crops, the price trend in the sugar market, the recovery rate and the reasonable margin for growers. It then recommends the FRP. Second, the Centre consults state governments and other stakeholders. Third, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs approves the FRP, which is announced for each sugar season (October-September) and linked to a basic recovery rate. States may announce a higher State Advised Price (SAP), as Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Haryana do. Elimination: CACP (b) is a recommending body with no approving power. The Directorate of Marketing and Inspection (c) deals with agricultural marketing, grading and standardisation. APMCs (d) are state-level market regulators for the sale of produce, and have no role in setting the FRP.
explanations: Correct: the CCEA gives the final approval of the FRP of sugarcane on the CACP's recommendation, after consulting the states.
Incorrect: the CACP only recommends the FRP (and MSPs for other crops). It does not approve them, and its recommendations are not binding on the government.
Incorrect: the Directorate of Marketing and Inspection works on agricultural marketing, grading and standardisation, and has no role in fixing cane prices.
Incorrect: APMCs are state-level market regulators that run mandis. They do not fix the national FRP.
keyfact: CACP recommends, CCEA approves the FRP of sugarcane; the FRP replaced the SMP in 2009-10 and states may set a higher SAP.
summary: The correct answer is (a) Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA). The CACP only recommends the FRP of sugarcane, and the CCEA, chaired by the Prime Minister, gives the final approval.

ocr: What explains the eastward flow of the equatorial counter-current? (a) The Earth’s rotation on its axis (b) Convergence of the two equatorial currents (c) Difference in salinity of water (ad) Occurrence of the belt of calm near the equator
subject: Geography
detail: In the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans, the trade winds drive the North Equatorial Current and the South Equatorial Current westward, on either side of the equator. Both currents push water against the western margins of the ocean basins and raise sea level there, by roughly 60 cm in the Pacific. The Coriolis force is nearly zero at the equator, so this piled-up water flows back eastward under gravity along the pressure gradient. It moves in the narrow doldrum belt between the two equatorial currents, where the trade winds are weak. This return flow is the Equatorial Counter-Current. It lies at about 3 to 10 degrees N, mostly in the northern hemisphere, and is a warm current. Its eastward flow is a compensation for the water that the two currents have converged on the west. In the Pacific, the counter-current weakens during El Niño events as the trade winds slacken, and the western pile-up shifts eastward. Elimination: rotation of the Earth explains the westward drift of the equatorial currents, not the eastward return. Salinity differences cause only minor density-driven flows. The doldrums provide the calm zone in which the counter-current can flow, but they are not its cause.
explanations: Incorrect: Earth's rotation, together with the trade winds, deflects surface water westward in the equatorial currents. It does not explain a flow in the opposite, eastward direction.
Correct: The North and South Equatorial Currents converge and pile up water in the west of the ocean. This water returns eastward as the counter-current under a pressure gradient.
Incorrect: Differences in salinity cause density-driven currents that are small and local. They do not produce a large, persistent surface current like the counter-current.
Incorrect: The doldrums are a calm belt where the counter-current can flow because the opposing winds are weak. Their presence is not the cause of the flow, so this is a misleading option.
keyfact: Equatorial counter-current: eastward return flow of water piled up by the converging North and South Equatorial Currents, running through the doldrums.
summary: The answer is (b): the equatorial counter-current flows eastward because of the convergence of the North and South Equatorial Currents. The two westward currents pile water up on the western side of the ocean, and this excess water returns eastward as a counter-current in the calm doldrum zone between them.

question:
Consider the following pairs : Place of Pilgrimage Location
1. Srisailam : Nallamala Hills
2. Omkareshwar : Satmala Hills
3. Pushkar : Mahadeo Hills Which of the above pairs is/are correctly matched?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Pilgrimage places are often tested through their geographical setting. Srisailam, in Kurnool district of Andhra Pradesh, hosts the Mallikarjuna Jyotirlinga and a Shakti Peetha. It sits on the Nallamala Hills, part of the Eastern Ghats, on the banks of the Krishna river. Omkareshwar, in Khandwa district of Madhya Pradesh, is a Jyotirlinga on Mandhata (Shivapuri) island in the Narmada. The surrounding region is the Vindhya-Satpura area, and the Satmala hills are in Maharashtra, with no link to Omkareshwar. Pushkar, in Ajmer district of Rajasthan, is famous for the Brahma temple and the sacred Pushkar lake. It lies in the Aravalli range, separated from Ajmer by Nag Pahar. The Mahadeo Hills are a Satpura range feature in Madhya Pradesh, with Pachmarhi and Dhupgarh, so they have nothing to do with Pushkar. Elimination logic: once pair 1 is known to be correct, options (b) is eliminated. Knowing that Pushkar is in Rajasthan and the Aravallis eliminates (c) and (d), leaving (a).
explanations: Correct: only pair 1 is rightly matched, since Srisailam is in the Nallamala Hills.
Wrong: pair 2 is incorrect because Omkareshwar is not in the Satmala hills, and pair 3 is incorrect too.
Wrong: pair 1 is correct, but pair 3 is wrong because Pushkar is in the Aravallis, not the Mahadeo Hills.
Wrong: pairs 2 and 3 are both incorrect, so all three cannot be correct.
keyfact: Srisailam = Nallamala Hills (Krishna river); Omkareshwar = Narmada island; Pushkar = Aravallis, Rajasthan.
statements: 1 — Correct: Srisailam is in the Nallamala Hills of Andhra Pradesh, on the Krishna river.
2 — Incorrect: Omkareshwar is on an island in the Narmada in Madhya Pradesh, in the Vindhya-Satpura region, not the Satmala hills.
3 — Incorrect: Pushkar is in Rajasthan near the Aravalli range, while the Mahadeo Hills are in the Satpura range of Madhya Pradesh.
summary: The answer is (a): only pair 1 is correctly matched. Srisailam lies in the Nallamala Hills, while Omkareshwar is on the Narmada in the Vindhyan/Satpura region and Pushkar is near the Aravalli range.

question:
With reference to Rowlatt Satyagraha, which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. The Rowlatt Act was based on the tecommendations of the ‘Sedition Committee’. B-AQN-0-JUA/63A
2. In Rowlatt Satyagraha, Gandhiji tried to utilize the Home Rule League.
3. Demonstrations against the arrival of Simon Commission coincided with Rowlatt Satyagraha. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Modern History
detail: The Rowlatt Act (Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act, March 1919) was passed on the recommendations of the Sedition Committee headed by Justice Sidney Rowlatt, set up in 1917 to investigate revolutionary activities. It allowed detention without trial for up to two years and trial by special courts without juries or appeals. All Indian members of the Imperial Legislative Council opposed it, and Jinnah, Madan Mohan Malaviya and Mazharul Haque resigned. Gandhi launched the Rowlatt Satyagraha by forming the Satyagraha Sabha in February 1919. He drew on the organisation of the Home Rule League, led by Annie Besant and Tilak, to spread the message, and the League's young activists became volunteers and organisers. A nationwide hartal was held on 6 April 1919, and the protests led to the Jallianwala Bagh massacre on 13 April 1919 in Amritsar. The Simon Commission, an all-white body, was announced in 1927 and arrived in India in 1928, when 'Simon Go Back' protests took place, including the one in which Lala Lajpat Rai was injured in Lahore. Elimination: statement 3 is chronologically wrong, which removes (c) and (d). Statement 1 is correct, which removes (c). Only (b) remains.
explanations: (a) Wrong: It is incomplete, because statement 2 is also correct (Gandhi utilised the Home Rule League).
(b) Right: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, and statement 3 is chronologically incorrect.
(c) Wrong: It includes statement 3, which is false, and leaves out statement 1, which is true.
(d) Wrong: It includes statement 3, as the Simon Commission arrived in 1928, nine years after the Rowlatt Satyagraha.
keyfact: Rowlatt Act and Satyagraha: 1919 (Sedition Committee, Home Rule League network used by Gandhi); Simon Commission: 1927-28.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Rowlatt Act of 1919 was based on the report of the Sedition Committee (Rowlatt Committee, 1917-18).
2 — Correct: Gandhi used the Home Rule League's organisation and its activists to mobilise support for the Satyagraha, alongside the Satyagraha Sabha.
3 — Incorrect: The Simon Commission protests were in 1928, while the Rowlatt Satyagraha was in 1919, so they did not coincide.
summary: The correct answer is (b): statements 1 and 2 are correct, while statement 3 is wrong. The Rowlatt Act (1919) followed the Sedition Committee's recommendations, and Gandhi used the Home Rule League's network for the Satyagraha. The Simon Commission came in 1928, nine years later.

question: Among the following, which were frequently mentioned in the news for the outbreak of Ebola virus recently?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: The question refers to the 2014 West African Ebola outbreak. It began in December 2013 in Guinea, in the Guéckédou area (Meliandou village), and spread to neighbouring Sierra Leone and Liberia. The WHO declared it a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) on 8 August 2014, and the epidemic was declared over in 2016. About 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths were reported, mostly in these three countries. Ebola is caused by a filovirus of the genus Ebolavirus, is named after the Ebola River in the DR Congo (first identified in 1976), and is a zoonotic disease with fruit bats as the likely natural reservoir. It spreads through direct contact with blood and body fluids. Elimination logic: Syria and Jordan are Middle Eastern and were in the news for conflict and refugees. The Philippines and Papua New Guinea are in Asia-Pacific. Jamaica, Haiti and Surinam are in the Americas. Only option (b) is in West Africa, so it is the only possible answer.
explanations: Wrong. Syria and Jordan were in the news for the Syrian civil war, ISIS and refugee flows, not Ebola. Both are in West Asia, far from the outbreak zone.
Correct. Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia were the three worst-hit countries in the 2014 West African outbreak. Guinea was the origin, and the two others saw the largest case counts.

Wrong. The Philippines and Papua New Guinea are in Southeast Asia and Oceania. The Philippines does have a Reston ebolavirus strain in animals, but it is not known to cause illness in humans, and there was no 2014 outbreak there.
Wrong. Jamaica, Haiti and Surinam are in the Caribbean and South America. Haiti was associated with cholera after the 2010 earthquake, not Ebola.
keyfact: The 2014-16 Ebola epidemic hit Guinea (origin), Sierra Leone and Liberia in West Africa, and the WHO declared it a PHEIC on 8 August 2014.
option_notes: Syria and Jordan are West Asian (Levant) countries. Syria has been in civil war since 2011, with ISIS, chemical weapons concerns and millions of refugees. Jordan hosts large numbers of Syrian refugees (for example the Zaatari camp) and is a constitutional monarchy. Neither has had a major Ebola outbreak.

Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia are West African nations. Guinea is the origin of the 2014 epidemic, with Conakry as its capital. Sierra Leone's capital is Freetown, and Liberia's is Monrovia. All three are among the poorest countries, with weak health systems, which let the virus spread widely. They received international aid and were declared Ebola-free in 2015-16.

The Philippines is a Southeast Asian archipelago, and Papua New Guinea is in Oceania and occupies the eastern half of New Guinea island. The Reston ebolavirus was found in monkeys and pigs in the Philippines, but it is not pathogenic to humans. Neither country had the 2014 epidemic.

Jamaica and Haiti are Caribbean island countries, and Surinam (Suriname) is a small country in northeastern South America. Haiti suffered a cholera epidemic after the 2010 earthquake. Chikungunya and Zika spread in the region later. No Ebola epidemic was recorded in these countries in 2014.
related: The 2014 Ebola outbreak began in Guinea in December 2013 and was declared a PHEIC by the WHO on 8 August 2014.
Ebola is caused by a filovirus and is named after the Ebola River in the DR Congo.
Fruit bats are the suspected natural reservoir of Ebola.
Ervebo (rVSV-ZEBOV) was the first licensed Ebola vaccine, approved in 2019.
The 2018-20 Kivu outbreak in the DR Congo was the second-largest Ebola outbreak.
The Reston ebolavirus is not known to cause disease in humans.
The WHO has declared PHEICs for H1N1, polio, Ebola, Zika, COVID-19 and mpox.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with body fluids, not through the air.
summary: The answer is (b) Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia. These three West African countries were the epicentre of the 2014-16 Ebola epidemic, the largest ever recorded, and accounted for almost all of its cases and deaths.
topic_notes: Ebola Virus Disease (EVD), earlier called Ebola haemorrhagic fever, is a severe, often fatal illness with a fatality rate of about 50% on average (25-90% in different outbreaks). It is caused by viruses of the family Filoviridae. There are six known species: Zaire, Sudan, Bundibugyo, Taï Forest, Reston and Bombali. The Zaire ebolavirus caused the 2014 epidemic. The virus was first identified in 1976 in two simultaneous outbreaks, one in Nzara, South Sudan, and one in Yambuku, DR Congo, near the Ebola River. Fruit bats of the Pteropodidae family are considered the natural hosts. Transmission to humans is through infected wild animals (chimpanzees, gorillas, antelopes), and then human to human through direct contact with blood, secretions and body fluids, or contaminated surfaces. Symptoms include fever, fatigue, muscle pain, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in some cases, internal and external bleeding. Incubation is 2 to 21 days. Treatment is supportive care, although monoclonal antibody therapies (Inmazeb, Ebanga) were later approved. The rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine (Ervebo, by Merck) was approved in 2019. The 2014 epidemic was declared a PHEIC on 8 August 2014. The 2018-20 outbreak in the DR Congo (Kivu) was the second largest and was also declared a PHEIC in 2019. Other WHO-declared PHEICs include H1N1 (2009), polio (2014), Zika (2016), COVID-19 (2020) and mpox (2022 and 2024). UPSC often asks about the causes of these diseases, whether they are zoonotic, vaccine details and where the outbreaks occurred.

ocr: With reference to ‘fly ash’ produced by the power plants using coal as fuel, which of the following statements is/are correct? 1. Fly ash can be used in the production of bricks for building construction. 2. Fly ash can be used as a replacement for some of the Portland cement contents of concrete. 3. Fly ash is made up of silicon dioxide and calcium oxide only, and does not contain any toxic & elements. Select the correct answer using the code given below. (a) 1 and 2 (b) 2 only feo} 1 and 3 (d) 3 only
subject: Environment
detail: Fly ash is the fine particulate residue carried off in flue gases when pulverised coal is burnt in thermal power plants, and it is collected by electrostatic precipitators. It is a pozzolanic material: it reacts with calcium hydroxide released during cement hydration to form additional cementitious compounds. This is why it is used in Portland Pozzolana Cement (PPC), in blended and high-volume fly ash concrete, in fly ash bricks and blocks, in road embankments, in mine-void filling and in soil stabilisation. Its main constituents are silica (SiO2), alumina (Al2O3), iron oxide (Fe2O3) and lime (CaO), with smaller amounts of magnesium oxide, sulphur trioxide and unburnt carbon. It also holds trace toxic elements such as arsenic, lead, mercury, cadmium, chromium and selenium, which can leach into groundwater from ash ponds. Statement 3 is therefore wrong for two reasons: it names only two oxides, and it denies toxic elements. Elimination logic: once statement 3 is rejected, options (c) and (d) fall away. Statement 1 is clearly true, so (b), which says '2 only', also falls away. That leaves (a). In India, MoEF notifications since 1999 require the use of fly ash products within a set radius of thermal plants.
explanations: Correct. Statements 1 and 2 are true and statement 3 is false, which matches this option exactly.
Wrong. Statement 1 is also true, since fly ash is used in bricks, so '2 only' leaves out a correct statement.
Wrong. It includes statement 3, which is false, and leaves out statement 2, which is true.
Wrong. Statement 3 alone is false, and this option rejects both of the true statements.
keyfact: Fly ash is a pozzolanic coal-combustion waste used in bricks and as a partial cement substitute, but it is a mix of oxides with toxic trace metals, not just SiO2 and CaO.
related: Fly ash is a pozzolanic material that reacts with calcium hydroxide to form cementitious compounds.
Portland Pozzolana Cement contains 15-35% fly ash (IS 1489).
Fly ash is captured from flue gas by electrostatic precipitators.
Class F fly ash is low in calcium and comes from bituminous coal; Class C is high in calcium.
The MoEF 1999 notification mandates the use of fly ash bricks within a set radius of thermal power plants.
Fly ash contains trace toxic metals such as arsenic, lead, mercury and cadmium.
Red mud is the waste from alumina (bauxite) refining, and phosphogypsum is a waste from fertiliser production.
Cenospheres are hollow, lightweight spheres recovered from fly ash.
statements: 1 — Correct: Fly ash is a standard raw material for bricks, blocks and tiles used in building construction. Fly ash bricks are made from fly ash, sand or stone dust, lime or cement and gypsum, and are cured by steam or water rather than burnt in kilns. They are lighter and stronger than clay bricks and save topsoil, since no clay is dug. The MoEF fly ash notification of 1999 (amended 2003 and 2009) mandates their use within 100 km (later 300 km) of coal or lignite thermal plants. The BIS standard is IS 12894. Fly ash bricks also help reduce coal-ash disposal problems and kiln emissions.

2 — Correct: Fly ash can replace part of the Portland cement in concrete, typically 15-35% and up to 50-60% in high-volume mixes. Because it is pozzolanic, it reacts with lime from cement hydration to form calcium silicate hydrate, which improves long-term strength, workability and durability, reduces heat of hydration and lowers permeability. Portland Pozzolana Cement (IS 1489) contains 15-35% fly ash. Replacing cement also cuts CO2 emissions, since cement production is highly carbon-intensive. Class F (low calcium, from bituminous coal) and Class C (high calcium) are the two ASTM classes of fly ash.

3 — Incorrect: Fly ash is not made only of SiO2 and CaO. Its principal components are silica, alumina and iron oxide, with lime in varying amounts (low in Class F, high in Class C). It also contains magnesium oxide, sulphates, unburnt carbon and trace heavy metals such as arsenic, lead, mercury, cadmium, chromium and selenium. These can leach into soil and groundwater from ash ponds, and fine particles (PM2.5) cause respiratory problems. Ash-pond breaches and ash dumping are recurring environmental issues in India, which is why disposal and utilisation rules exist.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 and 2. Fly ash is widely used in brick manufacture and as a partial replacement for Portland cement in concrete. Statement 3 is wrong because fly ash is not made of silicon dioxide and calcium oxide only, and it contains toxic trace elements.
topic_notes: Fly ash is the main solid waste of coal-based thermal power, and India produces well over 200 million tonnes of it a year. It consists of fine, glassy, spherical particles of silica, alumina, iron oxide and lime. Fly ash is collected from flue gas by electrostatic precipitators, while the coarser bottom ash falls to the bottom of the boiler. ASTM C618 classifies it as Class F (low calcium, from bituminous coal) and Class C (high calcium, from lignite or sub-bituminous coal). Uses include Portland Pozzolana Cement, ready-mix concrete, bricks, blocks and tiles, road and embankment construction, filling of mines and low-lying areas, soil conditioning in agriculture, and extraction of cenospheres. Environmental concerns include air pollution from fine dust, leaching of heavy metals into groundwater from ash ponds, loss of land to ash ponds and ash-dyke failures. Policy: the MoEF&CC notification of 1999, amended in 2003, 2009 and 2021, mandates use of fly ash-based products in construction within a specified radius of thermal plants and requires plants to achieve near-100% utilisation. Fly Ash Mission and the Fly Ash Utilisation Centre under the Department of Science and Technology have promoted its use. Fly ash bricks also help cut the soil erosion and emissions linked to clay brick kilns. Related topics UPSC may ask about include other pozzolanic materials (silica fume, ground granulated blast furnace slag), red mud from aluminium refining, phosphogypsum, and the use of industrial waste in cement. Questions may also cover the pollutants from thermal power plants (SO2, NOx, mercury, PM) and flue gas desulphurisation requirements.

question:
With reference to ‘dugong’, a mammal found in India, which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. Itis a herbivorous marine animal.
2. Itis found along the entire coast of India.
3. It is given legal protection under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. Select the correct answer using the cade given below
subject: Environment
detail: The dugong (Dugong dugon) is a large marine mammal of the order Sirenia, which also includes manatees. It is the only strictly marine herbivorous mammal, and its diet is almost entirely seagrass, which is why it is called the 'sea cow'. In India its distribution is patchy and confined to the Gulf of Mannar and Palk Bay (Tamil Nadu), the Gulf of Kutch (Gujarat), the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, and a few other places. It is absent from most of the east and west coast, so statement 2 fails on the word 'entire'. It is listed under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, which gives the highest protection. The IUCN status is Vulnerable, and it is on CITES Appendix I. It is also listed on CMS (Bonn Convention), and India signed the CMS Dugong MoU. Tamil Nadu declared the Dugong Conservation Reserve in Palk Bay in 2022, the first in India. Elimination logic: statement 2 is clearly wrong because of 'entire', so (a) and (b) go, and since statement 3 is true, (c) is correct and (d) is incomplete.
explanations: Wrong: it accepts statement 2, which is false because the dugong is found only in specific pockets and not along the entire coast.
Wrong: statement 2 alone is incorrect, and it leaves out the true statements 1 and 3.
Correct: statement 1 (herbivorous marine mammal) and statement 3 (Schedule I protection) are both true, and statement 2 is false.
Wrong: statement 3 is true, but it omits statement 1, which is also true.
keyfact: Dugong: herbivorous marine mammal (seagrass eater), found only in pockets of India, Schedule I of the WPA 1972, so the answer is 1 and 3.
option_notes: 1 and 2 only: this option pairs the true herbivore statement with the false 'entire coast' claim. The dugong occurs only in the Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, the Gulf of Kutch and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. It is not found along the whole coastline, and areas without seagrass lack it. Remember the pattern: UPSC often uses absolute words like 'entire' to make a statement false.

2 only: this would claim the dugong occurs along the entire Indian coast, which is false. Its range depends on seagrass meadows, which are found in a few places such as the Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, the Gulf of Kutch and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Seagrass loss from pollution, trawling and coastal development has shrunk its range further. The Palk Bay Dugong Conservation Reserve (2022) is India's first such reserve.

1 and 3: the official answer. The dugong is a herbivorous marine mammal (order Sirenia) that feeds on seagrass, and it has Schedule I protection under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. It is IUCN Vulnerable and on CITES Appendix I. The Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands are key habitats. It is also called the sea cow.

3 only: this option is correct about legal protection but incomplete. Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 gives absolute protection with the heaviest penalties, and covers species such as the tiger, elephant, Ganges river dolphin and dugong. It ignores that the dugong is also a herbivorous marine mammal, so it fails by omission.
related: The dugong is also called the 'sea cow' and is the state animal of Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
India's first Dugong Conservation Reserve was notified in Palk Bay, Tamil Nadu, in 2022.
Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve was India's first marine biosphere reserve (2001).
Gulf of Kutch Marine National Park (1980) was India's first marine national park.
Dugongs are in order Sirenia along with manatees; the dugong has a fluke tail.
Dugongs are IUCN Vulnerable and on CITES Appendix I.
India signed the CMS Dugong Memorandum of Understanding in 2008.
Seagrass meadows are blue carbon sinks and the dugong's key habitat.
statements: 1 — Correct: the dugong is a herbivorous marine mammal that grazes on seagrass. Facts: it belongs to the order Sirenia, family Dugongidae, and is the only living member of that family. It has a fluke-like tail, unlike the manatee's paddle-shaped tail. It lives in warm coastal waters of the Indo-Pacific, from East Africa to Australia, and it can live 70 years. Its slow breeding and dependence on seagrass meadows make it vulnerable to habitat loss, fishing nets and boat strikes.

2 — Incorrect: the dugong is not found along the entire coast of India. Facts: its presence is restricted to the Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, the Gulf of Kutch and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which have seagrass beds. Populations are small, and the Andamans are thought to hold the healthiest numbers. Seagrass degradation, coastal development, trawling and entanglement in gill nets are the main threats. The Wildlife Institute of India and state forest departments run monitoring. The Dugong Conservation Reserve in Palk Bay (Tamil Nadu, 2022) covers about 448 sq km.

3 — Correct: the dugong is listed in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. Facts: Schedule I gives the highest protection, with the strictest penalties for hunting or trade. Other Schedule I species include the tiger, Asiatic lion, snow leopard and Ganges river dolphin. The Act was amended in 2022 and now has four schedules in place of the earlier six. The dugong is IUCN Vulnerable and on CITES Appendix I, and India has signed the CMS Dugong Memorandum of Understanding.
summary: The answer is (c): statements 1 and 3 are correct. The dugong is a herbivorous marine mammal that feeds on seagrass, and it is protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. It is not found along the entire Indian coast, so statement 2 is wrong.
topic_notes: The dugong (Dugong dugon) is the only strictly marine herbivorous mammal. It belongs to order Sirenia, which includes the manatees (three species) and the extinct Steller's sea cow. Key identification point: the dugong has a whale-like fluke tail, while the manatee has a rounded paddle tail. It feeds on seagrasses such as Halophila and Halodule, so it depends on healthy seagrass meadows. Gestation lasts about 13 to 14 months and calves are born singly at long intervals, which makes recovery from population decline slow. In India it occurs in the Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, the Gulf of Kutch and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Legal status: Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972; IUCN Vulnerable; CITES Appendix I; CMS listing, with India a signatory to the CMS Dugong MoU (2008). Tamil Nadu notified the Dugong Conservation Reserve in Palk Bay in September 2022, covering about 448 sq km. The Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve, India's first marine biosphere reserve (2001), is a major habitat. Other marine reserves and species to link: Gulf of Kutch Marine National Park (the first marine national park in India, 1980), Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park in the Andamans, and Olive Ridley turtles, whose nesting site is Gahirmatha in Odisha. Threats include seagrass loss, bycatch in gill nets, boat strikes, pollution and traditional hunting for meat and oil. Related angles for UPSC: UN Convention on Migratory Species, seagrass ecosystems as blue carbon sinks, coral reefs and mangroves, and Schedule listing under the 2022 amendment to the Wildlife Act.

question:
Who of the following was/were economic critic/critics of colonialism in India?
1. Dadabhai Naoroji
2. G. Subramania lyer
3. R. C. Dutt Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The early nationalists, often called Moderates, built the economic critique of colonialism. Dadabhai Naoroji, the 'Grand Old Man of India', propounded the Drain of Wealth theory in 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901), and earlier in papers presented in the 1860s-70s. He argued that India's resources were being transferred to Britain without return, as home charges, interest, and salaries and pensions of officials. R. C. Dutt, an ICS officer and later Congress president (1899), wrote 'The Economic History of India' (2 vols, 1901 and 1903) and 'India in the Victorian Age', documenting de-industrialisation, heavy land revenue and famines. G. Subramania Iyer, co-founder of The Hindu (1878) and of the Tamil daily Swadesamitran, and a founder of the Madras Mahajana Sabha (1884), criticised British economic policy, its exploitation of India, and the resulting poverty. Other critics include M. G. Ranade and G. K. Gokhale. Elimination logic: knowing that Naoroji and Dutt are certain eliminates (a)-(c) only partly; recognising Iyer's economic writings makes (d) the only option containing all three.
explanations: (a) is wrong: it omits Iyer and Dutt, who were also economic critics of colonial rule.
(b) is wrong: it leaves out R. C. Dutt, author of 'The Economic History of India'.
(c) is wrong: it leaves out Dadabhai Naoroji, the chief exponent of the Drain theory.
(d) is right: Naoroji, Iyer and Dutt all criticised the colonial economy, so all three statements hold.
keyfact: Naoroji (Drain Theory, 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India'), R. C. Dutt ('Economic History of India') and G. Subramania Iyer were all economic critics of colonialism.
statements: 1 — Correct: Dadabhai Naoroji formulated the Drain of Wealth theory in 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India'.
2 — Correct: G. Subramania Iyer, founder of The Hindu, criticised British economic exploitation and the poverty it caused in India.
3 — Correct: R. C. Dutt wrote 'The Economic History of India' and exposed colonial economic exploitation.
summary: The answer is (d): all three, Dadabhai Naoroji, G. Subramania Iyer and R. C. Dutt, were economic critics of colonialism. Each analysed British rule as a system that drained India's wealth and caused impoverishment.

question: Which one of the following issues the ‘Global Economic Prospects’ report periodically?
options: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development
subject: Economy
detail: Global Economic Prospects is published by the World Bank's Development Prospects Group, in January and June each year. It reviews recent global economic developments, forecasts GDP growth for the world, advanced economies, and emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs), and covers regional outlooks including South Asia, where India's growth is highlighted. It also contains analytical special-focus chapters on topics such as inflation, debt, commodity markets and productivity. For UPSC, students should link each major report with its issuing body: World Bank issues GEP, Ease of Doing Business (discontinued in 2021), World Development Report, Human Capital Index and Logistics Performance Index; IMF issues World Economic Outlook, Global Financial Stability Report and Fiscal Monitor; UNDP issues the Human Development Report; WEF issues the Global Competitiveness Report and Global Gender Gap Report. Elimination logic: the Asian Development Bank publishes the Asian Development Outlook, the EBRD publishes the Transition Report, and the US Federal Reserve publishes the Beige Book and monetary policy reports. None of these three publishes GEP, so only the World Bank fits.
explanations: Incorrect: The Asian Development Bank publishes the Asian Development Outlook (ADO) and Key Indicators for Asia and the Pacific, not Global Economic Prospects.
Incorrect: The EBRD publishes the Transition Report and Regional Economic Prospects, focused on its countries of operation, not GEP.
Incorrect: The US Federal Reserve issues the Beige Book, the Monetary Policy Report and FOMC projections, which are national, not a global prospects report.
Correct: The World Bank publishes Global Economic Prospects twice a year, in January and June, giving global and regional growth forecasts.
keyfact: World Bank = Global Economic Prospects (Jan & June); IMF = World Economic Outlook; ADB = Asian Development Outlook.
summary: The correct answer is (d) The World Bank. Global Economic Prospects (GEP) is the World Bank Group's flagship twice-yearly report (January and June) analysing global growth and the outlook for emerging markets and developing economies.

ocr: When the Reserve Bank of India reduces the Statutory Liquidity Ratio by 50 basis points, which of the following is likely to happen? (a) India’s GDP growth rate increases drastically (b) Foreign Institutional Investors may bring more capital into our country (c) Scheduled Commercial Banks may cut their lending rates fd) It may drastically reduce the liquidity to the banking system
subject: Economy
detail: SLR is the minimum percentage of Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) that commercial banks must maintain with themselves in liquid form: cash, gold, or unencumbered approved securities such as G-secs and T-bills. It is a statutory requirement under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and the RBI sets it. The Act's floor is 0%, and the earlier ceiling of 40% was removed in 2007. The SLR was brought down to 18% in 2020 (it was 18.25% in 2015), and the RBI changes it only occasionally. Cutting the SLR by 50 basis points (0.5 percentage point) releases a small amount of lendable resources, because banks need to park less money in government securities. This eases liquidity, increases banks' capacity to lend, and puts downward pressure on lending rates, so the impact is moderate and gradual. The elimination logic is that words like 'drastically' signal an exaggeration in options (a) and (d). Option (b) is wrong because FII flows depend on global conditions, returns and the exchange rate, not directly on the SLR. Option (c) uses the cautious word 'may', which makes it the most plausible choice.
explanations: Wrong: a 50 bps SLR change is marginal and cannot make GDP growth rise 'drastically'. Growth depends on many other factors, and monetary transmission is slow and partial.
Wrong: FII inflows depend on global liquidity, relative returns, growth prospects and the exchange rate. They do not follow directly from an SLR cut, and the link is weak and uncertain.
Correct: a lower SLR releases funds that were locked in government securities, which raises banks' lendable resources. This lets them cut lending rates, hence 'may cut'.
Wrong: lowering the SLR increases liquidity in the banking system, not reduces it, and a 50 bps change would be small, not drastic.
keyfact: Lower SLR means more lendable funds with banks, hence easier credit and possibly lower lending rates. SLR is held in liquid assets (cash, gold, G-secs) as a percentage of NDTL.
summary: The answer is (c). A cut in the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) frees up funds that banks were required to hold in liquid assets such as government securities, cash and gold. Banks can then lend more, so they may reduce their lending rates.

ocr: With reference to the use of nano- technology in health sector, which of the following statements is/are correct? 1. Targeted drug delivery is made possible by nanotechnology. 2. Nanotechnology can largely contribute to gene therapy. Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa) 1 only (b} 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (a) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Nanotechnology works with materials at 1-100 nm, where properties differ from bulk matter. In health it is used for drug delivery, diagnostics, imaging, tissue engineering and gene therapy. Targeted drug delivery uses liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles, dendrimers, gold nanoparticles and carbon nanotubes. These carry a drug to diseased tissue, such as a tumour, either through the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect or by ligands/antibodies on the surface. This raises efficacy and reduces side effects, so Statement 1 is correct. Gene therapy needs safe vectors to deliver DNA, siRNA or CRISPR components into cells. Lipid nanoparticles, polymeric nanoparticles and gold nanoparticles serve as non-viral vectors and avoid the immunogenicity risks of viral vectors. Lipid nanoparticles were used in mRNA COVID-19 vaccines, which shows their delivery power. So Statement 2 is correct. Elimination logic: both statements describe well-established applications, so (a), (b) and (d) fail. UPSC questions on this theme are typically straightforward and reward knowing the applications and the risks (nanotoxicity, regulation, environmental concerns).
explanations: (a) is wrong because Statement 2 is also correct; nanotechnology does contribute to gene therapy.
(b) is wrong because Statement 1 is also correct; targeted drug delivery is a core nanomedicine application.
(c) is right because both statements are correct: targeted drug delivery and gene therapy are both enabled by nanotechnology.
(d) is wrong because both statements are correct, so 'neither' cannot hold.
keyfact: Nanotechnology in health enables both targeted drug delivery (nanocarriers) and gene therapy (non-viral nanoparticle vectors), so the answer is (c).
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', would hold if only targeted drug delivery were valid. Targeted delivery uses nanocarriers like liposomes and polymeric nanoparticles to concentrate drugs at diseased sites by passive (EPR effect) or active (ligand-receptor) targeting. Doxil, a liposomal doxorubicin, was approved by the US FDA in 1995 as the first nano-drug. Here it is incomplete because gene therapy applications also hold true.

Option (b), '2 only', would hold if only gene therapy were valid. Gene therapy introduces, edits or silences genes to treat disease, using viral vectors (adenovirus, AAV, lentivirus) or non-viral vectors such as nanoparticles. Examples include Luxturna for retinal disease and Zolgensma for spinal muscular atrophy (both viral vector based). It is wrong here because targeted drug delivery is also a correct statement.

Option (c), 'Both 1 and 2', is the official correct answer. It reflects that nanomedicine covers both drug delivery and gene delivery. Nanoparticles of 1-100 nm can be engineered to carry drugs or nucleic acids, cross biological barriers, target specific cells and release cargo in a controlled way. Applications also include imaging contrast agents, biosensors, antimicrobial coatings, tissue scaffolds and cancer therapy such as photothermal treatment with gold nanoshells.

Option (d), 'Neither 1 nor 2', would mean nanotechnology had no role in either area, which is false. Nanotechnology is widely researched and used in medicine, with approved products in oncology, vaccines (lipid nanoparticle mRNA), imaging and RNA interference drugs. Concerns exist about nanotoxicity, bioaccumulation and regulation, but these do not negate the applications. India's Nano Mission (2007, DST) supports such research.
related: Nanoscale range is 1-100 nm; 1 nm equals one billionth of a metre.
India's Nano Mission was launched in 2007 under the Department of Science and Technology.
Doxil (liposomal doxorubicin) was the first FDA-approved nano-drug in 1995.
Lipid nanoparticles delivered the mRNA in the Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna COVID-19 vaccines.
Patisiran (Onpattro, 2018) was the first approved siRNA drug and uses an LNP carrier.
The EPR effect lets nanoparticles accumulate in tumours through leaky blood vessels.
IFFCO's Nano Urea is a nano-fertiliser launched in 2021.
Silver nanoparticles are used for antimicrobial wound dressings and water purification.
statements: 1 — Correct: Nanocarriers can deliver drugs specifically to target cells or tissues. Liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles, dendrimers, quantum dots and gold nanoparticles act as carriers. Passive targeting uses the EPR effect in leaky tumour blood vessels, while active targeting uses surface ligands, antibodies or folate that bind receptors on diseased cells. Examples: liposomal doxorubicin (Doxil), the first FDA-approved nano-drug (1995), and albumin-bound paclitaxel (Abraxane). Benefits are lower dose, fewer side effects, controlled release and the ability to cross barriers such as the blood-brain barrier. Challenges are toxicity, cost, clearance by the immune system and regulation.

2 — Correct: Nanoparticles serve as non-viral vectors that carry DNA, RNA or gene-editing tools into cells. Lipid nanoparticles, polymeric nanoparticles, gold nanoparticles and dendrimers protect genetic material from degradation and aid cell entry. They avoid the immune reactions and insertional mutagenesis risks linked with viral vectors. Lipid nanoparticles carried the mRNA in the Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna COVID-19 vaccines, and the first siRNA drug, patisiran (Onpattro, 2018), uses an LNP. Nanotechnology is also used with CRISPR-Cas9 delivery. Gene therapy treats genetic disorders by correcting, replacing or silencing faulty genes.
summary: The answer is (c) Both 1 and 2. Nanotechnology enables targeted drug delivery through engineered nanocarriers, and it is a major enabler of gene therapy because nanoparticles can carry genetic material into cells.
topic_notes:
Nanotechnology deals with structures of 1-100 nanometres (1 nm = 10^-9 m). At this scale materials show altered optical, electrical, magnetic and chemical properties because of quantum effects and large surface-area-to-volume ratio. Types of nanomaterials: nanoparticles, nanotubes (carbon nanotubes), fullerenes, quantum dots, nanowires, dendrimers, liposomes and graphene.

Health applications: (1) targeted drug delivery, especially in cancer; (2) gene therapy and RNA delivery, using lipid nanoparticles; (3) diagnostics and imaging, including quantum dots, magnetic nanoparticles for MRI, and nano-biosensors; (4) tissue engineering and regenerative medicine, using nanofibre scaffolds; (5) antimicrobial uses, such as silver nanoparticles in wound dressings; (6) theranostics, combining therapy and diagnosis; (7) nanorobots, which are still experimental; (8) vaccines, such as mRNA-LNP COVID-19 vaccines.

Other sectors: water purification (nano-filters, silver and titanium dioxide), agriculture (nano-fertilisers such as IFFCO's Nano Urea, nano-pesticides), energy (solar cells, batteries), electronics, cosmetics (sunscreens with ZnO or TiO2), textiles and food packaging.

India: the Nano Mission was launched in 2007 by the Department of Science and Technology with Rs 1,000 crore over five years. It promotes basic research, infrastructure, applications, human resources and international collaboration. Nano Science and Technology Initiative (NSTI) preceded it in 2001. Centres exist at institutes such as IISc and IITs.

Risks and regulation: nanotoxicity, bioaccumulation, environmental release, and gaps in specific regulation. India has drafted guidelines for nanopharmaceuticals (2019) and the Department of Biotechnology and ICMR have related guidance. Possible future questions: carbon nanotube properties, graphene, nano-silver, quantum dots, nano urea, and the difference between top-down and bottom-up synthesis.

question: In India, markets in agricultural products are regulated under the
options: Agricultural Produce Market Committee Act enacted by States
Food Products Order, 1956 and Meat and Food Products Order, 1973
subject: Economy
detail: Agricultural marketing in India is regulated mainly through State-level APMC Acts (sometimes called Agricultural Produce Marketing (Regulation) Acts). Under these laws, a State notifies agricultural commodities and market areas, and the APMC, a statutory market committee, regulates trade within the mandi. It licenses traders and commission agents, collects market fees, and ensures sale through open auction. The constitutional basis is Entry 28 of the State List (Seventh Schedule), 'Markets and fairs', and agriculture is also a State subject (Entry 14). The Centre has tried to push reform through the Model APMC Act 2003 and the Model APLM Act 2017. The Farmers' Produce Trade and Commerce Act 2020 was later passed and repealed in 2021. The other options deal with different subjects. The Essential Commodities Act 1955 controls production, supply, distribution and prices of notified essential goods, and is used for stock limits and price control, not mandi regulation. The Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marking) Act 1937 provides for quality standards, the AGMARK certification. The Food Products Order 1956 and Meat and Food Products Order 1973 relate to licensing and hygiene of processed food and meat products. Eliminate (a), (c) and (d) by their subject matter.
explanations: Wrong: The Essential Commodities Act 1955 regulates production, supply, distribution and pricing of notified essential commodities, with tools like stock limits. It does not regulate mandis.
Correct: State APMC Acts establish and regulate agricultural produce markets, licensing traders and regulating auctions and market fees, under the State List entry on markets and fairs.
Wrong: The Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marking) Act 1937 deals with grading and quality marking (AGMARK), not the regulation of market yards.

Wrong: The Fruit Products Order-style orders, namely the Food Products Order 1956 and Meat and Food Products Order 1973, govern licensing, quality and hygiene in food processing and meat products, not agricultural markets.
keyfact: Mandis are regulated by State APMC Acts (Entry 28, State List: markets and fairs); AGMARK comes from the 1937 Grading and Marking Act.
summary: The correct answer is (b). Regulation of agricultural produce markets (mandis) in India is done through the Agricultural Produce Market Committee (APMC) Acts enacted by individual States, since 'markets and fairs' fall under the State domain.

ocr: Which one of the following is the national aquatic animal of India? (a) Saltwater crocodile (bj) Olive ridley turtle (c) Gangetic dolphin (ad) Gharial
subject: Environment
detail: India's National Aquatic Animal is the Gangetic river dolphin (Platanista gangetica gangetica), notified on 5 October 2009 at the first meeting of the National Ganga River Basin Authority (NGRBA), chaired by the Prime Minister. It is a freshwater, nearly blind mammal that navigates by echolocation, and it is found in the Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna and Karnaphuli-Sangu river systems of India, Bangladesh and Nepal. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List, placed in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, and in Appendix I of CITES. It is also covered under CMS (Bonn Convention). The Vikramshila Gangetic Dolphin Sanctuary in Bhagalpur, Bihar, is the only dolphin sanctuary in India. National Dolphin Day is observed on 5 October, and Project Dolphin was announced in 2020. Elimination logic: the saltwater crocodile and the olive ridley are marine or estuarine species, and neither has been given national status. The gharial is a freshwater, fish-eating crocodilian, but it is Critically Endangered and has no national symbol status. The question asks for a mammal that is truly aquatic and is a national symbol, which points to the dolphin.
explanations: Incorrect: the saltwater (estuarine) crocodile, Crocodylus porosus, is a reptile and is not India's national aquatic animal.
Incorrect: the olive ridley is a marine turtle famous for mass nesting (arribada) at Gahirmatha, Odisha, but it holds no national symbol status.
Correct: the Gangetic dolphin was declared National Aquatic Animal in 2009.
Incorrect: the gharial is a fish-eating crocodilian of Himalayan rivers and is Critically Endangered, but it is not the national aquatic animal.
keyfact: Gangetic river dolphin = National Aquatic Animal of India (2009); Endangered; Vikramshila Sanctuary, Bihar.
option_notes: The saltwater crocodile (Crocodylus porosus) is the largest living reptile. It lives in estuaries, mangroves and coasts, and in India it is found in Bhitarkanika (Odisha), the Sundarbans and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. It is listed under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act and as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. Bhitarkanika has a major crocodile conservation programme begun in the 1975 Crocodile Project.

The olive ridley turtle (Lepidochelys olivacea) is the most abundant sea turtle and is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. It is famous for mass nesting (arribada) at Gahirmatha, Rushikulya and Devi river mouth in Odisha. It is listed in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act and in CITES Appendix I. Odisha uses Turtle Excluder Devices to reduce bycatch in trawl nets.

The Gangetic river dolphin (Platanista gangetica) is a freshwater cetacean that is almost blind and uses echolocation. It is Endangered on the IUCN Red List and in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act. It was declared National Aquatic Animal in 2009. It is found in the Ganga, Brahmaputra and their tributaries. Vikramshila Sanctuary in Bihar protects it. Project Dolphin was announced in 2020, and 5 October is National Dolphin Day.

The gharial (Gavialis gangeticus) is a long-snouted, fish-eating crocodilian, listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List and in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act. It is found in the Chambal, Girwa, Gandak and Ramganga rivers. The National Chambal Sanctuary is its major stronghold. Males have a bulbous snout growth called a ghara.
related: The Gangetic dolphin was declared National Aquatic Animal in 2009.
The Gangetic dolphin is listed as Endangered by the IUCN.
Vikramshila Gangetic Dolphin Sanctuary is in Bhagalpur, Bihar.
National Dolphin Day is observed on 5 October.
Project Dolphin was announced on 15 August 2020.
The Irrawaddy dolphin is found in Chilika Lake, Odisha.
The Indus river dolphin (Platanista minor) is found in the Beas river, Punjab.
The gharial is Critically Endangered and found in the Chambal sanctuary.
summary: The correct answer is (c) Gangetic dolphin. The Gangetic river dolphin (Platanista gangetica) was declared India's National Aquatic Animal in 2009 by the Government of India (announced via the National Ganga River Basin Authority, NGRBA). It is a flagship species and an indicator of the health of the river ecosystem.
topic_notes: National symbols of India are a frequent UPSC prelims topic. National Animal: Tiger (Panthera tigris), which replaced the lion in 1972. National Bird: Indian peafowl. National Aquatic Animal: Gangetic river dolphin (2009). National Heritage Animal: Elephant (2010). National Reptile: King cobra is sometimes cited, though it is not officially notified, so treat it cautiously. National Flower: Lotus. National Tree: Banyan. National Fruit: Mango. The Gangetic dolphin belongs to the family Platanistidae. Its two subspecies are the Ganges river dolphin and the Indus river dolphin (Platanista minor, found in the Beas in Punjab). Both were treated as separate species in 1998. It is a mammal that breathes air, and it has no functional eye lens, so it relies on sound. Threats include habitat fragmentation by dams and barrages, pollution, entanglement in fishing nets, and poaching for oil used as fish bait. Legal protection includes Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, Appendix I of CITES and Appendix II of CMS. The Vikramshila Gangetic Dolphin Sanctuary lies in the Ganga between Sultanganj and Kahalgaon in Bihar. Project Dolphin, announced on 15 August 2020, resembles Project Tiger and Project Elephant. The first national survey of river dolphins reported roughly 6,000 individuals (2023). Other aquatic fauna questions may cover the Irrawaddy dolphin in Chilika Lake and the dugong in the Gulf of Mannar, which has a Dugong Conservation Reserve in Tamil Nadu (2022). The Namami Gange programme and the NGRBA also relate to the river's ecology.

ocr: With reference to Congress Socialist Party, consider the following statements : 1. It advocated the boycott of British goods and evasion of taxes. It wanted to establish the dicta- torship of proletariat. It advocated separate electorate for minorities and oppressed classes. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? 1 and 2 only (a} 3 only (b) fc) 1, 2 and 3 (dj None
subject: Modern History
detail: The Congress Socialist Party was founded in May 1934 at Patna (first conference presided over by Sampurnanand; Acharya Narendra Dev became president at the Meerut conference in 1936), with Jayaprakash Narayan as general secretary and Minoo Masani, Ram Manohar Lohia, Achyut Patwardhan and Asoka Mehta among its leaders. It worked inside the Congress, aiming to give it a socialist direction, and advocated socialism, the nationalisation of key industries, the abolition of landlordism and kisan and workers' organisation. It sought to make the Congress a radical, anti-imperialist mass body rather than to create a rival party. It did NOT want a 'dictatorship of the proletariat' as its stated goal (that was the Communist position), though it was Marxist-influenced. Boycott of British goods and evasion of taxes is a feature of Swadeshi (1905) and the Civil Disobedience Movement (no-tax campaigns), not a CSP programme. Separate electorates for minorities and oppressed classes were demanded by the Muslim League and Ambedkar (Communal Award, 1932; Poona Pact), and the Congress and the CSP opposed them. Since all three statements are wrong, the answer is (d).
explanations: (a) is wrong: it accepts statements 1 and 2, but neither describes the CSP; boycott/tax evasion was a Swadeshi and Civil Disobedience feature, and the CSP did not formally aim at proletarian dictatorship.
(b) is wrong: statement 3 is incorrect because the CSP opposed separate electorates; they were demanded by communal and depressed class groups and opposed by socialists.
(c) is wrong: it would require all three statements to be true, but none is a correct description of the CSP.
(d) is correct: all three statements are false, so None is the right option, matching the official UPSC answer.
keyfact: The Congress Socialist Party (Patna, 1934; JP, Narendra Dev, Lohia, Masani) was a socialist group within the Congress, not a body for boycott-and-tax-evasion, proletarian dictatorship or separate electorates.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Boycott of British goods and tax evasion belonged to the Swadeshi movement and Civil Disobedience (no-tax campaigns), not the CSP's programme, which centred on socialist economic reform within the Congress.

2 — Incorrect: The CSP was Marxist-influenced but did not declare dictatorship of the proletariat as its aim; it favoured democratic socialism and working within the nationalist movement. That idea was associated with the Communist Party.

3 — Incorrect: Separate electorates were demanded by the Muslim League and, initially, Ambedkar's depressed class leaders; the CSP, like the Congress, opposed communal electorates and stood for class-based, secular mobilisation.
summary: The correct answer is (d) None. The Congress Socialist Party (CSP), formed in 1934, was a Marxist-leaning socialist group within the Indian National Congress, and none of the three statements describes it accurately.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. The Rajya Sabha has no power either to reject or to amend a Money Bill. The Rajya Sabha cannot vote on the Demands for Grants. The Rajya Sabha cannot discuss the Annual Financial Statement. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: Under Article 109, a Money Bill cannot be introduced in the Rajya Sabha. After the Lok Sabha passes it, the Bill is transmitted to the Rajya Sabha, which must return it within 14 days with or without recommendations. The Lok Sabha may accept or reject those recommendations. If the Rajya Sabha does not return the Bill within 14 days, it is deemed passed in the form the Lok Sabha passed it. The Rajya Sabha therefore cannot effectively reject or amend a Money Bill; at most it can recommend changes, which are not binding. Under Article 113, Demands for Grants are submitted only to the Lok Sabha, which alone can assent, refuse or reduce them. The Rajya Sabha has no vote on them. Article 112 requires the Annual Financial Statement (Budget) to be laid before both Houses. The Rajya Sabha may hold a general discussion on the Budget, though it cannot vote on grants. Elimination: since statement 3 is wrong, any option containing it, namely (c) and (d), is out. Statement 2 is correct, so (a) is out. That leaves (b).
explanations: Incorrect: It omits statement 2, which is also correct, so it is incomplete.
Correct: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, and statement 3 is wrong because the Rajya Sabha can discuss the Budget.
Incorrect: It includes statement 3, which is false, and excludes statement 1, which is true.
Incorrect: It includes statement 3, which is false, because the Rajya Sabha can discuss the Annual Financial Statement.
keyfact: Rajya Sabha can discuss the Budget and recommend on Money Bills (14 days), but cannot reject or amend them or vote on Demands for Grants.
statements: 1 — Correct: Under Article 109 the Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes to a Money Bill within 14 days, and the Lok Sabha may ignore them. So it has no effective power to reject or amend it.
2 — Correct: Under Article 113 Demands for Grants go only to the Lok Sabha, which votes on them. The Rajya Sabha has no power to vote on them.
3 — Incorrect: The Budget is laid before both Houses under Article 112, and the Rajya Sabha can discuss it. It just cannot vote on the demands.
summary: The correct answer is (b): statements 1 and 2 are correct, statement 3 is incorrect. The Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations on a Money Bill and cannot vote on Demands for Grants, but it is free to discuss the Annual Financial Statement (Budget).

ocr: The Government of India Act of 1919 clearly defined (a) the separation of power between the judiciary and the legislature (b) the jurisdiction of the central and provincial governments the powers of the Secretary of State (e) for India and the Viceroy (d) None of the above B-AQN-O-—JUA/63A
subject: Polity
detail: The Government of India Act, 1919 implemented the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms and came into force in 1921. Its key administrative feature was the devolution of authority: the Devolution Rules classified subjects into Central and Provincial lists, so the jurisdiction of the centre and the provinces was clearly defined for the first time. Provincial subjects were further divided into 'transferred' subjects, administered by Indian ministers responsible to the legislature, and 'reserved' subjects, administered by the Governor and his Executive Council. This arrangement is called dyarchy. The Act also introduced a bicameral central legislature (Council of State and Legislative Assembly), direct elections on a limited franchise, and communal electorates were extended. It did not separate powers between the judiciary and legislature, since that doctrine was not adopted under colonial rule. Nor did it clearly define the powers of the Secretary of State and the Viceroy; the Secretary of State retained wide control, though his powers were somewhat reduced, as the India Council's role diminished and a High Commissioner for India in London took over some agency functions. Elimination logic: (a) and (c) are false, (d) is therefore false, and (b) is the only accurate statement.
explanations: Incorrect: The Act did not provide for separation of powers between the judiciary and the legislature; the colonial structure was not built on that doctrine.
Correct: The Devolution Rules under the 1919 Act created Central and Provincial lists of subjects, clearly demarcating the jurisdiction of central and provincial governments.
Incorrect: The relative powers of the Secretary of State and the Viceroy were not clearly defined; the Secretary of State retained overriding control and the Viceroy remained answerable to him.
Incorrect: Since option (b) is a correct statement of what the Act defined, 'None of the above' cannot be right.
keyfact: GoI Act 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford): dyarchy in provinces plus Central and Provincial lists that clearly demarcated centre-province jurisdiction.
summary: The correct answer is (b). The Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms) clearly demarcated the jurisdiction of the central and provincial governments by creating Central and Provincial lists of subjects, a process known as devolution.

ocr: Which of the following brings out the ‘Consumer Price Index Number for Industrial Workers’? (a) The Reserve Bank of India (b) The Department of Economic Affairs (c) The Labour Bureau (2) The Department of Personnel and Training
subject: Economy
detail: The CPI-IW measures the change in retail prices of a fixed basket of goods and services consumed by industrial workers. It is compiled by the Labour Bureau, Shimla/Chandigarh, an attached office of the Ministry of Labour and Employment, set up in 1920. The Bureau also compiles the CPI for Agricultural Labourers (CPI-AL) and Rural Labourers (CPI-RL). The CPI-IW is released monthly, and the current base year is 2016=100 (earlier 2001=100). It covers 88 centres across India. Its main uses are to determine the Dearness Allowance (DA) of central government employees and public sector workers, and to revise minimum wages. It is also used to fix wage rates in many industries. By contrast, the general CPI (Urban, Rural, Combined) is now released by the National Statistical Office (NSO) under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), since 2011. The Wholesale Price Index is published by the Office of the Economic Adviser in the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade. Elimination logic: RBI is the monetary authority and uses CPI but does not compile it. The Department of Economic Affairs handles fiscal and economic policy matters. The Department of Personnel and Training handles personnel administration. Only the Labour Bureau, which deals with labour statistics, fits.
explanations: Incorrect: The RBI regulates monetary policy and uses CPI (Combined) as its inflation target, but it does not compile CPI-IW.
Incorrect: The Department of Economic Affairs (Ministry of Finance) handles economic policy, budget and the Economic Survey, not the compilation of CPI-IW.
Correct: The Labour Bureau under the Ministry of Labour and Employment compiles and releases CPI-IW monthly, along with CPI-AL and CPI-RL.
Incorrect: The Department of Personnel and Training handles civil service personnel matters; it only applies the DA rates that are based on CPI-IW.
keyfact: CPI-IW (base 2016=100, 88 centres) is compiled by the Labour Bureau, Ministry of Labour and Employment, and is used to set Dearness Allowance.
summary: The correct answer is (c) The Labour Bureau. It compiles and publishes the Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW) every month. The Labour Bureau is an attached office of the Ministry of Labour and Employment.

ocr: In the context of modern scientific research, consider the following statements about TceCube’, a particle detector located at South Pole, which was recently in the news : 1. It is the world’s largest neutrino detector, encompassing a cubic kilometre of ice. 2. It is a powerful telescope to search for dark matter. 3. It is buried deep in the ice. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only fc} 1 and 3 only (da) 1, 2 and 3
subject: Environment
detail: IceCube Neutrino Observatory is operated by a collaboration led by the University of Wisconsin-Madison and located at the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station. Construction finished in December 2010. It has 5,160 digital optical modules (DOMs) on 86 vertical strings, frozen into holes melted with hot water at depths of about 1,450 m to 2,450 m. Neutrinos are nearly massless, chargeless particles that rarely interact; when one does, it produces a muon or cascade that emits Cherenkov light in the clear ice, which the DOMs record. This allows reconstruction of the neutrino's direction and energy, so IceCube works as a neutrino telescope for astrophysical sources such as active galactic nuclei, supernovae and gamma-ray bursts. In 2013 it reported the first high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, and in 2017-18 it traced one to the blazar TXS 0506+056. It also searches indirectly for dark matter (WIMP annihilation in the Sun or Galactic centre), studies neutrino oscillations, and, via DeepCore, probes lower energies. Elimination logic: statement 1 is the well-known descriptor; statement 3 is factual; statement 2 looks doubtful but dark-matter search is a stated goal, so (d) follows.
explanations: Incorrect: statement 1 is correct, but statements 2 and 3 are also correct, so '1 only' is incomplete.
Incorrect: statements 2 and 3 are correct, but statement 1 is also correct, so this omits it.
Incorrect: statements 1 and 3 are correct, but dark-matter search (statement 2) is also an IceCube objective, so this omits it.
Correct: all three statements are accurate. It is the largest neutrino detector, it works as a telescope that also searches for dark matter, and it lies buried deep in the South Pole ice.
keyfact: IceCube: the world's largest neutrino detector, a cubic kilometre of ice buried 1.45-2.45 km deep at the South Pole, which also searches for dark matter.
related: IceCube is at the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station and is run by a University of Wisconsin-Madison-led collaboration.
IceCube uses 5,160 DOMs on 86 strings at 1.45-2.45 km depth.
In 2018 IceCube traced a high-energy neutrino to the blazar TXS 0506+056.
Neutrino oscillation discovery earned the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physics (Kajita and McDonald).
India-based Neutrino Observatory (INO) is proposed in Theni district, Tamil Nadu.
Super-Kamiokande is a water Cherenkov neutrino detector in Japan.
Dark matter is about 27% of the universe's mass-energy; dark energy is about 68%.
Cherenkov radiation is light emitted when a charged particle moves faster than light in a medium.
statements: 1 — Correct: IceCube instruments one cubic kilometre of ice and is the largest neutrino detector in the world. It is at the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station, Antarctica, and is run by an international collaboration led by the University of Wisconsin-Madison with US National Science Foundation funding. It has 86 strings and 5,160 DOMs. Construction was completed in December 2010. Its volume far exceeds that of earlier detectors such as AMANDA, Super-Kamiokande (Japan) and ANTARES (Mediterranean).

2 — Correct: IceCube is described as a neutrino telescope, and one of its science goals is the indirect search for dark matter. If WIMPs (weakly interacting massive particles) accumulate in the Sun, Earth or Galactic halo and annihilate, they would produce high-energy neutrinos that IceCube could detect. Dark matter makes up about 27% of the universe's mass-energy and is detected only through gravity. Other experiments include LUX-ZEPLIN, XENON, and the AMS on the ISS. IceCube has set limits on WIMP cross-sections but has not yet detected dark matter.

3 — Correct: The detector is buried deep in the Antarctic ice, with strings lowered into holes 2.5 km deep drilled using hot water. The sensors sit at depths of 1.45 to 2.45 km, where the ice is extremely clear and free of air bubbles, so Cherenkov light can be seen. The overlying ice also shields against cosmic-ray muons. A surface array called IceTop sits above it to detect cosmic-ray air showers, and a denser infill, DeepCore, lowers the energy threshold.
summary: The correct answer is (d): all three statements are correct. IceCube is the world's largest neutrino detector, it instruments a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice at the South Pole, and it is buried 1.45-2.45 km below the surface. It also serves as a 'telescope' that searches for dark matter, among other things.
topic_notes: Neutrinos are elementary leptons of the Standard Model that come in three flavours: electron, muon and tau. They have extremely small mass, no electric charge, and interact only through the weak force and gravity, so trillions pass through the body each second. Sources include the Sun (fusion), supernovae, cosmic-ray interactions, the Big Bang relic background, and distant astrophysical accelerators. The 2015 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Takaaki Kajita and Arthur McDonald for discovering neutrino oscillations, which show that neutrinos have mass. Detectors must be large and shielded, so they are placed deep underground, underwater or in ice. Examples: Super-Kamiokande (Japan, water Cherenkov), SNO (Canada), KamLAND, ANTARES and KM3NeT (Mediterranean), Baikal-GVD (Siberia's Lake Baikal), and IceCube (Antarctica). India's proposed India-based Neutrino Observatory (INO) at Bodi West Hills, Theni district, Tamil Nadu, aims to study atmospheric neutrinos with an iron calorimeter (ICAL) but has faced environmental and legal delays. IceCube uses digital optical modules to detect Cherenkov radiation from charged particles created by neutrino interactions. In 2013 it announced the first detection of very-high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, and in 2018 it linked a neutrino to the blazar TXS 0506+056, launching multi-messenger astronomy. In 2023 it mapped neutrinos from the Milky Way plane. An upgrade, IceCube-Gen2, is planned.
