3 — Incorrect: Increasing Indian representation in the ICS was not part of the Cabinet Mission; that relates to earlier bodies such as the Aitchison Commission, Islington Commission and Lee Commission.
summary: The correct answer is (a) 1 only. The Cabinet Mission (1946) recommended a three-tier federal structure: a Union of India with limited subjects (foreign affairs, defence, communications), Provinces, and groups of provinces (Sections A, B, C). It had nothing to do with enlarging the powers of Indian courts or increasing Indian recruitment in the ICS.

ocr: Which one of the following National Parks has a climate that varies from tropical to subtropical, temperate and arctic? fa) Khangchendzonga National Park (b) Nandadevi National Park (c) Neora Valley National Park (a) Namdapha National Park
subject: Environment
detail: Namdapha National Park lies in the Changlang district of Arunachal Pradesh, in the Eastern Himalaya biodiversity hotspot, along the India-Myanmar border. It is bounded by the Patkai range on the east and the Dapha Bum ridge on the north. Its elevation runs from roughly 200 m to about 4,571 m (Dapha Bum), so the vegetation and climate change with height, from tropical wet evergreen forest through subtropical and temperate forest to alpine meadows and permanent snow. The park is drained by the Noa-Dihing river, a tributary of the Brahmaputra. It was declared a National Park in 1983 and a Tiger Reserve in 1983 under Project Tiger. It is the only park in the world with four large felid species: tiger, leopard, snow leopard and clouded leopard. It also has the hoolock gibbon, red panda and Namdapha flying squirrel. Elimination: Khangchendzonga (Sikkim) and Nandadevi (Uttarakhand) are high-altitude Himalayan parks with no tropical zone, and Neora Valley (West Bengal) is mostly subtropical to temperate. Namdapha's tropical-to-arctic range is the distinguishing feature.
explanations: (a) Incorrect: Khangchendzonga is a high-altitude Himalayan park in Sikkim. It spans subtropical to alpine zones, with no true tropical belt at its base, and it is known for glaciers and the third-highest peak.
(b) Incorrect: Nandadevi National Park in Uttarakhand is a high-altitude alpine and temperate area around Nanda Devi. It has no tropical zone.
(c) Incorrect: Neora Valley National Park in West Bengal is a lower-altitude park of subtropical and temperate forests (about 183 m to 3,200 m). It has no arctic or alpine climate.
(d) Correct: Namdapha's altitude range, about 200 m to over 4,500 m, produces tropical, subtropical, temperate and arctic climate zones. This is why UPSC accepts it as the answer.
keyfact: Namdapha National Park (Arunachal Pradesh) ranges from tropical to arctic climate and has four big cats: tiger, leopard, snow leopard and clouded leopard.
option_notes: Khangchendzonga National Park, in Sikkim, is a UNESCO mixed World Heritage Site (2016), India's first mixed site. It protects Mt Khangchendzonga (8,586 m), glaciers such as Zemu, lakes and the habitats of the snow leopard, red panda and blue sheep. It is a core part of the Khangchendzonga Biosphere Reserve and is sacred to the Sikkimese.

Nandadevi National Park, in Chamoli district, Uttarakhand, surrounds Nanda Devi (7,816 m), India's second-highest peak within the country. It forms the core of the Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve and, together with the Valley of Flowers, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1988, extended 2005). Its inner sanctuary is a glacial basin with the Rishi Ganga gorge. It is home to the snow leopard, Himalayan musk deer and bharal.

Neora Valley National Park is in Kalimpong district, West Bengal, and was notified in 1986. It holds some of the richest biodiversity in the state, with dense subtropical and temperate forests, bamboo and rhododendrons. It is a refuge of the red panda and also has clouded leopards, leopards and Asiatic black bears. It lies on the Sikkim and Bhutan border.

Namdapha National Park, in Changlang district, Arunachal Pradesh, is India's largest protected area in the Eastern Himalaya, about 1,985 sq km. It is a tiger reserve and has the Noa-Dihing river. It is the only park with four big cats: tiger, leopard, clouded leopard and snow leopard. It also has the hoolock gibbon, red panda and the critically endangered Namdapha flying squirrel.
related: Namdapha is in Changlang district, Arunachal Pradesh, on the India-Myanmar border.
Namdapha is the only park with four big cats: tiger, leopard, snow leopard and clouded leopard.
Khangchendzonga is India's first UNESCO mixed World Heritage Site (2016).
Nanda Devi and Valley of Flowers are a joint UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Keibul Lamjao in Manipur is the world's only floating national park, home of the sangai.
Neora Valley is in West Bengal and is a refuge of the red panda.
The Noa-Dihing river flows through Namdapha and joins the Brahmaputra system.
National parks are declared under Section 35 of the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972.
summary: The answer is (d) Namdapha National Park in Arunachal Pradesh. Because its altitude rises from about 200 m to over 4,500 m, the park passes through tropical, subtropical, temperate and arctic (alpine) climatic zones.
topic_notes: Indian national parks are classified by biogeographic zone. Altitude matters in the Himalayas, where climate changes from tropical in the foothills to alpine and arctic-like conditions at the top, and Namdapha shows the full sequence. Key facts on Namdapha: the Eastern Himalaya hotspot, the Patkai range, the Noa-Dihing river, Miao town as the entry point, and the Lisu and Chakma communities in and around the park. The Namdapha flying squirrel is critically endangered, and the park has orchids, rare birds, and the Mishmi takin in nearby areas. National parks are established under the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 (Section 35). Other notable parks and their features: Kaziranga (Assam, one-horned rhino, UNESCO site), Manas (Assam, UNESCO, tiger reserve and elephant reserve), Keibul Lamjao (Manipur, the only floating park, sangai deer), Sundarbans (West Bengal, mangroves and Royal Bengal tiger), Great Himalayan National Park (Himachal Pradesh, UNESCO 2014), Valley of Flowers (Uttarakhand), Silent Valley (Kerala, lion-tailed macaque), Bandipur and Nagarhole (Karnataka), and Gir (Gujarat, Asiatic lion). Related ideas UPSC may test include biosphere reserves, Project Tiger (1973), Ramsar sites, UNESCO natural and mixed sites, and hotspot regions: the Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, and Sundaland (Nicobar).

ocr: Amnesty International is fa) an agency of the United Nations to help refugees of civil wars (b} a global Human Rights Movement (c} a non-governmental voluntary organization to help very poor people (a) an inter-governmental agency to cater to medical emergencies in war-ravaged regions B-AQN-O-JUA/63A 18
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Amnesty International (AI) was founded in London in 1961 by the British lawyer Peter Benenson after his article 'The Forgotten Prisoners'. It began by campaigning for the release of prisoners of conscience, meaning people jailed for their beliefs, colour, sex, ethnic origin, language or religion who have not used or advocated violence. Today it describes itself as a global movement of more than 10 million supporters. It has its International Secretariat in London and national sections in many countries. It is independent of any government, political ideology, economic interest or religion, and it is funded mainly by membership fees and public donations, not government money. It won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1977 for its work against torture, and the UN Prize in the Field of Human Rights in 1978. Its work covers research, reporting, lobbying and campaigning against torture, the death penalty, and unfair trials, and for freedom of expression, refugee and women's rights. Elimination: (a) is wrong because UNHCR is the UN refugee agency, and AI is not part of the UN. (c) is wrong because AI is non-governmental but it is a rights-advocacy body, not a poverty-relief charity. (d) is wrong because AI is not intergovernmental, and medical emergency aid in war zones is the work of the ICRC and Médecins Sans Frontières.
explanations: Incorrect: Amnesty is an independent NGO and not a UN agency. The UN body for refugees is the UNHCR, and AI's work is much broader than refugees of civil wars.
Correct: Amnesty International describes itself as a global movement of people campaigning for internationally recognised human rights. This matches the official answer.
Incorrect: It is non-governmental, but its purpose is human rights advocacy, not relief for very poor people. Poverty relief is the work of groups like Oxfam or CARE.
Incorrect: AI is not intergovernmental, because governments are not its members. It does not provide medical aid, which is the role of the ICRC, MSF or the WHO.
keyfact: Amnesty International (founded 1961, London, by Peter Benenson; Nobel Peace Prize 1977) is a global NGO human rights movement.
option_notes: The UN agency for refugees is the UNHCR (United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees), set up in 1950 and headquartered in Geneva. It protects refugees under the 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol. It has won the Nobel Peace Prize twice, in 1954 and 1981. India is not a party to the 1951 Convention. The UNHCR is a UN body, which Amnesty is not.

Amnesty International was founded in 1961 by Peter Benenson in London. It is a global movement of over 10 million people, with its Secretariat in London. It won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1977 and publishes an annual State of the World's Human Rights report. It accepts no government funding for its human rights work, and it campaigns on prisoners of conscience, torture, the death penalty and freedom of expression.

A non-governmental organisation (NGO) is a voluntary, non-profit group independent of government. Examples of poverty-focused NGOs are Oxfam (founded in 1942 in Oxford), CARE and the Akshaya Patra Foundation. Amnesty is an NGO, but its focus is human rights advocacy and not poverty relief, so the description in this option does not fit it.

An inter-governmental organisation is one whose members are states, such as the UN, WHO, WTO or ASEAN. The WHO handles global health and emergencies. In war zones medical aid comes from the ICRC (founded in 1863, Geneva, a neutral humanitarian body) and Médecins Sans Frontières (founded in 1971, which won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1999). Amnesty is not inter-governmental.
related: Amnesty International was founded in 1961 in London by Peter Benenson.
Amnesty International won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1977.
The UNHCR was set up in 1950 and is headquartered in Geneva.
The UN Human Rights Council has 47 members and was established in 2006.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted on 10 December 1948.
India's NHRC was established under the Protection of Human Rights Act 1993.
Human Rights Watch is headquartered in New York.
Transparency International publishes the Corruption Perceptions Index.
summary: The answer is (b): Amnesty International is a global Human Rights Movement. It is a non-governmental, membership-based movement that campaigns for internationally recognised human rights; it is not a UN agency, not a poverty-relief charity, and not an intergovernmental medical body.
topic_notes:
Amnesty International: founded in 1961 in London by Peter Benenson. It is a membership-based movement with its International Secretariat in London. It has more than 10 million members and supporters and sections in many countries; Amnesty International India is based in Bengaluru. It campaigns for prisoners of conscience, a fair trial, and the abolition of the death penalty, and against torture, enforced disappearances and extrajudicial executions. It also works on refugee, women's and LGBT rights and on freedom of expression. Its logo is a candle wrapped in barbed wire. It won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1977 and the UN Human Rights Prize in 1978. It publishes an annual report on the state of human rights worldwide. Amnesty India stopped its work in India in September 2020 after its bank accounts were frozen under FCRA rules.

Other human rights bodies: Human Rights Watch (New York, founded in 1978 as Helsinki Watch) is an international NGO. The UN Human Rights Council (Geneva, established in 2006, replacing the Commission on Human Rights) has 47 members. The OHCHR is the UN human rights office. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted on 10 December 1948, which is observed as Human Rights Day. India's National Human Rights Commission was set up under the Protection of Human Rights Act 1993. Other NGOs: Transparency International (Berlin) publishes the Corruption Perceptions Index; Greenpeace works on the environment; Oxfam works against poverty; Reporters Without Borders publishes the press freedom index.

question: With reference to the art and archaeological history of India, which one among the following was made earliest?
subject: Geography
detail: Dhauli, near Bhubaneswar in Odisha, is the site of Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts (including the separate Kalinga Edicts) issued after the Kalinga War of about 261 BCE. Above the edicts is a rock-cut forepart of an elephant, carved around 250-260 BCE. It is one of the earliest Buddhist sculptures in India and symbolises the Buddha, or gaja. It is a classic example of Mauryan rock-cut art. The Varaha image at Udayagiri (Madhya Pradesh) is a Gupta work of the time of Chandragupta II, early 5th century CE, and shows the Vishnu avatar lifting Prithvi. The rock-cut monuments at Mahabalipuram (rathas, Arjuna's Penance) were made by the Pallavas under Narasimhavarman I Mamalla in the 7th century CE. The Lingaraja Temple at Bhubaneswar is a Kalinga-style nagara temple of the Somavamshi dynasty, built from the 11th century, with Ganga additions later. The elimination logic is the chronology Mauryan (3rd century BCE) < Gupta (5th century CE) < Pallava (7th century CE) < Somavamshi/Ganga (11th century CE).
explanations: Incorrect: The Lingaraja Temple was built in the 11th century CE by the Somavamshi dynasty and is the latest of the four.
Correct: The Dhauli elephant dates to Ashoka's Mauryan period, c. 260 BCE, making it the earliest.
Incorrect: The Mahabalipuram monuments are Pallava work of the 7th century CE, much later than the Mauryan period.
Incorrect: The Udayagiri Varaha is Gupta, from the early 5th century CE, so it is later than Dhauli.
keyfact: Dhauli elephant (Ashoka, c. 260 BCE) < Udayagiri Varaha (Gupta, 5th c. CE) < Mahabalipuram (Pallava, 7th c.) < Lingaraja (11th c.).
summary: The answer is (b) Rock-cut Elephant at Dhauli. It dates to the Mauryan period (Ashoka, c. 260 BCE), which is far earlier than the Gupta, Pallava and Ganga-era or later monuments in the other options.

question:
With reference to Indian history, which of the following is/are the essential element/elements of the feudal system?
1. A very strong centralized political authority and a very weak provincial or local political authority
2. Emergence of administrative structure based on control and possession of 1 and
3. Creation of lord-vassal relationship between the feudal lord and his overlord Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Feudalism is a politico-economic system in which political authority is fragmented and exercised by landholding lords. Its core features are: (i) land, granted by an overlord or king in return for military service, loyalty and tribute, is the basis of administration and power; (ii) a hierarchy of lord and vassal ties, with obligations flowing both ways, since the overlord offers protection and the vassal offers service; (iii) a weak central authority, with real power, justice, revenue and armed forces in the hands of local lords; (iv) an agrarian, largely self-sufficient manorial economy with serfs or peasants tied to the land. In Europe it flourished from roughly the 9th to the 13th centuries. In India, historians such as R.S. Sharma link 'Indian feudalism' to land grants (agrahara, brahmadeya) from the Gupta and post-Gupta period onward, with samantas rising in power. R.S. Sharma and D.N. Jha support the thesis, while others such as B.D. Chattopadhyaya and Harbans Mukhia reject or qualify it. Elimination: any option including statement 1 (a, d) is out because a strong centre contradicts feudalism. Statement 3 is clearly correct, so (c) is incomplete because statement 2 is also valid. That leaves (b).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 1, which describes the opposite of feudalism, since a strong centre is not a feudal feature.
Correct: statements 2 (land-based administrative structure) and 3 (lord-vassal relationship) are the essential elements of feudalism, while statement 1 is false.
Wrong: statement 3 is true, but statement 2 is also an essential element, so '3 only' is incomplete.
Wrong: it wrongly includes statement 1, because feudalism implies a weak central and strong local authority.
keyfact: Feudalism = land-based administration plus lord-vassal bond with a weak centre; a strong centralised authority is NOT feudal.
option_notes: Option (a) pairs statements 1 and 2. Statement 1, a strong centralised authority with weak local authority, describes a unitary bureaucratic empire like the Mauryan state under Ashoka, not feudalism. Feudal polities were fragmented, as in post-Carolingian Europe from the 9th century and in India after Harsha (7th century), when samantas grew powerful. Statement 2 is correct, but because 1 is wrong, this option fails. Remember that centralisation and feudalism are opposites, a distinction often tested in the form of 'strong centre' traps.

Option (b), 2 and 3 only, is the official answer. It captures the land-based administrative structure (fief, land grants, samanta holdings) and the reciprocal lord-vassal bond. Feudalism in Europe developed after Charlemagne's empire broke up, with the manor as the economic unit and serfs as labour. In India, R.S. Sharma's 'Indian Feudalism' (1965) argued that land grants from the Gupta and post-Gupta period led to a feudal order. Critics include Harbans Mukhia, who argued the peasantry was not servile as in Europe.

Option (c), 3 only, selects the lord-vassal relationship, which is indeed essential, but it omits the land-based administrative structure. It is therefore incomplete. The lord-vassal tie is the personal bond: homage, fealty, military service and protection. Its European form is the knight-vassal serving a baron or king. Its Indian parallel is the samanta paying tribute and providing troops to a mahārājādhirāja. UPSC often makes 'only' options as traps when an additional true statement exists.

Option (d), 1, 2 and 3, would be correct only if a strong centre were a feudal feature. It is not. The feudal state is decentralised, with power shared among landholding lords. The Delhi Sultanate's iqta system and the Mughal mansabdari-jagir system are sometimes compared with feudal arrangements, but they were controlled by a strong, centrally appointed and transferable administration, unlike hereditary feudal holdings. Hence statement 1 invalidates this option.
related: Feudalism: weak centre, strong local lords, land-for-service, lord-vassal bond.
R.S. Sharma wrote 'Indian Feudalism' (1965) and argued land grants led to feudal structures.
D.D. Kosambi proposed feudalism 'from above' and 'from below'.
Burton Stein proposed the 'segmentary state' model for the Cholas.
Brahmadeya and agrahara were land grants to Brahmanas; devadana to temples.
Samantas were subordinate chiefs owing tribute and military service to overlords.
The iqta (Delhi Sultanate) was a transferable revenue assignment, unlike a hereditary fief.
Harbans Mukhia argued that Indian peasants were not serfs as in Europe.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: feudalism is characterised by a weak centre and strong local or provincial authority, not the reverse. Political fragmentation is its hallmark. Under it, the king was often only the first among equals, and powerful barons or samantas ran their own armies, courts and revenue collection. In India, the decline of imperial authority after the Guptas and Harsha, and the rise of samantas, mahasamantas and regional kingdoms, illustrate this. In Europe, the weak Carolingian successors let counts and dukes become hereditary rulers. A strong centralised state such as the Mauryan empire is the opposite of the feudal model.

2 — Correct: feudal administration is based on control and possession of land. Land, not cash salary, was the means of rewarding officials and soldiers, so political and military power flowed from landholding. In Europe, the fief (feudum) was granted in return for service. In India, grants of land and revenue to Brahmanas and temples (brahmadeya, agrahara, devadana) and to officers (the later Rashtrakuta, Pratihara and Chola-era nadu systems, and the Rajput samanta or jagir structure) transferred fiscal and administrative rights. These grants often included immunities from taxes and interference by royal officers. This is the economic base of the manorial system, in which peasants worked the land.

3 — Correct: the lord-vassal relationship is the central social and political bond of feudalism. A vassal received land (fief) from the overlord and in return owed military service, counsel, loyalty and sometimes tribute. The overlord owed protection and justice. The chain could run from king to great lords to knights, a process called subinfeudation. Homage and fealty ceremonies sealed it. In India, the samanta system is analogous, with samantas owing military help, tribute and attendance at court to their overlord. Hierarchical, personal and reciprocal ties of this kind separate feudalism from bureaucratic or purely monarchical rule.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 and 3 only. Feudalism rests on an administrative structure built on control and possession of land (statement 2) and on a lord-vassal relationship between a feudal lord and his overlord (statement 3). Statement 1 is wrong because feudalism implies a weak central authority and strong local or provincial power.
topic_notes:
Feudalism (from Latin feudum, fief) is a system of political, military and economic organisation in which land is held in return for service. Classic European feudalism arose after the fragmentation of the Carolingian empire (9th century) and peaked in the 11th-13th centuries. Features: king at the top, then great lords or barons, knights, and at the base serfs working on the manor. Fealty and homage bound vassals to lords. The Church was itself a large feudal landholder.

In India the 'Indian feudalism' debate was led by D.D. Kosambi (feudalism 'from above' and 'from below'), R.S. Sharma (Indian Feudalism, c. 300-1200 CE), and D.N. Jha. Evidence includes land grants (copper plates) to Brahmanas and temples with administrative and fiscal immunities, the rise of samantas, decline of trade and towns (urban decay), the spread of self-sufficient village economies, and growth of forced labour (vishti). The Satavahanas gave early grants, but the practice became widespread from the Gupta period. Examples: Pallavas, Rashtrakutas, Pratiharas, Palas, Rajputs. Sceptics include B.D. Chattopadhyaya (who proposed 'integrative polity' and 'early medieval state formation'), Harbans Mukhia, and Burton Stein (the 'segmentary state' for the Cholas).

Other angles: Delhi Sultanate iqta (land assignment to nobles for salary, transferable), Mughal mansabdari and jagirdari (rank-linked, transferable, with revenue assignments), zamindari and Permanent Settlement (1793), and Rajput clan-based landholding. UPSC may also ask about land grant types: brahmadeya, devadana, agrahara, and nivartana as a land measure. The contrast with a bureaucratic-centralised state is the key test of understanding.

ocr: BioCarbon Fund Initiative for Sustain- able Forest Landscapes’ is managed by the (a) Asian Development Bank - (b) International Monetary Fund (c) United Nations Environment Programme (4) World Bank
subject: Economy
detail: The BioCarbon Fund Initiative for Sustainable Forest Landscapes (ISFL) was launched in 2013 and is managed by the World Bank. It is supported by donor countries such as the UK, the USA, Germany, Norway and others. It is a multilateral fund that rewards reduced greenhouse gas emissions from the land sector. This covers deforestation and forest degradation (REDD+), agriculture, and land-use planning, and it also promotes climate-smart agriculture and sustainable commodity supply chains. It works through programmes in selected jurisdictions (for example Colombia, Ethiopia, Zambia, Indonesia's Jambi province, Mexico, Côte d'Ivoire) and uses results-based payments for verified emission reductions. The older BioCarbon Fund, established in 2004, was also a World Bank-administered carbon fund, and the ISFL builds on it. Related World Bank-hosted funds worth remembering include the Forest Carbon Partnership Facility (FCPF) and the Carbon Fund. Elimination logic: the ADB works on Asia-Pacific development finance, and the IMF handles macroeconomic and balance-of-payments stability, so neither runs forest carbon funds. UNEP is a UN environmental coordinating body. It co-runs UN-REDD with FAO and UNDP, but it does not manage this fund. Hence the World Bank is the answer.
explanations: (a) Incorrect: The Asian Development Bank finances regional development projects in Asia and does not manage the BioCarbon ISFL.
(b) Incorrect: The IMF deals with monetary cooperation, exchange stability and balance-of-payments support, not forest or carbon funds.
(c) Incorrect: UNEP is a UN environmental body that partners in UN-REDD (with FAO and UNDP), but it does not manage the ISFL.
(d) Correct: The ISFL is a multilateral, donor-funded fund managed by the World Bank, which also hosts related funds such as the FCPF and the older BioCarbon Fund.
keyfact: BioCarbon Fund ISFL (2013) = World Bank-managed, results-based REDD+ and climate-smart land-use fund.
summary: The correct answer is (d) World Bank. The BioCarbon Fund Initiative for Sustainable Forest Landscapes (ISFL) is a multilateral fund supported by donor governments and managed by the World Bank. It promotes REDD+ and climate-smart land use.

ocr: India is a member of which among the following? 1. Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation 2. Association of South-East Asian Nations 3. East Asia Summit Select the correct answer using the code given below. {a} 1 and 2 only (b) 3 only fc) 1, 2 and 3 (d) India is a member of none of them
subject: Current Affairs
detail: India is a founding participant of the East Asia Summit (EAS), whose first meeting was held in Kuala Lumpur in December 2005 with 16 countries: the 10 ASEAN states plus India, China, Japan, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand. The USA and Russia joined in 2011, making 18 members. APEC, formed in 1989, is a forum of Pacific Rim economies. India has repeatedly applied for membership but has not been admitted, partly because of a long-standing moratorium on new members, which lapsed in 2010 but has not been followed by India's entry. ASEAN (founded 1967 by the Bangkok Declaration) has 10 members, all South-East Asian: Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Brunei, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar and Cambodia. India is a sectoral partner (1992), a dialogue partner (1996) and a summit-level partner (2002), and its 'Look East' policy, later 'Act East', is built on this engagement, but it is not a member. Elimination logic: knowing that India is not in ASEAN eliminates (a) and (c). Knowing that India is in the EAS eliminates (d). That leaves (b).
explanations: Wrong: it includes APEC and ASEAN, and India is a member of neither, while it omits the EAS, where India is a member.
Correct: India is a member only of the East Asia Summit among the three bodies listed.
Wrong: this would need India to be in APEC and ASEAN as well, which it is not.
Wrong: India is a member of the East Asia Summit, so it is not true that it belongs to none of them.
keyfact: India is in the EAS (since 2005) but not in APEC or ASEAN, where it is only a dialogue partner of ASEAN.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: India is not a member of APEC; its membership bid has not succeeded, and the Pacific Rim focus of the grouping has kept India out.
2 — Incorrect: ASEAN has only 10 South-East Asian members; India is a dialogue and summit-level partner, not a member.
3 — Correct: India has been a member of the East Asia Summit since its inception in 2005.
summary: The correct answer is (b) 3 only. India is a member of the East Asia Summit (since its first summit in 2005) but is not a member of APEC or ASEAN; it is only a dialogue partner of ASEAN.

question: In India, the steel production industry requires the import of
subject: Economy
detail: Steelmaking in the blast furnace route needs iron ore, coking coal (metallurgical coal) and limestone or dolomite as flux. India is rich in iron ore (Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Goa), but its coking coal, mostly in the Jharia and Raniganj fields, is of poor quality, with high ash content and often over 15-17% ash. Steelmakers therefore import low-ash coking coal, chiefly from Australia, and also from the USA, Russia, Mozambique and Canada. Imports cover roughly 85% or more of the demand for coking coal. The National Steel Policy 2017 aims to reduce this dependence. Saltpetre (potassium nitrate) is used in fertilisers, explosives and fireworks, and has no role in steel production. Rock phosphate is the raw material for phosphatic fertilisers such as DAP and SSP, and India imports it from Morocco, Jordan and others for the fertiliser industry, not for steel. Elimination logic: only coking coal is a steel input, so (a), (b) and (d) fall away.
explanations: Incorrect: Saltpetre (potassium nitrate) is used for fertilisers, gunpowder and explosives, not as a steelmaking input.
Incorrect: Rock phosphate is imported for the phosphatic fertiliser industry, not for steel production.
Correct: India lacks sufficient low-ash coking coal, which is essential for blast furnace steelmaking, so it imports it, mainly from Australia.
Incorrect: Since saltpetre and rock phosphate are not needed for steel, 'All of the above' cannot be right.
keyfact: India imports coking coal for steel because domestic coking coal is high in ash; rock phosphate and saltpetre serve fertiliser and explosives industries.
summary: The answer is (c) coking coal. India has limited reserves of good-quality low-ash coking coal, so the steel industry, especially the blast furnace-basic oxygen furnace route, must import it. Saltpetre and rock phosphate are not inputs to steelmaking.

question: The provisions in Fifth Schedule and Sixth Schedule in the Constitution of India are made in order to
options: protect the interests of Scheduled Tribes
determine the powers, authority and responsibilities of Panchayats
protect the interests of all the border States B-AQN-O-JUA/63A
subject: Polity
detail: Article 244 of the Constitution provides for the administration of Scheduled Areas and tribal areas. Under Article 244(1), the Fifth Schedule applies to Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in all States except Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. It provides for a Tribes Advisory Council (up to 20 members, three-fourths of them ST MLAs). It empowers the Governor to direct that an Act of Parliament or the State legislature does not apply to a Scheduled Area, or applies with modifications. The Governor can also make regulations on land transfer, money-lending and the allotment of land. Under Article 244(2), the Sixth Schedule covers tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. It creates Autonomous District Councils and Regional Councils with legislative, judicial and executive powers over land, forests, village administration and customary law. Both Schedules therefore exist to protect tribal interests. The other options fail. State boundaries are dealt with under Articles 3 and 4 and the First Schedule. Panchayat powers are in Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule (Article 243G). The Schedules are not meant for border States generally, since the Sixth Schedule is tied to tribal population, not to being a border State.
explanations: Correct: the Fifth and Sixth Schedules (Article 244) provide special administration for Scheduled Areas and tribal areas to protect Scheduled Tribes.
Incorrect: State boundaries are governed by Articles 3 and 4 and the First Schedule, which lists States and territories, not the Fifth or Sixth Schedule.
Incorrect: Panchayat powers and responsibilities are in Part IX (Articles 243-243O) and the Eleventh Schedule, added by the 73rd Amendment.
Incorrect: the Schedules concern tribal areas, not border States as such. Many border States are not covered, and some covered areas are not on a border.
keyfact: Fifth Schedule = Scheduled Areas in States other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram; Sixth Schedule = tribal areas of those four States with Autonomous District Councils (Article 244).
summary: The answer is (a). The Fifth and Sixth Schedules contain special provisions for administering Scheduled Areas and tribal areas, so that the interests, land, culture and autonomy of Scheduled Tribes are protected.

question: With reference to the Union Government, consider the following statements : 1 The Department of Revenue is responsible for the preparation of Union Budget that is presented to the Parliament. No amount can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India without the authorization from the Parliament of India. All the disbursements made from Public Account also need the authorization from the Parliament of India. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: The Union government has three funds. The Consolidated Fund of India (Article 266(1)) receives all revenues, loans raised and loan repayments received. No money can be withdrawn from it except under an appropriation made by law (Article 266(3) and Article 114(3)), so Parliament must authorise expenditure through an Appropriation Act. The Contingency Fund of India (Article 267) is an imprest placed at the President's disposal for urgent unforeseen expenditure, and Parliament approves it afterwards. The Public Account (Article 266(2)) holds money the government receives as a banker or trustee, such as provident funds, small savings, deposits and reserve funds. Payments from it are operated by executive action and need no parliamentary appropriation, because the money is not government revenue. The Budget Division of the Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance, prepares the Budget. The Department of Revenue deals with taxation, namely the CBDT and CBIC. Elimination logic: statement 3 is wrong, so (b) and (d) fall away. Statement 1 is wrong, so (a) falls away. That leaves (c).
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes statement 1, and the Budget is prepared by the Department of Economic Affairs, not the Department of Revenue.
(b) is wrong because it includes statement 3, and Public Account payments need no parliamentary authorisation.
(c) is correct because only statement 2 holds: Consolidated Fund withdrawals need parliamentary authorisation.
(d) is wrong because statements 1 and 3 are both incorrect.
keyfact: Budget is prepared by the Department of Economic Affairs; the Consolidated Fund needs Parliament's appropriation, while the Public Account does not.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Budget is prepared by the Department of Economic Affairs (Budget Division), not the Department of Revenue.
2 — Correct: Article 266(3) and Article 114(3) bar withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund without parliamentary appropriation by law.
3 — Incorrect: Public Account disbursements are made by executive action and do not need parliamentary authorisation, since the government holds this money as a banker.
summary: The answer is (c): only statement 2 is correct. Withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund of India need parliamentary authorisation under Article 266 and Article 114(3). The Union Budget is prepared by the Department of Economic Affairs, not the Department of Revenue, and Public Account disbursements do not need parliamentary authorisation.

question: Who/Which of the following is the custodian of the Constitution of India?
subject: Polity
detail: The Supreme Court is described as the 'custodian' or 'guardian' of the Constitution because it has the final authority to interpret constitutional provisions and to strike down laws or executive actions that violate them. Its powers include judicial review, which is implicit in Articles 13, 32, 131-137 and 226 (for High Courts), and original, appellate and advisory jurisdiction (Article 143). Article 32, which Dr B.R. Ambedkar called the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution, lets citizens approach the Supreme Court directly to enforce Fundamental Rights. Article 141 makes its rulings binding on all courts in India. In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) the Court laid down the Basic Structure doctrine, which limits Parliament's amending power under Article 368. The President takes an oath under Article 60 to 'preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law', and this is sometimes confused with custodianship. However, the President acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74), so the President is the constitutional head and not its interpreter. The Prime Minister is the head of the government and the Lok Sabha Secretariat is an administrative body that serves the House. Neither has any power to adjudicate on the Constitution. Hence only the Supreme Court fits.
explanations: Incorrect: The President is the nominal head of state and swears to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution. However, the President acts on ministerial advice and has no power to interpret the Constitution or strike down laws.
Incorrect: The Prime Minister heads the Council of Ministers and is accountable to the Lok Sabha. This is an executive role with no function of guarding or interpreting the Constitution.
Incorrect: The Lok Sabha Secretariat is an administrative and secretarial body that assists the House under the Speaker. It has no constitutional adjudicatory role.

Correct: The Supreme Court is the final interpreter and guardian of the Constitution. It exercises judicial review and enforces Fundamental Rights under Article 32, and it developed the Basic Structure doctrine.
keyfact: The Supreme Court is the guardian and final interpreter of the Constitution, through judicial review and Article 32.
summary: The correct answer is (d) The Supreme Court of India. The Supreme Court is the guardian and final interpreter of the Constitution, and it protects it through judicial review and its power to enforce Fundamental Rights.

ocr: Consider the following statements : 1. The Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme was launched during 1996-97 to provide loan assistance to poor farmers. The Command Area Development Programme was launched in 1974-75 for the development of water-use efficiency. , Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (a) 1 only fb) 2 only {c) Both 1 and 2 {d) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Both statements test the difference between irrigation schemes aimed at states and projects and schemes aimed at individual farmers. The AIBP was launched in 1996-97 by the Ministry of Water Resources. It gave central loan assistance, later a mix of grant and loan, to state governments so they could complete ongoing major and medium irrigation projects that were stuck for lack of funds, and thereby create irrigation potential quickly. Its beneficiaries are state governments and projects, not poor farmers directly. Statement 1 is therefore wrong, because it misstates the purpose and the target group. It was later folded into the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY) in 2015-16, whose components include AIBP, Har Khet Ko Pani, Per Drop More Crop and watershed development. The CAD Programme began in 1974-75 as a centrally sponsored scheme. It was meant to close the gap between irrigation potential created and potential actually used, through on-farm development, field channels, land levelling, warabandi (rotational water supply) and farmer participation. In 2004 it was restructured as CADWM, the Command Area Development and Water Management programme. Statement 2 is therefore correct. Elimination logic: once statement 1 is rejected because of the 'poor farmers' wording, only option (b) remains.
explanations: (a) Wrong: it treats statement 1 as correct and statement 2 as incorrect, but the reverse is true. AIBP assists state projects, not poor farmers.
(b) Correct: statement 2 is accurate, as CAD was launched in 1974-75 for efficient water use, and statement 1 is inaccurate about AIBP's beneficiaries.
(c) Wrong: statement 1 is false, so 'both' cannot be correct.
(d) Wrong: statement 2 is true, so 'neither' cannot be correct.
keyfact: AIBP (1996-97) = central loan help to states for unfinished irrigation projects; CAD Programme (1974-75) = better water-use efficiency in command areas.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: AIBP (1996-97) provides central loan assistance to state governments to complete major and medium irrigation projects, not to poor farmers.
2 — Correct: The CAD Programme was launched in 1974-75 to improve water-use efficiency and reduce the gap between irrigation potential created and utilised.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. The Command Area Development (CAD) Programme was launched in 1974-75 to improve water-use efficiency in irrigation commands. The Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme (AIBP) was launched in 1996-97 to give central loan assistance to states for completing major and medium irrigation projects, not to poor farmers.

question: The Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee is constituted under the
options: Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999
subject: Science & Tech
detail: GEAC is the apex statutory body that appraises activities involving large-scale use of hazardous microorganisms and recombinants in research and industrial production from the environmental angle. It also appraises proposals for the release of genetically engineered (GE) organisms and products, including GM crops, into the environment, including experimental field trials. It functions under the 'Rules for the Manufacture, Use, Import, Export and Storage of Hazardous Micro-organisms, Genetically Engineered Organisms or Cells, 1989', notified under Sections 6, 8 and 25 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. It is chaired by the Special Secretary/Additional Secretary of MoEFCC, with a co-chair from the Department of Biotechnology (DBT). Other bodies under the same Rules include the Recombinant DNA Advisory Committee (RDAC), the Institutional Biosafety Committee (IBSC), the Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation (RCGM, under DBT), the State Biotechnology Coordination Committee (SBCC) and the District Level Committee (DLC). Elimination: the Food Safety Act, 2006 created FSSAI, the GI Act, 1999 deals with registration of GIs, and the Wildlife Act, 1972 deals with species and protected areas. None of these concerns GM organisms. GEAC's approval is needed for commercial release, as in the Bt cotton approval of 2002.
explanations: Incorrect: the FSS Act, 2006 set up FSSAI for food standards. GM food is regulated under it, but GEAC is not constituted under this Act.
Incorrect: the GI Act, 1999 governs registration and protection of geographical indications through the GI Registry in Chennai. It has nothing to do with GEAC.
Correct: GEAC is constituted under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, through the 1989 Rules notified by MoEFCC.
Incorrect: the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 protects wild animals and plants and provides for sanctuaries, national parks and the NBWL. It has no role in appraising GM organisms.
keyfact: GEAC (MoEFCC) is the apex body for GM organism approvals, set up under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 via the 1989 Rules.
option_notes: The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 consolidated earlier food laws, including the PFA Act 1954, and established the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), headquartered in Delhi. It sets science-based food standards and regulates manufacture, storage, distribution, sale and import of food. It is administered by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. FSSAI's chairperson is appointed by the Centre. GM food regulation falls under it, with the GEAC giving environmental clearance.

The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999 came into force in 2003 and complies with the TRIPS Agreement. The GI Registry is in Chennai. A GI tag lasts 10 years and is renewable. Darjeeling Tea was the first Indian product registered, in 2004-05. The Act is administered by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.

The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 was enacted after the Bhopal gas tragedy (1984), under Article 253 to implement the 1972 Stockholm Conference decisions. It is an umbrella Act empowering the Centre to take measures to protect and improve the environment. Rules under it cover hazardous waste, EIA, noise pollution and GM organisms. Penalty for violation is up to 5 years' imprisonment or a fine up to Rs 1 lakh, or both.

The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 provides for protection of wild animals, birds and plants and for the management of their habitats. It created Schedules I-VI, with Schedule I giving the highest protection, and it provides for Sanctuaries, National Parks, Conservation and Community Reserves. It established the National Board for Wildlife and the Central Zoo Authority. The 2002 amendment created the NTCA, and the 2022 amendment reduced the Schedules to four.
related: GEAC functions under MoEFCC; its co-chair is from DBT.
The 1989 Rules were notified under Sections 6, 8 and 25 of the EPA, 1986.
Bt cotton, approved in 2002, is the only GM crop commercially grown in India.
Bt brinjal was put under a moratorium in 2010.
GM mustard (DMH-11) was cleared by GEAC in 2022; the Supreme Court delivered a split verdict in 2024.
Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (2000) regulates transboundary movement of living modified organisms.
RCGM, under DBT, monitors GM research; IBSC works at the institution level.
FSSAI regulates GM food under the FSS Act, 2006.
summary: The answer is (c) Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. The Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) is constituted under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) through the 1989 Rules framed under the EPA, 1986.
topic_notes: GEAC is the apex regulator for GM organisms in India. It sits in MoEFCC and is chaired by the Special Secretary/Additional Secretary of MoEFCC, with the DBT representative as co-chair. Its legal basis is the 1989 Rules under the EPA, 1986. The Rules also created other bodies. The IBSC works at the institutional level. The RCGM in DBT oversees research and monitoring. The SBCC and the DLC work at the state and district levels. The RDAC in DBT is advisory and reviews biotechnology developments. The GEAC approves commercial release of GM crops and large-scale use of hazardous microbes. It can also take punitive action under the EPA, 1986. Bt cotton, approved in 2002, is the only GM crop commercially cultivated in India. In 2022 GEAC cleared the environmental release of GM mustard (DMH-11), which was challenged in the Supreme Court. The Court delivered a split verdict in July 2024 and referred the matter to a larger bench, and it directed the Centre to frame a National Policy on GM crops. Bt brinjal was recommended by GEAC in 2009, but then Environment Minister Jairam Ramesh imposed a moratorium in 2010. Import of GM food needs GEAC approval and FSSAI regulation, and FSSAI's 2022 GM food regulations apply. India is a party to the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (2000), under the Convention on Biological Diversity. It regulates transboundary movement of living modified organisms. India hosted COP-11 of the CBD and the MOP-6 of the Cartagena Protocol at Hyderabad in 2012. The Nagoya-Kuala Lumpur Supplementary Protocol covers liability and redress. The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 is another related law, with NBA at Chennai.

ocr: In the Mekong-Ganga Cooperation, an initiative of six countries, which of the following is/are not a participant/ participants? 1. Bangladesh 2. Cambodia 3. China 4. Myanmar 5. Thailand 22 B-AQN-O-JUA/63A Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa) 1 only (b) 2, 3 and 4 (o} i and 3 (d) 1,2 and 5
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Mekong-Ganga Cooperation was launched in November 2000 at Vientiane, Laos. Its six member countries are India and five Mekong-basin countries: Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam. It focuses on four areas of cooperation: tourism, culture, education, and transport and communication. It is meant to link the Ganga and Mekong civilizations and to support India's Act East Policy and its engagement with ASEAN's CLMV states (Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Vietnam). The Mekong river flows through six countries: China, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam. China is a Mekong riparian state but is not part of MGC. It participates instead in the Lancang-Mekong Cooperation and the Greater Mekong Subregion programme. Bangladesh belongs to BIMSTEC and BBIN, but not to MGC. The elimination logic is as follows. Cambodia (2), Myanmar (4) and Thailand (5) are definite members, so any option containing 2, 4 or 5 is wrong. That eliminates (b) and (d). Option (a) leaves out China, so only (c) is left.
explanations: (a) Wrong: 1 only misses China, which is also not a participant.
(b) Wrong: Cambodia (2), Myanmar (4) are members, so they cannot be 'not participants'.
(c) Right: Bangladesh (1) and China (3) are the two listed countries outside MGC.
(d) Wrong: Cambodia (2) and Thailand (5) are members, and China (3) is left out.
keyfact: MGC (2000, Vientiane) = India + Thailand, Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam; China and Bangladesh are not members.
statements: 1 — Incorrect as a member claim, so it is a 'not a participant' item: Bangladesh is not an MGC member. It is in BIMSTEC and BBIN instead.
2 — Correct as a member, so it is not an answer: Cambodia is an MGC member (CLMV group).
3 — Incorrect as a member claim, so it is a 'not a participant' item: China is a Mekong riparian state but is not in MGC. It runs the separate Lancang-Mekong Cooperation.
4 — Correct as a member, so it is not an answer: Myanmar is an MGC member.
5 — Correct as a member, so it is not an answer: Thailand is an MGC member and one of its founders.
summary: The correct answer is (c) 1 and 3. The Mekong-Ganga Cooperation (MGC) has six members: India, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos and Vietnam. Bangladesh and China are not members, so they are the 'not a participant' options.

question: Basel II] Accord’ or simply ‘Basel IH’, often seen in the news, seeks to
options: develop national strategies for the conservation and sustainable use of biological diversity
improve banking sector’s ability to deal with financial and economic stress and improve risk management
reduce the greenhouse gas emissions but places a heavier burden on developed countries
transfer technology from developed countries to poor countries to enable them to replace the use of chiorofluorocarbons in refrigeration with harmless chemicals
subject: Environment
detail: Basel norms are global banking standards issued by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, which was set up in 1974 under the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), headquartered in Basel, Switzerland. Basel I (1988) introduced minimum capital against credit risk. Basel II (2004) rested on three pillars: minimum capital, supervisory review and market discipline. Basel III was agreed in 2010-11 after the 2008 crisis. It raises the quality and quantity of capital (Common Equity Tier 1), adds a capital conservation buffer and a countercyclical buffer, introduces a leverage ratio, and adds liquidity standards (Liquidity Coverage Ratio and Net Stable Funding Ratio). It also tightens rules on systemically important banks. The RBI has been implementing it in India in phases. Elimination: option (a) describes the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), whose Article 6 covers national strategies. Option (c) describes the Kyoto Protocol, with its common but differentiated responsibilities. Option (d) describes the Montreal Protocol on ozone-depleting substances. Only (b) concerns banking.
explanations: Wrong. National strategies for conserving and sustainably using biodiversity come from the Convention on Biological Diversity (1992), not from Basel norms.
Correct. Basel III strengthens bank capital, liquidity and leverage so that banks can withstand financial and economic stress, and it improves risk management and governance.
Wrong. Cutting greenhouse gas emissions with heavier burdens on developed countries describes the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the UNFCCC principle of common but differentiated responsibilities.
Wrong. Technology transfer to help poorer countries replace CFCs is a feature of the Montreal Protocol (1987), which has a Multilateral Fund for this purpose.
keyfact: Basel III (BCBS, post-2008) strengthens bank capital, liquidity and leverage to withstand financial stress and improve risk management.
option_notes: The Convention on Biological Diversity was opened at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit and came into force in 1993. Its three goals are conservation of biodiversity, sustainable use of its components, and fair sharing of benefits from genetic resources. Article 6 requires national biodiversity strategies and action plans (NBSAPs). The Cartagena Protocol covers biosafety and the Nagoya Protocol covers access and benefit sharing. The Aichi Targets were followed by the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022). India's Biological Diversity Act is from 2002.

This is the correct option. Basel III is a set of BCBS reforms from 2010-11 that followed the 2008 crisis. It sets a minimum CET1 ratio of 4.5 percent, a total capital ratio of 8 percent, a 2.5 percent capital conservation buffer, a countercyclical buffer of up to 2.5 percent, a leverage ratio, LCR and NSFR. It also adds extra requirements for global systemically important banks (G-SIBs). The RBI adopted it for Indian banks in phases from 2013.

The Kyoto Protocol was adopted in 1997 and came into force in 2005. It set binding emission reduction targets for developed (Annex I) countries, based on common but differentiated responsibilities. It introduced flexibility mechanisms: emissions trading, the Clean Development Mechanism and Joint Implementation. Its first commitment period ran 2008-12 and the Doha Amendment covered 2013-20. The Paris Agreement (2015) later replaced its approach with nationally determined contributions.

The Montreal Protocol (1987) phases out ozone-depleting substances such as CFCs, halons and HCFCs. It was adopted under the Vienna Convention (1985) and has achieved universal ratification. Developing countries get a longer phase-out schedule and financial and technical help through the Multilateral Fund. The Kigali Amendment (2016) added the phase-down of HFCs, which are potent greenhouse gases but not ozone-depleting.
related: BCBS was established in 1974 and sits under the Bank for International Settlements in Basel, Switzerland.
Basel III was a response to the 2008 global financial crisis.
Basel III liquidity measures are the LCR and the NSFR.
India's D-SIBs are SBI, HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank.
Basel II rested on three pillars: minimum capital, supervisory review and market discipline.
The Financial Stability Board was created by the G20 in 2009 and is based in Basel.
Basel norms are not legally binding; national regulators such as the RBI implement them.
summary: The answer is (b). Basel III is a global regulatory framework from the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) that makes banks stronger against financial and economic stress and improves risk management. It was drawn up after the 2008 global financial crisis.
topic_notes:
Basel norms are international banking regulations from the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS), formed in 1974 by G10 central bank governors and hosted by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) in Basel. The standards are not legally binding, and each country implements them through its own regulator, which in India is the RBI.

Basel I (1988) set a minimum capital of 8 percent of risk-weighted assets, mainly against credit risk. Basel II (2004) added operational and market risk and the three-pillar structure. Basel III (2010-11) responded to the 2008 crisis with these main elements:
- Higher and better-quality capital, centred on Common Equity Tier 1.
- A capital conservation buffer of 2.5 percent and a countercyclical buffer.
- A non-risk-based leverage ratio.
- Liquidity standards: the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (30-day stress) and the Net Stable Funding Ratio (one-year horizon).
- Extra loss-absorbency for G-SIBs and D-SIBs.

In India, the RBI began phasing in Basel III in 2013. Indian banks must keep a minimum total capital ratio of 9 percent, higher than the Basel minimum of 8 percent, plus a capital conservation buffer of 2.5 percent. The RBI also identifies domestic systemically important banks (D-SIBs): SBI, HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank. The final reforms, often called Basel IV or the Basel III endgame, revise the standardised approaches to credit risk and operational risk and add an output floor.

Other angles for UPSC: the Financial Stability Board (FSB), the BIS as the central banks' bank, Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital, risk-weighted assets, the Prompt Corrective Action framework, and the global bodies that govern finance (IMF, World Bank, FATF).

ocr: Consider the following statements : 1. The winds which blow between 30° N and 60° § latitudes through- out the year are known as westerlies, 2. The moist air masses that cause winter rains in North-Western region of India are part of westerlies. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? fa) 1 only (b) 2 only (co) Both 1 and 2 (da) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Geography
detail: Westerlies are prevailing winds that blow from the subtropical high-pressure belts (about 30°-35°) toward the sub-polar low-pressure belts (about 60°-65°) in both hemispheres. Because of the Coriolis effect they blow from the southwest in the Northern Hemisphere and from the northwest in the Southern Hemisphere. They are strongest in the Southern Hemisphere, where the vast oceans offer little obstruction. These are the 'Roaring Forties', 'Furious Fifties' and 'Screaming Sixties'. Statement 1 is wrong because the range given, 30° N to 60° S, mixes the two hemispheres. That range includes the equatorial belt and the tropical easterlies (trade winds), which blow in the opposite direction. The correct ranges are 30°-60° N and 30°-60° S. Statement 2 is right. Western disturbances are extratropical cyclonic systems that originate over the Mediterranean region and travel east in the westerly flow, with the subtropical westerly jet stream steering them. They bring winter rain and snow to Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, Himachal Pradesh and Jammu & Kashmir. This rain is very beneficial for rabi crops, especially wheat. Elimination logic: once statement 1 is seen to be geographically impossible, only (b) remains.
explanations: (a) Wrong: it accepts statement 1, which gives an incorrect latitudinal extent for westerlies, and it rejects the correct statement 2.
(b) Right: only statement 2 is correct, since western disturbances are carried by the westerlies. Statement 1 gives a wrong latitude range.
(c) Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect, so 'Both' cannot be true.
(d) Wrong: statement 2 is correct, since the winter rains of North-West India come from westerly-borne western disturbances.
keyfact: Westerlies blow between 30°-60° in each hemisphere, and western disturbances carried by them bring winter rain to North-West India (good for rabi wheat).
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Westerlies blow between about 30° and 60° latitude in each hemisphere (30°-60° N and 30°-60° S). The range '30° N to 60° S' wrongly spans the equator and the trade-wind belt, and the winds do not blow across it throughout the year.

2 — Correct: Winter rain in North-Western India is caused by western disturbances, which are moist air masses from the Mediterranean region carried eastward by the westerlies and the subtropical westerly jet stream.
summary: The correct answer is (b) 2 only. Westerlies blow from the subtropical high-pressure belts toward the sub-polar lows, so they lie between roughly 30°-60° latitude in each hemisphere, not across a continuous band from 30° N to 60° S. The winter rain in North-Western India comes from western disturbances, which are moist air masses carried by the westerlies.

ocr: With reference to Indian Ocean Rim Association for Regional Cooperation (IOR-ARC)’, consider the following statements : 1. It was established very recently in response to incidents of piracy and accidents of oil spills. 2. It is an alliance meant for maritime security only. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? fa) 1 only (6) 2 only (c} Both 1 and 2 (@) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Geography
detail: The Indian Ocean Rim Association (IORA), earlier called the Indian Ocean Rim Initiative and then the Indian Ocean Rim Association for Regional Cooperation (IOR-ARC), was formally launched in March 1997 in Mauritius, after the idea emerged from India-South Africa-Mauritius consultations in 1995. Its secretariat is at Ebene, Mauritius. It was renamed IORA in 2013. It is an intergovernmental organisation with about 23 member states and several dialogue partners, built on open regionalism. Its objectives are trade and investment facilitation, and economic and sustainable development in the region. Its priority areas are maritime safety and security, trade and investment facilitation, fisheries management, disaster risk management, academic and science-technology cooperation, tourism and cultural exchanges, and the Blue Economy. Maritime security is therefore only one of several pillars. It is also not a military alliance. Elimination logic: Statement 1 fails because the body is nearly three decades old and was not created in response to piracy or oil spills. Statement 2 fails because of the word 'only' and the word 'alliance'. UPSC often uses absolute words such as 'only' to make a statement wrong. Both statements are wrong, so (d) is the answer.
explanations: (a) Wrong: Statement 1 is incorrect because the body dates from 1997 and was founded for economic cooperation, not as a response to piracy or oil spills.
(b) Wrong: Statement 2 is incorrect because the mandate is multi-sectoral, not maritime security only, and the body is not an alliance.
(c) Wrong: Both statements cannot be correct, since each is factually flawed.
(d) Correct: Neither statement holds. IORA was founded in 1997 as a multi-sector regional cooperation forum, not a maritime-security-only alliance.
keyfact: IORA (ex-IOR-ARC): founded 1997, Mauritius; secretariat at Ebene; a multi-sector economic cooperation forum with maritime security as just one of its priority areas.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: IOR-ARC was established in 1997 (Mauritius), not very recently, and its purpose was regional economic cooperation, not a response to piracy or oil spills.

2 — Incorrect: IORA is a broad regional cooperation grouping covering trade, investment, fisheries, disaster management, tourism, the Blue Economy and more. Maritime safety and security is only one priority area, and it is not an alliance.
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is correct. IORA (formerly IOR-ARC) was established in 1997, not recently, and it is a broad regional economic and cooperation grouping, not an alliance for maritime security only.

question: Which one of the following movements has contributed to a split in the Indian National Congress resulting in the emergence of ‘moderates’ and ‘extremists’?
subject: Modern History
detail: The Partition of Bengal, announced by Lord Curzon in July 1905 and effective 16 October 1905, triggered the Swadeshi and Boycott movement. Moderates such as Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Pherozeshah Mehta and Dadabhai Naoroji favoured constitutional agitation, petitions and limited boycott of foreign goods. Extremists, notably Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal and Lala Lajpat Rai (Lal-Bal-Pal), along with Aurobindo Ghose, demanded Swaraj, boycott on a wide scale, national education and passive resistance. The disagreement over extending the movement beyond Bengal and over the Congress presidency (Tilak's camp wanted Lajpat Rai, the Moderates backed Rash Behari Ghosh) led to a breakdown at the Surat Session in December 1907, and the Moderates retained control of the Congress. The Congress reunited only in 1916 at the Lucknow Session under A. C. Majumdar's presidency. Elimination: the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22), Civil Disobedience Movement (1930) and Quit India Movement (1942) came much later, when the Moderate-Extremist labels were obsolete. They were mass movements led by Gandhi and did not cause that particular split.
explanations: Correct: the Swadeshi Movement (1905 onwards) after the Partition of Bengal divided the Congress over boycott and Swaraj, leading to the Surat split of 1907.
Incorrect: the Quit India Movement (1942) occurred decades after the Moderate-Extremist split and had nothing to do with it.

Incorrect: the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22) was launched under Gandhi after the Moderates and Extremists had reunited in 1916; some Moderates left the Congress in 1920, but that is not the Moderate-Extremist split.
Incorrect: the Civil Disobedience Movement (1930-34), begun with the Dandi March, came long after the 1907 split.
keyfact: Swadeshi Movement (1905, Partition of Bengal) led to the Surat Split of 1907 between Moderates and Extremists; they reunited at Lucknow in 1916.
summary: The answer is (a) Swadeshi Movement. The Swadeshi and Boycott movement that followed the 1905 Partition of Bengal sharply divided the Congress over methods, producing the Moderates and Extremists, and the split became formal at the Surat Session of 1907.

question: In a particular region in India, the local people train the roots of living trees into robust bridges across the streams. As the time passes, these bridges become stronger. These unique ‘living root bridges’ are found in
subject: Environment
detail: Living root bridges are a bio-engineering tradition of Meghalaya, found mainly in East Khasi Hills, West Jaintia Hills and South West Khasi Hills districts, around Cherrapunji (Sohra), Mawsynram, Nongriat and Pynursla. The Khasis and Jaintias guide the secondary aerial roots of Ficus elastica (Indian rubber tree, 'jing kieng jri' in Khasi) across a stream using betel-nut trunks or bamboo scaffolding. Over 10-15 years the roots fuse (inosculation) and thicken, so the bridge strengthens with age. Some are 100-500 years old, and some bridges can carry 50 or more people. The heavy rainfall, flash floods and steep terrain make wooden or steel bridges decay or wash away, while living bridges self-renew. The Umshiang double-decker bridge at Nongriat is the best known. Meghalaya's living root bridges are on UNESCO's Tentative List (2022) for World Heritage status as a cultural landscape. Elimination: Himachal Pradesh is known for Himalayan rope and wooden bridges, Jharkhand is a plateau region with no such tradition, and Tamil Nadu has no living root bridge culture. The rain-soaked northeast, with its rubber fig, is the clue.
explanations: Correct. Living root bridges belong to the Khasi and Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya, where Ficus elastica roots are trained across streams.
Wrong. Himachal Pradesh has Himalayan suspension and wooden cantilever bridges, but no tradition of living root bridges.
Wrong. Jharkhand is a plateau state known for tribal culture and minerals, not for root bridges.
Wrong. Tamil Nadu has no such tradition. Its famous bridge is the Pamban rail bridge, which links Rameswaram to the mainland.
keyfact: Living root bridges (Ficus elastica roots) are made by the Khasi and Jaintia peoples of Meghalaya.
option_notes: Meghalaya ('abode of clouds') became a state in 1972. It is home to the Khasi, Jaintia and Garo tribes and has a matrilineal society. Cherrapunji and Mawsynram are among the wettest places on Earth. It has the Sixth Schedule's autonomous district councils, and the living root bridges and Mawlynnong 'cleanest village' are well known. Sacred groves (Law Kyntang) are also found there.

Himachal Pradesh, a Himalayan state with Shimla as its capital, became a full state in 1971. It is known for apple orchards, the Kullu-Manali area, Kinnaur and Spiti, and the Great Himalayan National Park (UNESCO site, 2014). Its traditional bridges are wood or rope. The Kalka-Shimla railway is a UNESCO site.

Jharkhand was carved out of Bihar in 2000, with Ranchi as its capital. It lies on the Chota Nagpur Plateau and is rich in coal, iron ore and mica. Its tribes include the Santhal, Munda and Oraon. Parasnath Hill and Betla National Park are located there, and the Damodar and Subarnarekha are its rivers.

Tamil Nadu, with Chennai as its capital, lies on the south-eastern coast, with the Western and Eastern Ghats and the Kaveri delta. It has Dravidian temple architecture, including the Great Living Chola Temples (UNESCO). It also has the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve and Pamban Bridge. Jallikattu and Bharatanatyam are part of its culture.
related: Living root bridges use aerial roots of Ficus elastica (Indian rubber fig).
They are found mainly in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya.
The Umshiang double-decker bridge is at Nongriat, near Cherrapunji.
Meghalaya's living root bridges are on UNESCO's Tentative List (2022).
Cherrapunji and Mawsynram are among the wettest places on Earth.
Mawlynnong in Meghalaya is called Asia's cleanest village.
Meghalayan Age (4,200 years ago) is the latest stage of the Holocene.
Apatani valley in Arunachal Pradesh is a traditional agriculture site on the UNESCO Tentative List.
summary: The answer is (a) Meghalaya. Living root bridges are made by the Khasi and Jaintia peoples, who guide the aerial roots of the Indian rubber fig (Ficus elastica) across streams in the wet southern Khasi and Jaintia Hills. The roots strengthen as they grow and thicken over time.
topic_notes: Living root bridges are a form of 'living architecture' or bio-engineering. The species used is mostly Ficus elastica, which produces strong secondary roots from the trunk and grows well on rocky riverbanks. In the Jaintia Hills, a related practice uses the roots of Ficus benghalensis and similar species. Khasi names include 'jingkieng jri'. Examples: the Umshiang double-decker root bridge at Nongriat (near Cherrapunji), the Riwai root bridge near Mawlynnong, and the Mawsaw root bridge. The bridges are built and maintained by communities, often over generations, and can last for centuries. They are on the UNESCO Tentative List (2022) as the 'Jingkieng Jri: Living Root Bridge Cultural Landscapes of Meghalaya'. The bridges reflect traditional ecological knowledge and the community's relationship with the forest. The region has very heavy monsoon rainfall, which makes conventional bridges decay. Related Meghalaya topics: the Khasi, Jaintia and Garo hills; the Sixth Schedule; the Meghalaya Basin Age (Meghalayan stage of the Holocene, 4,200 years ago); Mawlynnong; Dawki and the Umngot river; sacred groves; and the Nokrek Biosphere Reserve. The Khasi Hills also have limestone caves, such as Krem Liat Prah. UPSC often asks about GI-tagged products, UNESCO sites and traditional practices of the northeast, such as Apatani paddy-cum-fish cultivation in Arunachal Pradesh and Zabo farming in Nagaland.

ocr: Tides occur in the oceans and seas due to which among the following? 1. Gravitational force of the Sun 2. Gravitational force of the Moon 3. Centrifugal force of the Earth Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa) 1 only (b}) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1,2 and 3
subject: Geography
detail: Tides are the periodic rise and fall of sea level. The main cause is the differential gravitational attraction of the Moon, which is much closer to Earth, so its tide-generating force is about twice that of the Sun even though the Sun is far more massive. The Sun's gravitational pull adds to or subtracts from the lunar effect. When the Sun, Moon and Earth are aligned (new moon and full moon), spring tides occur with the highest high tides and lowest low tides. At the quarter phases (first and last quarter), the Sun and Moon pull at right angles, producing neap tides with a lower range. Gravitational force dominates on the side of Earth facing the Moon, creating the 'toward' bulge. On the opposite side, the centrifugal force, arising from the revolution of the Earth and Moon about their common centre of mass, exceeds the Moon's weaker gravitational pull and creates the second bulge. This is why most coasts see two high tides roughly every 24 hours 52 minutes. Since the question asks which factors cause tides, and all three listed forces contribute, elimination leaves only option (d). Any option omitting the Sun, the Moon or the centrifugal force is incomplete.
explanations: (a) Wrong: It counts only the Sun and omits the Moon, the dominant factor, and the centrifugal force.
(b) Wrong: Moon and centrifugal force are valid causes, but it leaves out the Sun's gravitational influence, which is also a cause.
(c) Wrong: It leaves out the Moon, the principal tide-generating body, so it is clearly incomplete.
(d) Correct: The Sun's gravity, the Moon's gravity and the centrifugal force all contribute to tides, so all three statements hold.
keyfact: Tides = Moon's gravity (dominant) + Sun's gravity + centrifugal force (far-side bulge); spring tides at new and full moon, neap tides at quarter phases.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Sun's gravitational force contributes to tide generation, strengthening tides at spring tides and weakening them at neap tides.
2 — Correct: The Moon's gravitational force is the dominant tide-producing force because of its proximity to Earth.
3 — Correct: The centrifugal force from the Earth-Moon system's revolution about their common centre of mass counterbalances gravity on the far side and produces the second tidal bulge.
summary: The correct answer is (d) 1, 2 and 3. Tides are produced by the combined effect of the Moon's gravitational pull, the Sun's gravitational pull, and the centrifugal force arising from the Earth-Moon system's revolution, which together create the tidal bulges.

ocr: In which of the following activities are Indian Remote Sensing (IRS) satellites used? 1, Assessment of crop productivity 2. Locating grcundwater resources 3. Mineral exploration 4, Telecommunications 5S. Traffic studies Select the correct answer using the code given below. (a) 1, 2 and 3 only (b) 4 and 5 only fc) 1 and 2 only (@) 1,2,3,4and5
subject: Geography
detail: The Indian Remote Sensing (IRS) programme, started with IRS-1A in 1988, is one of the largest constellations of civilian earth-observation satellites in the world. The satellites are placed in sun-synchronous polar orbits, launched mainly by PSLV, and carry optical and multispectral sensors such as LISS (Linear Imaging Self-Scanning), PAN and AWiFS. Data are received and processed by NRSC (National Remote Sensing Centre), Hyderabad. Applications include crop acreage and yield estimation (e.g., the FASAL programme), groundwater prospect mapping (Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking Water Mission), mineral exploration, forest cover, land use and land cover, flood and drought monitoring, urban planning, and ocean and fisheries studies (potential fishing zones). Telecommunications and broadcasting are done by INSAT/GSAT series, which are geostationary communication satellites. Traffic studies are not a core IRS function, since the resolution and revisit times are unsuited to it. Elimination logic: statements 4 and 5 are the odd ones, so any option containing either (b) or (d) is out, and (c) leaves out mineral exploration, a classic remote sensing use.
explanations: Correct: it includes exactly the three valid applications (crop productivity, groundwater, mineral exploration) and excludes telecommunications and traffic studies.
Incorrect: 4 and 5 are not IRS applications; telecommunications belongs to INSAT/GSAT and traffic studies are not a core IRS use.
Incorrect: it omits mineral exploration (3), which is a valid IRS application, and so is incomplete.
Incorrect: it wrongly includes telecommunications (4) and traffic studies (5).
keyfact: IRS = earth observation (crops, groundwater, minerals, land use) in sun-synchronous orbit; INSAT/GSAT = telecommunications in geostationary orbit.
statements: 1 — Correct: IRS data are used for crop acreage and production estimation and for assessing crop productivity and health.
2 — Correct: IRS imagery helps map geomorphology and lineaments to identify groundwater prospect zones.
3 — Correct: Multispectral imagery helps identify rock types, structures and alteration zones useful in mineral exploration.
4 — Incorrect: Telecommunications is the function of INSAT/GSAT geostationary communication satellites, not IRS.
5 — Incorrect: Traffic studies are not a function of IRS satellites.
summary: The answer is (a) 1, 2 and 3 only. IRS satellites are earth-observation (remote sensing) satellites used for crops, groundwater and minerals, whereas telecommunications and traffic studies are not their functions.

ocr: Consider the following States : 1. Arunachal Pradesh 2. Himachal Pradesh 3. Mizoram In which of the above States do ‘Tropical Wet Evergreen Forests’ occur? (a) 1 only () 2 and 3 only (co) 1 and 3 only 1, 2 and 3 (d}
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Tropical wet evergreen forests (Champion and Seth classification) grow where annual rainfall exceeds about 200 cm, the mean annual temperature is around 22°C or more, and the dry season is short or absent. They are dense and multi-layered, with tall broad-leaved trees (30-45 m) such as mahogany, ebony, rosewood, dipterocarps, Hopea and Mesua. The main areas are the windward slopes of the Western Ghats, the Andaman & Nicobar Islands, upper Assam, and the north-eastern hill states including Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Tripura. In the north-east the forests occur mainly in the foothills and lower slopes, and Arunachal Pradesh also has them in its low-lying eastern districts. Mizoram has large areas of tropical wet evergreen and semi-evergreen forest. Himachal Pradesh lies in the western Himalaya, which has lower rainfall, a marked winter and altitudinal zonation. Its vegetation is mainly subtropical pine (chir), moist temperate, dry temperate, sub-alpine and alpine forests, plus some tropical dry deciduous forest in the lower Shiwalik foothills. Elimination: if you know Arunachal Pradesh has these forests, (b) and (d) can be dropped only if Himachal is excluded, and Himachal's temperate Himalayan character excludes it. The remaining pair, 1 and 3, gives (c).
explanations: (a) Incorrect: it omits Mizoram, which also has tropical wet evergreen forests.
