ocr: India With reference to the religious history of India, consider the following statements : 1, The concept of Bodhisattva is central to Hinayana_ sect of Buddhism. Bodhisattva is a compassionate one on his way to enlightenment. Bodhisattva delays achieving his own salvation to help all sentient beings on their path to it. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? — {a) 1 only {b} 2 and 3 only (c) 2 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 54. 51. ‘Doctors Without Borders {Medecins Sans Frontieres)’, often in the news, is fa) a division of World Health Organization (b) a non-governmental international org
subject: Ancient History
detail: Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) is an international, independent, non-profit humanitarian medical organization. A group of French doctors and journalists founded it in Paris in 1971, after their experience in the Biafra conflict in Nigeria. It delivers emergency medical aid in conflict zones, epidemics (Ebola, cholera, measles), natural disasters and areas with no healthcare access. It works on the principles of neutrality, impartiality and independence, and it relies mostly on private donations, which keeps it free of government control. It won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1999. Its international headquarters are in Geneva, and it has national sections in many countries. The elimination logic is simple. The WHO is a UN specialized agency, and MSF is not a division of it. MSF is not an inter-governmental body, because states are not its members; it is a private association of individuals. The EU does not sponsor it, and it deliberately avoids dependence on government funding. It is not a UN specialized agency, since those are created by inter-governmental agreement and linked to the UN through ECOSOC. Hence only (b) fits. Remember the Q51 pattern: UPSC often asks about the legal nature of well-known bodies (NGO, inter-governmental, UN agency).
explanations: Wrong. MSF is independent of the World Health Organization. WHO is an inter-governmental UN specialized agency, whereas MSF is a private NGO, though the two may cooperate in emergencies.
Correct. MSF is a non-governmental international humanitarian medical organization, founded in France in 1971 and awarded the 1999 Nobel Peace Prize.

Wrong. It is not inter-governmental, since its members are individuals and not states, and it is not sponsored by the European Union. It deliberately limits government funding to protect its independence.
Wrong. UN specialized agencies (WHO, FAO, UNESCO, ILO and others) are created by inter-governmental agreements. MSF is a private NGO and has no such status.
keyfact: MSF (Doctors Without Borders), founded in 1971 in France and Nobel Peace Prize winner of 1999, is a private non-governmental international medical humanitarian organization, not a UN or WHO body.
option_notes: The World Health Organization was established on 7 April 1948 (observed as World Health Day) and is headquartered in Geneva. It is a UN specialized agency that coordinates international public health. Its governing body is the World Health Assembly, and its members are states (194 member states). It eradicated smallpox (declared in 1980) and leads on pandemic response, the International Health Regulations and the Essential Medicines List. India is a member of its South-East Asia Region (SEARO, New Delhi).

A non-governmental international organization is a private, voluntary body that is not run by a government and not formed by treaty. Examples are MSF, Amnesty International, Greenpeace, the Red Cross movement (ICRC, a private Swiss association with a mandate under the Geneva Conventions), Oxfam and Transparency International. They often get consultative status with the UN ECOSOC. They work on humanitarian aid, human rights, environment and advocacy, and are funded mainly by donations.

An inter-governmental organization is formed by a treaty among sovereign states, which are its members. Examples are the UN, WTO, IMF, World Bank, ASEAN, SAARC and the African Union. The European Union is a unique political and economic union of 27 member states (after Brexit in 2020), based on the Maastricht Treaty (1993) and the Lisbon Treaty (2009), with its headquarters at Brussels. It funds humanitarian aid through ECHO, but it does not sponsor MSF.

UN specialized agencies are autonomous bodies established by inter-governmental agreement and brought into relationship with the UN under Article 57 and Article 63 of the UN Charter through ECOSOC. Examples are WHO, FAO, UNESCO, ILO, IMF, World Bank Group, ICAO, IMO, ITU, UPU, WMO, WIPO, IFAD, UNIDO and UNWTO. They have their own membership, budgets and governance, and the UN coordinates their work.
related: MSF was founded in 1971 in France and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1999.
MSF is headquartered in Geneva and is funded mainly by private donors.
WHO was established on 7 April 1948 and has its headquarters in Geneva.
ICRC was founded in 1863 by Henri Dunant, who shared the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901.
Amnesty International (founded 1961) won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1977.
The World Food Programme (Rome) won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2020.
UN specialized agencies are linked to the UN through ECOSOC under Articles 57 and 63 of the UN Charter.
The Bodhisattva question beside it: official answer is (b) 2 and 3 only, since the Bodhisattva concept is central to Mahayana, not Hinayana.
summary: The answer is (b): Doctors Without Borders (Médecins Sans Frontières, MSF) is a non-governmental international organization. It is a private humanitarian medical body founded in France in 1971, not part of the WHO, the EU or the UN.
topic_notes: Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders) was founded in 1971 in Paris by a group of French doctors and journalists, with Bernard Kouchner among the best-known founders. It grew out of the Biafra famine and civil war in Nigeria. Its charter rests on neutrality, impartiality, independence and witnessing (speaking out, or témoignage). It received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1999. Its international office is in Geneva, and it works through national sections and operational centres (for example Amsterdam, Brussels, Paris, Geneva, Barcelona). It runs medical programmes in war zones such as Syria, Yemen, South Sudan and Gaza, and during outbreaks such as the West Africa Ebola crisis of 2014-16. It also runs the Access Campaign for affordable medicines, and in India it has campaigned on TB, HIV and generic drug access (it has opposed evergreening of patents). It refuses funds from some governments to stay independent. Related bodies that UPSC may ask about: the International Committee of the Red Cross (founded 1863 by Henri Dunant, Nobel Peace Prize 1917, 1944 and 1963; the Red Cross and Red Crescent movement), Amnesty International (founded 1961, Nobel Peace Prize 1977), Greenpeace, Oxfam, Save the Children, CARE and Human Rights Watch. Also revise the UN system, with its six principal organs (General Assembly, Security Council, ECOSOC, Trusteeship Council, ICJ and Secretariat). Other typical comparison questions ask what an organization is, such as an NGO versus an IGO versus a specialized agency. Also learn the headquarters of major global bodies: WHO in Geneva, UNICEF in New York, UNHCR in Geneva, UNESCO in Paris, and the WFP in Rome (Nobel Peace Prize 2020).

ocr: With reference to an initiative called The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity (TEEB)’, which of the following statements is/are correct? 55. 1. It is an initiative hosted by UNEP, IMF and World Economic Forum. 2. It is a global initiative that focuses on drawing attention to the economic benefits of biodiversity. 3. It presents an approach that can help decision-makers recognize, demonstrate and capture the value of ecosystems and biodiversity. Select the correct answer using the code given below. . fa) 1 and 2 only (b) 3 only (c} 2 and 3 only {a} 1, 2 and 3
subject: Environment
detail: TEEB (The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity) grew out of a 2007 G8+5 meeting in Potsdam, Germany, where environment ministers proposed a study on the global economic cost of biodiversity loss. Pavan Sukhdev, an Indian economist, led the study, and UNEP hosts it, with support from the European Commission, Germany and the UK. Its main reports appeared in 2008 (interim) and 2010 (synthesis, released at CBD COP10 in Nagoya). Its purpose is to mainstream the values of nature into decision-making by making the benefits of ecosystem services visible in economic terms, and it works through a tiered approach: recognise value, demonstrate value, capture value. Later work includes TEEB for Agriculture and Food (TEEBAgriFood), TEEB for business, and national TEEB studies, including in India. Elimination logic: statements 2 and 3 are the standard description of TEEB's purpose and approach. Statement 1 names the IMF and the World Economic Forum as hosts, which is wrong because UNEP alone hosts the initiative. Dropping statement 1 leaves only option (c). Options (a) and (d) both include statement 1, and option (b) leaves out statement 2.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes statement 1, which names the IMF and the World Economic Forum as hosts, and it leaves out the correct statement 3.
(b) is wrong because statement 3 is correct, but statement 2 is also correct, so '3 only' is incomplete.
(c) is correct because statements 2 and 3 both describe TEEB accurately, and statement 1 is rejected because its hosting claim is false.
(d) is wrong because it includes statement 1, and TEEB is hosted by UNEP, not by the IMF and the WEF.
keyfact: TEEB is a UNEP-hosted initiative, led by Pavan Sukhdev, that shows the economic value of biodiversity and ecosystems; the IMF and the WEF do not host it.
option_notes: (a) '1 and 2 only' is a statement-number option, so there is no standalone entry for it.
(b) '3 only' is a statement-number option, so there is no standalone entry for it.
(c) '2 and 3 only' is a statement-number option, so there is no standalone entry for it.
(d) '1, 2 and 3' is a statement-number option, so there is no standalone entry for it.
related: TEEB is hosted by UNEP and led by Pavan Sukhdev.
TEEB was proposed at the G8+5 meeting in Potsdam in 2007.
The TEEB synthesis report was released at CBD COP10, Nagoya, in 2010.
TEEB follows a recognise, demonstrate and capture value approach.
The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (2005) classified ecosystem services as provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting.
IPBES was established in 2012 and its secretariat is in Bonn.
The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework was adopted in 2022 at CBD COP15.
The Dasgupta Review (2021) is a UK-commissioned report on the economics of biodiversity.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: TEEB is hosted by UNEP, not by the IMF or the World Economic Forum. The TEEB Office is in Geneva, under UNEP's Economics and Trade Branch. Funding came from the European Commission, Germany, the UK, Norway, the Netherlands and others. The IMF is a Bretton Woods financial institution and has no role in running TEEB. The WEF is a forum for business and political leaders, and it is not a TEEB host either. The 2007 Potsdam initiative began under the German presidency of the G8, with the European Commission, and Pavan Sukhdev led the study. UNEP continues to host the initiative and its follow-on programmes, including TEEBAgriFood.

2 — Correct: TEEB is a global initiative that draws attention to the economic benefits of biodiversity and ecosystem services, and to the growing cost of biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation. It began as a G8+5 proposal in Potsdam in 2007 and was led by Pavan Sukhdev. The Phase 1 interim report came out in 2008, and the final synthesis was presented at CBD COP10 in Nagoya in October 2010. It builds on the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (2005) and the Stern Review on climate economics. Its aim is to show that nature has economic value, so that policy, business and consumers account for it.

3 — Correct: TEEB offers a tiered approach to help decision-makers recognise, demonstrate and capture the value of ecosystems and biodiversity. Recognising value is the first step, because some cultures and communities already hold nature to be valuable. Demonstrating value means using economic tools to make it visible in decision-making. Capturing value means building it into mechanisms such as payments for ecosystem services, reforming subsidies, and creating protected areas. The approach is applied to policymakers, local administrators, businesses and citizens through separate TEEB reports. National and regional studies, including in India, use the framework.
summary: The correct answer is (c): statements 2 and 3 are correct, statement 1 is wrong. TEEB is a global initiative, hosted by UNEP, that draws attention to the economic benefits of biodiversity and offers an approach to help decision-makers recognise, demonstrate and capture the value of ecosystems and biodiversity. It is not hosted by the IMF or the World Economic Forum.
topic_notes: TEEB (The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity) is a global initiative to mainstream the values of biodiversity and ecosystem services into decision-making. Background: environment ministers of the G8+5 met in Potsdam, Germany, in 2007 and proposed a review of the global economic benefit of biodiversity and the cost of its loss, and of the failure to take protective action. Pavan Sukhdev, a former banker, led the study as Study Leader. UNEP hosts it, and the main funders have been the European Commission, Germany and the UK. Key outputs: an interim report in 2008, then the TEEB reports of 2009-2010 for policymakers, local administrators, business, and citizens, with the synthesis report 'Mainstreaming the Economics of Nature' released at CBD COP10 in Nagoya in 2010. A later programme, TEEBAgriFood, evaluates the full costs and benefits of agri-food systems. India has run its own TEEB-India initiative with the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. Core ideas: ecosystem services are classed as provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting, following the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (2005). Tools include natural capital accounting, payments for ecosystem services, and reform of harmful subsidies. Related items UPSC could test: the Convention on Biological Diversity (1992, Rio), the Aichi Targets (2010) and the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022), IPBES (2012), the Nagoya Protocol on access and benefit sharing, the Ramsar Convention, the Green GDP idea, and the Dasgupta Review (2021) on the economics of biodiversity. Remember who hosts what: UNEP is in Nairobi, the CBD Secretariat is in Montreal, IPBES is in Bonn, and Ramsar is in Gland.

ocr: With reference to ‘Red Sanders’, 56. sometimes seen in the news, consider the following statements : 1. Itisa tree species found in a part of ' South India. 2. itis one of the most important trees in the tropical rain forest areas of South India. So Ae Which of the statements given above ‘is/are correct? {a} 1 only {bj} 2 only fc) Both ] and 2 ‘(a) Neither 1 nor 2 .20 B-APM-P-CKB/65A Which of the following statements is/are correct? ee = Proper design and effective implemen- tation of UN-REDD+ Programme can significantly contribute to 1. protection of biodiversity 2. resilience of forest ecosy
subject: Environment
detail: Red Sanders, also called red sandalwood, Rakta Chandan or Yerra Chandanam, is a small tree endemic to a limited belt of the Eastern Ghats in southern Andhra Pradesh (Kadapa, Chittoor, Kurnool, Nellore) with marginal extension into Tamil Nadu and Karnataka. It grows in dry deciduous and scrub forests on rocky, red, gravelly soils with low rainfall and hot conditions. It is not a rain forest tree. Its heartwood is valued for its deep red colour, used in furniture, carvings, musical instruments (e.g. the Japanese shamisen), and dyes and medicines, which drives heavy smuggling to China and East Asia. The IUCN Red List classified it as Endangered earlier and later as Near Threatened (2018). It is listed in CITES Appendix II and in Schedule II of the Wild Life (Protection) Act 1972 (via the 2022 amendment). Export is restricted. Elimination logic: statement 1 is plainly true because it is endemic to a part of South India. Statement 2 is false because rain forest trees are associated with the Western Ghats, not the dry Eastern Ghats. So (a) is the only option consistent with both.
explanations: Correct: statement 1 is true because Red Sanders is endemic to a part of South India, and statement 2 is false because it is not a rain forest tree.
Wrong: statement 2 is false. Red Sanders grows in dry deciduous and scrub forests of the Eastern Ghats, not in the tropical rain forests.
Wrong: this would require statement 2 to be true, but it is not, so the option fails.
Wrong: statement 1 is true, so it cannot be that neither statement is correct.
keyfact: Red Sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus) is endemic to the dry Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh, not a rain forest tree; CITES Appendix II.
option_notes: Option (a) 1 only: it asserts that Red Sanders is a tree species found in a part of South India and rejects the rain forest claim. This matches the facts. Red Sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus) is endemic to the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh and is the only species valued as red sandalwood. It is a legume family tree with a deep red heartwood used for furniture, carving, dyes and medicine, and is heavily targeted by smugglers. It is listed in CITES Appendix II and was assessed Near Threatened by IUCN in 2018.

Option (b) 2 only: this would mean Red Sanders is an important rain forest tree but not a regionally restricted species, which is false. The tropical rain forests of South India are in the Western Ghats, with evergreen species such as Dipterocarpus, Mesua, Palaquium and Calophyllum, high rainfall above 200 cm and dense multi-layered canopy. Red Sanders instead prefers dry, hot, rocky terrain with scrub vegetation in the Eastern Ghats and is restricted in range.

Option (c) Both 1 and 2: this treats Red Sanders as both endemic to South India and a major rain forest tree. Only the first part is right. Rain forests need heavy, well distributed rainfall, while Red Sanders grows in semi-arid to dry deciduous forests with 500-1000 mm rainfall. Its restricted distribution in the Eastern Ghats (Seshachalam, Nallamala, Veligonda hills) is its key feature, linked with smuggling, CITES regulation and conservation concerns.

Option (d) Neither 1 nor 2: this would deny that Red Sanders is a South Indian species, which is wrong. The species is a well known endemic of southern Andhra Pradesh and neighbouring pockets of Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, often in the news for smuggling seizures, the Seshachalam encounter of 2015, and trade restrictions. It is regulated in international trade under CITES, and India restricts export of the wood.
related: Red Sanders: Pterocarpus santalinus, endemic to the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh.
Seshachalam Hills were notified as a Biosphere Reserve in 2010.
Red Sanders is under CITES Appendix II; IUCN status Near Threatened (2018).
True sandalwood is Santalum album, a root hemi-parasite.
Tropical wet evergreen forests of South India are mainly in the Western Ghats.
Red Sanders heartwood colour comes from the pigment santalin.
Red Sanders is a legume tree of the Fabaceae family.
The Nilgiri, Agasthyamalai and Seshachalam are biosphere reserves in South India.
statements: 1 — Correct: Red Sanders is a tree species endemic to a part of South India, the Eastern Ghats. It is Pterocarpus santalinus, of the Fabaceae (legume) family. Its natural range is a narrow belt in Andhra Pradesh covering the Seshachalam, Nallamala, Veligonda and Lankamala hills of Kadapa, Chittoor, Kurnool and Nellore districts. Its heartwood contains the red pigment santalin. It is slow growing and takes decades to mature. The Seshachalam Hills were notified as a biosphere reserve in 2010. It is prized for furniture, carving and traditional medicine, and is heavily smuggled. It was classed Endangered by IUCN and downlisted to Near Threatened in 2018. It is under CITES Appendix II.

2 — Incorrect: Red Sanders is not an important tree of the tropical rain forests of South India. It thrives in dry deciduous and scrub forest with low rainfall and rocky red soil in the Eastern Ghats. Tropical wet evergreen rain forests of South India lie in the Western Ghats, with species like Dipterocarpus, Palaquium, Mesua and Calophyllum. Red Sanders is valued for its heartwood, not for its role in the rain forest canopy. Its habitat is hot and dry, with rainfall roughly 800-1000 mm, which is far below the rain forest requirement, so it cannot be described as an important rain forest tree.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 only. Red Sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus) is an endemic tree species confined to a part of South India (the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh, chiefly Seshachalam hills). It is a tree of dry deciduous scrub and tropical dry forest, not of the tropical rain forest, so statement 2 is wrong.
topic_notes: Red Sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus), also known as red sandalwood, is a species of the Fabaceae family endemic to the Eastern Ghats of southern India. Its core range is in Andhra Pradesh (Kadapa, Chittoor, Kurnool, Nellore) in the Seshachalam and Nallamala ranges. Seshachalam Hills were declared a Biosphere Reserve in 2010. It prefers dry, hot, rocky red-soil terrain and dry deciduous or scrub forest. It is slow growing, with a heartwood that is deep red due to the pigment santalin. It is not related to true sandalwood (Santalum album), which is a hemi-parasite with fragrant heartwood and oil, mostly found in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Kerala (Marayoor in Kerala has natural sandal forests). Uses of Red Sanders include furniture, carving, musical instruments (shamisen), natural dye, cosmetics and traditional medicine. Demand from China, Japan and other East Asian countries has fuelled large scale illegal felling and smuggling. Conservation status: IUCN Red List Endangered, later changed to Near Threatened in 2018; CITES Appendix II, which regulates international trade through permits and non-detriment findings. In India it is protected through state forest laws, and export of the wood is banned or heavily restricted, with limited exceptions for value-added or cultivated material. Andhra Pradesh set up a Red Sanders Anti-Smuggling Task Force. Other angles UPSC may ask on: rain forests of the Western Ghats and their species, other endemic trees, difference between Eastern and Western Ghats vegetation, CITES appendices, IUCN categories, Wild Life (Protection) Act Schedules, true sandalwood, and biosphere reserves in South India (Nilgiri, Agasthyamalai, Gulf of Mannar, Seshachalam).

ocr: What is ‘Greenhouse Gas Protocol’? fa} It is an international accounting tool for government and business leaders to understand, quantify and Manage greenhouse gas emissions (b) It is an initiative of the United Nations to offer financial incentives to developing countrics to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and to adopt eco-friendly technologies fc) It is an _ inter-governmental agreement ratified by all the member countries of the United Nations to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to specified levels by the year 2022 {d) It is one of the multilateral RED))+ initiatives hosted by the World Bank
subject: Environment
detail: The FSDC was set up by the Government of India in December 2010 as an apex body for financial stability, financial sector development and inter-regulatory coordination. It was proposed in the 2010 Budget and arose from the Raghuram Rajan Committee on Financial Sector Reforms (2008). It was created by executive decision and has no statutory backing. The Union Finance Minister chairs it. Members include the heads of RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA and FMC (since merged into SEBI), the Finance Secretary, the Secretary of the Department of Financial Services, the Chief Economic Adviser and the Economic Affairs Secretary. A sub-committee chaired by the RBI Governor handles day-to-day issues. The FSDC monitors macroprudential supervision of the economy, including the working of large financial conglomerates, and promotes financial literacy and financial inclusion. It sits under the Ministry of Finance and has no link to NITI Aayog, which is the Planning Commission's successor think tank set up in 2015. Elimination logic: statement 1 is false because FSDC is not part of NITI Aayog. That rules out (a) and (d). Statement 3 is true, which rules out (a) and leaves (b) or (c). Statement 2 is also true, so (c) is the only consistent choice. The supplied key (d) would require statement 1 to be true, which is factually wrong.
explanations: (a) 1 and 2 only is wrong because statement 1 is false (FSDC is not a NITI Aayog organ) and it omits statement 3, which is true.
(b) 3 only is wrong because it omits statement 2: the Finance Minister does head FSDC.

(c) 2 and 3 only matches the facts: FSDC is headed by the Finance Minister and monitors macroprudential supervision, and it is not part of NITI Aayog. This is the factually correct option, though it differs from the supplied key.

(d) 1, 2 and 3 is the supplied official key, but it needs statement 1 to be true, and FSDC is not an organ of NITI Aayog. The key conflicts with the facts, so verify it against the official answer sheet.
keyfact: FSDC (2010): non-statutory, chaired by the Finance Minister, handles macroprudential supervision, and is not part of NITI Aayog.
related: FSDC was set up in December 2010 and is non-statutory.
The Union Finance Minister chairs the FSDC; the RBI Governor chairs its Sub-Committee.
The RBI publishes the Financial Stability Report twice a year.
NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015.
The Greenhouse Gas Protocol is an accounting standard from the WRI and the WBCSD.
The Financial Stability Board was established by the G20 in 2009.
Microprudential supervision targets individual institutions; macroprudential targets systemic risk.
The Raghuram Rajan Committee (2008) on financial sector reforms recommended an FSDC-like body.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: FSDC is not an organ of NITI Aayog. It is a Ministry of Finance body created by executive resolution in 2010, before NITI Aayog existed (2015). NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015 as a policy think tank with the Prime Minister as chairperson. FSDC has no statutory basis and sits within the financial-sector architecture of the Department of Economic Affairs. NITI Aayog has a Governing Council of Chief Ministers and Lieutenant Governors, a Vice-Chairperson and a CEO. It has no role in regulatory coordination of RBI, SEBI, IRDAI or PFRDA.

2 — Correct: The Union Finance Minister chairs the FSDC. Other members are the heads of the financial sector regulators (RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA), the Finance Secretary, the Secretary of the Department of Financial Services, the Economic Affairs Secretary, the Revenue Secretary and the Chief Economic Adviser. The RBI Governor chairs the FSDC Sub-Committee. The Council was set up in December 2010 after the global financial crisis. It meets periodically to review financial stability, inter-regulatory coordination, financial literacy and financial inclusion, and it can invite experts. Its secretariat is in the Ministry of Finance.

3 — Correct: One of FSDC's core functions is to monitor macroprudential supervision of the economy and the functioning of large financial conglomerates. It also focuses on financial stability, financial sector development, inter-regulatory coordination, financial literacy and financial inclusion. Macroprudential supervision means watching risks to the whole financial system, such as systemic risk and interconnectedness, rather than individual firms (microprudential). The RBI publishes a biannual Financial Stability Report, released after the FSDC Sub-Committee review. The Council does not replace the regulators' own powers.
summary: The image has two questions, and neither matches the supplied key (d) on the facts. I have taken Q54 to be the Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC) question. On the facts, FSDC is chaired by the Union Finance Minister and monitors macroprudential supervision, but it is not an organ of NITI Aayog, so the factually correct choice is (c) 2 and 3 only. The Greenhouse Gas Protocol question has the correct choice (a). Please check the key against the official UPSC answer sheet for your paper set.
topic_notes: The FSDC is the apex inter-regulatory forum of India's financial sector. It was constituted in December 2010 by executive order, after the 2008 global financial crisis, following the Raghuram Rajan Committee on Financial Sector Reforms (2008). The 2010-11 Budget announced it. It is not a statutory body. Functions: maintaining financial stability, financial sector development, inter-regulatory coordination, macroprudential supervision of the economy including large financial conglomerates, financial literacy and financial inclusion. The Union Finance Minister chairs it. Members include the heads of RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and PFRDA, the Finance Secretary, the Economic Affairs Secretary, the Secretary of the Department of Financial Services, the Revenue Secretary and the Chief Economic Adviser. The FSDC Sub-Committee is chaired by the RBI Governor and works through technical groups on financial inclusion and literacy. The Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission (Justice B. N. Srikrishna, 2013) proposed a statutory FSDC, but this was not enacted. The RBI's Financial Stability Report is published twice a year, in June and December. Related institutions: RBI (1935, monetary policy and banking regulator), SEBI (statutory since 1992), IRDAI (1999 Act), PFRDA (2003, statutory 2013), and the Financial Stability Board (G20, set up in 2009 and based in Basel). Possible future angles: composition, whether it is statutory, the head of the body, the sub-committee chair, comparison with the US Financial Stability Oversight Council, and macroprudential versus microprudential supervision. The Greenhouse Gas Protocol, in the other question, is the international accounting tool from the World Resources Institute and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development, correct option (a).

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q55.
ocr: What is ‘Greenhouse Gas Protocol’? fa} It is an international accounting tool for government and business leaders to understand, quantify and Manage greenhouse gas emissions (b) It is an initiative of the United Nations to offer financial incentives to developing countrics to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and to adopt eco-friendly technologies fc) It is an _ inter-governmental agreement ratified by all the member countries of the United Nations to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to specified levels by the year 2022 {d) It is one of the multilateral RED))+ initiatives hosted by the World Bank
subject: Environment
detail: The GHG Protocol is a voluntary global standard-setting partnership between the World Resources Institute (WRI), a US-based think tank, and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD), Geneva. It began in 1998, and the Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard was first published in 2001 and revised in 2004. It is the most widely used emissions-accounting framework. It underpins CDP disclosures, the Science Based Targets initiative, and national and city inventories. It classifies emissions into Scope 1 (direct emissions from owned sources), Scope 2 (indirect emissions from purchased electricity, steam, heat and cooling) and Scope 3 (all other value-chain emissions, with a standard published in 2011). It covers the seven Kyoto-basket gases: CO2, CH4, N2O, HFCs, PFCs, SF6 and NF3. Its standards include Corporate, Project, Product (Life Cycle), Scope 3, Policy and Action, and the Global Protocol for Community-Scale inventories (GPC) for cities. Elimination logic: the word 'Protocol' tempts students toward the Kyoto Protocol, which is option (c). But (c) fails on facts, because Kyoto was not ratified by all UN members, the US never ratified it, and its target years were 2008-12 and 2013-20, not 2022. Option (b) describes funds such as the Green Climate Fund, and option (d) describes the World Bank's Forest Carbon Partnership Facility. Neither is the GHG Protocol.
explanations: Correct. The GHG Protocol is an accounting and reporting standard, developed by WRI and WBCSD, that helps governments and businesses understand, quantify and manage emissions.

Wrong. It does not offer financial incentives. That description fits funding mechanisms such as the Green Climate Fund, the Global Environment Facility or the Clean Development Mechanism, and the GHG Protocol is not a UN initiative.
Wrong. This describes a treaty such as the Kyoto Protocol. The GHG Protocol is a voluntary standard, not an inter-governmental agreement, and no 2022 deadline is attached to it.
Wrong. REDD+ concerns forest-based mitigation, with World Bank facilities such as the FCPF and the UN-REDD Programme. The GHG Protocol is an accounting methodology run by WRI and WBCSD.
keyfact: The GHG Protocol (WRI plus WBCSD) is a voluntary emissions-accounting standard for governments and businesses, not a treaty or a funding scheme.
option_notes: The GHG Protocol is a voluntary accounting and reporting standard from WRI and WBCSD, launched in 1998, with the Corporate Standard published in 2001. It sets out the Scope 1, 2 and 3 framework and covers the seven Kyoto gases. It is compatible with ISO 14064. Companies report through CDP, and governments and cities use its related standards. It is the global baseline for carbon footprint measurement.

Financial incentives for developing countries are provided by the Green Climate Fund, set up at COP16 in Cancun (2010) and headquartered in Songdo, Incheon, South Korea. It is the UNFCCC's financial mechanism, with a target of mobilising $100 billion a year. The Clean Development Mechanism under Article 12 of the Kyoto Protocol allowed certified emission reduction credits (CERs). The Global Environment Facility and the Adaptation Fund are also climate finance channels.

The Kyoto Protocol was adopted in 1997 and entered into force in 2005. It bound Annex-I countries to cut emissions by about 5.2% below 1990 levels during 2008-12. The Doha Amendment (2012) set a second commitment period for 2013-20. The US never ratified it and Canada withdrew in 2011. It was succeeded by the Paris Agreement (2015), which relies on voluntary NDCs, not binding national targets.

REDD+ stands for Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and forest Degradation, plus conservation, sustainable management and enhancement of carbon stocks. It is a UNFCCC mechanism, framed by the Warsaw Framework (2013). The World Bank hosts the Forest Carbon Partnership Facility (2008) and the BioCarbon Fund. The separate UN-REDD Programme is run by FAO, UNDP and UNEP. Payments are results-based.
related: GHG Protocol: WRI plus WBCSD; Corporate Standard published 2001; Scopes 1, 2 and 3.
Seven Kyoto-basket gases: CO2, CH4, N2O, HFCs, PFCs, SF6, NF3 (NF3 added from 2013).
Kyoto Protocol: adopted 1997, in force 2005; the Doha Amendment covers 2013-20.
Green Climate Fund: headquartered in Songdo, Incheon, South Korea; created at COP16 in 2010.
REDD+: Warsaw Framework 2013; FCPF is hosted by the World Bank; UN-REDD is run by FAO, UNDP and UNEP.
Paris Agreement: COP21, 2015; NDCs; global stocktake every five years.
India's net-zero target is 2070, announced at COP26 Glasgow in 2021.
The Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC) is headed by the Union Finance Minister and is not an organ of NITI Aayog.
summary: The answer is (a). The Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol is an international accounting and reporting standard. It gives governments and businesses a common method to measure, quantify and manage greenhouse gas emissions. It is not a funding scheme, a treaty or a REDD+ initiative.
topic_notes: Emissions accounting is the base of climate policy: what cannot be measured cannot be managed. The GHG Protocol, from WRI and WBCSD, is the dominant framework. Its Scope 1 covers direct emissions, Scope 2 covers purchased energy, and Scope 3 covers the value chain, both upstream and downstream. It handles the seven Kyoto gases (CO2, CH4, N2O, HFCs, PFCs, SF6, NF3), each converted to CO2-equivalent using Global Warming Potentials. Related standards include the Product Life Cycle Standard, the Project Protocol for offsets, and the GPC for cities. The wider climate architecture is also examinable. The UNFCCC was adopted in 1992 at the Rio Earth Summit and came into force in 1994. The Kyoto Protocol (1997, in force 2005) set binding targets for developed countries on the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities. The Paris Agreement (COP21, 2015, in force 2016) aims to hold warming well below 2°C, and to pursue 1.5°C, through nationally determined contributions and a global stocktake every five years. India's NDC targets, updated in 2022, include a 45% reduction in emissions intensity of GDP by 2030 from 2005 levels, 50% non-fossil electric capacity by 2030, and net zero by 2070 announced at COP26 Glasgow. Market mechanisms include Kyoto's CDM, Joint Implementation and emissions trading, and Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. India has its own Carbon Credit Trading Scheme under the Energy Conservation Act amendment (2022). Disclosure frameworks include CDP, TCFD, SBTi, the ISSB standards and SEBI's BRSR. Finance bodies include the Green Climate Fund, the GEF and the Adaptation Fund. For forests, REDD+ runs through the FCPF and UN-REDD. UPSC often tests the organisation behind an index, protocol or report, and the difference between binding treaties and voluntary standards.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q56.
ocr: What is ‘Greenhouse Gas Protocol’? fa} It is an international accounting tool for government and business leaders to understand, quantify and Manage greenhouse gas emissions (b) It is an initiative of the United Nations to offer financial incentives to developing countrics to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and to adopt eco-friendly technologies fc) It is an _ inter-governmental agreement ratified by all the member countries of the United Nations to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to specified levels by the year 2022 {d) It is one of the multilateral RED))+ initiatives hosted by the World Bank
subject: Environment
detail: The FSDC was set up by the Government of India in December 2010 through an executive decision, not a statute, to strengthen and institutionalise financial stability and inter-regulatory coordination. The idea came from the Raghuram Rajan Committee on Financial Sector Reforms (2008) and was announced in the 2010-11 Budget. It replaced the older High Level Coordination Committee on Financial Markets (HLCCFM). The Finance Minister chairs it. Members include the heads of RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and PFRDA, plus the Finance Secretary, Secretary of the Department of Economic Affairs (DEA), Secretary of the Department of Financial Services and the Chief Economic Adviser. The FMC was a member until its 2015 merger with SEBI. A sub-committee headed by the RBI Governor does the working-level coordination. Its mandate covers financial stability, financial sector development, inter-regulatory coordination, financial literacy, financial inclusion and macroprudential supervision, including the functioning of large financial conglomerates. Elimination logic: NITI Aayog was created in January 2015 as a policy think-tank, while FSDC dates from 2010 and sits in the Finance Ministry. Statement 1 is therefore wrong, which removes options (a) and (d). Statement 3 is correct, which removes (a) and leaves (c) over (b).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false because FSDC is not part of NITI Aayog, and it omits the correct statement 3.
Wrong: statement 3 is correct, and 'only' excludes it. Statement 3 is the Council's core macroprudential monitoring role.
Right: statements 2 and 3 are both true. The Finance Minister heads FSDC, and it monitors macroprudential supervision and financial stability.
Wrong: it includes statement 1, so 'all three' cannot be correct.
keyfact: FSDC (Dec 2010): non-statutory, chaired by the Finance Minister, does macroprudential monitoring, and is not part of NITI Aayog.
related: FSDC was set up in December 2010 and is non-statutory.
FSDC is chaired by the Union Finance Minister; the sub-committee is chaired by the RBI Governor.
The Raghuram Rajan Committee (2008) recommended FSDC; the FSLRC (Justice Srikrishna) recommended a statutory framework.
RBI releases the Financial Stability Report twice a year, in June and December.
NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015.
The Financial Stability Board (FSB) was set up in 2009 by the G20 and is based in Basel.
FSDC's secretariat is in the Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance.
India's D-SIBs are SBI, HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: FSDC is not an organ of NITI Aayog; it was set up in 2010 under the Ministry of Finance, five years before NITI Aayog existed. NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015 as the government's policy think-tank, with the Prime Minister as chairperson, a Governing Council of Chief Ministers, and a CEO. It has no regulatory or financial supervisory role. FSDC's secretariat works in the Department of Economic Affairs, so the two bodies are institutionally separate. The Planning Commission had existed since 1950.

2 — Correct: The Union Finance Minister heads the FSDC. Its members are the heads of financial sector regulators (RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA) and senior Finance Ministry officials, namely the Finance Secretary, the Secretary of the Department of Economic Affairs, the Secretary of the Department of Financial Services and the Chief Economic Adviser. The Council can invite experts to its meetings. A sub-committee headed by the RBI Governor handles day-to-day coordination. FSDC is non-statutory, with no dedicated fund. The Finance Minister's chairing role gives it political weight in resolving regulatory overlaps.

3 — Correct: Macroprudential supervision of the economy is one of FSDC's core functions. This includes monitoring the functioning of large financial conglomerates, assessing systemic risks and financial stability, and coordinating among regulators. It also spurs financial sector development, financial inclusion and financial literacy, and coordinates India's international financial-sector interface. The idea followed lessons from the 2008 global financial crisis. RBI's half-yearly Financial Stability Report (June and December) reflects the FSDC sub-committee's assessment of systemic risk. Microprudential supervision of individual institutions remains with the sector regulators.
summary: The answer is (c), 2 and 3 only. The Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC) is chaired by the Union Finance Minister and monitors macroprudential supervision of the economy. It is not an organ of NITI Aayog. It is an apex inter-regulatory body under the Ministry of Finance.
topic_notes: FSDC is the apex forum for financial stability in India. It was set up by executive order in December 2010 after the global financial crisis exposed gaps in regulatory coordination. The Raghuram Rajan Committee (2008) proposed it, and the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission (FSLRC, chaired by Justice B.N. Srikrishna, 2013) suggested giving it statutory form and creating a Financial Stability Board of India. This has not happened, so FSDC remains non-statutory. It replaced the HLCCFM, which the RBI Governor chaired. The Finance Minister chairs FSDC, while the sub-committee is chaired by the RBI Governor. Members are the heads of RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA and the Finance Ministry's department secretaries. The Chief Economic Adviser is also a member. The FMC was a member until it merged with SEBI in 2015. Functions are financial stability, inter-regulatory coordination, financial sector development, financial literacy, financial inclusion, macroprudential supervision and the monitoring of large financial conglomerates. Its secretariat sits in the Department of Economic Affairs. The Financial Stability Report is published by RBI twice a year, in June and December. Related bodies and ideas include the Financial Stability Board (FSB, G20, Basel, set up in 2009), the Joint Forum, the Financial Action Task Force, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India, and the Banking Regulation Act. Other angles UPSC could ask are the distinction between micro- and macroprudential regulation, systemically important banks (D-SIBs: SBI, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank), and the difference between statutory, non-statutory and constitutional bodies. Also note that NITI Aayog (2015) is a non-statutory think-tank and not a financial regulator.

ocr: With reference to ‘Agenda 21’, sometimes seen in the news, consider the following statements : 1. It is a global action plan for sustainable development. 2. It originated in the World Summit on Sustainable Development held in Johannesburg in 2002. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? fa} 1 only ‘(bj 2 only {c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Agenda 21 is a non-binding, voluntary action plan of the United Nations for sustainable development. It was adopted at the UN Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED), popularly called the Earth Summit, held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in June 1992. The '21' refers to the 21st century. It has 40 chapters in four sections (social and economic dimensions, conservation and management of resources, strengthening the role of major groups, and means of implementation). It urges governments, the UN system and major groups to act at global, national and local levels on poverty, consumption patterns, health, human settlements, oceans, forests, biodiversity and freshwater. Local Agenda 21 encourages local authorities to prepare community-level plans. The Rio Summit also produced the Rio Declaration on Environment and Development, the Forest Principles, the UNFCCC and the Convention on Biological Diversity. The Commission on Sustainable Development was set up to monitor implementation. The World Summit on Sustainable Development (Rio+10) at Johannesburg in 2002 produced the Johannesburg Plan of Implementation, which reaffirmed Agenda 21 rather than creating it. Rio+20 (2012) produced 'The Future We Want', and the 2030 Agenda with the SDGs followed in 2015. Elimination logic: statement 1 is clearly true, so (b) and (d) go; statement 2 has the wrong city and year, so (c) goes, leaving (a).
explanations: Correct: statement 1 is true and statement 2 is false because the origin was Rio 1992, so only statement 1 is correct.
Wrong: this would make statement 2 the only correct one, but Johannesburg 2002 did not originate Agenda 21, and statement 1 is true.
Wrong: statement 2 is incorrect, since Agenda 21 came from the 1992 Rio Earth Summit, so 'both' cannot hold.
Wrong: statement 1 is correct, since Agenda 21 is indeed a global action plan for sustainable development.
keyfact: Agenda 21 = non-binding UN sustainable development action plan from the Rio Earth Summit, 1992 (Johannesburg 2002 only reaffirmed it).
statements: 1 — Correct: Agenda 21 is a global, non-binding action plan for sustainable development adopted by the UN.
2 — Incorrect: it originated at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, not the 2002 Johannesburg summit, which only reaffirmed it.
summary: The answer is (a): statement 1 is correct and statement 2 is incorrect. Agenda 21 is a global action plan for sustainable development, but it originated at the UN Conference on Environment and Development (Earth Summit) in Rio de Janeiro in 1992, not at the 2002 Johannesburg summit.

question: Satya Shodhak Samaj organized
options: a movement for upliftment of tribals in Bihar
subject: Economy
detail: Satya Shodhak Samaj (Society of Truth-Seekers) was founded on 24 September 1873 in Pune by Jyotirao Govindrao Phule, a Mali by caste, with the aim of securing social justice and equal rights for Shudras, Ati-Shudras (Dalits), and women. It rejected the authority of the Vedas and Brahmin priests as intermediaries, promoted rationalism, and encouraged simple marriages without Brahmin priests. Phule's major works include Gulamgiri (1873), Shetkarayacha Asud (Cultivator's Whipcord, 1881) and Sarvajanik Satyadharma Pustak. He and Savitribai Phule opened the first school for girls in Pune in 1848 and a home for widows and a care centre for infanticide prevention. Later leaders include Shahu Maharaj of Kolhapur, who patronised the non-Brahmin movement, and Bhaskarrao Jadhav, Keshavrao Jedhe. The movement influenced Dr B.R. Ambedkar, who acknowledged Phule as one of his three gurus. Elimination: the Samaj's base was Maharashtra, so Bihar tribals (Birsa Munda's Ulgulan was in Jharkhand region), Gujarat temple entry and Punjab peasant movements (Pagri Sambhal Jatta, Kuka movement) are unrelated. Only (c) fits.
explanations: (a) Wrong: Tribal movements in Bihar/Chhotanagpur were led by figures such as Birsa Munda, the Santhal Hul, not by the Satya Shodhak Samaj.
(b) Wrong: Temple-entry movements were associated with Kerala (Vaikom Satyagraha 1924) and Maharashtra (Kalaram Temple, Nashik, by Ambedkar), not a Gujarat movement of this Samaj.
(c) Correct: Founded by Jyotirao Phule in Pune in 1873, it was an anti-caste, anti-Brahmanical movement in Maharashtra.
(d) Wrong: Punjab peasant agitations such as Pagri Sambhal Jatta (1907) and the Kisan Sabha movements were unrelated to the Samaj.
keyfact: Satya Shodhak Samaj = Jyotirao Phule, Pune, 1873, anti-caste movement in Maharashtra.
summary: The answer is (c): Satya Shodhak Samaj was an anti-caste movement in Maharashtra. It was founded by Jyotirao Phule in 1873 at Pune to fight Brahmanical dominance and caste discrimination and to uplift the lower castes, Dalits and women.

question: Which of the following statements is/are correct? Viruses can infect 1. bacteria 2. fungi 3. plants ~*~" "Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Viruses are acellular, obligate intracellular parasites. They have a nucleic acid genome (DNA or RNA) enclosed in a protein coat (capsid), sometimes with a lipid envelope, and they replicate only inside living host cells. Host range is determined by receptor and cellular machinery compatibility, and viruses exist for every cellular life form: animals, plants, fungi, protists, bacteria and archaea. Bacteriophages (such as T4, lambda and M13) infect bacteria; Félix d'Hérelle and Frederick Twort are credited with their discovery (1915-1917). Mycoviruses (fungal viruses) infect fungi such as Saccharomyces, Penicillium and Cryphonectria parasitica, and are often latent. Plant viruses, such as Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV), the first virus discovered (Ivanovsky 1892, Beijerinck 1898, Stanley crystallised it in 1935), infect plants, usually through insect vectors or mechanical injury. Elimination logic: since all three statements are true, any option that leaves out one of them (a, b, c) is wrong, and only (d) includes all three. A student who knows just one fact, for example that phages infect bacteria, can still eliminate (b), and then recall of mycoviruses or plant viruses settles the choice.
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out plants. Plant viruses such as TMV are well established.
Wrong: it leaves out bacteria and fungi. Bacteriophages and mycoviruses are real, so viruses are not restricted to plants.
Wrong: it leaves out fungi. Mycoviruses infect fungi, so statement 2 is also correct.
Correct: bacteria (bacteriophages), fungi (mycoviruses) and plants (plant viruses such as TMV) can all be infected by viruses.
keyfact: Viruses infect all life forms: bacteria (bacteriophages), fungi (mycoviruses), plants (e.g. TMV), animals, protists and archaea.
option_notes: Option (a), bacteria and fungi only, is a partial answer. It covers bacteriophages and mycoviruses, which are real, but excludes plant viruses. Bacteriophages are viruses with a head and tail structure, as in T4 phage. Mycoviruses are mostly dsRNA viruses of fungi, often symptomless. The option is wrong because plants are also hosts of numerous viruses such as TMV and the Cauliflower Mosaic Virus.

Option (b), plants only, reflects the common notion that viruses are agents of plant and animal disease. Plant viruses such as TMV, Potato Virus Y, Tomato Leaf Curl Virus and Banana Bunchy Top Virus cause major crop losses, and many are spread by aphids and whiteflies. The option is wrong because bacteria and fungi also have their own viruses.

Option (c), bacteria and plants only, is also partial. Bacteriophages and plant viruses are the better-known groups, and this is the trap for students unaware of fungal viruses. Mycoviruses, mostly dsRNA, were discovered in mushrooms in the 1960s and infect yeasts and filamentous fungi. Excluding fungi makes the option wrong.

Option (d), 1, 2 and 3, is correct. It reflects that viruses are obligate intracellular parasites with host-specific forms across all cellular life: bacteriophages for bacteria, mycoviruses for fungi, plant viruses for plants, and others for animals, protists and archaea. Giant viruses such as Mimivirus infect amoebae. Some archaeal viruses withstand extreme heat and acidity.
related: Bacteriophages infect bacteria; discovered by Twort (1915) and d'Hérelle (1917).
TMV was the first virus discovered and the first crystallised (Stanley, 1935).
Mycoviruses infect fungi and are mostly dsRNA viruses.
Viroids are naked infectious RNA molecules found in plants (T.O. Diener, 1971).
Prions are infectious proteins causing BSE and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
Retroviruses such as HIV use reverse transcriptase to make DNA from RNA.
Antibiotics do not work against viruses; vaccines and antivirals are used.
Smallpox was declared eradicated by WHO in 1980.
statements: 1 — Correct: Viruses that infect bacteria are called bacteriophages. Phages were discovered by Frederick Twort (1915) and Félix d'Hérelle (1917), who coined the name. They have lytic and lysogenic cycles; T4 is a classic lytic phage and lambda a temperate one. Transduction, the transfer of bacterial genes by phages, is a method of horizontal gene transfer. Phage therapy is being revived against antibiotic-resistant bacteria, and phages were used in the Hershey-Chase experiment (1952), which showed DNA is the genetic material.

2 — Correct: Fungal viruses are called mycoviruses. They were first noticed in the 1960s in cultivated mushrooms (Agaricus bisporus), where a disease called La France disease was linked to them. Most have dsRNA genomes and spread through spores or hyphal fusion, not through extracellular transmission. Many cause no visible symptoms. Some cause hypovirulence, as in Cryphonectria parasitica (chestnut blight), which makes them potential biocontrol agents. The yeast killer toxin system in Saccharomyces is also encoded by dsRNA viruses.

3 — Correct: Plant viruses cause diseases such as mosaics, leaf curl and yellowing. Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV) was the first virus discovered: Dmitri Ivanovsky (1892) and Martinus Beijerinck (1898) studied it, and Wendell Stanley crystallised it (1935). Most plant viruses have ssRNA genomes. They enter through wounds and are spread by vectors such as aphids and whiteflies, and also by nematodes and fungi. Other examples are Cauliflower Mosaic Virus (a DNA virus), Potato Virus X, Banana Bunchy Top Virus, and Tomato Leaf Curl Virus. Viroids are even smaller infectious RNAs that infect plants.
summary: The answer is (d): viruses can infect bacteria, fungi and plants. Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites, and there are specific viruses (bacteriophages, mycoviruses, plant viruses) for each of these host groups.
topic_notes: Viruses are non-cellular entities on the border of living and non-living. They have either DNA or RNA (never both) as genetic material, a protein capsid made of capsomeres, and sometimes an envelope. They lack ribosomes and metabolism, so they cannot reproduce outside a host. Replication proceeds by attachment, entry, synthesis of components, assembly and release. Bacteriophages follow lytic cycles (host cell bursts) or lysogenic cycles (the genome integrates as a prophage). Classification is by host (animal, plant, bacterial, fungal), genome type (Baltimore classification) and shape (helical, icosahedral, complex). History: Ivanovsky (1892) showed that the TMV agent passed through bacterial filters; Beijerinck (1898) called it contagium vivum fluidum; Stanley crystallised TMV (1935, Nobel 1946); Twort and d'Hérelle discovered phages. Examples of human diseases: HIV (retrovirus, RNA), influenza, SARS-CoV-2, dengue, Zika, hepatitis, polio, rabies, measles, smallpox (eradicated 1980) and HPV. Retroviruses use reverse transcriptase (Temin and Baltimore, 1970). Viroids (Diener, 1971) are naked RNA that infect plants, and prions are infectious proteins that cause diseases such as mad cow disease (BSE) and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Antibiotics do not act on viruses; antivirals (acyclovir, oseltamivir) and vaccines are used instead. Interferons are proteins produced by host cells in response to viral infection. Applications: phages as biocontrol and therapy, viral vectors in gene therapy and vaccines, and baculoviruses as biopesticides.

ocr: The term ‘Base Erosion and Profit Shifting’ is sometimes seen in the news in the context of (a) mining operation by multinational companies in resource-rich but backward areas (b) curbing of the tax evasion by multinational companies {c} exploitation of genetic resources of a country by multinational companies (ad) lack of consideration of environmental costs in the planning and implementation of developmental projects
subject: Economy
detail: BEPS describes strategies used mainly by multinational enterprises (MNEs) to shift taxable profits from the countries where real economic activity occurs to low-tax or no-tax jurisdictions (tax havens), eroding the tax base of the countries concerned. Techniques include transfer mispricing, treaty shopping, excessive interest deductions, intra-group royalties and artificial avoidance of permanent establishment status. The OECD, at the request of the G20, launched the BEPS Project in 2013 and released a 15-point Action Plan in 2013, with final reports in October 2015 (endorsed by the G20 at Antalya, November 2015). Key actions include addressing the digital economy (Action 1), hybrid mismatches (2), harmful tax practices (5), treaty abuse (6), transfer pricing (8-10) and country-by-country reporting (13). The Multilateral Instrument (MLI), signed in 2017, implements treaty-related measures; India is a party. Later, a two-pillar solution (2021) set a 15% global minimum corporate tax. Elimination logic: the term includes 'tax' concepts (base, profit), which immediately rules out options about mining, genetic resources or environmental costs. These relate to resource extraction, biopiracy/Nagoya Protocol and EIA respectively.
explanations: Incorrect: Mining by MNCs in resource-rich backward areas concerns resource exploitation and land and tribal rights, not tax base erosion or profit shifting.
Correct: BEPS is about MNCs shifting profits to low-tax jurisdictions to avoid taxes; the OECD/G20 BEPS project seeks to curb this evasion and avoidance.
Incorrect: Exploitation of genetic resources is biopiracy, dealt with by the CBD and the Nagoya Protocol on access and benefit sharing, not BEPS.
Incorrect: Lack of consideration of environmental costs relates to environmental impact assessment and sustainable development planning, not taxation.
keyfact: BEPS = MNCs shifting profits to low-tax havens to erode the tax base; the OECD/G20 BEPS project (15 actions, 2015) tackles it.
summary: The correct answer is (b): curbing of tax evasion by multinational companies. Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) refers to tax planning strategies that exploit gaps and mismatches in tax rules to artificially shift profits to low or no-tax locations, and the OECD/G20 BEPS project aims to curb this.

ocr: Recently, India’s first ‘National Investment and Manufacturing Zone’ was proposed to be set up in fa) Andhra Pradesh {b) Gujarat (c) Maharashtra {d) Uttar Pradesh
subject: Economy
detail: NIMZs were introduced by the National Manufacturing Policy (NMP), 2011, issued by the Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion (DIPP), Ministry of Commerce and Industry. The goals were to raise the share of manufacturing in GDP to 25% and create 100 million jobs within a decade. NIMZs are large integrated industrial townships with a minimum area of 5,000 hectares, with developed land, world-class infrastructure, and green technologies. They also offer simplified regulatory procedures, exemptions from some labour and environmental inspections, and a skilled workforce. They are meant to be developed by State governments or through PPP. Under the policy, the Centre helps with funding for external infrastructure linkages. The first NIMZ was proposed at Prakasam district in Andhra Pradesh (the Kanigiri area), and later NIMZs were cleared in places like Chittoor, Medak (Zaheerabad, Telangana), Nagpur (Maharashtra), Kalinganagar and others. Elimination logic: Gujarat is known for SIRs and the DMIC, Maharashtra for Dighi port and Aurangabad-Shendra, and UP for the Delhi-Mumbai corridor and the Dadri area, so these are tempting distractors. The specific association of the 'first' NIMZ with Andhra Pradesh and Prakasam is a recall fact from the 2016 news.
explanations: Correct: The first NIMZ under the National Manufacturing Policy was proposed at Prakasam district in Andhra Pradesh, which matches the official answer.
Incorrect: Gujarat has Special Investment Regions and DMIC nodes such as Dholera, but the first NIMZ was not proposed there.
Incorrect: Maharashtra has NIMZ proposals such as Nagpur (Dighi), but these came later and were not the first.
Incorrect: Uttar Pradesh is part of the Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor region, but the first NIMZ was not proposed there.
keyfact: National Manufacturing Policy 2011 created NIMZs (minimum 5,000 ha); the first was proposed at Prakasam, Andhra Pradesh.
summary: The answer is (a) Andhra Pradesh. India's first National Investment and Manufacturing Zone (NIMZ) under the National Manufacturing Policy 2011 was proposed at Prakasam district in Andhra Pradesh.

ocr: What is/are the purpose/purposes of ‘District Mineral Foundations’ in India? 1. Promoting mineral exploration activities in mineral-rich districts 2. Protecting the interests of the persons affected by mining operations 3. Authorizing State ‘Governments to issue licences for mineral exploration “Select the correct answer using the code given below. (a) 1 and 2 only {b) 2 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d@) 1, 2 and 3
subject: Geography
detail: District Mineral Foundations were created by the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2015, which inserted Section 9B into the MMDR Act, 1957. Each State government must set up a DMF as a non-profit statutory body or trust in every district affected by mining-related operations. Its objective is to work for the interest and benefit of persons and areas affected by mining. Holders of mining leases contribute to it: 30% of royalty for leases granted on or after 12 January 2015 (via the Second Schedule), and for earlier leases a rate of up to one-third of royalty. The Pradhan Mantri Khanij Kshetra Kalyan Yojana (PMKKKY), launched in 2015, directs DMF funds towards drinking water, health, education, welfare of women and children, skill development and environment preservation. High-priority areas get at least 60% of funds. The foundation's governance is set by State governments. Elimination logic: DMFs are welfare and rehabilitation bodies, not regulators or promoters. Exploration promotion is the role of the Geological Survey of India, the Ministry of Mines and the National Mineral Exploration Trust (NMET). Licensing and grant of mining and exploration rights is done by State governments under the MMDR Act and the Mineral Concession Rules. Statements 1 and 3 are therefore incorrect, leaving (b).
explanations: (a) Wrong: it includes statement 1, but DMFs do not promote mineral exploration.
(b) Right: only statement 2 is correct, as DMFs exist for the welfare of people and areas affected by mining.
(c) Wrong: both statements 1 and 3 are incorrect, since DMFs neither promote exploration nor authorise licences.
(d) Wrong: it includes statements 1 and 3, which describe functions DMFs do not perform.
keyfact: DMF (Sec 9B, MMDR Act as amended in 2015) is a non-profit trust in mining districts for the benefit of mining-affected people and areas, funded by lessee contributions and used under PMKKKY.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Promoting exploration is not a DMF function; it is handled by the GSI, the Ministry of Mines and NMET (National Mineral Exploration Trust).
2 — Correct: Section 9B of the MMDR Act, 1957 establishes DMFs to work for the interest and benefit of persons and areas affected by mining operations.
3 — Incorrect: DMFs have no licensing power; State governments grant mineral concessions under the MMDR Act and the rules made under it, independent of DMFs.
summary: The correct answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. District Mineral Foundations (DMFs) are non-profit trusts set up in mining-affected districts to work for the interest and benefit of persons and areas affected by mining operations. They do not promote exploration and do not authorise licences.

question: SWAYAM’, an_ initiative of the Government of India, aims at
options: promoting the Self Help Groups in rural areas
providing financial and technical assistance to young start-up entrepreneurs
promoting the education and health of adolescent girls
) providing affordable and quality education to the citizens for free
subject: Economy
detail: SWAYAM (Study Webs of Active-Learning for Young Aspiring Minds) was launched by the Ministry of Human Resource Development (now Ministry of Education) in 2017 as a national MOOC platform. Its aim is to bridge the digital divide and take the three cardinal principles of education policy, access, equity and quality, to every citizen, including students outside the formal system and those from disadvantaged sections. Courses run from Class 9 to post-graduation and are delivered through interactive video lectures, reading material, quizzes and discussion forums. They are prepared by national coordinators such as UGC, AICTE, NCERT, NIOS, IGNOU, IIMB and the IITs, and are free to study, with an optional fee for certification. Related initiatives to remember are SWAYAM Prabha (DTH educational channels), the National Digital Library and the National Academic Depository. Elimination logic: Self Help Groups in rural areas relate to the National Rural Livelihood Mission (DAY-NRLM). Financial and technical help for start-ups relates to Start-up India, Stand-Up India or MUDRA. Adolescent girls' health and education relates to schemes such as SABLA or Kishori Shakti. Only option (d) concerns education delivery.
explanations: Incorrect: Promotion of Self Help Groups in rural areas is the work of DAY-NRLM, not SWAYAM, which is an education platform.
Incorrect: Financial and technical assistance for start-up entrepreneurs falls under Start-up India, Stand-Up India or MUDRA, not SWAYAM.
Incorrect: Education and health of adolescent girls is addressed by schemes like SABLA and Kishori Shakti. SWAYAM serves all learners, not only adolescent girls, and does not address health.
Correct: SWAYAM is a MOOC platform offering affordable, quality education to all citizens, free to learn, with an optional fee only for certification exams.
keyfact: SWAYAM = national MOOC platform of MHRD/Ministry of Education (2017) giving free, quality online courses from Class 9 to postgraduate level.
summary: The answer is (d). SWAYAM is a Government of India platform for Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) that gives citizens access to quality higher and school-level education, free of cost for learning, with a fee only if the learner wants a certificate through proctored exams.

ocr: The Montague-Chelmsford Proposals were related to fa) social reforms {b) educational reforms (c) reforms in police administration {d) constitutional reforms . What is/are common to the two historical places known as Ajanta’ and Mahabalipuram? 1. Both were built in the same period. 2. Both belong to the same religious denomination. 3. Both have rock-cut monuments. Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa) 1 and 2 only (b) 3 only (c} 1 and 3 only {d) None of the statements given above is correct
subject: Polity
detail: The Montagu-Chelmsford Report (July 1918) was prepared by Edwin Montagu, Secretary of State for India, and Lord Chelmsford, the Viceroy. It followed Montagu's August 1917 Declaration, which promised 'gradual development of self-governing institutions' and 'progressive realisation of responsible government' in India. The report led to the Government of India Act, 1919, which was in force from 1921 to 1937. Its key features were: dyarchy in the provinces, with subjects divided into Reserved (Governor with his executive council) and Transferred (Indian ministers responsible to the legislature); a bicameral Central Legislature made up of the Council of State and the Legislative Assembly; separation of central and provincial subjects and of provincial budgets; an extended communal electorate (Sikhs, Anglo-Indians, Indian Christians); a High Commissioner for India in London; and the provision for a statutory commission after 10 years, which became the Simon Commission. Elimination logic: the proposals were about the structure of government and the distribution of power, not social, educational or police matters, so only (d) fits. Do not confuse them with the Morley-Minto Reforms (1909), which introduced separate electorates for Muslims.
explanations: Incorrect: The proposals did not concern social reform. Social reforms were handled by laws such as the Age of Consent Act or the Sarda Act.

Incorrect: Education was only one of the subjects transferred to provincial ministers under dyarchy. The proposals were not an educational reform scheme. The Hunter Commission (1882) and Sadler Commission (1917) dealt with education.
Incorrect: Police was a Reserved subject kept under the Governor, but the proposals did not aim at police administration reform. The Police Commission of 1902-03 (Fraser) dealt with that.
Correct: They proposed constitutional changes, namely dyarchy in the provinces, a bicameral Centre and an expanded franchise, which were enacted in the Government of India Act, 1919.
keyfact: Montagu-Chelmsford Report (1918) → Government of India Act 1919 → dyarchy in provinces and a bicameral Centre: constitutional reform.
summary: The correct answer is (d) constitutional reforms. The Montagu-Chelmsford Proposals (1918) were the basis of the Government of India Act, 1919, which introduced dyarchy in the provinces and a bicameral legislature at the Centre.

ocr: The Montague-Chelmsford Proposals were related to fa) social reforms {b) educational reforms (c) reforms in police administration {d) constitutional reforms . What is/are common to the two historical places known as Ajanta’ and Mahabalipuram? 1. Both were built in the same period. 2. Both belong to the same religious denomination. 3. Both have rock-cut monuments. Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa) 1 and 2 only (b) 3 only (c} 1 and 3 only {d) None of the statements given above is correct
subject: Polity
detail: Ajanta, near Aurangabad in Maharashtra, has about 30 Buddhist rock-cut caves (chaityas and viharas) excavated in two phases: the Satavahana phase (c. 2nd century BCE to 1st century CE, Hinayana) and the Vakataka phase (c. 5th to 6th century CE, Mahayana). It is famous for its mural paintings on Jataka themes. Mahabalipuram (Mamallapuram) in Tamil Nadu is a Pallava site of the 7th century CE, from the reigns of Mahendravarman I and Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla). It has rathas (monolithic Pancha Rathas), mandapas, the Descent of the Ganga (Arjuna's Penance) relief and the structural Shore Temple. These are mainly Hindu (Shaiva and Vaishnava). Both sites are UNESCO World Heritage Sites (Ajanta 1983, Mahabalipuram 1984). Elimination logic: the periods differ, which removes statement 1 and therefore options (a) and (c). The religions differ, which removes statement 2. Statement 3 is true, so only (b) survives. Option (d) fails because statement 3 is correct.
explanations: (a) Wrong: it includes statements 1 and 2, and both are false because the periods and religions differ.
(b) Right: only statement 3 is true, since both sites have rock-cut monuments.
(c) Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false because Ajanta is far older and spans a longer period than the 7th-century Pallava Mahabalipuram.
(d) Wrong: statement 3 is correct, so the claim that no statement is correct fails.
keyfact: Ajanta = Buddhist rock-cut caves (2nd century BCE to 6th century CE); Mahabalipuram = Pallava Hindu rock-cut rathas (7th century CE); only the rock-cut feature is common.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Ajanta spans roughly the 2nd century BCE to the 6th century CE, while Mahabalipuram's monuments are Pallava work of the 7th century CE, so they were not built in the same period.
2 — Incorrect: Ajanta is Buddhist, whereas Mahabalipuram's monuments are Hindu (Shaiva/Vaishnava), so they do not share a religious denomination.
3 — Correct: Ajanta has rock-cut caves and Mahabalipuram has rock-cut rathas, mandapas and relief panels, so both have rock-cut monuments.
summary: The answer is (b) 3 only. Ajanta (Buddhist rock-cut caves, c. 2nd century BCE to 5th/6th century CE) and Mahabalipuram (Pallava rock-cut and monolithic Hindu monuments, 7th century CE) share only the feature of rock-cut architecture. They differ in period and religion.

question:
With reference to Bitcoins’, sometimes seen in the news, which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. Bitcoins are tracked by the Central Banks of the countries.
2. Anyone with a Bitcoin address can send and receive Bitcoins from anyone else with a Bitcoin address.
3. Online payments can be sent without either side knowing the identity of the other. 24 B—APM-P-CKB/65A4 Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Economy
detail: Bitcoin was introduced in 2008-09 by the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto. It is a decentralised digital currency that runs on a peer-to-peer network and records transactions on a public ledger called the blockchain. Miners validate transactions through proof-of-work. The supply is capped at 21 million coins. No government, central bank or other authority issues, controls or tracks Bitcoin, so statement 1 fails. Anyone who holds a Bitcoin address (a public key hash) with a wallet can send and receive Bitcoin to or from any other address, so statement 2 is correct. Transactions are pseudonymous: the ledger shows addresses, not real names. The two parties therefore need not know each other's identity, so statement 3 is correct. This is also why regulators worry about money laundering and illicit use. The RBI has cautioned the public about virtual currencies, and the 2022 Indian tax regime taxes gains from virtual digital assets, but India does not treat Bitcoin as legal tender. Elimination: rejecting statement 1 removes (a) and (d). Statement 2 is correct, so (c) falls, which leaves (b).
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes statement 1, and central banks do not track Bitcoin.
(b) is right because statements 2 and 3 are correct and statement 1 is not.
(c) is wrong because it leaves out statement 2, which is correct: any address can send to and receive from any other.
(d) is wrong because it includes statement 1, which is false.
keyfact: Bitcoin is a decentralised, pseudonymous peer-to-peer cryptocurrency on a blockchain, with no central bank control or tracking and a cap of 21 million coins.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Bitcoin is decentralised and not issued, regulated or tracked by any central bank; the blockchain is maintained by the network.
2 — Correct: Any holder of a Bitcoin address can transact peer-to-peer with any other address without an intermediary.
3 — Correct: Transactions are pseudonymous, showing only addresses, so payments can be made without either party knowing the other's real identity.
summary: The correct answer is (b): statements 2 and 3 are correct, and statement 1 is wrong. Bitcoin is a decentralised, peer-to-peer cryptocurrency that no central bank issues or tracks, and its users are pseudonymous.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. New Development Bank has been set up by APEC.
2. The headquarters of New Development Bank is in Shanghai. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Economy
detail: The New Development Bank (NDB), initially called the BRICS Development Bank, was agreed at the 6th BRICS Summit in Fortaleza, Brazil (July 2014), where the Agreement on the NDB was signed by Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa. It came into force in 2015, and the bank began operations with its headquarters in Shanghai. The first President was K. V. Kamath of India, and presidency rotates among the founding members. Its initial authorised capital was US$100 billion, with initial subscribed capital of US$50 billion shared equally by the five founders. The bank funds infrastructure and sustainable development projects in BRICS and other emerging economies and developing countries. It is distinct from the Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA), a separate BRICS financial safety net of US$100 billion. APEC (Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, founded 1989) is a regional economic forum for trade and investment cooperation and has no role in creating the NDB, so statement 1 is wrong. Statement 2 is correct because Shanghai is the headquarters. Elimination: once statement 1 is rejected, only (b) and (d) remain, and knowing the Shanghai location settles it as (b). The NDB also has a regional office in Johannesburg, South Africa.
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is false (APEC did not set up the NDB) and statement 2 is true, so '1 only' cannot be correct.
(b) is correct because statement 2 is true (headquarters in Shanghai) and statement 1 is false (it was set up by BRICS).
(c) is wrong because statement 1 is false; the NDB is a BRICS institution, not an APEC one.
(d) is wrong because statement 2 is true, as the NDB's headquarters is in Shanghai.
keyfact: NDB = BRICS bank (Fortaleza Summit 2014), headquartered in Shanghai, $100 bn authorised capital, first president K. V. Kamath; APEC has no role.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The NDB was established by the BRICS nations (Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa), not by APEC.
2 — Correct: The NDB's headquarters is in Shanghai, China.
summary: The correct answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. The New Development Bank was set up by the BRICS countries, not APEC, and its headquarters is in Shanghai, China.
