ocr: ‘Gadgil Committee Report’ and ‘Kasturirangan Committee Report’, sometimes scen in the news, are related to fa) constitutional reforms (b) Ganga Action Plan (c) linking of rivers (a) protection of Western Ghats
subject: Economy
detail: The Western Ghats, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2012 and one of the world's biodiversity hotspots, run through Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu. In 2010 the MoEF constituted the Western Ghats Ecology Expert Panel (WGEEP) under Madhav Gadgil. Its 2011 report proposed classifying the whole Western Ghats as an Ecologically Sensitive Area (ESA) with three graded zones (ESZ 1, 2 and 3), restrictions on mining, quarrying, thermal plants and large dams, and a bottom-up, community-involved governance model through a Western Ghats Ecology Authority. States objected that the report was too restrictive on development. The MoEF then formed a High-Level Working Group (HLWG) under K. Kasturirangan, which reported in 2013. It recommended that only about 37% of the Western Ghats (roughly 60,000 sq km) be declared ESA, with a ban on mining, quarrying and sand mining, no new thermal power plants, a ban on polluting 'Red category' industries, and restrictions on building and township projects. Elimination: constitutional reforms are handled by bodies like the Sarkaria or Venkatachaliah commissions; the Ganga Action Plan (1985) and river-linking (National Perspective Plan, NWDA) are unrelated to either committee. Remember that both reports are about ecology and the Western Ghats.
explanations: Incorrect: Constitutional reforms were examined by bodies such as the Sarkaria Commission, the Punchhi Commission and the Venkatachaliah Commission (NCRWC), not by Gadgil or Kasturirangan.
Incorrect: The Ganga Action Plan, launched in 1985, was an executive pollution-control programme and is not linked to either committee.
Incorrect: River linking is associated with the National Water Development Agency and the National Perspective Plan, not with these environmental committees.

Correct: Both committees dealt with the conservation and the ecologically sensitive area demarcation of the Western Ghats. The Gadgil report (2011) was the WGEEP, and the Kasturirangan report (2013) was the HLWG.
keyfact: Gadgil (WGEEP, 2011) wanted the whole Western Ghats as ESA; Kasturirangan (HLWG, 2013) cut this to about 37%, and both were about Western Ghats protection.
summary: The answer is (d) protection of the Western Ghats. The Gadgil Committee (2011) and the Kasturirangan Committee (2013) were both set up by the Ministry of Environment and Forests to recommend how to conserve and manage the ecologically sensitive Western Ghats.

ocr: Consider the following : 1. Calcutta Unitarian Committee 2. ‘Tabernacle of New Dispensation 3. Indian Reform Association Keshab Chandra Sen is associated with the establishment of which of ‘the above? fa) 1 and 3 only (b}) 2 and 3 only (c) 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Keshab Chandra Sen (1838-84) joined the Brahmo Samaj in 1857 and was made Acharya by Debendranath Tagore. His radical stance on caste, the sacred thread and inter-caste marriage led to the 1866 split: Sen's Brahmo Samaj of India, and Debendranath's Adi Brahmo Samaj. In 1870 he founded the Indian Reform Association, which had five sections: cheap literature, education, women's improvement, temperance, and charity. It also led to the Indian Mirror and to Sulabh Samachar, a penny newspaper. He campaigned for the Native Marriage Act (Civil Marriage Act) of 1872, which set the minimum marriage age at 18 for boys and 14 for girls. After his daughter's marriage to the Maharaja of Cooch Behar in 1878 broke his own principles, his followers split again and formed the Sadharan Brahmo Samaj. In 1881 Sen announced the Church of the New Dispensation (Nava Vidhan), at the Tabernacle, with a syncretic message. Elimination: statement 1 belongs to Rammohan Roy's era (1821), so any option with 1 is wrong. Options (a) and (d) are eliminated, and (c) is incomplete, which leaves (b).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 1, and the Calcutta Unitarian Committee is not Sen's creation. It was set up by Rammohan Roy and William Adam in 1821.
Correct: Sen founded the Tabernacle of New Dispensation (1881) and the Indian Reform Association (1870), and had no role in the Unitarian Committee.
Wrong: it is incomplete, because it leaves out the Tabernacle of New Dispensation, which Sen definitely founded in 1881.
Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is not associated with Sen but with Rammohan Roy and Adam.
keyfact: Keshab Chandra Sen: Indian Reform Association (1870) + Tabernacle of New Dispensation (1881); the Unitarian Committee (1821) was Rammohan Roy's.
option_notes: Options (a)-(d) here are combinations of numbered statements, so the notes follow the statements.

The combination 2 and 3 corresponds to the Nava Vidhan Tabernacle (1881) and the Indian Reform Association (1870), both Sen's creations. The Indian Reform Association worked for women's improvement, education, cheap literature, temperance and charity. The Nava Vidhan was a church of religious synthesis. Sen also set up the Brahmo Samaj of India (1866) and the Bharat Ashram (1872).

The combination 3 only would correctly include the Indian Reform Association (1870) and ignore the Tabernacle. The Indian Reform Association had five sections and led to the Native Marriage Act, 1872.
The combination 1, 2 and 3 is wrong because the Calcutta Unitarian Committee (1821) was formed by Rammohan Roy and William Adam long before Sen's activity.
related: Keshab Chandra Sen founded the Indian Reform Association in 1870.
Nava Vidhan (Church of New Dispensation) was proclaimed by Sen in 1881.
The Native Marriage Act 1872 was passed after Sen's campaign.
The Calcutta Unitarian Committee (1821) was founded by Rammohan Roy and William Adam.
Sadharan Brahmo Samaj was formed in 1878 after Sen's daughter's marriage with the Cooch Behar prince.
Prarthana Samaj (1867) in Bombay was inspired by Keshab Chandra Sen.
Sen's weekly Sulabh Samachar sold for one paisa.
Debendranath Tagore founded the Tattvabodhini Sabha in 1839.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Calcutta Unitarian Committee was formed in 1821 by Rammohan Roy with William Adam, not by Keshab Chandra Sen. Adam, a Baptist missionary, converted to Unitarianism and was called 'the second fallen Adam'. The Committee promoted Unitarian Christianity and pure monotheism. It was a precursor to the Brahmo Sabha of 1828, which became the Brahmo Samaj. Roy had also written 'The Precepts of Jesus' (1820), a book that stressed Christ's ethics over his miracles. Sen was born in 1838, so he could not have founded the Committee. It operated in Calcutta and was linked to the Unitarian Christians of Britain and America.

2 — Correct: The Tabernacle of New Dispensation (Nava Vidhan) was established by Keshab Chandra Sen in 1881, after the Brahmo split of 1878 over his daughter's underage marriage to the Maharaja of Cooch Behar. It was a church for a synthesis of religions: Hinduism, Christianity, Islam, Buddhism and others. Sen was influenced by Ramakrishna Paramahamsa, whom he met in 1875. The Nava Vidhan used a set of rituals, including homa and the 'pilgrimage to saints' idea. Sen held that he was working for a harmony of faiths. He died in 1884.

3 — Correct: The Indian Reform Association was founded by Keshab Chandra Sen in 1870 after his visit to England in 1870. It had five sections: Female Improvement, Education, Cheap Literature, Temperance, and Charity. It led to the Native Marriage Act, 1872, which legalised marriage in the Brahmo form and set the minimum marriage age at 18 for boys and 14 for girls. The weekly Sulabh Samachar sold at one paisa, and the Indian Mirror was another Sen publication. The Bamabodhini Patrika was a women's journal of the time.
summary: The answer is (b): Keshab Chandra Sen is associated with the Tabernacle of New Dispensation (Nava Vidhan, 1881) and the Indian Reform Association (1870). The Calcutta Unitarian Committee is linked to Raja Rammohan Roy and William Adam (1821), not to Sen.
topic_notes: Brahmo Samaj history. 1828: Rammohan Roy founded the Brahmo Sabha, renamed the Brahmo Samaj in 1830 on the opening of its Chitpur building. Roy campaigned against sati, which was banned in 1829 under Bentinck, and published Sambad Kaumudi and Mirat-ul-Akhbar. He received the title 'Raja' from the Mughal emperor Akbar II. He founded the Vedanta College in 1825 and the Atmiya Sabha in 1815. Debendranath Tagore founded the Tattvabodhini Sabha in 1839, with its journal Tattvabodhini Patrika (edited by Akshay Kumar Datta), and he revived the Brahmo Samaj in 1843. Keshab Chandra Sen joined in 1857. In 1866 the split came, with Sen's Brahmo Samaj of India. In 1878 came the second split, when the Sadharan Brahmo Samaj was formed by Ananda Mohan Bose, Sivanath Sastri and others. Sen's Nava Vidhan came in 1881. Other points: Prarthana Samaj (1867, Bombay) by Atmaram Pandurang, inspired by Sen, with M.G. Ranade and R.G. Bhandarkar as notable members. The Brahmo Marriage Act (Native Marriage Act) of 1872. Sen visited England in 1870 and met Queen Victoria and Max Muller. Related movements to compare include the Arya Samaj (1875, Dayananda Saraswati), Ramakrishna Mission (1897, Vivekananda), Theosophical Society (1875 New York, 1882 Adyar), the Satya Shodhak Samaj (1873, Jyotiba Phule), and the Servants of India Society (1905, Gokhale). Expect questions on who founded which body, on the dates of the Brahmo splits, and on the social legislation connected with these reformers.

ocr: Which of the following is not a member of ‘Gulf Cooperation Council’? (a) Iran (b) Saudi Arabia (c) Oman (ad) Kuwait
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Gulf Cooperation Council was founded on 25 May 1981 at a summit in Abu Dhabi. Its six founding and current members are Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain and Oman. The secretariat is in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The GCC was created mainly for political, security and economic coordination among the Arab Gulf monarchies, and its formation was shaped by the Iranian Revolution of 1979 and the Iran-Iraq War that began in 1980. This explains why Iran, a Persian and Shia-majority republic, was left out. Iraq and Yemen are Arab states in the neighbourhood but are also not members, and Yemen has long sought admission. The GCC has a joint military arm, the Peninsula Shield Force, and a customs union that began in 2003. Its member economies are major oil and gas exporters and are important for India's energy security and its large diaspora. For elimination, a student who knows that Saudi Arabia, Oman and Kuwait are all Arab monarchies on the Arabian Peninsula can rule out (b), (c) and (d), which leaves Iran.
explanations: Correct answer: Iran is not a GCC member. It is a non-Arab republic on the northern Gulf coast and has never belonged to the council.
Wrong option: Saudi Arabia is a founding member (1981) and hosts the GCC secretariat in Riyadh, so it is a member.
Wrong option: Oman is a founding member of the GCC from 1981, so it is a member.
Wrong option: Kuwait is a founding member of the GCC from 1981, so it is a member.
keyfact: GCC (1981, Abu Dhabi; HQ Riyadh) = Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, Oman; Iran, Iraq and Yemen are not members.
summary: The answer is (a) Iran. The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) is a six-member Arab monarchy bloc of the Persian Gulf, and Iran, though a major Gulf littoral state, has never been a member.

ocr: What is/are the purpose/purposes of Government’s ‘Sovereign Gold Bond Scheme’ and ‘Gold Monetization Scheme’? 1. To bring the idle gold lying with Indian households into the economy 2. To promote FDI in the gold and jewellery sector 3. To reduce India’s dependence on gold imports Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa) 1 only {b) 2 and 3 only {c) 1 and 3 only (a) 1,2 and 3
subject: Economy
detail: In November 2015 the Government of India launched two linked schemes to tackle India's large appetite for physical gold, which drives up imports and the current account deficit (CAD). India has some of the world's largest household and temple gold stocks, estimated at about 20,000+ tonnes, and most of it lies idle. The Gold Monetization Scheme (GMS) replaced the older Gold Deposit Scheme (1999) and Gold Metal Loan Scheme. Under it, households and institutions deposit gold with designated banks and earn interest on it, through Short (1-3 years), Medium (5-7 years) and Long (12-15 years) term deposits. The Sovereign Gold Bond Scheme (SGB) is issued by the RBI on behalf of the Government of India. The bonds are denominated in grams of gold, carry a fixed interest rate (2.75% initially, later 2.5%), and have an 8-year tenure with an exit option after year 5. They offer a paper-gold alternative to buying physical gold, which cuts demand for imports. Both schemes therefore serve statements 1 and 3. Neither has anything to do with foreign direct investment, so statement 2 is a distractor. Elimination logic: once statement 2 is rejected, only option (c) remains.
explanations: (a) Wrong: Statement 1 is correct, but the answer is incomplete because statement 3 is also correct.
(b) Wrong: It includes statement 2, which is incorrect, and omits statement 1, which is correct.
(c) Right: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The schemes mobilise idle gold and reduce import dependence, and neither aims at FDI.
(d) Wrong: It includes statement 2, and the schemes have no FDI-promotion objective.
keyfact: GMS and SGB (Nov 2015) mobilise idle household gold and curb physical gold imports; the SGB is issued by the RBI, is denominated in grams of gold, and has an 8-year tenure; neither scheme is about FDI.
statements: 1 — Correct: Both schemes aim to draw idle household and institutional gold into the formal financial system, either through deposits (GMS) or by diverting demand to paper gold (SGB).
2 — Incorrect: Neither scheme is designed to promote FDI in the gold and jewellery sector. They deal with domestic gold mobilisation and investment, not foreign capital inflows.
3 — Correct: By mobilising domestic gold stocks and offering paper-gold investment instead of physical gold, the schemes aim to reduce gold imports and ease the current account deficit.
summary: The correct answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. Both the Sovereign Gold Bond Scheme and the Gold Monetization Scheme (launched November 2015) aim to mobilise idle household gold and reduce dependence on physical gold imports. Neither is meant to promote FDI in the gold and jewellery sector.

ocr: ‘Belt and Road Initiative’ is sometimes mentioned in the news in the context of the affairs of - - . —-- (a) African Union (b) Brazil ; {c) European Union (dj China B-APM-P-CKB/65A
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Belt and Road Initiative (earlier called One Belt One Road, OBOR) was announced by Chinese President Xi Jinping in 2013, with the Silk Road Economic Belt unveiled in Kazakhstan (September 2013) and the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road in Indonesia (October 2013). The 'Belt' refers to overland corridors linking China with Central Asia, Russia, Europe and South Asia. The 'Road' refers to sea lanes through the South China Sea, Indian Ocean, Africa and the Mediterranean. It is financed through Chinese policy banks, the Silk Road Fund and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB, headquartered in Beijing). The China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), a flagship BRI project, passes through Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, so India objects on grounds of sovereignty and has stayed out of the BRI forums. Critics also cite debt-trap concerns, such as the Hambantota port in Sri Lanka. For elimination, the African Union and the European Union are regional organisations, not originators of the BRI, and Brazil is not associated with it. Only China is the initiator, so (d) is correct.
explanations: (a) African Union – Incorrect. The AU is a continental body of African states. Many African countries are BRI partners, but the BRI is not the AU's initiative.
(b) Brazil – Incorrect. Brazil is a BRICS member and has trade ties with China, but it has no connection with originating the BRI. It is not the context in which the BRI is mentioned.
(c) European Union – Incorrect. The EU is a recipient or partner and sometimes a critic of the BRI. Its own connectivity strategy is the separate Global Gateway.
(d) China – Correct. President Xi Jinping launched the BRI in 2013, and it is central to China's foreign policy and economic strategy.
keyfact: BRI = China's initiative (Xi Jinping, 2013); its flagship CPEC passes through PoK, which is why India objects.
summary: The correct answer is (d) China. The Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) is China's flagship global infrastructure and connectivity programme, launched by President Xi Jinping in 2013. It is covered in the news in the context of China's foreign, economic and strategic affairs.

question: Pradhan Mantri MUDRA Yojana is aimed at bringing the small entrepreneurs
options: into forma] financial system providing loans to poor farmers for
cultivating particular crops providing pensions to old and
destitute persons funding the voluntary organizations
involved in the promotion of skill development and employment generation
subject: Economy
detail: PMMY was launched on 8 April 2015. It operates through MUDRA (Micro Units Development and Refinance Agency Ltd), set up as a subsidiary of SIDBI and later converted into an NBFC. MUDRA does not lend directly. It refinances banks, regional rural banks, NBFCs and microfinance institutions (MFIs) that lend to non-corporate, non-farm small and micro enterprises such as shopkeepers, vendors, artisans, food-service units and small manufacturers. Loans are collateral-free and come in three categories: Shishu (up to Rs 50,000), Kishore (Rs 50,000 to Rs 5 lakh) and Tarun (Rs 5 lakh to Rs 10 lakh). Tarun Plus, with a limit of Rs 20 lakh, was added later in the 2024 Budget. The core aim is financial inclusion and funding the unfunded, so small entrepreneurs get access to formal credit rather than depending on moneylenders. Elimination: crop loans for farmers are handled by schemes like the Kisan Credit Card, so (b) is wrong. Pensions for the old and destitute fall under the National Social Assistance Programme and the Atal Pension Yojana, so (c) is wrong. Funding voluntary organisations for skill development is not MUDRA's role, so (d) is wrong.
explanations: Correct: MUDRA brings small and micro entrepreneurs into the formal financial system through collateral-free loans routed via banks, NBFCs and MFIs.
Incorrect: Loans to farmers for particular crops come under agricultural credit schemes such as the Kisan Credit Card. MUDRA targets non-farm micro enterprises.
Incorrect: Pensions for the old and destitute are provided by the NSAP (Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme) and the Atal Pension Yojana, not by MUDRA.
Incorrect: MUDRA funds small business units, not voluntary organisations. Skill development is the domain of Skill India and the PMKVY.
keyfact: PMMY (8 April 2015): collateral-free loans up to Rs 10 lakh (Shishu, Kishore, Tarun) to non-farm micro enterprises via MUDRA, a SIDBI subsidiary.
summary: The answer is (a). Pradhan Mantri MUDRA Yojana (PMMY), launched on 8 April 2015, brings small and micro entrepreneurs, especially those previously unbanked, into the formal financial system by giving them collateral-free institutional credit of up to Rs 10 lakh.

ocr: In which of the following regions of India are shale gas resources found? Cambay Basin T; Cauvery Basin ai 3. Krishna-Godavari Basin Select the correct answer using the code given below. 1 and 2 only (a) 3 only (b) 2 and 3 only {c) 1, 2 and 3 (d)
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Shale gas is natural gas trapped within fine-grained, organic-rich sedimentary rock (shale), and it is extracted using horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing (fracking). India's shale potential has been assessed by the USGS/EIA, the Directorate General of Hydrocarbons (DGH), ONGC and the Oil and Gas Industry. ONGC drilled India's first shale gas well in 2011 at Durgapur in West Bengal (Damodar Valley basin). The Government announced a Shale Gas and Oil Policy in October 2013 that allowed National Oil Companies (ONGC, OIL) to explore shale gas in their nominated blocks, and the policy did not extend to private bidders in that phase. The main shale-bearing basins are Cambay (Gujarat), Krishna-Godavari (Andhra Pradesh, coastal), Cauvery (Tamil Nadu), Damodar Valley (Jharkhand-West Bengal), Assam-Arakan, Vindhyan, Pranhita-Godavari and the Rajasthan basins. The elimination logic is simple: since all three of the listed basins are recognised shale-bearing basins, any option that excludes one is wrong. Knowing even two of the three correctly leads you to (d), because the only option that includes both Cambay and Cauvery along with KG basin is (d). Remember that potential resource does not equal commercial production, and India has no significant commercial shale gas output so far.
explanations: (a) 1 and 2 only is wrong because it omits statement 3; the Krishna-Godavari Basin also holds shale gas resources.
(b) 3 only is wrong because it excludes the Cambay and Cauvery basins, both of which have identified shale gas potential.
(c) 2 and 3 only is wrong because it omits statement 1; the Cambay Basin has recognised shale gas resources.
(d) 1, 2 and 3 is correct because Cambay, Cauvery and Krishna-Godavari basins all have shale gas resources, as confirmed by the official UPSC key.
keyfact: Cambay, Cauvery and Krishna-Godavari basins all have shale gas resources, so the answer is (d).
related: India's first shale gas well was drilled by ONGC at Durgapur (West Bengal) in 2011.
Shale Gas and Oil Policy was announced in 2013 for National Oil Companies.
HELP (2016) introduced OALP and a uniform licence for all hydrocarbons.
Shale gas is extracted by hydraulic fracturing (fracking).
Gas hydrates have been found in the Krishna-Godavari basin offshore.
Coal bed methane is found in Raniganj, Jharia, Bokaro and Sohagpur coalfields.
DGH is the technical advisory body under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.
The USA led the global shale gas revolution.
statements: 1 — Correct: Cambay Basin has shale gas potential. Located in Gujarat, it is a rift-graben basin filled with Tertiary sediments, and its Cambay Shale is a key source rock. It is one of India's oldest producing petroleum basins (Ankleshwar, Kalol, Gandhar fields). ONGC has identified shale formations here, and DGH has assessed it among the prospective shale basins. Mehsana, Ahmedabad, Cambay and Broach are the major sub-blocks.

2 — Correct: Cauvery Basin has shale gas potential. Spread over Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, onshore and offshore, it is a pericratonic rift basin with Mesozoic-Tertiary sediments. Source rocks include the Andimadam and Sattapadi shales. Existing production includes oil and gas from fields such as Narimanam and Kovilkalappal, and ONGC has drilled exploratory shale wells there. It is among the basins listed by the DGH and EIA for shale potential.

3 — Correct: Krishna-Godavari (KG) Basin has shale gas potential. This east-coast basin spans Andhra Pradesh, both onshore and deep-water offshore, and is famous for the Reliance D6 gas field and ONGC finds. Permian-Triassic and Cretaceous shales such as the Kommugudem shale are source rocks. The EIA and DGH list KG among the most promising shale gas basins in India, and ONGC has tested shale wells there.
summary: The correct answer is (d) 1, 2 and 3. Shale gas resources in India have been identified in the Cambay, Cauvery and Krishna-Godavari basins, along with others such as Damodar Valley and Assam-Arakan. All three listed basins therefore qualify.
topic_notes: Shale gas is unconventional natural gas held in low-permeability, organic-rich shale. It is extracted through horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing, which pumps water, sand and chemicals at high pressure. Concerns include heavy water use, groundwater contamination, induced seismicity and methane leakage. Major producers are the USA (the shale revolution), Canada, China and Argentina. India's potential: the EIA and USGS have estimated sizeable technically recoverable resources, and the Indian assessments (DGH, ONGC) identify basins such as Cambay, KG, Cauvery, Damodar Valley, Assam-Arakan, Vindhyan and Pranhita-Godavari. ONGC drilled the first shale gas well at Durgapur, West Bengal, in 2011 (RB-1). The Government's Shale Gas and Oil Policy of 2013 permitted National Oil Companies to explore in their nominated blocks under existing PSC and nomination licences. Later, the Hydrocarbon Exploration and Licensing Policy (HELP, 2016) introduced a uniform licence, the Open Acreage Licensing Policy (OALP) and a revenue-sharing model, covering all hydrocarbons including shale gas, coal bed methane and gas hydrates. Related unconventional resources: coal bed methane (Raniganj, Jharia, Bokaro, Sohagpur), tight gas, and gas hydrates (found in the KG basin offshore, Mahanadi and Andaman). Regulatory bodies: the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, the DGH (technical arm) and PNGRB for downstream. The key limiting factors for India are water scarcity, high population density, land acquisition and lack of technology and rigs.

question: Global Financial Stability. Report’ is prepared by the European, Central Bank
options: Reconstruction and Development Organization for Economic
subject: Economy
detail: The Global Financial Stability Report is a flagship publication of the International Monetary Fund. It is issued twice a year, in April and October, alongside the World Economic Outlook and the Fiscal Monitor. It assesses risks to the global financial system, such as market volatility, asset valuations, leverage, capital flows and emerging-market vulnerabilities, and it suggests policy responses. It is produced by the IMF's Monetary and Capital Markets Department as part of the Fund's surveillance role under Article IV of its Articles of Agreement. The IMF was established at Bretton Woods in 1944 and is headquartered in Washington, D.C. The elimination logic is to match each body to its own flagship reports. The European Central Bank publishes a regional Financial Stability Review. The World Bank (IBRD) publishes the World Development Report, Doing Business (since discontinued) and Global Economic Prospects. The OECD publishes the Economic Outlook and the PISA assessments. Only the IMF produces the GFSR.
explanations: (b) is the official answer: the IMF prepares and publishes the Global Financial Stability Report, as part of its global surveillance work.
The European Central Bank publishes the Financial Stability Review, which covers the euro area. It does not publish the GFSR, so this option is wrong.
The World Bank (IBRD) publishes the World Development Report and Global Economic Prospects, not the GFSR, so this option is wrong.
The OECD publishes the Economic Outlook and PISA, not the GFSR, so this option is wrong.
keyfact: GFSR = IMF (twice yearly, April and October), alongside the World Economic Outlook and the Fiscal Monitor.
summary: The Global Financial Stability Report (GFSR) is prepared by the International Monetary Fund, so the answer is (b). The IMF's mandate to monitor global financial stability and surveillance makes it the publisher of this report.

ocr: Regarding ‘Atal Pension Yojana’, which of the following statements is/are correct? l. It is a minimum guaranteed pension scheme mainly targeted at unorganized sector workers. 2. Only one member of a family can join the scheme. 3. Same amount of pension is guaranteed for the spouse for life after subscriber’s death. Select the correct answer using the code given below, fa) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c} 1 and 3 only (da) 1, 2 and 3
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Atal Pension Yojana was launched on 9 May 2015 (announced in the Budget 2015-16) under the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA), and is administered through the National Pension System (NPS) architecture. It targets workers in the unorganised sector who lack a formal pension. Any Indian citizen aged 18 to 40 with a savings bank or post office account can join. The subscriber chooses a fixed monthly pension of Rs 1,000, 2,000, 3,000, 4,000 or 5,000, guaranteed from age 60. Contributions depend on the entry age and chosen pension amount, so joining earlier means lower contributions. The government guarantees the minimum pension. In the original design it also co-contributed 50% of the subscriber's contribution (or Rs 1,000 a year, whichever was lower) for five years for those who joined before 31 March 2016 and were not income tax payers or members of statutory social security schemes. After the subscriber's death, the spouse receives the same pension for life. After both die, the accumulated corpus goes to the nominee. Because APY is individual-based, husband and wife can each hold a separate account. Elimination logic: statement 2 is incorrect, so options (b) and (d) are eliminated. Statement 1 is certainly correct, so only (c) remains once statement 3 is confirmed.
explanations: (a) Wrong: Statement 1 is correct, but statement 3 is also correct, so '1 only' is incomplete.
(b) Wrong: Statement 2 is incorrect because there is no restriction to one family member, and this option leaves out the correct statement 1.
(c) Right: Statements 1 and 3 are correct, and statement 2 is false. This matches the official answer.
(d) Wrong: It includes statement 2, which is false, since multiple family members can each join as individual subscribers.
keyfact: APY (launched 9 May 2015, PFRDA): ages 18-40, guaranteed pension Rs 1,000-5,000 a month from age 60, same pension to the spouse after the subscriber's death, and the corpus to the nominee after both die.
statements: 1 — Correct: APY is a guaranteed minimum pension scheme, run by PFRDA, aimed mainly at unorganised sector workers.
2 — Incorrect: There is no one-per-family limit. Each eligible individual aged 18-40 with a bank account can join, and spouses can both subscribe separately.
3 — Correct: After the subscriber's death, the spouse gets the same guaranteed pension for life. After the spouse's death, the accumulated corpus is returned to the nominee.
summary: The correct answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. Atal Pension Yojana (APY) is a government-backed guaranteed minimum pension scheme aimed at unorganised sector workers, and the same pension continues to the spouse for life after the subscriber's death. The claim that only one family member can join is wrong, because APY is an individual-based scheme.

ocr: The term ‘Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership’ often appears in the news in the context of the affairs of a group of countries known as {a} G20 (b) ASEAN fc) SCO (dq) SAARC
subject: Current Affairs
detail: RCEP was formally launched at the ASEAN Summit in Phnom Penh in November 2012. It brings together the 10 ASEAN members (Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam) and the six countries with which ASEAN already has FTAs: China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand and India. The aim is to consolidate these separate ASEAN+1 agreements into a single, broader trade pact covering trade in goods and services, investment, economic and technical cooperation, intellectual property, competition and dispute settlement. Negotiations were led by ASEAN, which is why the grouping is described as being in the news in the context of ASEAN's affairs. India withdrew from the negotiations in November 2019, citing trade deficit concerns, especially with China, and inadequate protection for sensitive sectors. The remaining 15 countries signed RCEP in November 2020, and it came into force on 1 January 2022, creating one of the world's largest trading blocs by GDP and population. Elimination logic: G20 is a forum of major economies on global financial issues; SCO is a Eurasian political, security and economic grouping; SAARC is a South Asian regional body. None of these is associated with RCEP, so ASEAN is the answer.
explanations: (a) G20 is a forum of the world's major economies for global economic and financial coordination, not the originator of RCEP; it has no link to this trade negotiation. Incorrect.
(b) ASEAN launched RCEP in 2012 and led the negotiations with its six FTA partners (China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand, India). Correct.
(c) SCO is a Eurasian security, political and economic organisation (China, Russia, Central Asian states, India, Pakistan), unconnected with RCEP. Incorrect.
(d) SAARC is a South Asian regional grouping with SAFTA as its trade arrangement; RCEP is not its initiative. Incorrect.
keyfact: RCEP = ASEAN-led mega FTA (ASEAN-10 + China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand; India withdrew in 2019); launched 2012, signed 2020, in force 1 Jan 2022.
summary: The correct answer is (b) ASEAN. The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) is a proposed mega free trade agreement launched by ASEAN and driven by ASEAN centrality, covering its six FTA partners.

ocr: On which of the following can you find - the Bureau of Energy Efficiency Star Label? 1. Ceiling fans 2. Electric geysers 3. Tubular fluorescent lamps B-APM-P-CKB/65A 28 Select the correct answer using the code given below, {a) 1 and 2 only (b) 3 only (c}) 2 and 3 only fd) 1, 2 and 3
subject: Science & Tech
detail: The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) is a statutory body under the Ministry of Power, set up on 1 March 2002 under the Energy Conservation Act, 2001. Its Standards & Labelling (S&L) programme, launched in 2006, rates appliances on a 1-to-5 star scale, where 5 stars means the most energy-efficient. The label helps consumers compare the energy consumption of similar products. The programme began with frost-free refrigerators, tubular fluorescent lamps, room air conditioners and distribution transformers. Coverage later grew to ceiling fans, electric geysers (storage water heaters), colour TVs, washing machines, LED lamps, induction motors, pump sets and others. Labelling became mandatory (notified under the Act) for items such as tubular fluorescent lamps, room ACs, frost-free refrigerators, distribution transformers, and later ceiling fans, geysers, colour TVs and LED lamps. Other items remain voluntary. Elimination logic: all three items in the question have been on the BEE list, so any option that leaves one out is wrong. Options (a), (b) and (c) each omit one item, so only (d) is correct.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it leaves out tubular fluorescent lamps, which do carry the BEE Star Label.
(b) is wrong because it names only tubular fluorescent lamps and omits ceiling fans and geysers, which are also labelled.
(c) is wrong because it omits ceiling fans, which also carry the BEE Star Label.
(d) is correct because ceiling fans, electric geysers and tubular fluorescent lamps all fall under the BEE Standards & Labelling programme.
keyfact: BEE's Standards & Labelling programme (star ratings from 1 to 5) covers ceiling fans, electric geysers and tubular fluorescent lamps, so the answer is (d).
related: BEE was set up in March 2002 under the Energy Conservation Act, 2001 and works under the Ministry of Power.
The BEE star label rates appliances from 1 to 5 stars, and 5 stars means the most energy-efficient.
The PAT scheme falls under the National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency (NMEEE), part of the NAPCC.
The Energy Conservation Building Code (ECBC) was launched in 2007 for commercial buildings.
EESL implements the UJALA LED bulb scheme, launched in January 2015.
The S&L programme began in 2006 with refrigerators, tubular fluorescent lamps, room ACs and distribution transformers.
The Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022 introduced carbon credit trading and mandated renewable energy use for large consumers.
statements: 1 — Correct: Ceiling fans carry the BEE Star Label. Ceiling fans were brought under the S&L programme (voluntary from 2009, mandatory from 2010 and later). The label shows star ratings based on service value, i.e. air delivery per watt (m³/min per watt). Fans are a major household load in India, so efficiency gains matter. BLDC (brushless DC) fans can reach 5 stars and use roughly half the power of ordinary fans.

2 — Correct: Electric geysers (storage water heaters) carry the BEE Star Label. They were covered under the S&L programme from about 2009, with mandatory labelling later. Ratings depend on standing-loss (heat loss while the water is kept hot) and on the capacity of the storage tank. Star ratings help consumers choose models with better insulation and lower electricity use. Water heating is a significant share of household electricity use in cold regions and in winter.

3 — Correct: Tubular fluorescent lamps (TFL) were among the first four appliances labelled by BEE in 2006 and were made mandatory in 2009. Ratings are based on luminous efficacy (lumens per watt). Fluorescent tubes are more efficient than incandescent bulbs, though LEDs have since largely replaced them. Under the UJALA scheme (2015), LED bulbs were distributed and also carry BEE ratings.
summary: The correct answer is (d): ceiling fans, electric geysers and tubular fluorescent lamps all carry the BEE Star Label. The Bureau of Energy Efficiency's Standards & Labelling (S&L) programme covers all three, and the label is mandatory for some appliances and voluntary for others.
topic_notes: The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) was set up on 1 March 2002 under the Energy Conservation Act, 2001. It is a statutory body under the Ministry of Power and is headquartered in New Delhi. Its job is to reduce the energy intensity of the Indian economy through market-based approaches and regulation. The Act was amended in 2010 and 2022. The 2022 amendment introduced carbon markets and mandated renewable energy use by designated consumers. Main programmes: (1) Standards & Labelling (S&L), launched in 2006, with star ratings from 1 to 5. Labels are mandatory for some products and voluntary for others, and cover more than 25 appliances, including ACs, refrigerators, TVs, geysers, fans, LED lamps, washing machines, transformers, pump sets and motors. (2) Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT), launched in 2012 under the National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency (NMEEE), one of the eight missions of the National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC). PAT sets energy-saving targets for energy-intensive industries called Designated Consumers and issues tradable Energy Saving Certificates (ESCerts). (3) Energy Conservation Building Code (ECBC), launched in 2007 for commercial buildings, with ECBC 2017 and the residential code Eco Niwas Samhita. (4) UJALA (Unnat Jyoti by Affordable LEDs for All), launched in January 2015 and run by EESL, an energy-services company under the Ministry of Power, along with the Street Lighting National Programme (SLNP). (5) Demand-side management and agricultural pumping programmes. (6) The Energy Efficiency Financing Platform and the Partial Risk Guarantee Fund. Related UPSC angles include the star label colours, the ECBC and EESL, and India's NDC targets under the Paris Agreement.

question: India is an important member of the International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor’. If this experiment succeeds, what is the immediate advantage for India?
options: It can use thorium in place of uranium for power generation
It can attain a global role in satellite navigation
It can drastically improve the efficiency of its fission reactors in power generation
It can build fusion reactors for power generation
subject: Science & Tech
detail: ITER (International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor) is a collaborative project to demonstrate that nuclear fusion can produce energy on a commercial scale. It is being built at Cadarache in southern France. It uses a tokamak, a doughnut-shaped magnetic confinement device, to hold deuterium-tritium plasma at about 150 million degrees Celsius. The aim is Q greater than or equal to 10, meaning fusion output of about 500 MW from about 50 MW of input heating power. The ITER Agreement was signed in 2006 and entered into force in 2007. The members are the EU (host), India, China, Japan, South Korea, Russia and the USA. India formally joined in 2005 and contributes mostly in kind, including the cryostat, in-wall shielding, cooling water systems and power supplies, with the Institute for Plasma Research (IPR), Gandhinagar, as the lead agency. Elimination: (a) thorium use relates to India's three-stage nuclear programme, which is fission-based, and has nothing to do with ITER. (b) Satellite navigation relates to ISRO's NavIC. (c) Fusion is a different process from fission and does not improve fission reactors. So only (d) follows directly from ITER's success.
explanations: Wrong. Using thorium in place of uranium is the aim of India's three-stage fission programme (the AHWR and fast breeder reactors). ITER is about fusion and does not enable this.
Wrong. Satellite navigation is ISRO's domain (IRNSS/NavIC) and has no connection with a fusion experiment.
Wrong. ITER does not improve fission reactors. Fusion joins light nuclei, while fission splits heavy nuclei, so they are separate technologies.

Correct. ITER's success would demonstrate the feasibility of fusion power. As a member sharing the technology and intellectual property, India could then build its own fusion reactors for power generation.
keyfact: ITER is a fusion (not fission) tokamak project at Cadarache, France, and its success would let India build fusion reactors for power.
option_notes: Thorium is a fertile material, and Th-232 converts to fissile U-233 in a reactor. India has about a quarter of the world's thorium reserves, mostly in monazite sands in Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Odisha. Homi Bhabha's three-stage programme runs from PHWRs to fast breeder reactors to thorium-based reactors. The Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) is designed for thorium, and the PFBR at Kalpakkam is the second-stage reactor.

NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation), formerly IRNSS, is India's regional satellite navigation system run by ISRO. It has a constellation of seven satellites, in geostationary and inclined geosynchronous orbits. It covers India and about 1,500 km beyond its borders, and provides the Standard Positioning Service and a restricted service. Global systems include GPS (USA), GLONASS (Russia), Galileo (EU) and BeiDou (China).

Fission reactors split heavy nuclei such as U-235 or Pu-239 and release heat, which is used to make steam. India's fleet includes PHWRs, BWRs at Tarapur, and VVER units at Kudankulam. Efficiency depends on fuel, moderator and coolant design. Fusion research does not feed into these designs. The Indo-US civil nuclear deal of 2008 and the NSG waiver gave India access to fuel and reactors.

Fusion combines light nuclei such as deuterium and tritium into helium and releases neutrons and energy. It is the process that powers the Sun. Its advantages are abundant fuel, no chain reaction, little long-lived waste and no carbon emissions. ITER is a tokamak experiment. A follow-on demonstration reactor, DEMO, would be the step towards commercial power.
related: ITER is located at Cadarache, southern France.
ITER uses a tokamak, which confines plasma with magnetic fields.
ITER members: EU, India, China, Japan, South Korea, Russia and the USA.
India's lead agency for ITER is the Institute for Plasma Research, Gandhinagar.
Fusion fuel is deuterium and tritium, and tritium is bred from lithium.
India's SST-1 is a steady-state superconducting tokamak.
Stage 3 of India's nuclear programme uses thorium and U-233.
PFBR at Kalpakkam is India's prototype fast breeder reactor.
summary: The answer is (d). ITER is an experimental nuclear fusion project, so if it succeeds, India, as a member, gains access to fusion technology and can build fusion reactors for power generation. It has no direct link to thorium use, satellite navigation or fission reactor efficiency.
topic_notes:
ITER is the world's largest fusion experiment, being built at Saint-Paul-lez-Durance (Cadarache), France. Its members are the EU (host, with the largest share), the USA, Russia, Japan, China, South Korea and India, covering over half the world's population. The ITER Agreement was signed in November 2006 and ITER Organization was established in 2007. India joined in 2005. India's contribution is mainly in kind, through the Institute for Plasma Research (IPR) in Gandhinagar under the Department of Atomic Energy; the cryostat was made by L&T. The design is a tokamak, a magnetic confinement device with superconducting magnets, and the fuel is a deuterium-tritium plasma. Tritium is bred from lithium. The target is Q of 10 (500 MW from 50 MW input) and first plasma has been delayed, with research operations now planned for the 2030s.

Fusion versus fission: fusion joins light nuclei, needs extremely high temperatures, has no runaway chain reaction and produces little long-lived waste. Fission splits heavy nuclei. Indian fusion work includes the SST-1 tokamak at IPR and the earlier Aditya tokamak. India's nuclear energy base is the three-stage programme conceived by Homi Bhabha, using natural uranium PHWRs in stage 1, plutonium fast breeder reactors in stage 2 (PFBR at Kalpakkam) and thorium-U233 reactors in stage 3. Other ideas that UPSC may ask about: the Atomic Energy Act 1962, the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act 2010 and the NSG membership issue. Related facility: the Large Hadron Collider at CERN, in which India is an associate member.

ocr: In the context of the history of India, - consider the following pairs : Term Description. 1. Eripatti : Land, revenue from which was set apart for the main- tenance of the village tank 2. Taniyurs ; Villages donated to a single Brahmin or a group of Brahmins 3. Ghatikas : Colleges generally attached to the temples Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched? : fa} 1 and 2 (b} 3 only (c) 2 and 3 (d) 1 and 3
subject: Art & Culture
detail: This question tests the vocabulary of South Indian (Pallava-Chola) agrarian and local administration, which UPSC often asks about. Irrigation was central to the agrarian economy of Tamil country. Eripatti was land assigned, or its revenue earmarked, for maintaining the eri (village tank). Villages were classified by the dominant group or tenure. Ur was a non-Brahmin peasant settlement, Sabha or Mahasabha was the assembly of a Brahmadeya or Agrahara village, and Nagaram was a merchant settlement. Brahmadeya or Agrahara villages were donated to Brahmins, either a single Brahmin or a group. Taniyur was a big village or group of villages that stood alone as a separate administrative unit, often with a dominant community, and it is not the same as a Brahmadeya. Ghatikas were centres of higher learning attached to temples in early medieval South India. The Kanchi Ghatika under the Pallavas is the best-known example. Elimination logic: if you know that Ghatikas are temple colleges, pair 3 is correct, which leaves (b), (c) or (d). Knowing that Eripatti is correct gives (a) or (d). Together these point to (d).
explanations: Wrong: pair 1 is correct, but this option adds pair 2, which is incorrect because Taniyurs were not villages donated to Brahmins.
Wrong: pair 3 is correct, but pair 1 is also correct, so '3 only' is incomplete.
Wrong: pair 2 is incorrect (Taniyurs were not Brahmin donated villages), so including it makes the option wrong.
Correct: Eripatti (land for tank maintenance) and Ghatikas (temple colleges) are rightly matched. Pair 2 is the only incorrect one.
keyfact: Eripatti = land for tank upkeep; Ghatikas = temple colleges; Taniyur = a separate large village, not a Brahmin gift (that is Brahmadeya), so the answer is 1 and 3.
option_notes: Pairs 1 and 2: this combination pairs Eripatti with Taniyurs as Brahmin-donated villages. Eripatti was land assigned for tank maintenance in Chola-era Tamil Nadu, while Brahmin-donated villages were called Brahmadeya or Agrahara, and were run by a Sabha. Taniyur was a separate large village or group of villages treated as an independent unit.

3 only: Ghatikas were temple-attached colleges in early medieval South India. The Kanchi Ghatika under the Pallavas was the best known. They taught Vedic learning, grammar and philosophy with royal grants. Other terms to know are Salai (a Chola-period school) and Matha (a monastic centre). The option is incomplete because pair 1 is also correct.

Pairs 2 and 3: this combines the incorrect pair 2 (Taniyurs) with the correct pair 3 (Ghatikas). A Brahmadeya was a gift village for Brahmins, managed by a Sabha, with Uttaramerur as the best-known example. Taniyurs were independent large villages. Ghatikas were temple colleges, as at Kanchi.

Pairs 1 and 3: this is the correct option. Eripatti was land or revenue assigned for tank maintenance, important for Chola irrigation. Ghatikas were temple colleges, with Kanchi the famous example. Both belong to the Pallava-Chola south Indian system of agrarian and educational institutions.
related: Eripatti: land or its revenue assigned for maintaining the village tank (eri) in Tamil country.
Brahmadeya or Agrahara: village gifted to Brahmins, run by the Sabha or Mahasabha.
Taniyur: a large village, or group of villages, forming a separate administrative unit.
Ghatikas: temple-linked colleges; the Kanchi Ghatika under the Pallavas was famous.
Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I describe the Sabha's election by lot (kudavolai).
Devadana: land granted to temples. Pallichchhandam: land granted to Jain institutions.
Vellanvagai: land of non-Brahmin peasants. Salabhoga: land for the maintenance of a school.
Chola divisions: mandalam, valanadu, nadu, ur.
statements: 1 — Correct: Eripatti was land, or the revenue from it, set apart for maintaining the village tank (eri). Eri means tank in Tamil, and patti or pattu means a grant or share. Tank irrigation was the backbone of agriculture in the Tamil plains under the Pallavas and Cholas. Village assemblies and temples managed tanks through committees such as the Eri-variyam (tank supervision committee), which looked after tank maintenance and desilting. Inscriptions record land and income assigned for repairs, called kudimaramat in later usage. Besides Eripatti, there were other tenures such as Devadana (to temples), Pallichchhandam (to Jain institutions), Salabhoga (for schools) and Vellanvagai (non-Brahmin peasant land).

2 — Incorrect: Taniyurs were not villages donated to Brahmins. A Taniyur was a large, separate village, or a group of villages, that formed an independent administrative unit, often dominated by a particular community or institution. Villages donated to Brahmins were Brahmadeya (Brahmin gift) or Agrahara villages, managed by the Sabha or Mahasabha, which had committees (variyams) for tanks, gardens and justice. Under the Cholas, the Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I (c. 919 and 921 CE) describe the rules for electing members to these committees. The Chola kingdom was divided into mandalams, valanadus and nadus. The nadu was administered by the Nattar, the Ur was a non-Brahmin peasant village, and the Nagaram was a merchant settlement.

3 — Correct: Ghatikas were colleges or centres of learning attached to temples in early medieval South India. The Kanchi Ghatika under the Pallavas was famous, and Kadamba and Chalukya records also mention Ghatikas. They taught Vedic and Sanskrit learning, grammar, philosophy and the sciences, and rulers patronised them with grants. Related institutions include the Salai (a Chola-period school, for example Ennayiram and Tirumukkudal), the Mathas (monastic centres), and the Mahavihara of Nalanda. Temples in this period also served as centres of education, banking and charity. Mathas and Ghatikas helped spread Brahmanical learning and Sanskrit culture across South India.
summary: The answer is (d): pairs 1 and 3 are correctly matched. Eripatti was land whose revenue maintained the village tank (Chola-period South India), and Ghatikas were colleges attached to temples. Pair 2 is wrong because Taniyurs were large, independent villages or a group of villages with a dominant community, not villages donated to Brahmins.
topic_notes: The topic is the agrarian, administrative and educational terminology of early medieval South India (Pallava, Chola, Pandya, c. 6th-13th century CE). Villages were of several types. The Ur was a non-Brahmin peasant settlement run by an assembly of the same name. The Brahmadeya or Agrahara was a village gifted to Brahmins and run by the Sabha or Mahasabha. The Nagaram was a merchant settlement. The Taniyur was a large independent village or group of villages. Land grants and tenures included Devadana (to temples), Tirunamattukkani (temple land free of tax), Pallichchhandam (to Jain institutions), Salabhoga (for the maintenance of a school), Vellanvagai (land of non-Brahmin peasants), and Eripatti (for tank maintenance). Chola local government is best known from the Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I, which describe elections to the Sabha by lot (kudavolai) from qualified candidates, and its committees (variyams), such as the Eri-variyam for tanks and the Thotta-variyam for gardens. Administrative divisions ran from mandalam to valanadu to nadu to kurram or ur. Revenue was collected mainly as land revenue, often around one-third of the produce, and was called Kadamai or Irai. Land survey and classification were carried out under Rajaraja I and Kulottunga I. Temples were major economic and educational centres: they held land, lent money, employed people and supported learning. Education institutions included Ghatikas (Kanchi), Salais (Kanchipuram, Ennayiram, Tirumukkudal) and Mathas. The Chola bronze tradition, Dravidian temple architecture (Brihadeshwara at Thanjavur, Gangaikondacholapuram) and naval expeditions (Srivijaya under Rajendra I) are other angles UPSC may ask about.

ocr: Consider the following statements : 1. The International Solar Alliance was launched at the United Nations Climate Change Conference in 2015. 2. The Alliance’ includes all the member countries of the United Nations. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? fa) 1 only (b) 2 only (c} Both 1 and 2 fd) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The International Solar Alliance was jointly launched by India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi and French President Francois Hollande on 30 November 2015 at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP21) in Paris. It is a treaty-based intergovernmental organisation with its headquarters in Gurugram, Haryana (the interim secretariat was set up at the National Institute of Solar Energy). The ISA Framework Agreement came into force on 6 December 2017. Its main aim is to promote solar energy deployment, reduce the cost of solar technology and finance, and mobilise investments (the target is about USD 1 trillion by 2030). Originally, membership was limited to sunshine countries lying fully or partly between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn. The Framework Agreement was later amended (effective 2020) to open membership to all UN member states. Even so, joining requires signing and ratifying the Framework Agreement, so the Alliance does not automatically include every UN member. Statement 2 is therefore wrong, as the word 'all' makes it an absolute claim. Elimination: Statement 1 is correct, so (b) and (d) fall away; Statement 2 is wrong, so (c) falls away, leaving (a). A tip for UPSC: absolute words such as 'all' are frequently a warning sign.
explanations: (a) is correct: Statement 1 is true, and Statement 2 is false because not all UN member countries are ISA members.
(b) is wrong: it says only Statement 2 is correct, but 2 is false and 1 is true.
(c) is wrong: Statement 2 is false because the ISA does not comprise all UN members, so both cannot be correct.
(d) is wrong: Statement 1 is true, since the ISA was launched at COP21 in Paris in 2015.
keyfact: ISA: launched 30 Nov 2015 at COP21 Paris by India and France, HQ Gurugram; not all UN members belong to it.
statements: 1 — Correct: The ISA was launched on 30 November 2015 at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP21) in Paris, by India and France.

2 — Incorrect: The Alliance does not include all UN member countries. Membership was designed for sunshine countries between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, and even after being opened to all UN members, countries must sign and ratify the Framework Agreement to join.
summary: The correct answer is (a) 1 only. The International Solar Alliance (ISA) was launched on 30 November 2015 at COP21 (UNFCCC) in Paris, but it is not a grouping of all UN member countries; it is open to solar-resource-rich countries lying between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn.

ocr: ‘European Stability Mechanism’, sometimes seen in the news, is an (a) agency created by EU to deal with ' the impact of millions of refugees arriving from Middle East (b) agency of EU that provides financial assistance to eurozone countries (c) agency of EU to deal with all the bilateral and multilateral agreements on trade Yd) agency of EU to deal with the conflicts arising among the member countries
subject: Environment
detail: The European Stability Mechanism was set up in October 2012 as a permanent rescue fund for the eurozone. It replaced the temporary EFSF (European Financial Stability Facility) and the EFSM. It is based in Luxembourg and was created by a treaty among the euro-area states, so it is an intergovernmental organisation under international public law and not strictly an EU agency. UPSC treated it as an EU body providing financial help. Its lending capacity is about €500 billion, backed by a subscribed capital of roughly €704.8 billion. It can give loans to governments under macroeconomic adjustment programmes, precautionary credit lines, loans to recapitalise banks, and it can buy bonds in primary and secondary markets. Assistance is tied to conditionality, meaning fiscal consolidation and structural reforms. Greece, Spain, Cyprus, Portugal and Ireland received support from the ESM or its predecessors. The ESM was created in response to the sovereign debt crisis that began in 2009-10. Elimination logic: (a) refugee management is handled by Frontex, EASO and similar bodies. (c) Trade agreements are negotiated by the European Commission, which acts for the EU's common commercial policy. (d) Disputes among members go to the Court of Justice of the EU. Only (b) matches the financial-stability meaning of the name.
explanations: Wrong: the ESM has nothing to do with refugees. Migration and asylum matters are handled by bodies such as Frontex and the European Asylum Support Office, and the ESM is purely financial.
Correct: the ESM lends to eurozone countries in financial distress, on strict conditions, to safeguard the stability of the euro area as a whole.
Wrong: trade agreements are negotiated by the European Commission under the EU's common commercial policy, with the Council and Parliament involved. The ESM has no trade role.
Wrong: conflicts among member states are dealt with through EU institutions such as the Court of Justice of the EU and the Council. The ESM does not mediate disputes.
keyfact: ESM (2012, Luxembourg) = permanent eurozone bailout fund giving conditional financial assistance to euro-area countries, successor to the EFSF.
option_notes: Refugee response in the EU involves Frontex (the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, Warsaw), the European Asylum Support Office (now the EU Agency for Asylum), the Dublin Regulation, and relocation schemes. The 2015-16 migration crisis brought over a million arrivals, mainly from Syria, Afghanistan and Iraq. The EU-Turkey deal of March 2016 aimed to curb crossings. None of this is the ESM's role.

The ESM is the permanent eurozone financial safety net, operating since October 2012 and based in Luxembourg. It replaced the EFSF and EFSM. Its lending capacity is about €500 billion. It provides loans, precautionary credit lines, bank recapitalisation loans and bond purchases, always with conditionality. It is governed by a Board of Governors made up of euro-area finance ministers. Its managing director is Pierre Gramegna (since 2022).

Trade policy is an exclusive EU competence under the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU (Articles 206-207). The European Commission negotiates trade deals on behalf of the EU, the Council authorises them, and the European Parliament gives consent. Examples are the EU-Canada CETA, EU-Japan EPA and EU-Mercosur talks. The EU also speaks for its members at the WTO.

Disputes between members and EU law enforcement fall mainly to the Court of Justice of the EU (Luxembourg), which hears infringement cases brought by the Commission or by member states. The European Council and the Council of the EU handle political disagreements. The Court's rulings bind all members, and Article 7 TEU provides for sanctions over breaches of EU values.
related: ESM: permanent eurozone rescue fund, operational since October 2012, headquartered in Luxembourg.
ESM replaced the temporary EFSF and EFSM.
ESM lending capacity is about €500 billion.
Greece exited its ESM-funded programme in August 2018.
The eurozone has 20 members; Croatia joined on 1 January 2023.
The ECB is headquartered in Frankfurt; the euro was introduced in 1999 as a currency and in 2002 as notes and coins.
The Stability and Growth Pact sets limits of 3% of GDP for deficit and 60% for debt.
Frontex is the EU's border agency, based in Warsaw.
summary: The answer is (b). The European Stability Mechanism (ESM) is a permanent intergovernmental crisis-resolution institution of the eurozone. It provides financial assistance, mainly loans, to euro-area members facing or threatened by severe financing problems, in return for strict policy conditionality.
topic_notes: The eurozone debt crisis began in late 2009 when Greece revealed much larger deficits than reported. It spread to Ireland (2010), Portugal (2011), Spain and Cyprus (2012-13). The EU first created temporary tools: the European Financial Stabilisation Mechanism (EFSM, EU budget-backed) and the European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF, a Luxembourg company set up in 2010). In 2012 the permanent ESM took over. It was established by a treaty signed by euro-area states in 2011 and came into force in 2012. The ESM is headquartered in Luxembourg, and the governing Board of Governors consists of the finance ministers of the euro countries. The ESM can lend up to about €500 billion. Greece received three bailout programmes totalling over €260 billion in all, with the third one (2015-18) funded by the ESM, and it exited the programme in August 2018. The ESM also supported Spain's bank recapitalisation, as well as Cyprus. The IMF often took part alongside the European Commission and the European Central Bank, together known as the 'Troika'. Related architecture includes the Stability and Growth Pact (3% deficit and 60% debt limits), the Fiscal Compact (2012), the Banking Union (Single Supervisory Mechanism under the ECB, Single Resolution Mechanism), and the ECB's Outright Monetary Transactions programme (2012), announced after Mario Draghi's 'whatever it takes' statement. In 2020 the ESM introduced a Pandemic Crisis Support credit line for Covid-19 health costs. A reform of the ESM treaty was agreed to make it a backstop for the Single Resolution Fund. The eurozone has 20 members, with Croatia joining in 2023. Future questions could ask about the eurozone's membership, the ECB's role, or Brexit, which took effect on 31 January 2020.

ocr: Which of the following is/are the advantage/advantages of practising drip irrigation? 1. Reduction in weed 2. Reduction in soil salinity 3. Reduction in soil erosion B-APM-P-CKB/65A Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa} 1 and 2 only {b) 3 only {c}) 1 and 3 only {dj None of the above is an advantage of practising drip irrigation
subject: Geography
detail: Drip (trickle) irrigation applies water slowly, drop by drop, through emitters placed at or near the plant root zone, usually via a network of valves, pipes and tubing. Because only the root zone is wetted, the soil between plants stays dry, so weed seeds get little moisture and weed growth falls (statement 1). Water is applied at a rate lower than the soil infiltration rate, so there is no surface runoff, no overland flow and little splash, which reduces soil erosion (statement 3). Other well-known advantages are 40-70% water saving over flood irrigation, higher water-use efficiency, fertigation (fertiliser applied with water), lower labour and suitability for undulating land and water-scarce areas. Salinity is the trap. Drip irrigation applies small volumes and does not leach salts deeply; salts tend to accumulate at the edge of the wetted bulb and can be pushed to the root zone periphery, and saline water use can worsen the problem. Salinity reduction typically needs heavy leaching or flooding with good drainage. Hence statement 2 is wrong, so only 1 and 3 are correct. Options (a), (b) and (d) are eliminated by the validity of statements 1 and 3.
explanations: (a) Wrong: It includes statement 2 (reduction in soil salinity), which is not an advantage of drip irrigation, and it leaves out statement 3, which is correct.
(b) Wrong: Statement 3 is correct, but 'only 3' ignores statement 1 (reduction in weeds), which is also an advantage.
(c) Correct: Statements 1 (fewer weeds) and 3 (less soil erosion) are advantages; statement 2 is not.
(d) Wrong: Drip irrigation does have advantages, including weed reduction and erosion control, so 'none' is false.
keyfact: Drip irrigation: saves water, cuts weeds and erosion, enables fertigation, but does not leach or reduce soil salinity.
statements: 1 — Correct: Water is delivered only to the root zone, leaving inter-row areas dry, so weed germination and growth are reduced.
2 — Incorrect: Drip irrigation applies limited water and does not leach salts; salts can accumulate at the wetted-zone margin, so it does not reduce soil salinity (it may aggravate it).
3 — Correct: Slow, low-rate application avoids runoff and surface flow, thereby reducing soil erosion.
summary: The correct answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. Drip irrigation delivers water directly to the root zone, so the inter-row area stays dry, which suppresses weeds, and the absence of surface runoff and flooding reduces soil erosion. It does not reduce soil salinity in the way flooding or leaching does.

ocr: Regarding ‘DigiLocker’, sometimes scen in the news, which of the following statements is/are correct? 1. It is a digital locker system offered by the Government under Digital India Programme. 2. It allows you to access your e-documents irrespective of your physical location, Select the correct answer using the code given below. . (a) 1 only (b) 2 only — (c) Both 1 and 2 (dj) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Science & Tech
detail: DigiLocker is a flagship e-governance service of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), launched by PM Narendra Modi on 1 July 2015 as part of the Digital India Programme. It gives every Indian citizen a secure cloud-based space, linked to Aadhaar (and now also a mobile number), to store and share authentic digital copies of documents such as Aadhaar, PAN, driving licence, vehicle registration, and school and university certificates. Issuer organisations push documents directly into the locker as 'Issued Documents', while users can upload their own scans as 'Uploaded Documents' and self-attest them with eSign. Each document is linked to a URI (Uniform Resource Identifier). The service is run by the National e-Governance Division (NeGD), and the IT (Preservation and Retention of Information by Intermediaries providing Digital Locker Facilities) Rules, 2016 give legal backing to it. Rule 9A of the Information Technology Act framework, as amended in 2017, treats documents in DigiLocker as at par with originals. Elimination logic: Statement 1 is plainly true, which rules out (b) and (d). Statement 2 describes the cloud-based, location-independent nature of the service, which rules out (a). So (c) is correct.
explanations: (a) 1 only is wrong. Statement 1 is true, but statement 2 is also true, because the cloud-based locker can be accessed from anywhere.
(b) 2 only is wrong. Statement 2 is true, but statement 1 is also true, since DigiLocker is an official government service under Digital India.
(c) Both 1 and 2 is correct. DigiLocker is a government service under Digital India and it gives location-independent access to e-documents.
(d) Neither 1 nor 2 is wrong. Both statements accurately describe DigiLocker.
keyfact: DigiLocker: MeitY's cloud-based document locker under Digital India, launched 1 July 2015, accessible from anywhere, with issued documents legally equal to originals.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only, would mean that DigiLocker is a government service but has no location-independent access. That is not so. DigiLocker was launched on 1 July 2015 by MeitY and run by NeGD. It is a cloud-based platform with a website and a mobile app, which lets users get at issued and uploaded documents from anywhere. It is linked to Aadhaar or a mobile number, and documents carry a URI. The 2016 IT rules recognise the facility legally. Options built on only part of its features are traps.

Option (b), 2 only, would mean that DigiLocker offers location-independent access but is not a government system under Digital India. In fact it is a flagship Digital India initiative of MeitY. Digital India was launched on 1 July 2015 and has pillars such as broadband highways, universal phone access, public internet access, e-governance, eKranti, information for all, electronics manufacturing, IT for jobs and early harvest programmes. DigiLocker falls under the e-governance and eKranti themes. It is administered by NeGD, a division of MeitY.

Option (c), Both 1 and 2, is the correct answer. DigiLocker is a government digital locker under Digital India, launched in July 2015. It is run by MeitY through NeGD. Citizens sign up with Aadhaar or a mobile number and get cloud storage for issued and uploaded documents. Because it is cloud-based, it can be used from anywhere through the web or the mobile app. Documents shared through it are legally valid as per the 2016 IT rules and the 2017 amendment. It also integrates with UMANG and many other services.

Option (d), Neither 1 nor 2, is wrong because it denies both true features. It would imply that DigiLocker is not a government service and that it lacks location-independent access. In fact it is a MeitY service launched on 1 July 2015 and serves hundreds of millions of users. Its issuers include CBSE, the Income Tax Department, the Transport Department, universities and insurers. Its documents are accessible by internet from any location, which is why this option fails.
related: DigiLocker was launched on 1 July 2015 under the Digital India Programme.
DigiLocker is run by MeitY through the National e-Governance Division (NeGD).
DigiLocker registration uses a mobile number and Aadhaar-based verification.
DigiLocker has 'Issued Documents' (pushed by issuers, linked by URI) and 'Uploaded Documents' (user scans).
eSign is an Aadhaar-based online electronic signature service.
UMANG is a unified mobile app for accessing many government services.
India Stack includes Aadhaar, eKYC, eSign, UPI and DigiLocker.
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act was passed in 2023.
statements: 1 — Correct: DigiLocker is a government digital locker system launched under the Digital India Programme. It was launched on 1 July 2015 by MeitY, and the National e-Governance Division (NeGD) runs it. It offers each citizen cloud storage (initially 1 GB, later increased) tied to Aadhaar or a mobile number. Issuers such as CBSE, the Income Tax Department and transport authorities push verified documents straight into the locker. The IT Rules of 2016 set out the framework for digital locker facilities. Digital India itself was launched on 1 July 2015, with the vision of a digitally empowered society and knowledge economy.

2 — Correct: Because DigiLocker is cloud-based and works through a web portal and a mobile app, users can reach their e-documents from any location with an internet connection. This removes the need to carry physical copies. Documents are shared through secure links, and the locker has a 'Issued', 'Uploaded' and 'Shared' structure. Under the 2017 amendment to the IT rules, documents shared through DigiLocker are treated as valid and equal to originals. The Motor Vehicles rules and many universities accept it. The locker integrates with UMANG, and its Aadhaar-based sign-up gives authenticated access. This portability is the key benefit of the system.
summary: The answer is (c) Both 1 and 2. DigiLocker is a government-run digital document locker launched under the Digital India Programme, and because it is cloud-based, you can access your e-documents from anywhere with internet access.
topic_notes: DigiLocker is one of the best-known Digital India initiatives. Digital India was launched on 1 July 2015 with the vision of transforming India into a digitally empowered society and knowledge economy. DigiLocker is run by the National e-Governance Division (NeGD) under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY). Citizens register with a mobile number and Aadhaar-based verification. Each user gets a digital space to store documents. Issued documents come directly from government departments or other issuers and are linked by a URI, so they are verified and authentic. Uploaded documents are user scans, which can be self-attested using eSign. The Information Technology (Preservation and Retention of Information by Intermediaries providing Digital Locker Facilities) Rules, 2016 govern the service. A 2017 notification under the IT Act (Rule 9A of the Motor Vehicles framework and related rules) gives documents in DigiLocker the same validity as physical originals. Usage rose sharply during COVID-19 when physical documents were hard to carry. Related initiatives UPSC could ask about include UMANG (a unified mobile app for government services), eSign (an online electronic signature service built on Aadhaar e-KYC), BHIM (a UPI-based payments app), MyGov (a citizen engagement platform), e-Hospital, Jeevan Pramaan (digital life certificates for pensioners), the National Scholarship Portal, the Government e-Marketplace (GeM), Aadhaar (run by UIDAI under the Aadhaar Act, 2016) and CoWIN. Other angles are data protection and privacy: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and the Puttaswamy judgment of 2017 recognising privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21. Another is the India Stack, which includes Aadhaar, eKYC, eSign, UPI and DigiLocker. Students should also learn which ministry or body runs which service.

ocr: Recently, linking of which of the following rivers was undertaken? P fa} Cauvery and Tungabhadra (b) Godavari and Krishna {c) Mahanadi and Sone (d) Narmada and Tapti
subject: Geography
detail: India's river-linking programme is guided by the National Perspective Plan (1980) of the Ministry of Water Resources, which has two components: Himalayan Rivers and Peninsular Rivers. The National Water Development Agency (NWDA, set up 1982) prepares feasibility studies. The Ken-Betwa link was the first project identified under the Himalayan component, while the Godavari-Krishna link belongs to the Peninsular component. In 2015 Andhra Pradesh commissioned the Pattiseema lift irrigation scheme, which diverts Godavari flood water to the Krishna through the Polavaram right canal. It was widely reported as the first completed river-linking project, which is why the question uses the word 'recently'. The Polavaram project is a national project on the Godavari. Elimination: the Cauvery-Tungabhadra pairing is not a link in the NWDA plan, since the Tungabhadra is a Krishna tributary. Mahanadi-Sone and Narmada-Tapti are not the linking projects reported in news around 2015-16. The Mahanadi-Godavari link is in the plan, while the Sone is linked in the Himalayan component to the southern Ganga tributaries. Narmada-Tapti is a proposed link, but not the one carried out at that time.
explanations: Incorrect: The Tungabhadra is a tributary of the Krishna, and a Cauvery-Tungabhadra link was not the project undertaken. The peninsular plan includes a Krishna-Pennar-Cauvery link, not this pair.

Correct: The Godavari-Krishna link was carried out through the Pattiseema lift scheme (Polavaram right canal) in Andhra Pradesh, commissioned in 2015-16 and reported as India's first completed river-linking project.
Incorrect: The Mahanadi and Sone are not the pair linked recently. The peninsular plan links the Mahanadi to the Godavari, while the Sone is part of the Himalayan component.
Incorrect: The Narmada-Tapti link is only a proposal in the National Perspective Plan and was not the one actually carried out at the time.
keyfact: Godavari-Krishna link (Pattiseema/Polavaram right canal, Andhra Pradesh, 2015) was India's first completed river-linking project under the National Perspective Plan.
summary: The answer is (b) Godavari and Krishna. The Godavari-Krishna link (Polavaram-Pattiseema link, commissioned in 2015-16 in Andhra Pradesh) was the river-linking project actually undertaken recently at the time of the 2016 paper. It is part of the Peninsular Rivers Component of the National Perspective Plan.

ocr: In the cities of our country, which among the following atmospheric gases are normally considered in calculating the value of Air Quality Index? 1. Carbon dioxide 2 Carbon monoxide 3. Nitrogen dioxide 4. Sulfur dioxide 5 Methane \ Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa) 1, 2 and 3 only (b) 2, 3 and 4 only fc) 1, 4 and 5 only (da) 1, 2,3, 4 and 5
subject: Environment
detail: The National Air Quality Index was launched on 17 September 2014 by the Union Environment Ministry under the Swachh Bharat campaign. It was developed by the CPCB with IIT Kanpur and experts. It converts complex air-quality data into a single number and colour category so the public can understand it. It covers eight pollutants: PM10, PM2.5, nitrogen dioxide (NO2), sulphur dioxide (SO2), carbon monoxide (CO), ozone (O3), ammonia (NH3) and lead (Pb). The index has six categories: Good (0-50), Satisfactory (51-100), Moderately polluted (101-200), Poor (201-300), Very Poor (301-400) and Severe (401-500). The AQI is computed from at least three pollutants, one of which must be PM10 or PM2.5, using 24-hour averages (8-hour for CO and O3). The worst sub-index fixes the overall AQI. Elimination: CO2 and methane are climate-forcing gases, not direct health-hazard pollutants at ambient levels, so statements 1 and 5 are out. Options (a), (c) and (d) each include CO2 or methane, leaving only (b).
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes carbon dioxide (1), which is not part of the AQI, and it omits sulphur dioxide (4), which is.
(b) is right because CO, NO2 and SO2 are all AQI pollutants, while CO2 and methane are excluded.
(c) is wrong because it includes CO2 and methane, which are not AQI pollutants, and it leaves out CO and NO2.
(d) is wrong because it includes CO2 and methane, which are greenhouse gases but not AQI components.
