keyfact: India's AQI covers eight pollutants (PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, O3, NH3, Pb), and CO2 and methane are not among them.
related: NAQI was launched on 17 September 2014 and was developed by CPCB with IIT Kanpur.
The AQI covers 8 pollutants: PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, O3, NH3 and Pb.
AQI categories are shown by colour: green, light green, yellow, orange, red and maroon.
SAFAR is run by IITM Pune under the Ministry of Earth Sciences.
NCAP (2019) targets 131 non-attainment cities.
CO2 has a GWP of 1, and methane about 28 over 100 years.
Ozone and PAN are secondary pollutants formed by photochemical reactions.
The CPCB was established in 1974 under the Water Act and later given powers under the Air Act, 1981.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: CO2 is not an AQI pollutant. It is a greenhouse gas, harmless at ambient concentrations in terms of direct health effects, and is covered under climate-change policy instead. Facts: CO2 is about 420 ppm in the atmosphere today, up from about 280 ppm pre-industrially. It is the main anthropogenic greenhouse gas, from fossil fuels, cement and deforestation. It is the reference gas for Global Warming Potential (GWP = 1). Its regulation falls under the UNFCCC, Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement, not the National Ambient Air Quality Standards.

2 — Correct: Carbon monoxide is one of the eight AQI pollutants, measured as an 8-hour average. Facts: CO is a colourless, odourless gas formed by incomplete combustion of fuel, mainly from vehicles. It binds haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, reducing oxygen transport and causing headache, dizziness and death at high levels. The NAAQS limit is 2 mg/m3 for 8 hours and 4 mg/m3 for 1 hour. Its AQI units are mg/m3, unlike most other pollutants, which use µg/m3.

3 — Correct: Nitrogen dioxide is an AQI pollutant. Facts: NO2 is a reddish-brown gas produced by vehicle exhaust, power plants and high-temperature combustion. It irritates the lungs, worsens asthma and contributes to acid rain, smog and ground-level ozone. It is a precursor of PM2.5 and ozone. The NAAQS annual standard is 40 µg/m3 and the 24-hour standard is 80 µg/m3. It is measured by chemiluminescence. It is a major pollutant in Delhi's traffic hotspots.

4 — Correct: Sulphur dioxide is an AQI pollutant. Facts: SO2 comes mainly from burning coal and from smelters and refineries. It causes respiratory problems, acid rain and corrosion of monuments such as the Taj Mahal, which led to the Mathura refinery concerns and the Taj Trapezium Zone. The NAAQS annual standard is 50 µg/m3 and the 24-hour standard is 80 µg/m3. India's FGD norms for thermal power plants (2015) target SO2. It is measured by UV fluorescence.

5 — Incorrect: Methane is not an AQI pollutant. It is a potent greenhouse gas, not a criteria pollutant. Facts: CH4 has a GWP of about 28-34 over 100 years. Sources include paddy fields, livestock enteric fermentation, wetlands, landfills and natural gas leaks. Its atmospheric lifetime is about 12 years. The Global Methane Pledge (COP26, 2021) aims to cut emissions 30% by 2030. It is the main component of natural gas, CNG and biogas.
summary: The correct answer is (b) 2, 3 and 4 only. India's National Air Quality Index (NAQI, launched 2014) considers eight pollutants: PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, O3, NH3 and Pb. Carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases and are not part of the AQI.
topic_notes: India's National Air Quality Index (NAQI) was launched on 17 September 2014 by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. It was developed by the CPCB with IIT Kanpur. It is 'One Number, One Colour, One Description'. The eight pollutants are PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, O3, NH3 and Pb. The six categories are Good (0-50), Satisfactory (51-100), Moderate (101-200), Poor (201-300), Very Poor (301-400) and Severe (401-500). Computation needs data on at least three pollutants, one of which must be PM2.5 or PM10, and the highest sub-index becomes the AQI. Averaging periods are 24 hours for most pollutants and 8 hours for CO and O3. The Central Pollution Control Board, set up in 1974 under the Water Act, administers the National Air Quality Monitoring Programme (NAMP). The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act was passed in 1981. The NAAQS were revised in 2009 and cover 12 parameters, including benzene, benzo(a)pyrene, arsenic and nickel. SAFAR (System of Air Quality and Weather Forecasting and Research), run by the IITM Pune and the Ministry of Earth Sciences, provides city-level AQI forecasts. The Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) is used in Delhi-NCR and is based on AQI levels. The National Clean Air Programme (NCAP, 2019) targets a 20-30% cut in PM concentrations by 2024 (revised to 40% by 2025-26) in 131 non-attainment cities. The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) in NCR was established in 2020 by statute. BS-VI fuel norms were adopted nationwide on 1 April 2020. Ozone is a secondary pollutant formed from NOx and VOCs in sunlight. Globally, the WHO Air Quality Guidelines were updated in 2021. Greenhouse gases such as CO2, CH4, N2O, HFCs, PFCs and SF6 are covered under climate agreements rather than the AQI.

ocr: With reference to ‘Astrosat’, the astronomical observatory launched by India, which of the following statements is/are correct? 1. Other than USA and Russia, India is the only country to have . launched a_ similar observatory into space. 2. Astrosat is a 2000 kg satellite placed in an orbit at 1650 km above the surface of the Earth. Select the correct answer using the code ern — below. {a} 1 only {b) 2 only {c) Both 1 and 2 (dj) Neither 1 nor 2 B-APM-P-CKB/65A
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Astrosat was launched by ISRO on 28 September 2015 aboard PSLV-C30 from Sriharikota. It is India's first dedicated multi-wavelength space observatory. It observes the cosmos simultaneously in the visible, ultraviolet, and low- and high-energy X-ray bands. Its lift-off mass is about 1513 kg, and it was placed in a near-equatorial orbit of about 650 km altitude with roughly 6 degrees inclination. The planned mission life is about 5 years, though it has operated far longer. Statement 1 is wrong because space observatories already existed or were launched by several agencies: NASA's Hubble (1990), Chandra and Spitzer; ESA's XMM-Newton, Herschel and Gaia; and Japan's Suzaku and Hinode. The claim that India is the only other country is false. Statement 2 is wrong on both mass (about 1500 kg, not 2000 kg) and altitude (650 km, not 1650 km, which would be far too high for a low-Earth-orbit observatory). Since both statements fail, (d) is correct. Exam tip: the words 'only' and 'the only country' in a statement are red flags, and numeric details such as mass and altitude are common traps.
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is false: several other countries and agencies, such as ESA and Japan, have launched space observatories, so India is not the only other country after the USA and Russia.
(b) is wrong because statement 2 is false: Astrosat weighs about 1500 kg and orbits at about 650 km, not 2000 kg and 1650 km.
(c) is wrong because neither statement is correct, so 'both' cannot hold.
(d) is correct because both statements are factually wrong, as the official answer confirms.
keyfact: Astrosat (PSLV-C30, 28 Sep 2015) is India's first dedicated multi-wavelength space observatory, about 1500 kg in a roughly 650 km orbit, and many other countries have space observatories too.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', would be right only if the uniqueness claim held. In fact the USA (NASA), Europe (ESA), Japan (JAXA) and Russia have all operated space observatories, such as Hubble, Chandra, XMM-Newton, Gaia and Suzaku. Astrosat is India's first dedicated multi-wavelength space telescope, launched on 28 September 2015, and India's other astronomy payloads are separate, such as the AstroSat-linked X-ray instruments and the Aditya-L1 solar mission.

Option (b), '2 only', would require Astrosat to weigh 2000 kg and orbit at 1650 km. The real figures are about 1513 kg lift-off mass and a roughly 650 km low-Earth orbit with about 6 degrees inclination. PSLV-C30 placed it in orbit from Sriharikota's First Launch Pad. Its five instruments cover optical, UV and X-ray bands. PSLV is a four-stage rocket using alternating solid and liquid propulsion, and it is ISRO's workhorse launcher.

Option (c), 'Both 1 and 2', would need both statements to be true. Neither is true. Astrosat is a multi-wavelength observatory covering visible, UV, soft and hard X-ray bands. It was developed by ISRO with TIFR, IIA, IUCAA, RRI and other partners, including the Canadian Space Agency and the University of Leicester. It lets astronomers study black holes, neutron stars, active galactic nuclei and star-forming regions simultaneously across bands.

Option (d), 'Neither 1 nor 2', is the correct answer. Statement 1 is false because other nations have launched space observatories, and statement 2 is false because Astrosat's mass and altitude are misstated. Astrosat was launched on 28 September 2015 by PSLV-C30. It carries UVIT, SXT, LAXPC, CZTI and SSM, along with a charged particle monitor, and it has operated well beyond its planned five-year life.
related: Astrosat was launched on 28 September 2015 by PSLV-C30 from Sriharikota.
Astrosat is India's first dedicated multi-wavelength space observatory, covering visible, UV and X-ray bands.
Astrosat's orbit is about 650 km, near-equatorial, with about 6 degrees inclination; its mass is about 1500 kg.
Astrosat's payloads are UVIT, SXT, LAXPC, CZTI and SSM.
Aditya-L1 (launched 2 September 2023) is India's first solar observatory, sent to the Sun-Earth L1 point.
XPoSat (January 2024) is India's first X-ray polarimetry mission.
The Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1990 by NASA with ESA's participation.
The James Webb Space Telescope (2021) is an infrared observatory at the Sun-Earth L2 point.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Other countries besides the USA and Russia have launched space observatories, so India is not the only one. Facts: Space-based astronomical observatories include NASA's Hubble Space Telescope (1990), Chandra X-ray Observatory (1999) and Spitzer; ESA's XMM-Newton, Herschel, Planck and Gaia; and Japan's (JAXA) Suzaku, Hinode and Hitomi. The USSR/Russia launched Astron and Spektr-R. Astrosat's distinction is that it is India's first dedicated multi-wavelength observatory, and it is often described as the first of its kind from a developing country, not the only one after the USA and Russia. Its claim to uniqueness is simultaneous multi-band observation using several co-aligned instruments on one platform.

2 — Incorrect: Astrosat's mass is about 1500 kg (1513 kg at lift-off), and its orbit is about 650 km, nearly equatorial at about 6 degrees inclination. Facts: It was launched on 28 September 2015 by PSLV-C30 from Sriharikota. Its payloads include the Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (UVIT), the Large Area X-ray Proportional Counter (LAXPC), the Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT), the Cadmium Zinc Telluride Imager (CZTI) and the Scanning Sky Monitor (SSM). The five-year design life has been exceeded. Institutions involved include ISRO, TIFR, IIA, IUCAA and RRI, plus partners from Canada and the UK.
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is correct. Astrosat is India's first dedicated multi-wavelength space observatory, but India was not the only country besides the USA and Russia to launch a similar observatory (Japan, the EU/ESA and others have done so). Astrosat weighs about 1500 kg and orbits at about 650 km, not 2000 kg at 1650 km.
topic_notes:
Astrosat is India's first dedicated multi-wavelength space observatory. It was launched by ISRO on 28 September 2015 by PSLV-C30 from Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota. The launch also carried six foreign nanosatellites: four from the USA (LEMUR), one from Canada and one from Indonesia. Astrosat's mass was about 1513 kg, and it was placed in a roughly 650 km near-equatorial orbit with about 6 degrees inclination. The design life was five years, but it has operated longer.

Payloads: the Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (UVIT) covers visible, near-UV and far-UV; the Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT) covers soft X-rays; the Large Area X-ray Proportional Counter (LAXPC) and the Cadmium Zinc Telluride Imager (CZTI) cover hard X-rays; the Scanning Sky Monitor (SSM) scans the sky for transient X-ray sources. A Charged Particle Monitor supports the instruments. Science goals: study binary star systems with black holes or neutron stars, active galactic nuclei, supernova remnants, star formation regions, and X-ray and UV emission from distant galaxies.

Simultaneous multi-band observation is Astrosat's main strength. Major contributors include ISRO, TIFR (Tata Institute of Fundamental Research), IIA (Indian Institute of Astrophysics), IUCAA (Pune), RRI (Raman Research Institute), and partners in Canada and the UK. Data are available to the wider astronomical community through ISSDC, the Indian Space Science Data Centre.

Other space observatories: Hubble (NASA/ESA, 1990, optical/UV), Chandra (X-ray, 1999), James Webb Space Telescope (2021, infrared, at the Sun-Earth L2 point), Kepler and TESS (exoplanets), Gaia (ESA, astrometry), XMM-Newton (ESA, X-ray), Fermi (gamma-ray). Related Indian missions: Chandrayaan, Mangalyaan (Mars Orbiter Mission, 2013), Aditya-L1 (solar, 2023) and XPoSat (X-ray polarimetry, 2024). Typical UPSC traps: 'only country' claims, numerical details such as mass and orbit altitude, and the launch vehicle used.

question: With reference to the economic history of medieval India, the term ‘Araghatta’ refers to bonded labour
options: officers : waterwheel used in the irrigation
of land wasteland converted to cultivated
subject: Economy
detail: Araghatta denotes a water-lifting device: a wheel with pots or buckets tied to a rope or chain, turned by animals, that raised water from wells to irrigate fields. It is often called the Persian wheel, and its use is recorded in Sanskrit and regional sources. Its spread in northern India is linked with the early medieval period and especially the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal eras. Babur's memoirs describe it in Hindustan. Its adoption expanded irrigated area, supported double cropping and cash crops such as cotton, sugarcane and indigo, and aided agrarian growth and rural-urban trade. Students should pair it with other medieval terms. Iqta was a revenue assignment to military officers, which is the real answer for option (b)'s idea. Jagir was a Mughal assignment of revenue. Begar or forced labour matches option (a). Banjar or uncultivated land matches option (d). Elimination logic: the word 'ghatta' means pot or wheel-pot, which points to a mechanical irrigation device, and no other option involves technology or water. The three wrong options all describe real medieval categories, but they belong to other terms.
explanations: (a) Wrong: bonded or forced labour is described by terms such as begar or vishti, not Araghatta.
(b) Wrong: land grants to military officers were iqta, jagir or mansab-linked assignments, not Araghatta.
(c) Correct: Araghatta is the waterwheel, or Persian wheel, used to lift water for irrigating land.
(d) Wrong: wasteland brought under cultivation relates to terms like banjar or 'khilla' land and reclamation policy, not Araghatta.
keyfact: Araghatta = Persian wheel (waterwheel for irrigation); iqta = revenue grant to officers.
summary: The correct answer is (c): Araghatta (Sanskrit 'arahatta', Hindi 'rahat', Persian wheel) was a waterwheel used to lift water for irrigating land. It is a technology term from medieval Indian agrarian history, not a term for labour, land grants or land reclamation.

ocr: With reference to the cultural history of India, the memorizing of chronicles, dynastic histories and epic tales was the profession of who of the following? Shramana fa) Parivraajaka (b) Agrahaarika - (a) Maagadha (d)
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Sutas and Maagadhas formed a class of hereditary court bards and genealogists in ancient Indian society. The Suta traditionally recited the Puranas and epic material (Lomaharshana and his son Ugrashravas Sauti are the classic Suta narrators of the Mahabharata and Puranas), while the Maagadha was the panegyrist and chronicler who praised kings and preserved dynastic genealogies (vamsha) and heroic traditions. They accompanied kings, recited at sacrifices and court functions, and thereby preserved oral history before it was written down in the Puranas and Itihasa literature. The other options refer to different categories: Shramanas and Parivraajakas were ascetic or wandering religious seekers belonging to non-Vedic or heterodox traditions (Buddhists, Jains, Ajivikas), and Agrahaarikas were officials or holders connected with agrahara land grants made to Brahmins. Elimination logic: any option denoting a religious ascetic (a, b) or a land-grant-related person (c) has nothing to do with memorizing chronicles, leaving Maagadha as the bard-chronicler.
explanations: Incorrect: Shramana refers to an ascetic or renunciant in the non-Vedic traditions such as Buddhism, Jainism and Ajivika; their role was spiritual, not memorizing royal chronicles.
Incorrect: Parivraajaka means a wandering mendicant or ascetic who renounced household life in search of spiritual truth; not a chronicler profession.
Incorrect: Agrahaarika relates to agrahara, land granted to Brahmins or temples (or the people or officials associated with such grants); it is not a bardic profession.
Correct: Maagadha was the hereditary bard and genealogist who memorized and recited chronicles, dynastic histories and epic tales, often paired with the Suta.
keyfact: Sutas and Maagadhas were hereditary bards and chroniclers who preserved genealogies, dynastic histories and epic tales orally in ancient India.
summary: The correct answer is (d) Maagadha. In ancient India, the Maagadhas (along with Sutas) were hereditary bards and chroniclers who memorized and recited genealogies, dynastic histories, royal chronicles and epic tales.

ocr: Recently, for the first time in our country, which of the following States has declared a particular butterfly as ‘State Butterfly’? “Arunachal Pradesh- —+— fa} - Himachal Pradesh (b) Karnataka (c) Maharashtra (dj
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Maharashtra announced the Blue Mormon as its State Butterfly in June 2015 (the notification and wide publicity came in 2015-16), and it is regarded as the first state in India to do so. The Blue Mormon is a large swallowtail butterfly found in the Western Ghats, peninsular India and Sri Lanka. It is on Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (as amended 2022 it is protected as a scheduled species), and it resembles the Common Mormon but is larger and bluer. Later, Uttarakhand (Common Peacock), Karnataka (Southern Birdwing), Kerala (Malabar Banded Peacock, 2020), Tamil Nadu (Tamil Yeoman, 2019), Himachal Pradesh (Krishna Peacock, 2021) and Arunachal-linked species were named. Elimination logic: Karnataka had proposed the Southern Birdwing (India's largest butterfly) earlier but did not formally declare it first; Himachal and Arunachal declared much later. The 'first time in our country' phrase plus 2016 timing points to Maharashtra. State symbols are declared by state governments, usually on recommendation of the State Wildlife Board, and have no constitutional basis.
explanations: Incorrect. Arunachal Pradesh is rich in butterflies (Kaiser-i-Hind is associated with it) but it did not become the first state to declare a state butterfly.
Incorrect. Himachal Pradesh declared the Krishna Peacock (Papilio krishna) as state butterfly only in 2021, years after Maharashtra.
Incorrect. Karnataka's Southern Birdwing (Troides minos) was formally declared in 2017 or later after proposals; it was not first. Karnataka had earlier proposed it in 2015 but Maharashtra was first.
Correct. Maharashtra declared the Blue Mormon (Papilio polymnestor) as its State Butterfly, the first Indian state to do so.
keyfact: Maharashtra: first state to declare a State Butterfly, the Blue Mormon (Papilio polymnestor).
option_notes: Arunachal Pradesh: northeastern state in the Eastern Himalaya, a biodiversity hotspot with over 600 butterfly species. Kaiser-i-Hind (Teinopalpus imperialis) occurs here. Namdapha National Park is a major butterfly area. Its state animal is Mithun, state bird Great Hornbill and state flower Foxtail Orchid. Capital Itanagar.

Himachal Pradesh: Western Himalayan state with Great Himalayan National Park (UNESCO site, 2014). It declared the Krishna Peacock (Papilio krishna) as state butterfly in 2021. State animal is Snow Leopard, state bird Western Tragopan (Jujurana), state flower Pink Rhododendron.

Karnataka: Home to the Southern Birdwing (Troides minos), India's largest butterfly, found in the Western Ghats. It was later named state butterfly. Karnataka also has the Butterfly Park at Bannerghatta near Bengaluru, India's first enclosed butterfly park in a national park setting. State animal is Elephant, bird Indian Roller.

Maharashtra: Declared the Blue Mormon (Papilio polymnestor) as State Butterfly, the first Indian state to do so. The butterfly is velvety black with sky-blue patches and found in Western Ghats and Konkan. Other symbols: Giant Squirrel (Shekru) state animal, Green Imperial Pigeon state bird, Jarul state flower, Mango state tree.
related: Maharashtra was the first state to declare a State Butterfly: Blue Mormon.
Blue Mormon scientific name: Papilio polymnestor.
Southern Birdwing (Troides minos) is India's largest butterfly.
Kerala's state butterfly is the Malabar Banded Peacock (Papilio buddha).
Tamil Nadu's state butterfly is the Tamil Yeoman, declared 2019.
Kaiser-i-Hind is a Himalayan swallowtail found in Arunachal, Sikkim and Northeast.
Bannerghatta Biological Park has India's first large butterfly park.
Western Ghats became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012.
summary: The answer is (d) Maharashtra. In 2016 Maharashtra became the first Indian state to declare a State Butterfly, choosing the Blue Mormon (Papilio polymnestor). Other states adopted state butterflies only afterwards.
topic_notes: State symbols are a recurring UPSC theme. A state butterfly is a conservation flagship that draws attention to pollinators and habitat. Maharashtra's choice, the Blue Mormon, is a swallowtail of the family Papilionidae, widely seen in the Western Ghats, Konkan and urban gardens, with a wingspan of about 120-150 mm. It is a mimic of the unpalatable Common Rose butterfly in some forms. The Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 lists several butterflies in schedules; the Kaiser-i-Hind, Southern Birdwing and others have protected status. India's national butterfly has been proposed but not formally declared; the Orange Oakleaf (Kallima inachus) was suggested in 2018 by a butterfly body. Other states: Uttarakhand declared the Common Peacock as its state butterfly in 2016, Tamil Nadu the Tamil Yeoman (Cirrochroa thais) in 2019, Kerala the Malabar Banded Peacock (Papilio buddha) in 2020, Himachal the Krishna Peacock in 2021, Odisha (Tawny Coster) in 2021, Karnataka the Southern Birdwing, and Goa and Maharashtra link to Western Ghats fauna. India has around 1,300+ butterfly species. Largest Indian butterfly: Southern Birdwing; smallest: Grass Jewel; Golden Birdwing is also large. Related Western Ghats biodiversity: UNESCO World Heritage listing in 2012. Pollination services, indicator species role and butterfly parks (Bannerghatta, Tungareshwar in Maharashtra, Lalbagh) are possible angles. Also remember national symbols: tiger, peacock, lotus, Ganges river dolphin (national aquatic animal), Indian elephant (national heritage animal), and Banyan.

ocr: Consider the following statements : The Mangalyaan launched by ISRO 1. is also called the Mars Orbiter Mission 2. made India the second country to have a_ spacecraft orbit the Mars after USA 3. made India the. only country to be successful in making its spacecraft orbit the Mars in its very first ‘ attempt : Which of the statements given above is/are correct? {a) 1 only {b) 2 and 3 only {ec} 1 and 3 only (a) 1, 2 and 3
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Mangalyaan, officially the Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM), was launched by ISRO on 5 November 2013 from Sriharikota on PSLV-C25 (XL variant). It entered Martian orbit on 24 September 2014, making India the first Asian nation to reach Mars orbit and the first country in the world to do so on its maiden attempt. Several earlier Mars missions had failed, including Japan's Nozomi (2003), China's Yinghuo-1 (lost with Russia's Phobos-Grunt in 2011) and many Soviet probes. The mission cost about Rs 450 crore (around USD 74 million), among the cheapest interplanetary missions. It is a technology demonstrator, and its payloads include the Mars Colour Camera, the Methane Sensor for Mars, the Lyman Alpha Photometer, a thermal infrared imaging spectrometer and an energetic neutral analyser. Elimination logic: statement 1 is plainly true, so option (a) 'only 1' must be tested against 3. The claim of being second after the USA is false, since the Soviet Union's Mars 2 (1971) became the first to orbit Mars, and NASA's Mariner 9 (1971) followed. Statement 2 is therefore wrong, which eliminates (b) and (d). That leaves (c), and statement 3 is true because it is the only first-attempt success.
explanations: (a) is wrong: statement 1 is correct, but statement 3 is also correct, so 'only 1' is incomplete.
(b) is wrong: it includes statement 2, which is false because the USSR and ESA reached Mars orbit before India, and it leaves out statement 1, which is true.
(c) is right: statement 1 (Mars Orbiter Mission) and statement 3 (success on the first attempt) are correct, while statement 2 is false.
(d) is wrong: it includes statement 2, and India was the fourth space agency, not the second country, to orbit Mars.
keyfact: Mangalyaan (MOM), launched 5 Nov 2013 and in Mars orbit from 24 Sept 2014, made India the only country to succeed on its first attempt, and the fourth space agency to reach Mars.
option_notes: Option (a), 'only 1', would mean that the only correct fact is the name. The name is true: Mangalyaan means 'Mars craft' in Sanskrit and Hindi, and the mission is formally the Mars Orbiter Mission. It is India's first interplanetary probe, launched on 5 Nov 2013 by PSLV-C25 and inserted into Mars orbit on 24 Sept 2014. The mission cost around Rs 450 crore, and the orbiter weighed about 1,337 kg at launch. Option (a) is incomplete because it ignores the first-attempt success.

Option (b), '2 and 3 only', combines a false statement with a true one. The 'second after USA' claim is false because earlier orbiters included the USSR's Mars 2 and 3 in 1971 and ESA's Mars Express in 2003. The first-attempt success is true. India is the fourth agency to reach Mars, after the Soviet space programme, NASA and ESA.

Option (c), '1 and 3 only', is the correct option. It captures that Mangalyaan is the Mars Orbiter Mission and that India succeeded in orbiting Mars on its first try. Key facts are the launch on 5 Nov 2013 from Sriharikota, orbit insertion on 24 Sept 2014, a low cost of about Rs 450 crore, and India being the first Asian nation to reach Mars orbit. Its payloads were five instruments for studying Mars.

Option (d), '1, 2 and 3', is wrong because statement 2 is false. India was not the second country after the USA to orbit Mars, since the Soviet Union (Mars 2 and 3 in 1971) and ESA (Mars Express in 2003) had done it earlier. India is the fourth space agency to reach Mars. The UAE's Hope probe and China's Tianwen-1 both arrived in Feb 2021.
related: MOM was launched on 5 Nov 2013 by PSLV-C25 from Sriharikota.
MOM entered Mars orbit on 24 Sept 2014.
India is the first Asian country to reach Mars orbit and the first in the world to do so on its first attempt.
MOM's cost was about Rs 450 crore, among the cheapest Mars missions.
MOM payloads include the Methane Sensor for Mars and the Mars Colour Camera.
Chandrayaan-3 landed near the lunar south pole on 23 Aug 2023.
The UAE's Hope probe reached Mars orbit in Feb 2021.
AstroSat (2015) is India's first dedicated astronomy satellite.
statements: 1 — Correct: Mangalyaan is the popular name of ISRO's Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM). It was India's first interplanetary mission, approved in 2012 and launched on 5 Nov 2013 by PSLV-C25 from Sriharikota. It was injected into Mars orbit on 24 Sept 2014 with a planned mission life of six months, but it operated for several years. It carried five scientific payloads, including the Mars Colour Camera and the Methane Sensor for Mars, and its aim was to demonstrate deep-space technology and study the Martian surface and atmosphere. Communication with the orbiter was lost in 2022.

2 — Incorrect: India was not the second country to orbit Mars after the USA. The USSR's Mars 2 and Mars 3 (1971) were the first to orbit Mars, and NASA's Mariner 9 (Nov 1971) was the first to orbit it successfully for sustained study. Later orbiters came from NASA (Mars Global Surveyor, Odyssey, MRO, MAVEN) and from ESA (Mars Express, 2003). India became the fourth space agency to reach Mars, after the Soviet space programme, NASA and ESA. The UAE's Hope (2021) and China's Tianwen-1 (2021) came afterwards.

3 — Correct: India is the only country to succeed in placing a spacecraft in Mars orbit on its first attempt. The US, USSR and ESA had earlier failures or later successes: the USSR had many failed probes, and Japan's Nozomi (1998) failed to enter orbit. China's Yinghuo-1 was lost with Phobos-Grunt in 2011. The UAE's Hope (2021) also succeeded on its first try, but it came after India. The 'only' in the statement is accepted as correct in the official key, and India was also the first to do so.
summary: The answer is (c): statements 1 and 3 are correct, and statement 2 is incorrect. Mangalyaan is the Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM), and India is the only country to reach Mars orbit on its very first attempt. India was not the second country to orbit Mars after the USA, because the USSR, ESA and others had already done so.
topic_notes: Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM), or Mangalyaan, was India's first interplanetary mission, run by ISRO. It was launched on 5 Nov 2013 from Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota, by PSLV-C25 in its XL configuration. The spacecraft first went into Earth orbit, was raised through several orbit-raising manoeuvres, and then did a trans-Mars injection on 1 Dec 2013. It entered Mars orbit on 24 Sept 2014 in an elliptical orbit of about 421 km by 76,000 km. The cost was about Rs 450 crore, and the planned life was 6 months but it lasted about 8 years. Payloads: Mars Colour Camera (MCC), Methane Sensor for Mars (MSM), Lyman Alpha Photometer (LAP), Thermal Infrared Imaging Spectrometer (TIS) and Mars Exospheric Neutral Composition Analyser (MENCA). Signals were lost in 2022 after prolonged eclipses drained the battery. India was the first Asian country to reach Mars orbit and the fourth space agency after the Soviet space programme, NASA and ESA. Other Mars missions: NASA's Mariner 4 (1965, first flyby), the USSR's Mars 3 (1971, first soft landing), NASA's Viking (1976), Curiosity (2012), Perseverance (2021), and MAVEN (2014). The UAE's Hope and China's Tianwen-1 reached Mars in 2021, and Tianwen-1 also landed a rover (Zhurong). ISRO's follow-up, Mangalyaan-2 or Mars Lander Mission, is planned. Other ISRO milestones: Chandrayaan-1 (2008, found water molecules with NASA's M3), Chandrayaan-3 (23 Aug 2023, soft landing near the lunar south pole), Aditya-L1 (solar mission, launched 2023), AstroSat (2015, first Indian multi-wavelength space observatory), and Gaganyaan (human spaceflight programme).

question: What was the main reason for the split in the Indian National Congress at Surat in 1907?
options: Introduction of communalism into Indian politics by Lord Minto
Extremists’ lack of faith in the capacity of the moderates to negotiate with the British Government
Aurobindo Ghosh’s inability to be elected as the President of the Indian National Congress
subject: Modern History
detail: The Congress was founded in 1885 and for two decades the Moderates (Dadabhai Naoroji, Gokhale, Pherozeshah Mehta, Surendranath Banerjee) pursued constitutional agitation. The Partition of Bengal (1905) and the Swadeshi and Boycott movement exposed a rift. The Extremists, or Radical Nationalists, believed British rulers would not respond to petitions and favoured passive resistance, boycott and self-reliance. At Calcutta (1906), under Dadabhai Naoroji, a compromise resolution endorsed Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott and National Education. The Extremists wanted Lala Lajpat Rai or Tilak as president at the next session, while the Moderates backed Rash Behari Ghosh. The venue shifted from Nagpur to Surat, and the session in December 1907 ended in chaos, with shoes thrown and the session suspended. The Moderates then held a separate convention and adopted a constitution restricting Congress to constitutional means. The government then repressed the Extremists, and Tilak was jailed in 1908. Elimination: Minto's communal policy (Morley-Minto reforms, 1909) came after Surat. The Muslim League was founded in December 1906 but was not the cause of the split. Aurobindo was never a presidential candidate in this dispute.
explanations: Incorrect: Lord Minto's communal electorates came with the Indian Councils Act 1909, after the split, and were not its cause.
Correct: The fundamental difference was the Extremists' loss of faith in the Moderates' petitioning and negotiation with the British, which led to the Surat split.
Incorrect: The Muslim League was founded in 1906 at Dhaka, but this had no direct bearing on the Moderate-Extremist rift at Surat.
Incorrect: The dispute concerned the choice of president (Lajpat Rai versus Rash Behari Ghosh) and the ideological direction. Aurobindo's candidature was not the issue.
keyfact: Surat split (December 1907): Extremists vs Moderates over methods; Rash Behari Ghosh presided, and Tilak's faction was expelled.
summary: The correct answer is (b). The Surat split of December 1907 arose because the Extremists (Tilak, Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal, Aurobindo) had lost faith in the Moderates' method of petitions, prayers and constitutional negotiation with the British, and wanted a more assertive programme built on Swadeshi, boycott and national education.

ocr: The plan of Sir Stafford Cripps envisaged that after the Second World War {a) India should be granted complete __- - — _ independence. {b) India should be partitioned into two before granting independence (c} India should be made a republic : with the condition that she will join the Commonwealth (dj) India should be given Dominion status B-APM-P-CKB/65A
subject: Geography
detail: In March 1942, with Japan advancing in Southeast Asia and Britain under pressure from the USA, China and the Labour Party, the British War Cabinet sent Sir Stafford Cripps, Lord Privy Seal and Leader of the House of Commons, to India. The Draft Declaration offered: (1) Dominion status for India after the war, with the freedom to secede from the Commonwealth; (2) a Constituent Assembly elected by provincial assemblies and nominated by princely states to frame the Constitution; (3) the right of any province to stay out of the Union and negotiate its own arrangements with Britain (the 'local option' clause, seen as a seed of Pakistan); (4) Britain retaining control of defence during the war. Congress rejected it because of Dominion status instead of full independence, the provincial opt-out provision and the unequal representation of princely states. Gandhi reportedly called it 'a post-dated cheque on a crumbling bank'. The Muslim League disliked it because Pakistan was not explicitly conceded. Elimination: complete independence (a) was demanded, not offered; partition (b) was not proposed explicitly; a republic (c) was not mentioned. Remember Dominion status was the keyword.
explanations: Incorrect: Complete independence (Purna Swaraj) was the Congress demand, not what Cripps offered; the offer was only Dominion status after the war.
Incorrect: The plan did not propose partition. It only allowed provinces to opt out of the Union, which indirectly hinted at it, but there was no explicit division into two before independence.
Incorrect: A republic was not offered. The plan offered Dominion status under the Crown, with the freedom to leave the Commonwealth, not a republic conditional on joining it.
Correct: The Cripps proposals promised Dominion status after the war, plus a Constituent Assembly and a provincial opt-out right.
keyfact: Cripps Mission (March 1942) offered Dominion status after WWII, a Constituent Assembly and a provincial opt-out; Congress rejected it.
summary: The correct answer is (d): the Cripps Mission (March 1942) offered India Dominion status after the Second World War. The offer was to be implemented after the war, with a Constituent Assembly to frame the Constitution and a right for provinces to opt out.

ocr: Consider the following pairs : Famous place Region 1. Bodhgaya §: —_‘ Baghelkhand 2. Khajuraho : Bundelkhand 3. Shirdi : Vidarbha 4. Nasik (Nashik) : Malwa 5. Tirupati- Rayalaseema Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched? fa} 1, 2 and 4 (b) 2, 3, 4 and 5 (c) 2 and 5 only fd) 1, 3,4 and 5
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This is a cultural-geography question testing the link between famous places and historical-cultural regions. Khajuraho (Chhatarpur district, Madhya Pradesh) is a UNESCO World Heritage Site built by the Chandela dynasty (c. 950-1050 CE) in Bundelkhand, so pair 2 is right. Tirupati (Chittoor district, Andhra Pradesh) lies in Rayalaseema, the southern interior region comprising Anantapur, Kurnool, Kadapa and Chittoor, so pair 5 is right. Bodhgaya is in Gaya district, Bihar, in the ancient Magadha region; Baghelkhand is the eastern Madhya Pradesh/Rewa region, around Rewa and Satna, so pair 1 is wrong. Shirdi is in Ahmednagar district, Maharashtra, in the Khandesh/Western Maharashtra region, while Vidarbha is the eastern Maharashtra region around Nagpur and Amravati, so pair 3 is wrong. Nashik, on the Godavari, is in north Maharashtra; Malwa is the plateau region of western Madhya Pradesh around Ujjain and Indore, so pair 4 is wrong. Elimination logic: knowing that Khajuraho and Tirupati are correct while Bodhgaya is wrong immediately leaves only option (c), since every other option includes pair 1, 3 or 4.
explanations: (a) Wrong: it includes pairs 1 and 4, both mismatched (Bodhgaya is not in Baghelkhand and Nasik is not in Malwa).
(b) Wrong: it includes pairs 3 and 4, which are incorrect (Shirdi is not in Vidarbha, Nasik is not in Malwa).
(c) Right: only pairs 2 (Khajuraho-Bundelkhand) and 5 (Tirupati-Rayalaseema) are correctly matched.
(d) Wrong: it includes pairs 1, 3 and 4, all incorrect, and omits the correct pairs 2 and 5.
keyfact: Khajuraho = Bundelkhand and Tirupati = Rayalaseema; Bodhgaya = Magadh, Shirdi = western Maharashtra, Nashik = north Maharashtra (not Malwa).
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Bodhgaya is in Gaya district, Bihar (Magadh region); Baghelkhand is in eastern Madhya Pradesh around Rewa.
2 — Correct: Khajuraho, the Chandela temple site, lies in the Bundelkhand region of Madhya Pradesh.
3 — Incorrect: Shirdi is in Ahmednagar district, western Maharashtra; Vidarbha is eastern Maharashtra (Nagpur region).
4 — Incorrect: Nashik is in north Maharashtra on the Godavari; Malwa is in western Madhya Pradesh.
5 — Correct: Tirupati in Chittoor district lies in the Rayalaseema region of Andhra Pradesh.
summary: The correct answer is (c): only pairs 2 and 5 are correctly matched. Khajuraho lies in Bundelkhand and Tirupati lies in Rayalaseema, whereas Bodhgaya is in Magadh (Bihar, not Baghelkhand), Shirdi is in Maharashtra's Khandesh/Marathwada-Nashik belt (not Vidarbha), and Nasik is in North Maharashtra (not Malwa).

question: The Parliament of India acquires the power to legislate on any item in the State List in the national interest if a resolution to that effect is passed by the
options: ’ Lok Sabha by a simple majority of its total membership
Lok Sabha by a majority of not less than two-thirds of its total - .. membership
Rajya Sabha by a simple majority of its total membership
Rajya Sabha by a majority of not less than two-thirds of its members present and voting
subject: Polity
detail: Article 249 is an exception to the normal federal division of powers in Schedule VII. If the Rajya Sabha declares by a resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of members present and voting that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest for Parliament to legislate on a matter in the State List, Parliament gets the power to make laws on that matter for the whole or any part of India. The resolution must specify the matter. It remains in force for up to one year and can be renewed any number of times, each renewal for up to one year. Laws made under it cease to have effect six months after the resolution lapses. Only the Rajya Sabha initiates this, the Lok Sabha has no role in passing the resolution. The majority is a special one: two-thirds of those present and voting, not of total membership. Do not confuse it with Article 250 (during a National Emergency, Parliament can legislate on State List matters), Article 252 (legislation by consent of two or more states) or Article 253 (implementing international agreements). Elimination: options (a) and (b) wrongly name the Lok Sabha, option (c) names the correct House but the wrong majority (simple majority of total membership).
explanations: Incorrect: The Lok Sabha does not pass the Article 249 resolution, and a simple majority of total membership is not the required threshold.
Incorrect: The Lok Sabha has no role in this resolution, so a two-thirds majority of its total membership is irrelevant.
Incorrect: The House is correct, but the majority is wrong. Article 249 requires two-thirds of members present and voting, not a simple majority of total membership.
Correct: Article 249 requires a Rajya Sabha resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of members present and voting.
keyfact: Article 249: Rajya Sabha resolution by two-thirds of members present and voting lets Parliament legislate on a State List subject for up to 1 year, renewable.
summary: The answer is (d). Under Article 249, Parliament can legislate on a State List subject in the national interest only after the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution supported by at least two-thirds of members present and voting. The Rajya Sabha represents the states, so it is given this safeguard role.

ocr: Recently, which of the following States 98. has explored the _ possibility of constructing an artificial inland port to be connected to sea by a_.long navigational channel? ‘ fa) Andhra Pradesh (b) Chhattisgarh (c) Kamataka (da) Rajasthan
subject: Geography
detail: The question is based on a 2016 news item. The Rajasthan government, backed by the Union Ministry of Shipping, considered an artificial inland port in the state, connected to the sea by a long navigational channel. Rajasthan is landlocked and has no natural coastline or navigable river system for sea access. The proposal was to link the port to the Arabian Sea via a channel running through Gujarat, with the Gulf of Kutch or the Kandla and Mundra area as the sea end. A feasibility study was discussed under the Sagarmala initiative. Sagarmala was launched in 2015 to promote port-led development, modernise ports, and improve coastal and inland water connectivity. The key logic for elimination is geographic. Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka already have long coastlines and many natural and major ports, so they have no need for an artificial inland port linked to the sea by a long channel. Chhattisgarh is landlocked but has no desert or arid-region rationale and was not in the news for this proposal. Rajasthan is the landlocked state with the Thar desert and a long distance to the coast, which fits the idea of a long channel. Students should link such current-affairs items to the scheme behind them (Sagarmala) and to the ministry involved (Shipping).
explanations: Incorrect: Andhra Pradesh has a long coastline of about 970 km and several ports (Visakhapatnam, Krishnapatnam, Kakinada), so it needs no artificial inland port linked by a long channel.
Incorrect: Chhattisgarh is landlocked, but it was not the state that explored this proposal. The idea was not associated with it.
Incorrect: Karnataka has a coastline with ports such as New Mangalore and Karwar, so it has no need for an artificial inland port connected by a long channel.
Correct: Rajasthan is landlocked and explored an artificial inland port linked to the sea (via Gujarat's coast) by a long navigational channel, in the context of the Sagarmala initiative.
keyfact: Rajasthan (landlocked) explored an artificial inland port linked to the sea by a long navigational channel through Gujarat, in the Sagarmala context.
summary: The answer is (d) Rajasthan. The state explored building an artificial inland port in its desert interior, linked to the sea by a long navigational channel. The idea was to cut a channel from the Gulf of Kutch in Gujarat to Rajasthan, giving the landlocked state access to maritime trade.

question:
With reference to the Agreement at the UNFCCC Meeting in Paris in 2015, which of the following statements is/are correct? ‘1. The Agreement was signed by all 99. the member countries of the UN and it will go into effect in 2017.
2. The Agreement aims to limit the greenhouse gas emissions so that the rise in average global temperature by the end of this century does not exceed 2°C or ‘even 1:5°C -above pre-industrial levels. 100.
3. Developed countries acknowledged their historical responsibility in global warming and committed to donate $ 1000 billion a year from 2020 to help developing countries to cope with climate change. Select the correct answer using the code _. .Biven below
subject: Environment
detail: The Paris Agreement was adopted on 12 December 2015 at COP21 of the UNFCCC by consensus of 195 parties. It was opened for signature on 22 April 2016 in New York. It entered into force on 4 November 2016, after the double threshold was met: ratification by at least 55 parties accounting for at least 55% of global emissions. Its central goal under Article 2 is to hold the temperature rise well below 2°C and pursue efforts toward 1.5°C. It works through bottom-up Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), reviewed through a five-yearly global stocktake, rather than binding top-down targets as under the Kyoto Protocol. On finance, developed countries reaffirmed a goal of mobilising USD 100 billion a year from 2020, with a new higher goal to be set by 2025. This is a mobilisation goal drawn from public and private sources, not a donation, and it is not 1000 billion. Elimination: statement 1 fails on 'all UN members signed' and on '2017', so options (a) and (d) go. Statement 3 fails on the amount, so option (c) goes. That leaves (b).
explanations: Wrong: it pairs statement 1 (not all UN members signed at adoption, and entry into force was 2016) with statement 3 (the amount is 100 billion, not 1000 billion). Both are incorrect.
Right: only statement 2 is correct, on the well below 2°C and 1.5°C goal. Statements 1 and 3 contain factual errors.
Wrong: statement 3 is false because the finance goal is USD 100 billion a year, not 1000 billion, and it is a mobilisation goal rather than a donation.
Wrong: statements 1 and 3 are both incorrect, so 'all three' cannot be right.
keyfact: Paris Agreement (COP21, 2015): in force 4 Nov 2016; goal well below 2°C, pursue 1.5°C; finance USD 100 bn a year from 2020 (not 1000 bn).
option_notes: Options 1 and 3 only: this combines two flawed claims. The Paris Agreement was adopted by 195 parties in December 2015, opened for signature in April 2016, and entered into force on 4 November 2016. The finance goal is USD 100 billion a year from 2020, drawn from public and private sources and channelled through bodies like the Green Climate Fund, the Adaptation Fund and the GEF. The goal was later raised at COP29 to USD 300 billion a year by 2035.

Option 2 only: this is the correct answer. Article 2 of the Paris Agreement commits parties to holding the temperature rise well below 2°C and pursuing 1.5°C. It rests on NDCs submitted by each country, transparency requirements under the Enhanced Transparency Framework, and a five-year global stocktake. The Agreement also covers mitigation, adaptation, loss and damage (Article 8), finance, technology and capacity building. It replaced the Kyoto Protocol's top-down approach with a bottom-up one.

Options 2 and 3 only: this pairs the correct statement 2 with the wrong statement 3. The finance figure in Paris was USD 100 billion a year from 2020, to be revisited by 2025. Developed countries recognised their leadership role under CBDR-RC, but the Agreement does not frame finance as a donation based on historical responsibility. Loss and damage was included, with a clause that it does not involve liability or compensation. India stressed climate justice and equity throughout.

Options 1, 2 and 3: this accepts all statements and is wrong because of statements 1 and 3. Not every UN member state signed on the same day, since signature opened on 22 April 2016. Entry into force came on 4 November 2016, less than a year after adoption and much faster than the Kyoto Protocol, which was adopted in 1997 and took effect in 2005. The finance goal is USD 100 billion, not 1000 billion.
related: Paris Agreement: adopted 12 Dec 2015; in force 4 Nov 2016; India ratified 2 Oct 2016.
Entry into force threshold: 55 parties covering at least 55% of global GHG emissions.
Goal: well below 2°C, pursue 1.5°C; NDCs reviewed through five-yearly global stocktake.
Finance goal: USD 100 bn a year from 2020; COP29 Baku set USD 300 bn a year by 2035.
International Solar Alliance was launched at COP21 Paris by India and France.
Kyoto Protocol: adopted 1997, in force 2005; binding targets only for Annex I countries.
India's net-zero target is 2070, announced at COP26 Glasgow (2021).
COP27 Sharm el-Sheikh (2022) agreed to set up a loss and damage fund.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Not all UN members signed at the start, and the Agreement entered into force in 2016, not 2017. Facts: it was adopted on 12 December 2015 by 195 parties and opened for signature on 22 April 2016 at UN headquarters, when 175 parties signed on the first day, a record. Entry into force needed 55 parties covering 55% of emissions, achieved on 5 October 2016, so it took effect on 4 November 2016. India ratified on 2 October 2016. The USA withdrew in 2020, rejoined in 2021, and announced withdrawal again in 2025.

2 — Correct: Article 2 sets the goal of holding the temperature rise well below 2°C and pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels. Facts: the IPCC Special Report on 1.5°C (2018) later showed the greater benefits of the lower limit. Parties also aim for global peaking of emissions as soon as possible and net-zero balance of emissions and removals in the second half of the century. The Agreement is legally binding as a treaty, but NDC targets are nationally determined. Every five years parties submit more ambitious NDCs, and the first global stocktake concluded at COP28 in 2023.

3 — Incorrect: The figure is USD 100 billion per year from 2020, not 1000 billion, and it is a mobilisation goal rather than a donation. Facts: the 100 billion goal was first made at Copenhagen (COP15, 2009) and confirmed at Cancun (2010). The Paris decision extended it to 2025, after which a new collective quantified goal would be set. At COP29 in Baku (2024) that goal was set at USD 300 billion a year by 2035, within a wider aspiration of 1.3 trillion. The Green Climate Fund (Songdo, South Korea) is the main channel. The principle underlying this is Common But Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC).
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. The Paris Agreement (COP21, December 2015) aims to hold the rise in global average temperature well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C. Statements 1 and 3 are factually wrong on the signatories and entry-into-force date, and on the finance figure.
topic_notes: The UNFCCC was adopted at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992 and entered into force in 1994. Its secretariat is in Bonn, and the Conference of the Parties (COP) is its supreme body. The Kyoto Protocol (1997, in force 2005) set binding targets for developed (Annex I) countries only. Its first commitment period ran 2008-12 and the second, under the Doha Amendment, ran 2013-20. The Paris Agreement (COP21, 2015) is universal: all parties, developed and developing, submit NDCs. Key elements are the 2°C and 1.5°C temperature goals, a five-year ratchet cycle, a global stocktake (first one in 2023), the Enhanced Transparency Framework, Article 6 carbon markets and cooperative approaches, adaptation goals, and loss and damage. Finance: USD 100 billion a year from 2020, with the new goal of USD 300 billion by 2035 agreed at COP29 in Baku. India's NDC was updated in 2022: reduce emissions intensity of GDP by 45% from 2005 levels by 2030, and reach about 50% non-fossil electric capacity by 2030. India also announced net zero by 2070 at COP26 Glasgow (2021) and the Panchamrit commitments. Other milestones: Bali Action Plan (2007), Copenhagen (2009), Cancun (2010) and the Green Climate Fund, Warsaw Mechanism on loss and damage (2013), Lima (2014), COP26 (phase-down of unabated coal), COP27 (loss and damage fund established), COP28 Dubai (transition away from fossil fuels). Related groups include the International Solar Alliance (launched by India and France at COP21), CBDR-RC, the Emissions Gap Report (UNEP), and the IPCC (WMO-UNEP, 1988).

ocr: Consider the following statements : 1. The Sustainable Development Goals were first proposed in 1972 by a global think tank called the ‘Club of Rome’. 2. The Sustainable Development Goals have to be achieved by 2030. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? fa) 1 only (b}) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 fd) Neither 1 nor 2 A recent movie titled The Man Who Knew Infinity is based on the biography of fa) S. Ramanujan (b) S, Chandrasekhar jc) 5S. N. Bose {d@) C. V. Raman
subject: Science & Tech
detail: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are 17 global goals with 169 targets, adopted by all UN member states on 25 September 2015 in the resolution 'Transforming our World: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development'. They took effect on 1 January 2016 and run to 2030. They replaced the eight Millennium Development Goals (2000-2015). The idea of SDGs was proposed by Colombia (with Guatemala) at the UN Conference on Sustainable Development, Rio+20, in 2012. An Open Working Group then drafted the goals. The Club of Rome is a think tank founded in 1968. In 1972 it published 'The Limits to Growth', a report on resource depletion and population growth modelled by MIT researchers. It influenced environmental thinking but did not propose the SDGs. The year 1972 is also linked to the Stockholm UN Conference on the Human Environment, which created UNEP, and this is probably what the question setter wanted students to confuse. Elimination logic: Statement 2 is a well-known fact, so options (a) and (d) can be dropped. Statement 1 has a wrong origin and date, so (c) is also out. That leaves (b).
explanations: (a) 1 only is wrong. Statement 1 is factually incorrect because the Club of Rome did not propose the SDGs in 1972, and Statement 2 is correct, so 'only 1' fails on both counts.
(b) 2 only is correct. The SDGs have a 2030 deadline, but their origin is Rio+20 (2012) and the 2015 UN adoption, not the Club of Rome in 1972.
(c) Both 1 and 2 is wrong. Statement 2 is correct, but Statement 1 wrongly attributes the SDGs to the Club of Rome in 1972.
(d) Neither 1 nor 2 is wrong because Statement 2 is correct: the target year for the SDGs is 2030.
keyfact: SDGs: 17 goals, deadline 2030, adopted in September 2015 and proposed at Rio+20 (2012); the Club of Rome's 1972 report was 'The Limits to Growth', not the SDGs.
related: The Club of Rome was founded in 1968; its 1972 report was 'The Limits to Growth'.
The SDGs were adopted at the UN General Assembly on 25 September 2015 and took effect on 1 January 2016.
There are 17 SDGs with 169 targets; the MDGs were 8 goals running from 2000 to 2015.
The SDG concept was proposed by Colombia and Guatemala at Rio+20 (2012).
The Brundtland Report 'Our Common Future' (1987) defined sustainable development.
The 1972 Stockholm Conference led to the creation of UNEP, and 5 June became World Environment Day.
NITI Aayog is India's nodal body for SDGs and publishes the SDG India Index.
SDG 13 is Climate Action, SDG 6 is Clean Water and Sanitation, and SDG 17 is Partnerships for the Goals.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: the SDGs were not proposed in 1972 by the Club of Rome. They originated at Rio+20 (2012) on a proposal from Colombia and Guatemala. The Club of Rome is a global think tank founded in 1968 by Aurelio Peccei and Alexander King, and it is based in Winterthur, Switzerland. In 1972 it published 'The Limits to Growth', which used the World3 computer model built by MIT researchers (Donella Meadows and others). The report warned that exponential growth in population, industrial output and resource use would hit planetary limits within about a century. It raised early alarms on sustainability, but it did not propose any goals. The year 1972 also saw the Stockholm Conference and the creation of UNEP.

2 — Correct: the SDGs are to be achieved by 2030, which is why the framework is called Agenda 2030. The UN General Assembly adopted it on 25 September 2015 and it came into force on 1 January 2016. It has 17 goals, 169 targets and about 232 global indicators. The goals include No Poverty (1), Zero Hunger (2), Good Health (3), Quality Education (4), Gender Equality (5), Clean Water (6), Clean Energy (7), Decent Work (8), Industry and Innovation (9), Reduced Inequalities (10), Sustainable Cities (11), Responsible Consumption (12), Climate Action (13), Life Below Water (14), Life on Land (15), Peace and Justice (16) and Partnerships (17). The High-Level Political Forum (HLPF) reviews progress each year. In India, NITI Aayog is the nodal body for SDG implementation and publishes the SDG India Index.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 only. The SDGs are to be achieved by 2030 under the UN's Agenda 2030. They were not proposed in 1972 by the Club of Rome. The SDG idea came from Colombia and Guatemala at the Rio+20 conference in 2012, and the UN General Assembly adopted the goals in September 2015.
topic_notes: Background: The SDGs follow a line of UN sustainability milestones. These are the Stockholm Conference (1972, which created UNEP), the Brundtland Report 'Our Common Future' (1987, which defined sustainable development as meeting present needs without compromising future generations), the Rio Earth Summit (1992, which produced Agenda 21 and the UNFCCC, CBD and UNCCD), the Millennium Summit (2000, which set the 8 MDGs for 2015), the Johannesburg Summit (2002) and Rio+20 (2012, 'The Future We Want'). The SDGs were adopted on 25 September 2015 as Agenda 2030, with 17 goals, 169 targets and about 232 indicators. They are universal, applying to developed and developing countries alike, and they are not legally binding. They are described around the '5 Ps': People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace and Partnership. Monitoring is done through the HLPF under ECOSOC and the General Assembly, and through Voluntary National Reviews. The UN Statistical Commission maintains the indicators. In India, NITI Aayog is the nodal agency. It publishes the SDG India Index (first released in 2018) and ranks states, with Kerala and Himachal Pradesh among the top performers in early editions. Other angles UPSC could ask: which MDG goals were replaced or expanded, the content of specific goals (such as Goal 13 on climate action and Goal 6 on water), the Sustainable Development Solutions Network and its SDG Index, and the Club of Rome's other publications. Also remember the Paris Agreement (2015), the Sendai Framework (2015-2030) and the Addis Ababa Action Agenda (2015, on financing).

ocr: Consider the following statements : 1. The minimum age prescribed for any person to be a member of Panchayat is 25 years. 2. A Panchayat reconstituted after _ premature dissolution continues only for the remainder period. Which of the statements given above . is/are correct? (a) 1 only (b) 2 only fc) Both 1 and 2 {d) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Polity
detail: Caution for the student: the official UPSC key for this question is (a), and that is the answer to mark. However, the constitutional position needs to be learned precisely. Article 243F disqualifies a person from membership of a Panchayat if he is disqualified under any law for the time being in force for the purposes of elections to the State Legislature, or under State law, but a person cannot be disqualified on the ground that he is less than 25 years of age if he has attained 21 years. Thus the minimum age for Panchayat membership is 21, not 25, and the 25-year benchmark applies to the State Legislative Assembly. Article 243E(1) fixes a five-year term from the first meeting. Article 243E(3) requires elections before the expiry of the term or, in case of dissolution, within six months. Article 243E(4) says a Panchayat constituted upon dissolution continues only for the remainder of the period for which the dissolved Panchayat would have continued. Applying these facts, statement 1 is wrong in substance and statement 2 is right in substance, which gives (b) 2 only. This conflicts with the stated official key (a). Since the instruction is to treat (a) as the official answer, mark (a) in the exam context, but verify against the constitutional text (Articles 243F and 243E) and the original UPSC answer key before relying on this note.
explanations: (a) 1 only: this is the official UPSC answer key, so it is the option to mark, though the constitutional text on age (21 years under Article 243F) should be double-checked.
(b) 2 only: this matches the constitutional position under Article 243E(4) for statement 2, but it does not match the official key.
(c) Both 1 and 2: not the official answer; statement 1 conflicts with the 21-year minimum age rule.
(d) Neither 1 nor 2: not the official answer; statement 2 aligns with Article 243E(4).
keyfact: Panchayat membership minimum age is 21 (Art. 243F); a reconstituted Panchayat serves only the remainder of the term (Art. 243E(4)); the official key for this question is (a).
statements: 1 — Treated as correct per the official key (a); note that Article 243F actually sets the minimum age at 21 years, so verify against the constitutional text.

2 — Treated as incorrect per the official key (a); note that Article 243E(4) states a reconstituted Panchayat continues only for the remainder of the original term, so verify against the constitutional text.
summary: The answer is (a): only statement 1 is correct. The minimum age to contest Panchayat elections is 21 years (Article 243F), not 25, so statement 1 as printed is treated as correct per the official key... but see detail for the nuance. Statement 2 is incorrect because a Panchayat reconstituted after premature dissolution continues only for the remainder period, which is actually correct under Article 243E(4), so the official key must be read carefully.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q100.
ocr: Consider the following statements : 1. The minimum age prescribed for any person to be a member of Panchayat is 25 years. 2. A Panchayat reconstituted after _ premature dissolution continues only for the remainder period. Which of the statements given above . is/are correct? (a) 1 only (b) 2 only fc) Both 1 and 2 {d) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Polity
detail: Part IX of the Constitution (Articles 243 to 243O), inserted by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 and in force from 24 April 1993, governs Panchayati Raj. Article 243F lays down the disqualifications for membership: a person is disqualified if disqualified under any law for the time being in force for the purposes of elections to the State Legislature, or under any law made by the State Legislature. The minimum age is 21 years, which is lower than the 25 years required for a Legislative Assembly member. Many students confuse this with the Assembly age. Article 243E fixes the duration of Panchayats at five years from the date of first meeting. Article 243E(3) requires that an election to constitute a Panchayat be completed before the expiry of its term, or, in case of dissolution, within six months of the date of dissolution. Article 243E(4) states that a Panchayat constituted upon dissolution before expiry of its duration shall continue only for the remainder of the period for which the dissolved Panchayat would have continued. No fresh five-year term begins. Elimination logic: statement 1 is wrong because the age is 21, so options (a) and (c) fall; statement 2 is right, so (d) falls, leaving (b).
explanations: (a) Wrong: it treats statement 1 as correct, but the minimum age is 21 years under Article 243F, and it also ignores that statement 2 is correct.
(b) Correct: statement 1 is false because the age is 21 years, and statement 2 is true under Article 243E(4), so only statement 2 holds.
(c) Wrong: it requires statement 1 to be correct, but the minimum age is 21 years, not 25 years.
(d) Wrong: statement 2 is correct, because a reconstituted Panchayat serves only the remainder of the original term.
keyfact: Panchayat member minimum age is 21 years (Art. 243F); a Panchayat reconstituted after premature dissolution serves only the remainder of the term (Art. 243E(4)).
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Article 243F sets the minimum age for Panchayat membership at 21 years, not 25 years.
2 — Correct: Under Article 243E(4), a Panchayat reconstituted after premature dissolution continues only for the unexpired remainder of the original five-year term.
summary: The correct answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. Under Article 243F, the minimum age to be a Panchayat member is 21 years, not 25, while Article 243E(4) provides that a Panchayat reconstituted after premature dissolution continues only for the remainder of the original five-year term.

question:
With reference to the Parliament of India, 3. consider the following statements :
1. A private member’s bill is a_ bill presented by a Member of Parliament who is not elected but only nominated by the President of India.
2. Recently, a priyate member's bill has ’ been passed in the Parliament of India for the first time in its history. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Polity
detail: In Parliament, bills are classified as Government Bills (introduced by a minister) and Private Members' Bills (introduced by any MP who is not a minister). The status of the member as elected or nominated is irrelevant. Nominated members (12 in Rajya Sabha, up to 2 Anglo-Indians in Lok Sabha at the time) are only a small subset of private members, and elected MPs introduce most such bills. Private members' bills are taken up on Friday afternoons, in the last 2.5 hours of sitting, and they require a one-month notice. Government bills have priority and are backed by the government's support; their defeat can signal loss of confidence, whereas the rejection of a private member's bill carries no such implication. Historically, very few private members' bills have been passed: about 14 have become law since Independence, and the Rajya Sabha passed the Rights of Transgender Persons Bill, 2014 (Tiruchi Siva) in 2015, which is the only such bill passed by one House in 45 years. It did not become law because the Lok Sabha did not take it up. Hence statement 2, which says it was passed for the first time in history, is wrong because earlier private bills were passed (the last in 1970, the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Bill). Both statements fail, so (d).
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 wrongly restricts private members' bills to nominated members; any non-minister MP can introduce one.
(b) is wrong because statement 2 is factually incorrect; passage of private members' bills has happened before, so it is not a first in history.
(c) is wrong because both statements are incorrect, so they cannot both be correct.
(d) is correct because statement 1 misdefines a private member's bill and statement 2 makes a false 'first time' claim.
keyfact: A private member's bill is introduced by any non-minister MP (elected or nominated); about 14 have become law, the last in 1970.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: A private member's bill is introduced by any MP other than a minister, whether elected or nominated; it is not limited to nominated members.

2 — Incorrect: Private members' bills have been passed before (about 14 enacted since Independence, the last in 1970); the 2015 Rajya Sabha passage of the Transgender Persons Bill was only passage by one House, and not a first in history.
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is correct. A private member's bill can be introduced by any MP who is not a minister, whether elected or nominated, and no such bill has been passed in the recent past in the way the statement claims.

ocr: With reference to the difference between the culture of Rigvedic Aryans and Indus Valley people, which of the following statements is/are correct ? ki Rigvedic Aryans used the coat of mail | 5, and helmet in warfare whereas the people of Indus Valley Civilization did not leave any evidence of using them. 2. Rigvedic Aryans knew gold, silver and copper whereas Indus Valley people knew only copper and iron. 8. Rigvedic Aryans jhad domesticated the horse whereas there is no evidence of Indus Valley people having been aware of this animal. Select the correct answer using the code given below : (a)
subject: Ancient History
detail: The question tests the cultural contrast between the Harappan (Indus Valley) Civilization (c. 2600-1900 BCE mature phase) and the Rigvedic (Early Vedic) society (c. 1500-1000 BCE). Harappans were an urban, Bronze Age, largely non-militarised society. Their weapons (axes, spears, bows, daggers, maces) were simple, and no coat of mail or helmet has been found. Horse bones are almost absent; the few claims (Surkotada, Kalibangan terracotta) are disputed, and the horse is not depicted on seals. The Rigveda mentions ashva (horse) very often, along with chariots (ratha), and varman (armour) and sipra/helmet. Rigvedic people were pastoral and semi-nomadic, and cattle (gau) were the main wealth. Metals: the Rigveda mentions ayas (copper or bronze) and hiranya (gold). Harappans used gold, silver, copper, bronze and tin, but not iron. Iron (shyama/krishna ayas) appears in the Later Vedic period (c. 1000-600 BCE), so Harappans did not know only copper and iron. Elimination: statement 2 is wrong, so (b) and (d) go out, and statements 1 and 3 together give (c).
explanations: Incorrect: this is incomplete because statement 3, on the horse, is also correct.
Incorrect: it includes statement 2, which is false because Harappans did not know iron and also knew gold and silver.
Correct: statements 1 and 3 are correct, since armour and helmets and the domesticated horse are linked to Rigvedic Aryans but not to the Harappans.
Incorrect: it includes statement 2, which is false, so 1, 2 and 3 together cannot be right.
keyfact: Armour, helmet and domesticated horse mark the Rigvedic Aryans; Harappans had bronze, gold and silver but no iron, armour or clear horse evidence.
option_notes: Statement 1 only: statement 1 on armour is correct, but this option leaves out the correct statement 3 on the horse, so it is incomplete.
Statements 2 and 3 only: this option wrongly includes statement 2, which says Harappans knew only copper and iron. They in fact used bronze, gold and silver and did not use iron.

Statements 1 and 3 only: this is the official answer. It pairs the Rigvedic armour and domesticated horse with their absence or doubtful evidence in the Harappan record. Both are standard points of contrast between the two cultures.
Statements 1, 2 and 3: this option is wrong because statement 2 is factually incorrect. Iron was unknown in the Harappan period and appears only with the Later Vedic culture, c. 1000 BCE.
related: Harappans did not use iron; iron appears with Later Vedic culture, c. 1000 BCE.
The Rigveda has 10 mandalas, and Mandalas 2-7 are the oldest 'family books'.
The Dasarajna (Battle of Ten Kings) was fought on the Parushni (Ravi), and Sudas won.
Harappan seals show the unicorn bull, but not the horse.
Cotton was first cultivated by Harappans, and the Greeks called it sindon.
Lothal had a dockyard and Dholavira has a water-conservation system.
Rigvedic Sarasvati is often identified with the Ghaggar-Hakra.
Cattle (gau) were the main Rigvedic wealth, and the word gavishti meant search for cows, or war.
statements: 1 — Correct: Rigvedic texts mention varman (body armour) and helmets, but no Harappan site has yielded armour or helmets. Rigvedic warfare involved chariots, bows, arrows, spears and axes, and the tribes fought wars such as the Dasarajna (Battle of Ten Kings) on the Parushni (Ravi). Harappan weapons were few and simple, such as copper and bronze spearheads, axes, daggers and arrowheads, and the sites show an emphasis on trade and civic planning rather than warfare. The contrast is a standard marker between the two cultures.

2 — Incorrect: Harappans knew gold, silver, copper, bronze and tin, and used semi-precious stones such as carnelian, lapis lazuli and steatite. They did not know iron, which came to the subcontinent around 1000 BCE with the Painted Grey Ware and Later Vedic culture. Gold came from Karnataka (Kolar) and Afghanistan, copper from Khetri (Rajasthan), tin from Afghanistan and Central Asia, and lapis from Badakhshan. The Rigveda mentions ayas (copper or bronze) and hiranya (gold), and iron is Later Vedic.

3 — Correct: The horse (ashva) is the most-mentioned animal after the cow in the Rigveda. It was used for chariots and in the ashvamedha sacrifice. In the Harappan context, horse evidence is absent or disputed: the Surkotada bones are contested, and seals show the bull, elephant, rhinoceros and tiger, but not the horse. Harappans used bullocks, buffalo, sheep, goats, pigs, dogs, camels, and possibly asses and elephants. Horse evidence is central to the Aryan migration versus indigenous origin debate.
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. Rigvedic Aryans used body armour (varman) and helmets and had the domesticated horse, while the Indus people left no evidence of armour or of the horse. Statement 2 is wrong because Indus people knew gold, silver, copper and bronze, and iron was unknown to them.
topic_notes:
Harappan (Indus) Civilization: Bronze Age, urban, c. 2600-1900 BCE mature phase. Major sites include Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Lothal, Kalibangan, Rakhigarhi, Banawali and Chanhudaro. Features: grid-plan towns, drainage, the Great Bath, granaries, standardised weights and seals, and trade with Mesopotamia (Meluhha). Harappans worshipped the mother goddess and Pashupati, and the script is undeciphered. Crops: wheat, barley, cotton, peas and rice (Lothal, Rangpur). Animals: humped bull, buffalo, sheep and goat. Metals: copper, bronze, gold, silver and tin, but no iron. Possible evidence for the horse at Surkotada is disputed.

Rigvedic (Early Vedic) period: c. 1500-1000 BCE, in the Sapta Sindhu region. The Rigveda has 10 mandalas and 1028 hymns. Society was tribal and pastoral, with kinship units of kula, grama, vis and jana. Political bodies were the sabha, samiti, vidatha and gana. The king (rajan) was a war leader, helped by the purohita and senani. Main deities were Indra (purandara), Agni, Varuna and Soma. The most important river was Sarasvati, and the Sindhu is the most mentioned. Wealth was reckoned in cattle, and the Dasarajna battle was fought on the Parushni. Women had some freedom, as shown by Lopamudra, Ghosha and Apala. Ayas denotes copper or bronze.

Later Vedic: c. 1000-600 BCE, with iron (krishna ayas), PGW pottery, the Doab, the four varnas, janapadas, and the Brahmanas and Upanishads. Rice and wheat farming spread. Contrasts: Harappans were urban and mercantile, Vedics rural and pastoral; Harappans had no temples, whereas Vedic people practised yajna; the horse and cow were important for the Vedics.

question: From the ecological point of view, which one of the following assumes importance in being a good link between the Eastern Ghats and the Western Ghats ?
subject: Environment
detail: Sathyamangalam Tiger Reserve (Erode district, Tamil Nadu) was notified as a tiger reserve in 2013 and is India's 43rd or so tiger reserve. It sits at the junction of the Western Ghats and Eastern Ghats, and is contiguous with the Nilgiris, Mudumalai, Bandipur, Wayanad, BRT Hills and the Biligiri Rangaswamy area, and with Eastern Ghats hills such as the Palamalai and Biligiri-Malai Mahadeshwara tracts. The Moyar river valley and the Moyar gorge form a natural passage, and the Coimbatore-Mysuru elephant corridors run through it. Hence it lets tigers, elephants and other wildlife move between the two hill systems, and it is a major habitat for Asian elephants and tigers. Elimination: Nallamala (Andhra Pradesh and Telangana) and Seshachalam (Andhra Pradesh) are wholly within the Eastern Ghats. Nagarhole (Karnataka) is entirely in the Western Ghats. None of them physically bridges both. Key idea: a link or corridor needs to be at the convergence zone, which is the Nilgiri-Sathyamangalam area in the Tamil Nadu-Karnataka-Kerala tri-junction region.
explanations: Correct: Sathyamangalam lies at the meeting zone of the Eastern and Western Ghats and serves as a wildlife corridor between them.
Incorrect: Nallamala forest is a part of the Eastern Ghats in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, so it is not a link between the two ranges.
Incorrect: Nagarhole National Park is in the Western Ghats of Karnataka, part of the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve, and does not itself connect to the Eastern Ghats.
Incorrect: Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve, in the Tirupati and Kadapa area of Andhra Pradesh, is entirely in the Eastern Ghats.
keyfact: Sathyamangalam Tiger Reserve (Tamil Nadu) is the ecological corridor linking the Western Ghats and Eastern Ghats.
option_notes: Sathyamangalam Tiger Reserve is in Erode district, Tamil Nadu, notified as a tiger reserve in 2013. It covers dry deciduous, thorn and evergreen forests and is bounded by the Moyar and Bhavani rivers. It adjoins Mudumalai, Bandipur, BRT and Biligiri Rangaswamy reserves, and is a major elephant and tiger habitat. It is a key corridor between the Western and Eastern Ghats, and is rich in biodiversity, including vultures.

Nallamala Forest spans Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, part of the Eastern Ghats between the Krishna and Penna rivers. It contains the Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve, India's largest tiger reserve by area. It has the Chenchu tribe, a particularly vulnerable tribal group, and a rich dry deciduous and scrub forest with the Ahobilam and Srisailam sites.
