Related genetics for UPSC: gene therapy, CRISPR-Cas9 germline editing (He Jiankui's 2018 case), and the sickle cell and thalassemia gene-therapy approvals, including Casgevy, the first CRISPR therapy, approved in the UK in 2023. Other angles: autosomal dominant, recessive and X-linked inheritance; the Y chromosome passes from father to son; pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD); India's ART (Regulation) Act 2021 and the Surrogacy (Regulation) Act 2021; ICMR guidelines on germline editing; and the Human Genome Project (completed 2003).

question: Bollgard I and Bollgard II technologies are mentioned in the context of
subject: Environment
detail: Bollgard is the trade name of Bt cotton developed by Monsanto and introduced in India through Mahyco (Mahyco Monsanto Biotech). Bollgard I contains a single gene, cry1Ac, which gives protection against American bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera). Bollgard II, approved in India in 2006, has two genes, cry1Ac and cry2Ab, widening protection to include Spodoptera (tobacco caterpillar) and reducing the chance of pest resistance. Bt cotton was approved for commercial cultivation in India in 2002 by the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC, now Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee) under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the Rules of 1989. Cotton remains the only GM crop approved for commercial cultivation in India. The Cry proteins bind to receptors in the insect midgut, forming pores that kill the larva. Elimination: clonal propagation means tissue culture or cuttings, plant growth substances mean hormones such as auxin, and biofertilizers mean Rhizobium, Azotobacter or BGA. None of these has a link to Bollgard. The word 'technology' plus a Monsanto cotton brand points to genetic modification. Pink bollworm resistance to Bollgard II has since emerged in parts of India, and HTBt cotton remains unapproved.
explanations: Incorrect: clonal propagation produces genetically identical plants by vegetative methods or tissue culture. Bollgard involves inserting foreign genes, not cloning.
Correct: Bollgard I (cry1Ac) and Bollgard II (cry1Ac + cry2Ab) are Bt transgenic cotton technologies, so they relate to developing genetically modified crop plants.
Incorrect: plant growth substances such as auxins, gibberellins and cytokinins are hormones. Bollgard is not about producing them.
Incorrect: biofertilizers are microbial inoculants such as Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Azolla and mycorrhiza. Bollgard concerns pest resistance in cotton, not nutrient supply.
keyfact: Bollgard I (cry1Ac) and Bollgard II (cry1Ac + cry2Ab) are Bt cotton, GM technologies against bollworms.
option_notes: Clonal propagation is asexual multiplication that gives genetically identical copies (clones). Methods include cuttings, layering, grafting, and micropropagation by tissue culture from meristems or explants. It is used for banana, sugarcane, orchids, potato and teak. It preserves desirable traits and gives disease-free plantlets, but it does not add new genes.

Genetically modified crops carry genes transferred by recombinant DNA technology. In India, Bt cotton (2002) is the only GM crop approved for commercial cultivation. GM mustard DMH-11 received GEAC environmental release approval in 2022 but is stalled in the Supreme Court. Bt brinjal had a moratorium imposed in 2010. GEAC under MoEFCC is the regulator.

Plant growth substances (phytohormones) are organic compounds that regulate growth in small amounts. They include auxins (IAA), gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and ethylene. Auxins promote rooting and cell elongation, gibberellins cause bolting and stem elongation, cytokinins promote cell division, ABA induces dormancy and stomatal closure, and ethylene ripens fruit.

Biofertilizers are living microorganisms that improve soil fertility. Examples are Rhizobium (legumes), Azotobacter and Azospirillum (free-living nitrogen fixers), blue-green algae and Azolla (rice), phosphate-solubilising bacteria and mycorrhiza. In India, the Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana and National Project on Organic Farming promote them. They are cheap and eco-friendly, and they reduce chemical fertilizer use.
related: Bt cotton is the only GM crop commercially cultivated in India (approved 2002).
Bollgard II carries cry1Ac and cry2Ab genes; Bollgard I carries only cry1Ac.
GEAC under MoEFCC is the regulator for GM crop approvals in India.
Bt brinjal was put under a moratorium in 2010 by the Environment Minister.
GM mustard DMH-11 was cleared by GEAC in 2022; its release is subject to Supreme Court proceedings.
Flavr Savr tomato was the first commercially sold GM food (1994).
The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety deals with living modified organisms.
Pink bollworm has developed resistance to Bt cotton in parts of India.
summary: The answer is (b): Bollgard I and Bollgard II are technologies for developing genetically modified (transgenic) cotton. They insert genes from the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) so the plant produces proteins toxic to bollworm pests.
topic_notes: Bt cotton is the centrepiece of India's GM crop story. Bacillus thuringiensis is a soil bacterium that produces crystal (Cry) proteins which are toxic to specific insect groups. Cry1Ac targets Lepidoptera such as bollworms. Bollgard I was developed by Monsanto, with Mahyco as the Indian partner, and approved in 2002. Bollgard II, with cry1Ac and cry2Ab, was approved in 2006. Later, unapproved HTBt (herbicide-tolerant, with the cp4-epsps gene) cotton has been a regulatory controversy. India is among the world's largest cotton producers, with Bt varieties covering over 90 percent of the area. Pink bollworm resistance has been seen in Gujarat and Maharashtra. Regulation falls under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the 1989 Rules for hazardous microorganisms and GMOs, with GEAC in MoEFCC as the apex approving body. The Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation sits under DBT. The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (2000) governs transboundary movement of living modified organisms. Other GM topics include Golden Rice (beta-carotene), Flavr Savr tomato (first commercial GM food, 1994), Bt brinjal (moratorium 2010), GM mustard DMH-11 (developed by Delhi University, with the bar, barnase and barstar gene system), and the FSSAI rules on GM food. Related technologies are RNA interference, CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing (SDN-1 and SDN-2 genome-edited plants exempted from GM rules in India in 2022), and gene drives. Also remember tissue culture, biofertilizers and growth hormones, as these are the usual distractors.

ocr: In a pressure cooker, the temperature at which the food is cooked depends mainly upon which of the following? 1. Area of the hole in the lid 2. Temperature of the flame 3. Weight of the lid Select the correct answer using the code given below. (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (aq) 1,2 and 3
subject: Geography
detail: A pressure cooker raises the boiling point of water by raising the pressure above the liquid. Water boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure, so a higher pressure means a higher boiling point (about 120 °C at roughly 2 atm absolute, versus 100 °C at 1 atm). Steam builds up inside the sealed vessel until its pressure is enough to lift the weighted valve over the vent hole. At that point the steam escapes and the pressure stays roughly constant. The limiting pressure is approximately atmospheric pressure plus (weight of the valve ÷ area of the hole), P = P0 + mg/A. So a heavier lid/valve gives a higher pressure and temperature, and a larger hole area gives a lower pressure and temperature. The flame only controls how fast the steam is produced and how quickly the cooker reaches that pressure. Once the valve is venting, extra heat just makes more steam escape and does not raise the temperature. Elimination: statement 2 is wrong, so options (a), (b) and (d) are ruled out, leaving (c).
explanations: (a) Wrong: It includes statement 2 (flame temperature), which does not set the cooking temperature, and it omits statement 3 (weight of the lid), which does.
(b) Wrong: It includes statement 2, which is incorrect, and it omits statement 1 (hole area), which is relevant.
(c) Correct: The hole area and the weight of the lid together fix the limiting steam pressure and so the boiling point of water in the cooker. The flame temperature is irrelevant to that limit.
(d) Wrong: It includes statement 2, and the flame temperature does not determine the final cooking temperature.
keyfact: Pressure cooker temperature is set by the pressure at which the weighted valve lifts, P = P0 + mg/A, so it depends on the valve weight and the hole area, not on the flame.
statements: 1 — Correct: The area of the vent hole decides how much pressure is needed to lift the valve (P = P0 + mg/A), so it fixes the steam pressure and the boiling temperature.
2 — Incorrect: The flame temperature only changes how fast steam forms. Once the valve vents, the temperature is capped by the pressure limit, not by the flame.
3 — Correct: The weight of the lid/valve determines the pressure at which steam is released, and therefore the maximum cooking temperature.
summary: The correct answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. In a pressure cooker, the cooking temperature is set by the steam pressure at which the weighted vent (regulator) lifts. That pressure depends on the weight of the lid/valve and the area of the hole it covers. The flame temperature does not control it.

question:
Consider the following :
1. Bacteria
2. Fungi
3. Virus Which of the above can be cultured in artificial/synthetic medium?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Culturing an organism in an artificial or synthetic medium requires that the organism can carry out its own metabolism and reproduction once given nutrients. Bacteria (prokaryotes) and fungi (eukaryotes) both qualify. Bacteria grow on nutrient agar, MacConkey agar, blood agar and similar media. Fungi grow on Sabouraud dextrose agar and potato dextrose agar. Viruses are acellular. They have no ribosomes and no metabolic machinery, and they carry only DNA or RNA in a protein coat (capsid). They can replicate only inside living host cells. Viruses are therefore cultured in living systems: embryonated hen's eggs, primary or continuous cell lines, or live animals. Some bacteria are also obligate intracellular, such as Chlamydia, Rickettsia and Mycobacterium leprae, and cannot be grown on cell-free media either. The question, however, refers to bacteria as a group, and most bacteria can be cultured. The elimination logic is simple: viruses cannot be grown on synthetic media, so any option containing 3 (b, c, d) is wrong. Only (a) remains.
explanations: Correct. Bacteria and fungi have their own metabolic machinery and grow on artificial media, while viruses do not.
Wrong. It includes viruses (3), which cannot be cultured on synthetic media, and it leaves out bacteria (1), which can.
Wrong. It includes viruses (3) and leaves out fungi (2), which grow readily on media like Sabouraud agar.
Wrong. It includes viruses, which need living host cells. Only bacteria and fungi can be grown on artificial media.
keyfact: Bacteria and fungi grow on artificial media; viruses, being obligate intracellular parasites, need living host cells.
option_notes: 1 and 2 only means bacteria and fungi. Both are cellular organisms that can be grown in pure culture on nutrient agar, Sabouraud agar and similar media. This is the right answer. Koch's postulates rely on pure cultures of bacteria. Fungal cultures are used in industry (yeast fermentation, penicillin from Penicillium) and in diagnosis.

2 and 3 only pairs fungi with viruses. Fungi can be cultured on synthetic media, but viruses cannot because they are obligate intracellular parasites without ribosomes or metabolism. Viruses are grown in embryonated eggs, cell lines or animals. Wrong because it includes viruses and omits bacteria.

1 and 3 only pairs bacteria with viruses. Bacteria do grow on artificial media, but viruses do not. Fungi are wrongly left out, though they grow on Sabouraud and potato dextrose agar. Some bacteria (Chlamydia, Rickettsia) are obligate intracellular, but bacteria as a class are culturable.

1, 2 and 3 would hold only if viruses could grow without a host. They cannot. Viruses are acellular, lack metabolism outside a host, and need living cells. In 2002 poliovirus was chemically synthesised from its genome sequence, but that is not culturing, and the virus still needs host cells to replicate.
related: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites and are cultured in living cells, embryonated eggs or animals.
Sabouraud dextrose agar is the standard medium for fungi.
MacConkey agar is selective and differential for Gram-negative enteric bacteria.
Chlamydia and Rickettsia are bacteria that are obligate intracellular and cannot be grown on cell-free media.
Viroids are infectious RNA without a protein coat, discovered by T.O. Diener in 1971.
Prions are infectious proteins that cause BSE and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
Robert Koch developed pure culture techniques and the postulates; Julius Petri invented the Petri dish.
Influenza vaccines have traditionally been produced in embryonated hen's eggs.
statements: 1 — Correct: Most bacteria grow on artificial media. Bacteria are prokaryotic, single-celled organisms with their own ribosomes and enzymes. Robert Koch pioneered pure culture methods with solid media in the 1880s, and Fanny Hesse suggested agar. Common media are nutrient agar, MacConkey agar (selective and differential for enteric bacteria), blood agar and Luria-Bertani broth. Exceptions are obligate intracellular bacteria such as Chlamydia, Rickettsia, Coxiella and Mycobacterium leprae, which need host cells or animals like armadillos. Treponema pallidum also cannot be cultured in vitro.

2 — Correct: Fungi grow on artificial media. Fungi are eukaryotic, heterotrophic organisms (yeasts, moulds, mushrooms) with chitinous cell walls. They are cultured on Sabouraud dextrose agar (acidic pH about 5.6, which inhibits bacteria) and potato dextrose agar. Antibiotics such as chloramphenicol are often added to suppress bacteria. Yeasts like Saccharomyces cerevisiae are routine lab organisms. Fungi such as Candida, Aspergillus and Cryptococcus are identified by culture in clinical labs. Pneumocystis jirovecii is a notable fungus that is hard to culture.

3 — Incorrect: Viruses cannot be grown on cell-free synthetic media. They are obligate intracellular parasites, acellular and non-metabolising outside a host. They are cultured in embryonated hen's eggs (influenza vaccine production), in cell lines such as HeLa, Vero and primary monkey kidney cells, or in laboratory animals. Bacteriophages need bacterial hosts. Viral growth is detected by cytopathic effects or plaque assays. Wendell Stanley crystallised tobacco mosaic virus in 1935, and Ivanovsky (1892) and Beijerinck (1898) discovered viruses.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 and 2 only. Bacteria and fungi are cellular and have their own metabolism, so they grow on artificial media such as nutrient agar and Sabouraud's agar. Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites and need living host cells.
topic_notes:
Microbial culture is the growth of microorganisms in controlled lab conditions. Media may be liquid (broth) or solid (with about 1.5% agar). They may also be defined (synthetic, with known chemical composition) or complex (peptone, beef extract). Special types are selective, differential, enriched and transport media. Examples are MacConkey (selective and differential), blood agar (enriched and differential), Sabouraud agar (fungi) and Thayer-Martin (Neisseria).

Bacteria are prokaryotes with no nucleus, 70S ribosomes and a peptidoglycan cell wall. Fungi are eukaryotes with chitin walls. Viruses are acellular, contain either DNA or RNA, and are about 20-300 nm. They replicate only in host cells. Viral culture systems include embryonated eggs (chorioallantoic membrane, allantoic cavity), cell cultures (primary, diploid, continuous) and animals. Bacteriophages are grown on bacterial lawns.

Other angles UPSC could ask: viroids (infectious RNA only, discovered by T.O. Diener in 1971) and prions (infectious proteins causing BSE and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease), which are also not culturable on artificial media. Also useful: Koch's postulates, Petri dish (Julius Petri, 1887), Pasteur's disproof of spontaneous generation, Alexander Fleming's penicillin from Penicillium notatum (1928), the Gram stain (Hans Christian Gram, 1884), and PCR-based and tissue-culture-based vaccine production, such as the polio vaccine grown in monkey kidney cells. Obligate intracellular bacteria and Treponema pallidum are standard exceptions.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. Adenoviruses have single-stranded DNA genomes whereas retroviruses have double-stranded DNA genomes.
2. Common cold is sometime caused by an adenovirus whereas AIDS is caused by a retrovirus. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Viruses are classified by the type and strandedness of their nucleic acid. Adenoviruses are non-enveloped viruses with a linear double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) genome. They infect the respiratory tract, eyes, gut and urinary tract, and are one of the causes of the common cold, along with rhinoviruses and coronaviruses. They are also used as vectors in gene therapy and in vaccines, such as the Oxford-AstraZeneca/Covishield and Sputnik V COVID-19 vaccines. Retroviruses are enveloped viruses with two copies of a single-stranded positive-sense RNA genome. They carry reverse transcriptase, which makes DNA from the RNA, and this DNA is then integrated into the host genome by integrase. HIV-1 and HIV-2 are retroviruses (genus Lentivirus) that destroy CD4+ T-helper cells and cause AIDS. Elimination logic: statement 1 is wrong because a retrovirus cannot have a DNA genome, since its defining feature is reverse transcription from RNA. That eliminates (a) and (c). Statement 2 is factually correct, so (d) is out, leaving (b).
explanations: Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect, since adenoviruses have dsDNA and retroviruses have ssRNA genomes.
Right: only statement 2 is correct. Adenoviruses can cause the common cold and HIV, a retrovirus, causes AIDS.
Wrong: statement 1 is false, so 'both' cannot be correct.
Wrong: statement 2 is correct, so 'neither' is incorrect.
keyfact: Adenoviruses are dsDNA viruses (one cause of colds); retroviruses like HIV are ssRNA viruses that use reverse transcriptase.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only: this would require adenoviruses to be ssDNA viruses and retroviruses to be dsDNA viruses, which is false. Adenoviruses are dsDNA viruses, and retroviruses carry ssRNA and copy it into DNA by reverse transcription. Single-stranded DNA viruses include parvoviruses (such as B19) and bacteriophage M13. Double-stranded DNA viruses include herpesviruses, poxviruses, papillomaviruses and adenoviruses. Hepatitis B is a partially double-stranded DNA virus that uses reverse transcription.

Option (b), 2 only: this is the official and correct answer. Adenoviruses sometimes cause common colds, and HIV, a retrovirus, causes AIDS. Retroviruses use reverse transcriptase to convert RNA into DNA, which integrates into the host genome as a provirus. Adenoviruses are dsDNA viruses linked to respiratory, eye and gut infections. They are used as vectors in vaccines and gene therapy. HIV infection damages CD4+ T cells and causes immune deficiency.

Option (c), both 1 and 2: this is wrong because statement 1 mixes up the genomes of the two virus groups. Retroviruses are RNA viruses, not dsDNA viruses. Examples of retroviruses are HIV, HTLV-1 (adult T-cell leukaemia) and the Rous sarcoma virus, the first oncogenic virus, discovered by Peyton Rous in 1911 (Nobel 1966). Adenoviruses are dsDNA viruses. Only statement 2 is correct.

Option (d), neither: this is wrong because statement 2 is correct. Adenoviruses are among the causes of the common cold (also called acute viral rhinitis or upper respiratory infection), and HIV, a retrovirus, causes AIDS. The common cold is self-limiting, usually lasts 7-10 days, and has no specific cure or vaccine. Rhinoviruses are the most common cause. Treatment is symptomatic, and antibiotics do not work against viruses.
related: Adenoviruses have linear dsDNA genomes and no envelope.
HIV is a retrovirus with two copies of ssRNA and reverse transcriptase.
Covishield uses a chimpanzee adenovirus vector (ChAdOx1).
SARS-CoV-2 is a positive-sense ssRNA coronavirus.
Hepatitis B is a DNA virus that replicates through reverse transcription.
Rhinoviruses are the commonest cause of the common cold.
Smallpox (variola, a dsDNA virus) was declared eradicated in 1980.
Reverse transcriptase was discovered in 1970 by Temin and Baltimore.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Adenoviruses have double-stranded DNA, not single-stranded, and retroviruses have single-stranded RNA, not double-stranded DNA. Adenoviruses were first isolated in 1953 from human adenoid tissue, which gives them their name. They are non-enveloped, icosahedral, about 70-90 nm, with a linear dsDNA genome of roughly 26-45 kb. There are over 50 human serotypes. They cause respiratory illness, conjunctivitis, gastroenteritis and cystitis. Retroviruses (family Retroviridae) include HIV, HTLV-1 and Rous sarcoma virus. They have a diploid ssRNA genome and use reverse transcriptase, discovered by Temin and Baltimore in 1970 (Nobel 1975).

2 — Correct: Adenoviruses are a recognised cause of the common cold and other upper respiratory infections. AIDS is caused by HIV, a retrovirus. The common cold is mostly caused by rhinoviruses, with coronaviruses, adenoviruses, RSV and others also involved. HIV was identified in 1983-84 by Luc Montagnier and Françoise Barré-Sinoussi, and Robert Gallo was credited with related work. It spreads through blood, sexual contact and mother-to-child transmission. HIV targets CD4+ T cells. Diagnosis uses ELISA and Western blot, and treatment is antiretroviral therapy (ART). India's National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) runs the national programme, and World AIDS Day is on 1 December.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. Adenoviruses sometimes cause the common cold and HIV, a retrovirus, causes AIDS. Statement 1 reverses the genome facts: adenoviruses have double-stranded DNA and retroviruses have single-stranded RNA genomes.
topic_notes: Virus classification: the Baltimore system groups viruses into seven classes by genome type and the way mRNA is made. Class I is dsDNA (adenovirus, herpes, pox, papilloma). Class II is ssDNA (parvovirus). Class III is dsRNA (rotavirus, reovirus). Class IV is positive-sense ssRNA (polio, SARS-CoV-2, dengue, hepatitis C, rhinovirus). Class V is negative-sense ssRNA (influenza, measles, rabies, Ebola). Class VI is ssRNA with reverse transcriptase (retroviruses, such as HIV). Class VII is dsDNA with reverse transcriptase (hepatitis B). Retroviruses: HIV has two copies of ssRNA and key enzymes reverse transcriptase, integrase and protease. Its envelope proteins gp120 and gp41 bind CD4 and the co-receptors CCR5 or CXCR4. Antiretroviral drug classes include NRTIs (zidovudine), NNRTIs, protease inhibitors and integrase inhibitors. Related ideas: reverse transcriptase is used in RT-PCR, and the Nobel Prize 1975 went to Baltimore, Temin and Dulbecco. Adenoviral vector vaccines: Covishield (ChAdOx1, a chimpanzee adenovirus), Sputnik V (Ad26 and Ad5) and Johnson & Johnson's Janssen vaccine. mRNA vaccines (Pfizer, Moderna) use no viral vector. Viral diseases and agents: common cold (rhinovirus, coronavirus, adenovirus), influenza (orthomyxovirus), SARS-CoV-2 (coronavirus, +ssRNA), Hepatitis A (picornavirus), HPV (dsDNA), and smallpox (variola, dsDNA, eradicated in 1980). Viroids are infectious RNA without a protein coat, and prions are infectious proteins. UPSC often asks about genome types, vectors in vaccines, gene therapy and diseases caused by particular viruses.

question: Water can dissolve more substances than any other liquid because
options: it is a good conductor of heat
it has high value of specific heat
it is an oxide of hydrogen
subject: Economy
detail: Water (H2O) has a bent geometry with an H-O-H angle of about 104.5 degrees. Oxygen is much more electronegative than hydrogen, so the O-H bonds are polar and the molecule has a permanent dipole: a partial negative charge (delta-) on oxygen and partial positive charges (delta+) on hydrogens. When an ionic solid such as NaCl is placed in water, the oxygen ends attract Na+ and the hydrogen ends attract Cl-. This ion-dipole attraction overcomes the lattice energy, and the ions become surrounded by water molecules (hydration). Water also forms hydrogen bonds with polar molecules such as sugars, alcohols and ammonia, so these dissolve readily. Its high dielectric constant (about 80) further weakens the attraction between separated ions in solution. Non-polar substances like oils and fats do not dissolve well, following the 'like dissolves like' rule, so water is the best, but not a perfect, solvent. Other properties such as high specific heat, good heat conduction and chemical composition explain water's thermal behaviour and identity, not its solvent power. For elimination, ask which property involves charge interaction with solutes: only polarity does.
explanations: Correct. Water's dipolar nature lets it attract positive and negative ions and polar molecules, causing hydration and dissolution; this makes it the universal solvent.
Wrong. Heat conduction concerns thermal energy transfer, not the interaction between solvent and solute particles. Water is actually a poor conductor of heat compared with metals.
Wrong. High specific heat explains why water heats and cools slowly, moderating climate. It does not determine how well it dissolves substances.

Wrong. Being an oxide of hydrogen merely describes its composition. Other hydrogen oxides such as hydrogen peroxide are not described as general solvents because of this fact, and composition alone doesn't explain solvency.
keyfact: Water is the 'universal solvent' because its polar (dipolar) molecules and hydrogen bonding hydrate ions and dissolve polar substances.
summary: The answer is (a). Water is a dipolar (polar) molecule, with partial negative charge on oxygen and partial positive charge on hydrogen, so it can interact with and dissolve many ionic and polar substances, which is why it is called the 'universal solvent'.

question:
With reference to street-lighting, how do sodium lamps differ from LED lamps?
1. Sodium lamps produce light in 360 degrees but it is not so in the case of LED lamps.
2. As street-lights, sodium lamps have longer life span than LED lamps.
3. The spectrum of visible light from sodium lamps is almost monochromatic while LED lamps offer significant colour advantages in street-lighting. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Street-lighting has moved from high-pressure sodium vapour (HPSV) and low-pressure sodium (LPS) lamps to LEDs. Sodium lamps are gas-discharge lamps. They radiate omnidirectionally, so reflectors and fixtures are needed to push light downward, and much light is wasted as spill and sky glow. LEDs are solid-state semiconductor devices (p-n junction electroluminescence) that emit light in a roughly 120-180 degree cone. This makes them directional and efficient for roads. LPS lamps emit almost purely at about 589 nm (the sodium D-line), so the light is nearly monochromatic and colour rendering is very poor (CRI close to 0). HPSV is broader but still yellowish-orange, with CRI of about 20-25. White LEDs have CRI of 70 or more, and colour temperature can be tuned. Lifespan is the reason statement 2 fails. Sodium lamps last roughly 12,000-24,000 hours, while LEDs last 50,000-100,000 hours. LEDs also use 50% or more less energy, switch on instantly and contain no mercury. India's Street Lighting National Programme (SLNP, by EESL) replaces conventional lamps with LEDs. Elimination: statement 2 is false, so (b) and (d) are out. Statement 3 is true, so (a) is out, leaving (c).
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is also correct, so '3 only' is incomplete.
(b) is wrong because statement 2 is false. LEDs, not sodium lamps, have the longer life span.
(c) is correct because statements 1 and 3 are true and statement 2 is false.
(d) is wrong because it includes statement 2, which is false.
keyfact: Sodium lamps: omnidirectional (360 degrees), near-monochromatic yellow, shorter life; LEDs: directional, good colour rendering, 50,000+ hours.
option_notes: 3 only: Statement 3 is true, but the option leaves out statement 1. It is a trap for students who know the spectrum difference but not the emission geometry. Sodium vapour lamps are gas-discharge lamps, and low-pressure types emit at about 589 nm. Their CRI is very low, so they are suited to uses where colour does not matter, such as roads and security lighting. They have been widely replaced by LEDs.

2 only: This is the false statement. Sodium lamps last roughly 12,000-24,000 hours, while LEDs last 50,000 hours or more. LEDs have lower maintenance and lower lifetime cost. Sodium lamps also need warm-up time, and their output declines with age. Sodium lamps contain sodium metal and sometimes a small amount of mercury, which makes disposal harder.

1 and 3 only: This is the official answer. Sodium lamps are omnidirectional and give a near-monochromatic yellow light. LEDs are directional and offer good colour rendering and tunable colour temperature. LEDs have a longer life and higher efficacy, typically 100-150 lumens per watt. Government schemes such as SLNP and UJALA promote LEDs in India.

1, 2 and 3: This option is wrong because it counts the false lifespan claim. It tests whether students assume that older technology lasts longer. Modern LED street-lights use heat sinks and drivers to reach 50,000-100,000 hours. A common mistake is to confuse the lifespan of a lamp with the lifespan of its driver or power supply, which can fail earlier.
related: Low-pressure sodium lamps emit near-monochromatic light at about 589 nm.
LEDs have a life of about 50,000-100,000 hours, far longer than sodium lamps.
UJALA (2015) is run by EESL under the Ministry of Power.
Street Lighting National Programme (SLNP) was launched in January 2015.
The 2014 Physics Nobel was awarded for the blue LED (Akasaki, Amano, Nakamura).
CRI measures how faithfully a light source shows colours; LPS sodium is near 0.
The Minamata Convention restricts mercury in products such as certain lamps.
BEE's Standards and Labelling programme gives star ratings to appliances.
statements: 1 — Correct: Sodium lamps are omnidirectional, emitting light through 360 degrees, while LEDs are directional and emit in a limited cone. Sodium vapour lamps are gas-discharge lamps in which an electric arc excites sodium vapour. The two main types are low-pressure sodium (LPS), which is very efficient but gives a monochromatic yellow light, and high-pressure sodium (HPS), which gives a broader golden-white light. Both need reflectors or refractors to direct light downward, and much light is wasted as spill and sky glow. LEDs are semiconductor diodes whose light comes from a flat chip, so they naturally emit in a roughly 120-180 degree cone. This reduces the need for reflectors, improves road-surface efficiency and reduces light pollution.

2 — Incorrect: LEDs have the longer life, not sodium lamps. Typical LED street-lights last about 50,000-100,000 hours, against about 12,000-24,000 hours for HPS lamps and roughly 18,000 for LPS. LEDs fade gradually, a measure called lumen depreciation (L70), instead of failing suddenly. They save 50-70% of energy, switch on instantly, can be dimmed and contain no mercury. Sodium lamps need a warm-up of several minutes and their output falls over time. India's Street Lighting National Programme (SLNP), run by EESL under the Ministry of Power, and the UJALA scheme (launched in 2015) promote the shift to LEDs. Lower maintenance and energy cost are the key advantages of LEDs.

3 — Correct: Sodium lamps, especially low-pressure ones, emit nearly monochromatic light at about 589 nm (the sodium D-lines), so the colour rendering index (CRI) is close to zero. Objects appear in shades of yellow and grey, which makes colour identification hard. HPS lamps have a CRI of about 20-25. White LEDs have a CRI of 70-90 and a tunable correlated colour temperature (warm to cool white), and they can also produce coloured light. This improves visibility, recognition of objects and safety. Warm-white or amber LEDs can also reduce effects on wildlife and astronomy. Note that blue-rich LEDs can raise glare and light-pollution concerns.
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. Sodium lamps emit light in all directions (360 degrees) while LEDs are directional, and sodium lamps give a near-monochromatic yellow light while LEDs offer a wide choice of colours and better colour rendering. Statement 2 is wrong because LEDs last much longer than sodium lamps.
topic_notes: Street-lighting technologies: incandescent lamps were replaced by mercury vapour, then sodium vapour (LPS and HPS), metal halide, CFL, and now LEDs. Sodium lamps are gas-discharge lamps. Low-pressure sodium gives about 589 nm monochromatic yellow light, with efficacy up to about 180 lm/W but a CRI near 0. High-pressure sodium gives a golden-white light with a CRI of about 20-25 and efficacy of about 80-140 lm/W. LEDs work by electroluminescence in a semiconductor p-n junction. They are directional, instant-on and dimmable, can be controlled by smart systems, and have a long life of 50,000 hours or more. They use no mercury, and white LEDs are made with blue LEDs plus phosphor. The 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura for efficient blue LEDs. In India, UJALA (2015) distributes LED bulbs, tubelights and fans through EESL (Energy Efficiency Services Limited, a joint venture of PSUs under the Ministry of Power). SLNP (Street Lighting National Programme, 2015) replaces conventional street-lights with LEDs. The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) runs the Standards and Labelling programme. Light pollution and sky glow are concerns, especially with blue-rich, high colour temperature LEDs. These can disrupt circadian rhythms and harm insects and turtle hatchlings. Related concepts include lumen (light output), lux (illuminance), efficacy (lm/W), CRI and CCT (correlated colour temperature in kelvin). Other angles UPSC can ask: OLED, the Minamata Convention on mercury (CFLs and mercury lamps are being phased out), solar street-lights, and the Montreal Protocol and Kigali Amendment, which concern cooling rather than lighting.

ocr: The term ‘ACE2’ is talked about in the context of (a) genes introduced in the genetically modified plants (b) development of India’s own satellite navigation system (c) radio collars for wildlife tracking (ad) spread of viral diseases 33 BXC-U-FTHI/68A
subject: Science & Tech
detail: ACE2 stands for Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme 2. It is a membrane-bound enzyme found on the surface of cells in the lungs, heart, kidneys, intestines and blood vessels. Physiologically it helps regulate blood pressure through the renin-angiotensin system, by converting angiotensin II into angiotensin (1-7), which dilates blood vessels. Its link to disease spread came with the COVID-19 pandemic. The spike (S) protein of SARS-CoV-2 binds to the ACE2 receptor through its receptor-binding domain. The host protease TMPRSS2 then primes the spike protein, and the virus fuses with the cell and enters. The earlier SARS-CoV (2002-03) also used ACE2. Because of this, ACE2 is a target for vaccine and drug design, including soluble ACE2 decoys and antibodies that block the spike. Elimination logic: genes in GM plants are usually named as Bt, cry or EPSPS genes, not ACE2. India's own navigation system is NavIC, also called IRNSS. Radio collars are a wildlife telemetry tool, not a biological term. ACE2 is a biological, medical term, so (d) fits.
explanations: Incorrect. Genes in GM plants are things like Cry genes (Bt cotton) or the cp4-EPSPS gene (herbicide tolerance). ACE2 is a human protein receptor and is not introduced into plants.
Incorrect. India's regional navigation system is NavIC (IRNSS), run by ISRO. ACE2 has nothing to do with satellites.
Incorrect. Radio collars are telemetry devices used to track animals such as tigers and elephants. ACE2 is a biological molecule, not a tracking technology.
Correct. ACE2 is the cell-surface receptor that SARS-CoV-2 (and SARS-CoV) uses to enter human cells. It is therefore central to how viral diseases like COVID-19 spread.
keyfact: ACE2 is the human cell receptor that SARS-CoV-2 binds through its spike protein to enter cells, so it is linked to the spread of viral disease.
option_notes: Genes in genetically modified plants are DNA sequences introduced to give new traits. Bt cotton carries Cry1Ac and Cry2Ab from Bacillus thuringiensis for bollworm resistance. Herbicide-tolerant crops use the cp4-EPSPS gene. Bt cotton has been the only GM crop commercially approved in India, since 2002. GM mustard (DMH-11) was under regulatory and judicial scrutiny. GEAC, under the Environment Ministry, is the regulator. Golden Rice carries genes for beta-carotene.

NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation), formerly IRNSS, is India's regional satellite navigation system developed by ISRO. It uses 7 satellites (IRNSS-1A to 1G) and covers India and about 1,500 km beyond its borders. It provides the Standard Positioning Service and a restricted service. It operates in the L5 and S bands. Its first satellite was launched in 2013. Other systems include GPS (USA), GLONASS (Russia), Galileo (EU) and BeiDou (China). GAGAN is India's SBAS augmentation system.

Radio collars are devices fitted to animals that transmit signals (VHF or GPS-satellite) so researchers can track their movement, range and behaviour. They are used for tigers, elephants, leopards and snow leopards. In India the Wildlife Institute of India, Dehradun, runs many such studies. Radio collaring was used in tiger reintroduction in Sariska and Panna. It supports human-wildlife conflict management and corridor planning. Tracking also uses camera traps and GPS tags.

Viral diseases are caused by viruses, which are obligate intracellular parasites that spread through droplets, vectors, contact, water or blood. Examples are COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2), dengue, influenza, Ebola, Nipah and HIV. SARS-CoV-2 uses the ACE2 receptor and the TMPRSS2 protease to enter cells. Vaccine types include mRNA, viral-vector and inactivated. India's vaccines were Covaxin (inactivated, Bharat Biotech) and Covishield (viral vector, Oxford-AstraZeneca/Serum Institute). Variants of concern include Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta and Omicron.
related: ACE2 is the host cell receptor for SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV; MERS-CoV uses DPP4.
TMPRSS2 is the host protease that primes the spike protein for cell entry.
SARS-CoV-2 is an enveloped positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus.
INSACOG is India's consortium for genome sequencing of SARS-CoV-2 variants.
ZyCoV-D by Zydus Cadila is the world's first DNA-based COVID vaccine.
Covaxin is an inactivated vaccine developed by Bharat Biotech with ICMR and NIV Pune.
NavIC is India's regional navigation system, with 7 satellites.
Bt cotton is India's only commercially approved GM crop.
summary: The answer is (d). ACE2 (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme 2) is a receptor protein on human cells that the SARS-CoV-2 virus uses to enter and infect them, so the term comes up in discussions of how viral diseases such as COVID-19 spread.
topic_notes: ACE2 (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme 2) is a zinc-containing carboxypeptidase on the surface of cells in the lungs (type II alveolar cells), heart, kidney, gut and endothelium. In the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), ACE converts angiotensin I to the vasoconstrictor angiotensin II, while ACE2 converts angiotensin II into angiotensin (1-7), which dilates vessels. ACE2 therefore acts as a counterbalance to ACE. Its role in infection: the S1 subunit of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein binds ACE2 through its receptor-binding domain. The host protease TMPRSS2 (and furin) cleaves the spike, which allows the viral and cell membranes to fuse. SARS-CoV (2003) also used ACE2, whereas MERS-CoV uses DPP4 as its receptor. Research angles: soluble ACE2 as a decoy, monoclonal antibodies against the spike, and concern over ACE inhibitors and ARBs in COVID patients (the evidence showed no harm). Coronaviruses are enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses. COVID-19 was declared a pandemic by WHO on 11 March 2020. Diagnostic tests: RT-PCR (gold standard), rapid antigen test, antibody (serology) test. Vaccine platforms: mRNA (Pfizer, Moderna), viral vector (Covishield, Sputnik V, J&J), inactivated (Covaxin, Sinovac), DNA (ZyCoV-D, the world's first DNA vaccine, from Zydus Cadila) and protein subunit (Covovax, Corbevax). Genome sequencing in India is coordinated by INSACOG. Variant naming by WHO uses Greek letters.

question: Bisphenol A (BPA), a cause of concern, is a structural/key component in the manufacture of which of the following kinds of plastics?
subject: Economy
detail: Bisphenol A (BPA) is an industrial organic chemical, (CH3)2C(C6H4OH)2, used chiefly as a monomer. Reacting BPA with phosgene or diphenyl carbonate gives polycarbonate, a hard, transparent, heat-resistant plastic used in water cooler bottles, reusable baby bottles, CDs/DVDs, spectacle lenses and food-storage containers. BPA is also a key component of epoxy resins, which line metal food cans and water pipes. It is a concern because it is an endocrine disruptor that mimics oestrogen; it can leach from plastic into food and drink, especially when heated or when the plastic is worn, and has been linked to reproductive, developmental, metabolic and behavioural effects. The EU and several countries have banned BPA in baby feeding bottles, and the US FDA has done likewise. Elimination logic: low-density polyethylene is made from ethylene, PVC from vinyl chloride (with phthalates as common plasticisers, a separate concern), and PET from terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol. None of these uses BPA as a monomer. Recycling code 7 (other) generally includes polycarbonate.
explanations: Incorrect: LDPE is polymerised from ethylene; BPA is not a structural component.
Correct: Polycarbonate is made by polymerising BPA with phosgene or a carbonate source, so BPA is its core monomer.
Incorrect: PET is made from terephthalic acid (or dimethyl terephthalate) and ethylene glycol, with no BPA in its structure.
Incorrect: PVC is made from vinyl chloride monomer; its health concerns relate to phthalates and additives, not BPA as a building block.
keyfact: BPA is the monomer of polycarbonate (and epoxy resins); it is an oestrogen-mimicking endocrine disruptor banned in baby bottles in many countries.
summary: The answer is (b) Polycarbonate. BPA is the monomer that is polymerised with phosgene (or a carbonate source) to make polycarbonate plastics, so it is a structural building block of that plastic.

question: Triclosan’, considered harmful when exposed to high levels for a long time, is most likely present in which of the following?
subject: Environment
detail: Triclosan (and the related triclocarban) is a synthetic, broad-spectrum antimicrobial chemical used since the 1970s in personal-care products (toothpaste such as those aimed at gingivitis, antibacterial soaps, body washes, deodorants, shaving creams, mouthwash), and also in some cosmetics, textiles, kitchenware and toys. Concerns include endocrine (thyroid and reproductive hormone) disruption seen in animal studies, possible contribution to antimicrobial resistance, and aquatic toxicity because it passes through wastewater and bioaccumulates in algae and fish. It can also form dioxins and chloroform on reacting with sunlight or chlorinated water. The US FDA banned it in over-the-counter consumer antiseptic wash products in 2016, and the EU has restricted its use in several product types, including hygiene products such as soaps. Elimination logic: food preservatives are substances such as benzoates, sorbates, nitrites and sulphites, not triclosan. Fruit ripening agents are calcium carbide (which releases acetylene), ethephon and ethylene. Reused plastic containers are linked with chemicals such as BPA and phthalates. Triclosan is a classic toiletry ingredient, so (d) is correct.
explanations: Incorrect: food preservatives are agents like sodium benzoate, sorbic acid, nitrites and sulphites. Triclosan is not a food additive.
Incorrect: fruit ripening uses ethylene, ethephon or illegally calcium carbide (acetylene). Triclosan has no role in ripening.
Incorrect: reused plastic containers are associated with leaching of BPA and phthalates, not triclosan, which is the standard association for this question's distractor.
Correct: triclosan is an antimicrobial in toothpaste, soaps, hand washes, deodorants and other toiletries, with concerns about endocrine disruption and resistance on prolonged high exposure.
keyfact: Triclosan = antibacterial agent in toiletries (toothpaste, soaps, deodorants); endocrine-disruption and antimicrobial-resistance concerns.
option_notes: Food preservatives are substances that prevent spoilage by microbes or oxidation. Examples include class I (salt, sugar, vinegar, natural) and class II (benzoates, sorbates, sulphites, nitrites, nitrates). In India the FSSAI regulates them under the Food Safety and Standards Act 2006 and its additive regulations. Excess sulphite can trigger asthma, and nitrites are linked to nitrosamine formation.

Fruit-ripening substances include ethylene gas (permitted, a natural plant hormone) and ethephon, which releases ethylene. Calcium carbide, which produces acetylene and may contain arsenic and phosphorus traces, is banned by FSSAI for ripening. Artificial ripening with it can cause mouth ulcers, gastric problems and neurological effects. Ethylene is permitted in regulated concentrations in ripening chambers.

Reused plastic containers, especially PET bottles and polycarbonate, may leach chemicals like bisphenol A (BPA), phthalates and antimony on heating, scratching or repeated use. BPA is an endocrine disruptor, and India (BIS and FSSAI) regulates BPA in baby feeding bottles. Plastic recycling codes 1-7 indicate resin types, and number 7 often involves polycarbonate.

Toiletries are personal-care items such as soap, toothpaste, shampoo, deodorant, and mouthwash. Triclosan is an antibacterial and antifungal added to many of them. It is regulated by the US FDA (banned in consumer antiseptic washes in 2016) and the EU, and it is a persistent water pollutant that may disrupt thyroid hormones and promote resistant bacteria.
related: Triclosan is an antibacterial and antifungal agent used in toothpaste, soaps and deodorants.
The US FDA banned triclosan in consumer antiseptic wash products in 2016.
Triclosan inhibits the bacterial enzyme enoyl-ACP reductase (FabI).
BPA is an endocrine disruptor in polycarbonate plastics and epoxy resins.
Calcium carbide, used illegally for ripening fruit, is banned by FSSAI.
Microbeads in scrubs are a source of microplastic pollution in water bodies.
Endocrine-disrupting chemicals interfere with hormone systems; examples are BPA, phthalates and some pesticides.
FSSAI, set up under the Food Safety and Standards Act 2006, regulates food additives in India.
summary: The answer is (d) Toiletries. Triclosan is an antibacterial and antifungal agent added to toothpastes, soaps, hand washes, deodorants and similar personal-care products, and long-term exposure to high levels is a health and environmental concern.
topic_notes: Triclosan is a chlorinated aromatic compound (a polychloro phenoxy phenol) with antibacterial and antifungal action. It works by inhibiting the bacterial enzyme enoyl-acyl carrier protein reductase (FabI), which is needed for fatty acid synthesis. It was introduced in the 1960s-70s, first in hospital settings as a surgical scrub, and then moved into consumer products. Uses: toothpaste (Colgate Total used triclosan with a copolymer to reduce plaque and gingivitis), antibacterial soaps, hand sanitisers, deodorants, cosmetics, and some plastics, clothes and kitchen items. Health and environmental concerns: studies in animals show lowered thyroid hormone levels and reproductive effects, there are concerns about antibiotic cross-resistance, and it is toxic to algae and aquatic life. It is found in sewage sludge and rivers, and it bioaccumulates. In sunlight it can degrade into dioxins, and with chlorinated tap water it can form chloroform. Regulation: the US FDA 2016 final rule banned triclosan and triclocarban, among other ingredients, in consumer antiseptic washes; the EU progressively restricted its use in cosmetics and food-contact materials; the Stockholm Convention committee has discussed related persistent chemicals. Related UPSC angles include other chemicals of concern in daily life: BPA in plastics, phthalates, parabens in cosmetics, microbeads in scrubs (banned in several countries), PFAS ('forever chemicals'), and endocrine-disrupting chemicals generally. Also remember FSSAI's role in food additives, BIS's role in standards, and the Plastic Waste Management Rules, which restrict single-use plastics.

question: Which one of. the following is a reason why astronomical distances are measured in light-years?
options: Distances among stellar bodies do not change
Gravity of stellar bodies does not change
Light always travels in straight line
Speed of light is always same. [P.7.0
subject: Science & Tech
detail: A light-year is a unit of length, not of time. It equals about 9.46 x 10^12 km (about 9.46 trillion km). It is the distance light covers in one Julian year (365.25 days) in vacuum. The unit is meaningful only because the speed of light in vacuum, c = 299,792,458 m/s, is the same for all observers and in all inertial frames. This is a postulate of Einstein's special relativity (1905), and the metre has been defined through c since 1983. Because c is constant, 'distance = c x time' gives an unambiguous distance. Kilometres give unwieldy numbers: the nearest star, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.24 light-years away, and the Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years across. Elimination: (a) is false because stars and galaxies move, so distances change over time. (b) is false because gravity varies with mass and distance, and it is irrelevant to the choice of unit. (c) is partly true in a uniform medium, but light bends near massive bodies (gravitational lensing) and in different media, and straight-line travel alone does not define a unit of length. Only constant speed makes the unit reliable. Other units: the astronomical unit (AU) is used inside the solar system, and the parsec (about 3.26 light-years) is used in professional astronomy.
explanations: Wrong. Distances among stars and galaxies do change, because of proper motion, orbital motion and cosmic expansion. Even if they were fixed, that would not explain why light-years are chosen as the unit.
Wrong. Gravity depends on mass and distance and varies from body to body. It has no role in defining a light-year.

Wrong. Light travels straight in a uniform medium, but gravity can bend it (gravitational lensing, confirmed in the 1919 eclipse observations) and refraction bends it in other media. Straight-line travel does not by itself justify a unit; constant speed does.

Correct. The speed of light in vacuum is a universal constant, so the distance light travels in a year is a fixed, well-defined length. That is why the light-year serves as a standard unit for astronomical distances.
keyfact: A light-year (about 9.46 x 10^12 km) is a unit of distance, usable because the speed of light in vacuum is constant.
option_notes: Constancy of stellar distances: this is not true. Stars move relative to one another (Barnard's Star has the largest proper motion, about 10.4 arcseconds a year). Galaxies recede because the universe is expanding (Hubble's law, 1929). The Andromeda galaxy, by contrast, is approaching the Milky Way at about 110 km/s. Distances in space are therefore dynamic, not fixed.

Constancy of gravity: gravitational force follows Newton's inverse-square law, F = GMm/r^2. It varies with mass and separation. Einstein's general relativity (1915) describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime. Surface gravity differs between bodies, for example Earth 9.8 m/s^2, Moon about 1.6 m/s^2, Sun about 274 m/s^2. It plays no part in defining distance units.

Straight-line propagation of light: light follows straight paths only in a uniform medium (the rectilinear propagation property). It bends by refraction, diffraction and gravitational lensing. Eddington's 1919 solar-eclipse observations confirmed that starlight is deflected near the Sun. Light-years do not depend on straightness; they depend on a constant speed.

Constant speed of light: in vacuum c = 299,792,458 m/s, about 3 x 10^8 m/s. It is independent of the motion of source and observer (special relativity, 1905). One light-year is about 9.46 x 10^12 km. The speed is lower in media (about 2 x 10^8 m/s in glass). This constancy makes the light-year a dependable unit.
related: 1 light-year is about 9.46 trillion km.
1 parsec is about 3.26 light-years.
1 AU is about 149.6 million km; sunlight takes about 8 min 20 s to reach Earth.
Proxima Centauri (about 4.24 ly) is the nearest known star after the Sun.
Speed of light in vacuum is about 3 x 10^8 m/s, the maximum possible speed.
Andromeda galaxy lies about 2.5 million ly away and is approaching the Milky Way.
The metre has been defined via the speed of light since 1983.
ISRO's AstroSat (2015) is India's first dedicated astronomy satellite.
summary: The answer is (d). A light-year is the distance light travels in one year in vacuum, and it works as a unit of distance because the speed of light in vacuum is a universal constant (about 299,792,458 m/s). That constancy gives a fixed, reliable yardstick for the vast distances in space.
topic_notes: Astronomical distance units: (1) Astronomical Unit (AU) is the mean Earth-Sun distance, about 1.496 x 10^8 km (149.6 million km). It is used within the solar system, and light takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to travel this distance. (2) Light-year (ly) is about 9.46 x 10^12 km. (3) Parsec (pc) is the distance at which 1 AU subtends an angle of 1 arcsecond of parallax. It equals about 3.26 ly or 3.09 x 10^13 km. Kiloparsec, megaparsec and gigaparsec are used for galactic and cosmological scales. Key distances: Moon is about 1.3 light-seconds away. Sun is about 8.3 light-minutes away. Proxima Centauri, the nearest star after the Sun, is about 4.24 ly away. Sirius is about 8.6 ly away. Andromeda galaxy is about 2.5 million ly away. The Milky Way's disc is about 100,000 ly across. The observable universe has a radius of about 46 billion ly. The Sun is about 26,000 ly from the galactic centre. Light-year is a unit of distance, not time. Methods of measuring distance: radar ranging in the solar system; trigonometric parallax for nearby stars (the Gaia mission); standard candles such as Cepheid variables (Henrietta Leavitt) and Type Ia supernovae for far-off galaxies; and redshift with Hubble's law for very distant galaxies. Related physics: speed of light is the maximum speed of information transfer. Looking far into space means looking back in time, because light from distant objects is old. Indian context: ISRO's AstroSat (2015) is India's first dedicated multi-wavelength space observatory, and Aditya-L1 (2023) studies the Sun.

ocr: We adopted parliamentary democracy based on the British model, but how does our model differ from that model? 1. As regards legislation, the British Parliament is supreme or sovereign but in India, the power of the Parliament to legislate is limited. 2. In India, matters related to the constitutionality of the Amendment of an Act of the Parliament are referred to the Constitution Bench by the Supreme Court. Select the correct answer using the code given below. (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 : (ad) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Polity
detail: India adopted the Westminster model of parliamentary government (collective responsibility, a nominal head of state, a bicameral legislature, a Cabinet drawn from the legislature). It departs from the British model in important ways. Britain follows parliamentary sovereignty (Dicey): Parliament can make or unmake any law and no court can strike it down, because the constitution is largely unwritten and flexible. India has a written Constitution with a federal division of powers (Seventh Schedule, Article 246), justiciable Fundamental Rights (Article 13, Articles 32 and 226), and judicial review. The Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that Parliament's amending power under Article 368 cannot alter the basic structure. Parliament's legislative power is therefore limited, which makes Statement 1 correct. Article 145(3) requires a minimum of five judges to decide a case involving a substantial question of law on the interpretation of the Constitution, or a Presidential reference under Article 143. Challenges to the validity of a constitutional Amendment Act raise exactly such a question and go to a Constitution Bench, as in Kesavananda (13 judges) and the NJAC case (5 judges). Statement 2 is therefore correct. Elimination: once both statements are verified, only (c) remains. Also, India has an elected President as head of state, unlike the British hereditary monarch.
explanations: (a) 1 only is wrong because Statement 2 is also correct under Article 145(3).
(b) 2 only is wrong because Statement 1 is also correct; Indian Parliament's legislative power is limited unlike the sovereign British Parliament.
(c) Both 1 and 2 is right: India has limited parliamentary power and Constitution Bench references for constitutional questions.
(d) Neither 1 nor 2 is wrong because both statements are accurate.
keyfact: UK: parliamentary sovereignty; India: constitutional supremacy with judicial review, and Article 145(3) requires a bench of at least 5 judges for substantial constitutional questions.
statements: 1 — Correct: British Parliament is sovereign, whereas India's Parliament is bound by the written Constitution, federal distribution of powers, Fundamental Rights and judicial review, including the basic structure doctrine.

2 — Correct: Under Article 145(3), substantial questions on the interpretation of the Constitution, including the constitutionality of an Amendment Act, are heard by a Constitution Bench of at least five Supreme Court judges.
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. British Parliament is sovereign, while India's Parliament is limited by a written Constitution, federal division of powers, fundamental rights and judicial review. Under Article 145(3), questions on the interpretation of the Constitution, which include the constitutionality of Amendment Acts, must be heard by a Constitution Bench of at least five judges.

ocr: With reference to the Union Government, consider the following statements : 1, (aN Gopalaswamy Iyengar Committee suggested that a minister and a_ secretary be designated solely for pursuing the subject of administrative reform and promoting it. 2. in 1970, the Department of Personnel. was _ constituted on the recommendation of the Administrative Reforms Commission, 1966, and this was placed under the Prime Minister’s charge. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (ad) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Polity
detail: Administrative reform in India has been examined by many bodies. N. Gopalaswamy Ayyangar, a Minister without Portfolio, was asked in 1949 to report on the reorganisation of the central government machinery. His report led to the creation of the Organisation and Methods (O&M) Division in 1954 in the Cabinet Secretariat. The Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC) of 1966, first chaired by Morarji Desai and later by K. Hanumanthaiya, made many recommendations on the machinery of government. One of them was to set up a Department of Personnel, which was established in 1970 and placed under the Prime Minister's charge, in the Cabinet Secretariat. It was later developed into the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) within the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions. The ARC also recommended the Lokpal and Lokayukta institutions. For elimination, statement 2 is a well-known, verifiable fact, so options (a) and (c) fall away. Statement 1 is not supported as a Gopalaswamy Ayyangar recommendation, so options (c) and (d) are removed and (b) remains. The UPSC key confirms (b).
explanations: (a) Wrong: it accepts statement 1 as correct and rejects statement 2, but statement 2 is correct and statement 1 is not.
(b) Right: only statement 2 is correct, which matches the official answer. The 1970 Department of Personnel followed the ARC (1966) and was under the Prime Minister.
(c) Wrong: it requires statement 1 to be correct as well, which the official key does not accept.
(d) Wrong: statement 2 is a correct historical fact, so it cannot be that neither statement is correct.
keyfact: Department of Personnel: set up in 1970 on the ARC (1966) recommendation, under the Prime Minister's charge (later DoPT).
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Gopalaswamy Ayyangar Committee did not suggest designating a minister and a secretary solely to pursue and promote administrative reform; its main outcome was the O&M Division (1954) and a restructured central machinery. UPSC treats this statement as wrong.
2 — Correct: The Department of Personnel was constituted in 1970 on the recommendation of the Administrative Reforms Commission (1966) and was placed under the Prime Minister's charge.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. The Department of Personnel was set up in 1970 on the Administrative Reforms Commission's (1966) recommendation and placed under the Prime Minister's charge. The N. Gopalaswamy Ayyangar report (1949) did not suggest a minister and a secretary solely for administrative reform; that suggestion is attributed to the A.D. Gorwala report (or the Gopalaswamy Ayyangar-era proposals on O&M), so statement 1 is treated as incorrect.

question: Right to Privacy’ is protected under which Article. of the Constitution of India?
subject: Polity
detail: The Right to Privacy is not explicitly mentioned in the Constitution. It was read into Article 21 ('No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law') through judicial interpretation. Earlier, M.P. Sharma (1954, eight judges) and Kharak Singh (1962, six judges) had denied privacy the status of a fundamental right. Later cases such as Gobind v. State of MP (1975) and R. Rajagopal (1994) recognised it in part. On 24 August 2017, in Puttaswamy, a nine-judge bench unanimously overruled M.P. Sharma and the relevant part of Kharak Singh. It held privacy to be a fundamental right under Article 21, and also as part of the freedoms in Part III, including Articles 14 and 19. Privacy covers bodily autonomy, informational privacy, and decisional autonomy, and is subject to restrictions that are legal, necessary and proportionate. Elimination logic: Article 15 prohibits discrimination, Article 19 gives the six freedoms (speech, assembly, etc.), and Article 29 protects the cultural and educational interests of minorities. The question asks for the primary source, which is Article 21. The case later shaped the Aadhaar judgment (2018) and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.
explanations: Incorrect: Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. It is not the source of privacy.

Incorrect: Article 19 guarantees freedoms such as speech and expression, assembly and movement. Privacy was held to be linked to these, but its primary home is Article 21, so this is not the best answer.
Correct: Puttaswamy (2017) held privacy to be an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21.
Incorrect: Article 29 protects the interests of minorities, including their language, script and culture. It has no bearing on privacy.
keyfact: Puttaswamy v. Union of India (24 Aug 2017, 9 judges): Right to Privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21.
summary: The answer is (c) Article 21. In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017), a nine-judge Supreme Court bench held that the Right to Privacy is an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21.

question: Consider the following statements : 1, In India, there is no law restricting the candidates from contesting in one Lok Sabha election from three constituencies. In 1991 Lok Sabha Election, Shri Devi Lal contested from three Lok Sabha constituencies. As per the existing rules, if a candidate contests in one Lok Sabha election from many constituencies, his/her _ party should bear the cost of byeelections to the constituencies vacated by him/her in the event ‘ of him/her winning in all the constituencies. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: Before 1996 there was no limit on how many constituencies one person could contest in a single election. Devi Lal used this freedom in 1989 (Sikar, Rohtak and Ghatampur) and again in 1991 (Sikar, Rohtak and Firozpur). The Representation of the People (Amendment) Act, 1996 inserted Section 33(7) into the RP Act, 1951. It bars a person from contesting a general election, or a group of bye-elections or biennial elections held together, from more than two constituencies. This is a statutory restriction, not a constitutional one. If a candidate wins both seats, he or she must resign one within 14 days under Section 70 of the RP Act read with the Representation of the People (Conduct of Elections) Rules, otherwise both seats fall vacant. The Election Commission has recommended raising the cost to the candidate: Rs 5 lakh for a vacated Assembly seat and Rs 10 lakh for a Lok Sabha seat. The Law Commission's 255th Report (2015) also backed the idea of limiting a candidate to one seat. Neither proposal has been enacted. So there is no current rule making the party bear the cost. Eliminating statements 1 and 3 leaves only statement 2, which gives option (b).
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is false. Since 1996 the law limits a candidate to two constituencies.
(b) is correct because only statement 2 is true. Devi Lal contested three seats in 1991, before the two-seat cap.
(c) is wrong because it relies on statements 1 and 3, and both are false.
(d) is wrong because it includes statement 3, which describes a rule that does not exist.
keyfact: Section 33(7) of the RP Act, 1951 (amended in 1996) caps a candidate at two constituencies, and no law makes the party pay for bye-elections.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Section 33(7) of the RP Act, 1951, inserted in 1996, restricts a candidate to a maximum of two constituencies in one general election.
2 — Correct: Devi Lal contested three Lok Sabha seats in 1991, when no cap existed. The cap came in 1996.
3 — Incorrect: No existing rule makes the party bear bye-election costs. The Election Commission and the Law Commission have only recommended that the candidate bear the cost.
summary: The most defensible answer is (b), statement 2 only. Since the 1996 amendment to Section 33(7) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, a candidate can contest from at most two constituencies in one general election, so statement 1 is wrong. No rule makes the party pay for bye-elections, so statement 3 is wrong. Devi Lal did contest three seats in 1991, before the cap came in, so statement 2 is correct.
why_dropped: The printed options and statements appear to have been garbled or inconsistent across paper sets, and the Devi Lal fact (three seats in both 1989 and 1991) invited confusion. UPSC probably dropped the question for these ambiguities.

ocr: Consider the following statements : 1. ‘Right to the City’ is an agreed human right and the UN-Habitat monitors the commitments made by each country in this regard. 2. ‘Right to the City’ gives every occupant of the city the right to reclaim public spaces and public participation in the city. 3. ‘Right to the City’ means that the State cannot deny any public service or facility to the unauthorized colonies in the city. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (a) 1 only (b) 3 only (c) 1 and 2 (@ 2and3
subject: Polity
detail: The 'Right to the City' idea was first articulated by Henri Lefebvre in 'Le Droit à la ville' (1968) and later developed by David Harvey. It asserts that all inhabitants, whatever their legal or tenure status, have the right to use, occupy, produce and shape urban space, and to take part in decisions about the city. It was promoted through the World Charter on the Right to the City (Social Forum of the Americas, Quito, 2004; World Urban Forum, Barcelona, 2004), and it informed Brazil's City Statute (2001) and Ecuador's constitution. It also appears in the New Urban Agenda adopted at Habitat III (Quito, 2016), where it is expressed as 'right to the city' in a soft-law, aspirational sense. It is not a codified human right in any binding UN treaty, and UN-Habitat has no mechanism to monitor each country's commitments on it. That makes statement 1 wrong. Statement 2 matches the core idea of reclaiming public space and participating in city life. Statement 3 follows from the principle of non-discrimination in access to services: residents of unauthorised colonies cannot be denied basic services such as water, sanitation and public facilities because of their tenure status. Elimination logic: statement 1 is incorrect, so (a) and (c) are out. Statement 3 is correct, so (b) is out. That leaves (d).
explanations: (a) 1 only: Wrong. Statement 1 is incorrect, since the right is not an agreed human right monitored by UN-Habitat, and it also leaves out the correct statements 2 and 3.
(b) 3 only: Wrong. Statement 3 is correct, but this option omits statement 2, which is also correct.
(c) 1 and 2: Wrong. It includes the incorrect statement 1 and omits the correct statement 3.
(d) 2 and 3: Correct. Both statements reflect the inclusive, participatory and non-discriminatory content of the Right to the City, and statement 1 is the only incorrect one.
keyfact: Right to the City (Lefebvre, 1968; World Charter 2004) is an evolving, non-binding concept of inclusive access, public space and participation. It is not a codified human right monitored by UN-Habitat.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: 'Right to the City' is not an agreed, binding human right in any UN treaty. It is a soft-law, aspirational concept, and UN-Habitat does not monitor each country's commitments on it.
2 — Correct: The concept gives every inhabitant a claim to use and reclaim public spaces and to take part in urban decision-making and governance.

3 — Correct: The concept rests on inclusion and non-discrimination, so the State cannot deny public services or facilities to residents of unauthorised colonies on the ground of their informal status.
summary: The correct answer is (d): statements 2 and 3 are correct, statement 1 is not. 'Right to the City' is not an agreed, binding human right monitored by UN-Habitat; it is an evolving concept about inclusive, participatory urban spaces and equal access to city services.

question:
With reference to India, consider the following statements :
1. Judicial custody means an accused is in the custody of the concerned magistrate and such accused is locked up in police station, not in jail.
2. During judicial custody, the police officer in charge of the case is not allowed to interrogate the suspect without the approval of the court. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, there are two forms of custody. Police custody means the accused is held in a police station lock-up under the investigating agency. Judicial custody means the accused is under the magistrate's custody and is sent to a jail (prison), run by the prison department, not the police. Section 167 CrPC governs remand: the magistrate may authorise detention for up to 15 days in police custody, and the total period of detention during investigation can extend to 60 or 90 days depending on the gravity of the offence, after which default (statutory) bail arises. Article 22(2) of the Constitution requires production before a magistrate within 24 hours of arrest, excluding travel time. Once the accused is in judicial custody, the investigating officer cannot interrogate the person at will. They must seek the magistrate's permission, and the interrogation is usually conducted inside the jail. Elimination logic: Statement 1 fails because of the claim that the accused is locked in a police station. That describes police custody. Since statement 1 is wrong, (a), (c) and (d) are eliminated, leaving (b).
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is incorrect. Judicial custody means confinement in jail, not in a police station.
(b) is right because statement 2 is correct and statement 1 is incorrect.
(c) is wrong because statement 1 wrongly places the accused in a police station.
(d) is wrong because statement 2 is correct, so at least one statement holds.
keyfact: Police custody = police station lock-up (max 15 days under Sec 167 CrPC); judicial custody = magistrate's custody in jail, where police need court permission to interrogate.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: In judicial custody the accused is under the magistrate's control and is lodged in jail. Confinement in a police station lock-up is police custody.
2 — Correct: While the accused is in judicial custody, the investigating police officer needs the court's permission to interrogate the person.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. In judicial custody the accused is under the magistrate's control and is lodged in jail, not a police station, and the police can question the accused only with the court's permission.

question:
With reference to India, consider the following statements :
1. When a prisoner makes out a sufficient case, parole cannot be denied to such prisoner because it becomes a matter of his/her right.
2. State Governments have their own Prisoners Release on Parole Rules. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Parole is a conditional, temporary release of a prisoner for a specified purpose such as a family emergency, death or illness of a relative, or marriage, after part of the sentence has been served. It differs from furlough and from remission. Courts have repeatedly held that parole is not a matter of right. It is an administrative decision by the competent authority, taken after considering factors such as the prisoner's conduct, the nature of the offence, the likelihood of absconding, and public interest and law and order. Even if a prisoner shows a sufficient case, the authority may refuse for valid reasons, so statement 1 wrongly says it cannot be denied. 'Prisons' and 'persons detained therein' are Entry 4 of the State List (Seventh Schedule). Because of this, each State has its own prison rules, for example the Punjab Good Conduct Prisoners (Temporary Release) Act, 1962, and the Rajasthan or Delhi Prisons Rules. The Model Prison Manual 2016 gives only guidance. Elimination logic: once statement 1 is seen as false because of the discretionary nature of parole, options (a) and (c) fall. Statement 2 is true, so (d) falls, leaving (b).
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is incorrect: parole is discretionary, not a right, and statement 2 is also correct, so 1 alone cannot be the answer.
(b) is right because only statement 2 is correct. States have their own parole rules, and parole remains an administrative discretion.
(c) is wrong because statement 1 wrongly treats parole as an enforceable right once a sufficient case is shown.
(d) is wrong because statement 2 is correct: State-specific parole rules exist under the State's power over prisons.
keyfact: Parole is a discretionary, conditional release, not a right; prisons are a State List subject (Entry 4), so each State has its own parole rules.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Parole is not an absolute right. It is discretionary and can be denied on grounds such as the prisoner's conduct, the gravity of the offence, or public interest, even if a case is made out.
2 — Correct: Prisons are a State subject (Entry 4, State List), so State Governments have framed their own parole and temporary release rules.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. Parole is not an absolute right of a prisoner, even when a sufficient case is made out, because the competent authority retains discretion. Prisons are a State subject, so States have framed their own parole rules.

question: At the national level, which ministry is the nodal agency to ensure effective implementation of the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006?
options: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
subject: Environment
detail: The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 came into force on 31 December 2007 (rules notified 1 January 2008; amended rules in 2012). It aims to correct the 'historical injustice' done to forest dwellers by recognising individual rights (habitation and self-cultivation, Section 3(1)(a)), community rights (nistar, minor forest produce, grazing, fishing, Section 3(1)(b-m)), and community forest resource rights (Section 3(1)(i)). The Ministry of Tribal Affairs is the nodal agency at the national level, issuing guidelines and monitoring progress. At the state level, the tribal or social welfare department usually acts as the nodal agency. The process begins at the Gram Sabha, which constitutes a Forest Rights Committee and initiates claims. The claim then goes to the Sub-Divisional Level Committee, then the District Level Committee, which makes the final decision. The state-level monitoring committee oversees the process. Elimination: MoEFCC administers conservation laws such as the Forest Conservation Act 1980 and the Wildlife Protection Act 1972. MoPR deals with Part IX and PESA only indirectly. MoRD runs poverty and rural development schemes. None of these is the FRA's nodal ministry.
explanations: Incorrect: MoEFCC administers conservation laws (Forest Conservation Act 1980, Wildlife Protection Act 1972, Environment Protection Act 1986). It gives forest clearances and is consulted under FRA, but it is not the FRA's nodal agency.

Incorrect: MoPR oversees Panchayati Raj institutions and the Part IX constitutional framework. The Gram Sabha has a role under FRA, but MoPR does not implement the Act. PESA 1996 is administered by MoPR, which is a separate matter.
Incorrect: MoRD runs schemes such as MGNREGA, PMAY-G and DAY-NRLM. It has no role as nodal agency for FRA.
Correct: The Ministry of Tribal Affairs is the designated nodal ministry for the FRA 2006, issuing rules and guidelines and monitoring state implementation.
