(c) Correct: S3i focuses on affordable housing, health care and renewable energy, which makes three; mass rapid transport is excluded.
(d) Wrong: all four would require mass rapid transport to be an S3i focus, which it is not.
keyfact: UNOPS S3i invests in three sectors: affordable housing, health care and renewable energy, not mass rapid transport.
option_notes: Only one: this would mean S3i is a single-sector fund. In fact S3i is a multi-sector impact investing initiative of UNOPS covering housing, health and renewable energy. UNOPS itself is a UN body headquartered in Copenhagen, working on infrastructure, procurement and project management, and is self-financing rather than funded from the UN regular budget.

Only two: this would mean any two of the listed sectors alone. S3i has three pillars, not two. It was launched by UNOPS to mobilise private capital for the SDGs in developing markets, using blended finance and impact investing, and partners with governments, DFIs and private investors.

Only three: this is the correct count. S3i, the Sustainable Investments in Infrastructure and Innovation initiative of UNOPS, invests in affordable housing, health care and renewable energy in low and middle-income countries. It aims for measurable social and environmental impact alongside financial returns, and supports SDGs 3, 7, 9 and 11.

All four: this would require mass rapid transport to be an S3i focus. Mass rapid transport (metros, BRT, suburban rail) is typically financed by big multilateral lenders such as the World Bank, ADB, AIIB and national governments, not by the S3i platform. India's metro projects, for instance, draw on JICA, AFD and EIB loans.
related: UNOPS is headquartered in Copenhagen, Denmark.
UNOPS became an independent, self-financing UN entity in 1995.
S3i focus sectors: affordable housing, health care, renewable energy.
S3i is UNOPS's impact investing initiative launched around 2018.
AIIB is headquartered in Beijing and began operating in 2016.
NIIF was set up in India in 2015 as a quasi-sovereign wealth fund.
SDG 7 is affordable and clean energy; SDG 11 is sustainable cities and communities.
The National Infrastructure Pipeline was launched in December 2019.
statements: 1 — Correct: Affordable housing is one of S3i's core sectors. S3i aims to deliver housing for low-income groups through partnerships with governments and developers. It uses blended finance, with UNOPS investing alongside private partners, to bring down the cost of housing. This links to SDG 11 (sustainable cities and communities). UNOPS has experience building shelters and housing in post-disaster and developing settings, and S3i uses that experience to scale up housing finance in emerging markets.

2 — Incorrect: Mass rapid transport (metro, BRT, urban rail) is not among S3i's stated focus sectors. It usually needs very large, sovereign-backed or multilateral bank financing, such as from the World Bank, ADB, AIIB or NDB, and S3i is a smaller impact investment platform. UNOPS does work on roads, bridges and transport in other programmes, but this sector is not part of S3i's three-pillar focus.

3 — Correct: Health care infrastructure is a core S3i sector. It covers hospitals, clinics and related facilities, linked to SDG 3 (good health and well-being). UNOPS has built and refurbished health facilities in many countries and procured medical supplies, for example during COVID-19. S3i channels investment into health infrastructure in underserved regions, using public-private partnership models to improve access to care.

4 — Correct: Renewable energy is a core S3i sector. It covers solar, wind and decentralised mini-grids, linked to SDG 7 (affordable and clean energy) and SDG 13 (climate action). S3i seeks to cut carbon emissions and expand energy access in developing countries, often through blended finance that attracts private capital to projects that would otherwise be considered too risky.
summary: The answer is (c) Only three. UNOPS S3i focuses its impact investments on affordable housing, health care (social infrastructure) and renewable energy, while mass rapid transport is not one of its stated focus sectors.
topic_notes:
UNOPS is the United Nations Office for Project Services, founded in 1973 and made an independent, self-financing UN entity in 1995. It is headquartered in Copenhagen, Denmark. It supports UN agencies, governments and other partners with infrastructure, procurement and project management, in particular in fragile and post-conflict settings. It is not a funding agency in the manner of UNDP. It reports to the UN Executive Board of UNDP/UNFPA/UNOPS.

S3i, launched in 2018, is its impact investing initiative. It has three focus areas: affordable housing, health care infrastructure and renewable energy. It uses blended finance, in which concessional or catalytic public money reduces risk for private investors, to close the infrastructure gap in developing countries. It targets the SDGs, mainly SDG 3, 7, 9, 11 and 13. UNOPS has published an Impact Investing framework, and it reports on outcomes such as housing units delivered, megawatts of renewable capacity and health facilities built.

India connections: UNOPS has had an office in India, and has worked on projects such as the Social Impact Investments in Affordable Housing, and with the Government of India on Affordable housing finance and the Global Housing Technology Challenge India (GHTC-India) through MoHUA is a related but separate programme. Other related UPSC themes include the Global Infrastructure Facility (World Bank), the National Infrastructure Pipeline (NIP), the National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF), the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB, Beijing, 2016), the New Development Bank (Shanghai, 2015), and the Green Climate Fund. UPSC often asks about the functions and headquarters of international organisations, so link each body with its location and mandate.

question: In essence, what does Due Process of Law’ mean?
subject: Economy
detail: Due process of law is an American constitutional doctrine (5th and 14th Amendments of the US Constitution). It has two aspects: procedural due process (fair hearing, notice, an unbiased adjudicator) and substantive due process (the law itself must be reasonable and not arbitrary). Both rest on natural justice, namely nemo judex in causa sua (no one should be a judge in their own cause) and audi alteram partem (hear the other side). Article 21 of the Indian Constitution uses the phrase 'procedure established by law', borrowed from the Japanese Constitution. In A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950), the Supreme Court read it narrowly: a validly enacted law with a prescribed procedure was enough. In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), the Court held that the procedure must be just, fair and reasonable, which brought due process ideas into Article 21 and linked Articles 14, 19 and 21. Elimination: (b) is the contrasting Indian phrase, (d) is Article 14 and a separate concept, and (c) is too vague and is not the standard description of the doctrine. (a) is the best fit.
explanations: Correct: due process is rooted in natural justice, requiring fair procedure, an unbiased decision-maker and a fair hearing, and also reasonableness of the law itself.
Incorrect: 'procedure established by law' is the phrase in Article 21 and is the contrasting, narrower standard. It checks only that a duly enacted procedure was followed, not that the law is fair.

Incorrect: 'fair application of law' captures only a part of procedural fairness. It does not express the doctrine's essence, which is the underlying natural justice and the substantive reasonableness of the law.
Incorrect: equality before law is in Article 14 (borrowed from the British idea of rule of law). It is a different concept from due process.
keyfact: Due process = natural justice (procedural and substantive fairness); 'procedure established by law' (Art. 21, Gopalan) was widened toward it by Maneka Gandhi (1978).
summary: The official answer is (a): 'Due Process of Law' in essence means the principle of natural justice. It goes beyond checking whether a procedure was followed and asks whether the law and its procedure are fair, just and reasonable.

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement-I : In India, prisons are managed. by State Governments with their own rules and _ regulations for the day-to-day administration of prisons. Statement-Il : ’ In India, prisons are governed by the Prisons Act, 1894 which expressly kept the subject of prisons in the control of Provincial Governments. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-Il are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-Il is correct
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Prisons and persons detained therein fall under Entry 4 of List II (State List) in the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution. So administration, management and day-to-day running of prisons rest with State Governments, each framing its own Prison Manual, rules and regulations. The Union role is advisory and coordinating: the Ministry of Home Affairs issues advisories, the Model Prison Manual (2016, and the Model Prisons and Correctional Services Act, 2023 replacing the older model) and funds modernisation. The Prisons Act, 1894 is the colonial central legislation that still governs prison administration, covering classification of prisoners, discipline, offences in prison and the powers of officers. Its Section 59 empowers State Governments to make rules, and it left the control of prisons with Provincial Governments, a position carried into the Government of India Act, 1935 and then the Constitution of India as a State subject. Hence the constitutional and statutory position links directly: the 1894 Act's devolution to provinces is the historical reason why States now run prisons with their own rules. Elimination: (c) and (d) fail because both statements are factually correct; (b) fails because Statement-II does explain Statement-I.
explanations: (a) is correct: both statements are true, and the 1894 Act's retention of prisons under Provincial Governments explains why States manage prisons today.
(b) is wrong: although both statements are correct, Statement-II is a valid explanation of Statement-I, not an unrelated fact.
(c) is wrong: Statement-II is correct, since the Prisons Act, 1894 does keep prisons under Provincial control.
(d) is wrong: Statement-I is correct, since prisons are a State subject managed by State Governments under their own rules.
keyfact: Prisons = Entry 4, State List; the Prisons Act, 1894 left them with Provincial Governments, hence State control today.
statements: 1 — Correct: Prisons are a State subject (Entry 4, List II), and State Governments manage them through their own prison manuals, rules and regulations.
2 — Correct: The Prisons Act, 1894 governs prisons and left their control with Provincial Governments, which is the historical basis of State control, so it explains Statement-I.
summary: The answer is (a). Both statements are correct. Prisons are a State subject managed by State Governments under their own rules, and this arrangement traces to the Prisons Act, 1894, which expressly left prisons under Provincial Governments, so Statement-II explains Statement-I.

question: Which one of the following statements best reflects the Chief purpose of the ‘Constitution’ of a country?
options: It determines the objective for the making of necessary laws
It enables the creation of political offices and a government
It defines and limits the powers of government
It secures social justice, social equality and social security. [ P.T.O
subject: Economy
detail: A constitution is the supreme law of a country. Its core function is to set up the structure of government (legislature, executive, judiciary), define the powers and jurisdiction of each organ, and place limits on them so that power is not exercised arbitrarily. This is the idea of constitutionalism, or limited government, which is the rule of law over rule by individuals. In India, limits operate through Fundamental Rights (Part III, Articles 12-35), which bind the State and can be enforced under Articles 32 and 226, through the separation and distribution of powers (including federal division in the Seventh Schedule), and through judicial review. The Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that Parliament's amending power is limited by the basic structure. Elimination logic: options (a), (b) and (d) describe real but secondary or specific features. Creation of offices is a means, and social justice is a goal found in Directive Principles (Part IV) and the Preamble, not in every constitution. Only (c) captures the universal, defining purpose that applies to all constitutions, including those with no social-welfare agenda.
explanations: (a) Incorrect: Constitutions may state objectives (e.g. the Preamble), but determining the objective of lawmaking is not their chief purpose. Their main role is to organise and restrain power.
(b) Incorrect: Creating political offices and a government is an important function, but it is only an enabling step. The distinctive purpose is to regulate and limit that government's powers.
(c) Correct: A constitution defines the powers of the organs of government and limits them through rights, separation of powers and judicial review. This is the essence of constitutionalism.
(d) Incorrect: Social justice, equality and security are aspirational goals, mainly in India's Preamble and Directive Principles. They are not universal or chief purposes of every constitution.
keyfact: A constitution's chief purpose is constitutionalism: it creates government and, above all, defines and limits its powers.
summary: The answer is (c): the chief purpose of a constitution is to define and limit the powers of government. It is the fundamental law that creates the organs of the state, allocates power among them and restrains them, which is the essence of constitutionalism.

question: °In India, which one of the following Constitutional Amendments was widely believed to be enacted to overcome the judicial interpretations of the Fundamental Rights?
subject: Polity
detail: The 1st Amendment Act, 1951 was the first major response of Parliament to judicial interpretation of Fundamental Rights. Courts had held that state laws restricting press freedom (Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras, Brij Bhushan v. State of Delhi, 1950) violated Article 19(1)(a), and State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) struck down communal reservations in educational institutions. Zamindari abolition laws were also being challenged under Article 31 and Article 19(1)(f). The amendment added 'public order', 'friendly relations with foreign states' and 'incitement to an offence' as grounds for restricting speech in Article 19(2), made restrictions 'reasonable' yet justiciable, inserted Article 15(4) enabling special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, added Articles 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule to protect land reform laws from challenge, and clarified that state trading and nationalisation were valid under Article 19(6). Other options: the 42nd Amendment (1976) overrode Kesavananda and Minerva Mills-type limits and expanded DPSP primacy, so it also fits; the 44th (1978) restored rights, removing the right to property as a Fundamental Right; the 86th (2002) inserted Article 21A, the right to education, and was not a response to a judgment. The 1st and 42nd are both plausible, but the 1st is the classic example, with the 24th and 25th Amendments also overriding Golaknath.
explanations: (a) Correct: The 1st Amendment overcame judicial rulings in Romesh Thappar, Brij Bhushan and Champakam Dorairajan by adding Article 15(4), Article 19(2) restrictions and Articles 31A and 31B.

(b) Plausible but weaker: The 42nd Amendment (1976) sought to curb judicial review and prioritise DPSPs, but it was a broad political overhaul of the Constitution, not primarily a response to interpretations of Fundamental Rights.
(c) Incorrect: The 44th Amendment (1978) undid Emergency excesses and made property a legal right under Article 300A; it was a restoration, not an override of the courts.
(d) Incorrect: The 86th Amendment (2002) inserted Article 21A and Article 51A(k); it was a policy initiative on education, not a reaction to a court judgment.
keyfact: The 1st Amendment (1951) was the first to override judicial rulings on Fundamental Rights, adding Article 15(4), Articles 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule.
summary: The most defensible answer is (a), the 1st Amendment (1951). It was enacted to overcome court rulings such as Romesh Thappar, Brij Bhushan and the Champakam Dorairajan case, which struck down or limited state action on free speech, caste-based reservations and land reforms.
why_dropped: Both the 1st and 42nd Amendments (and arguably others) could be said to have been enacted to overcome judicial interpretations, so the question had more than one defensible answer. The phrase 'widely believed' was also vague.

question:
Consider the following organizations/ bodies in India :
1. The National Commission for Backward Classes
2. The National Human _ Rights Commission
3. The National Law Commission
4. The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission How many of the above are constitutional bodies?
subject: Polity
detail: A constitutional body is one directly established by a provision of the Constitution itself. The NCBC began as a statutory body under the National Commission for Backward Classes Act, 1993. The 102nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2018 inserted Article 338B, which gave it constitutional status. It examines complaints and safeguards for socially and educationally backward classes, and it replaced the earlier statutory commission. The National Human Rights Commission was set up under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, so it is statutory. The Law Commission of India is neither constitutional nor statutory. It is an executive body created by a government resolution or notification, and it is reconstituted periodically for fixed terms. The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission is a quasi-judicial statutory body set up under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, and it now functions under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Elimination logic: once you know that only NCBC was elevated by amendment while the other three derive from Acts or executive orders, the count is one. Related examples: Article 338 (NCSC), Article 338A (NCST), Article 280 (Finance Commission), Article 324 (Election Commission).
explanations: Correct. Only NCBC has constitutional status (Article 338B), so the count of constitutional bodies is one.
Incorrect. Two bodies are not constitutional, because NHRC is statutory and the Law Commission is executive in origin, so the count is not two.
Incorrect. Three would require NHRC, Law Commission or NCDRC to be constitutional, and none of them is.
Incorrect. NHRC, Law Commission and NCDRC are not constitutional, so not all four qualify.
keyfact: NCBC became constitutional via the 102nd Amendment (2018), Article 338B; NHRC and NCDRC are statutory, and the Law Commission is only executive.
statements: 1 — Correct: NCBC is a constitutional body under Article 338B, inserted by the 102nd Amendment Act, 2018.
2 — Incorrect: NHRC is statutory, set up under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.
3 — Incorrect: The Law Commission is a non-statutory, non-constitutional executive body created by government notification.
4 — Incorrect: NCDRC is a statutory quasi-judicial body under the Consumer Protection Act (1986, now 2019).
summary: The answer is (a) Only one. Only the National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC) is a constitutional body, having been given constitutional status by the 102nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2018 (Article 338B). The NHRC, Law Commission and NCDRC are statutory or executive creations.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. If the election of the President of India is declared void by the Supreme Court of India, all acts done by him/her in the performance of duties of his/her office of President before the date of decision become invalid.
2. Election for the post of the President of India can be postponed on the ground that some Legislative Assemblies have been dissolved and elections are yet to take place.
3. When a Bill is presented to the President of India, the Constitution prescribes time limits within which he/she has to declare his/her assent. How many of the above statements are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: Statement 1 is tested through Article 71. The Supreme Court has exclusive jurisdiction to inquire into and decide disputes about the election of the President or Vice-President. If the election is declared void, Article 71(2) protects all acts done by the person in the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of the office on or before the date of the decision, so they are not invalidated. Statement 2 relates to Article 54 and Article 62. The electoral college consists of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States (and of the NCT of Delhi and Puducherry). Article 62 requires the election to be completed before the expiry of the term. Under the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952 (Section 4), the election cannot be postponed because of a vacancy in an Assembly, including dissolution, and the Supreme Court upheld this in the 1974 Presidential Reference (Re: Presidential Election, 1974). Statement 3 relates to Article 111. The President may assent, withhold assent or, for non-Money Bills, return the Bill for reconsideration, but no time limit is prescribed. This leaves room for a pocket veto, as in the Indian Post Office Bill, 1986. Because every statement is incorrect, (d) follows.
explanations: (a) is wrong because not even one statement is correct; each of the three fails against the Constitution.
(b) is wrong because no pair of statements is correct, since all three are incorrect.
(c) is wrong because it would require every statement to be correct, but each contradicts Article 71(2), Article 62 or Article 111.
(d) is correct because acts remain valid after a void election, the election cannot be postponed for dissolved Assemblies, and no time limit exists for assent.
keyfact: Art. 71(2): acts of a President whose election is voided stay valid; Art. 111 sets no time limit for assent (pocket veto); Presidential election can't be delayed over dissolved Assemblies.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Article 71(2) says acts done by the President before the Supreme Court's decision voiding the election remain valid.

2 — Incorrect: Election cannot be postponed because of dissolved Assemblies or vacancies; Article 62 requires it to be held before the term ends, and the 1974 Presidential Reference confirmed that vacancies do not invalidate or delay it.
3 — Incorrect: Article 111 prescribes no time limit for the President to give assent, which allows a pocket veto.
summary: The answer is (d) None. All three statements are incorrect: acts of a President whose election is voided remain valid, the Presidential election cannot be postponed because of dissolved Assemblies, and the Constitution sets no time limit for the President's assent to a Bill.

question:
With reference to Finance Bill and Money Bill in the Indian Parliament, consider the following statements :
1. When the Lok Sabha transmits Finance Bill to the Rajya Sabha, it can amend or reject the Bill.
2. When the Lok Sabha transmits Money Bill to the Rajya Sabha, it cannot amend or reject the Bill, it can only make recommendations.
3. In the case of disagreement between the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, there is no joint sitting for Money Bill, but a joint sitting becomes necessary for Finance Bill. How many of the above statements are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: Under Article 110, a Money Bill deals only with the matters listed there, such as taxation, borrowing and the Consolidated Fund of India. It can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, on the President's recommendation, and the Speaker certifies it as a Money Bill. Under Article 109, the Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations on it, and it must return the bill within 14 days. The Lok Sabha may accept or reject those recommendations. If the Rajya Sabha does nothing within 14 days, the bill is deemed passed. There is no joint sitting for a Money Bill, because the Lok Sabha's will prevails. Finance Bills are of two kinds. Under Article 117(1), a Finance Bill (I) contains Money Bill matters plus other matters, and is treated like a Money Bill only in that it can be introduced solely in the Lok Sabha. The Rajya Sabha has full powers over it, and a disagreement can lead to a joint sitting under Article 108. Under Article 117(3), a Finance Bill (II) is treated as an ordinary bill, with a few financial-bill restrictions. Elimination logic: statement 1 fails because the Rajya Sabha, not the Lok Sabha, has the amend-or-reject power over a Finance Bill, and the statement misattributes it. Statements 2 and 3 match Articles 109 and 108, so exactly two are correct.
explanations: (a) Wrong: this would hold only if just one statement were correct, but both statements 2 and 3 are correct.
(b) Right: statements 2 and 3 are correct and statement 1 is incorrect, so exactly two are correct. This is the official answer.
(c) Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect, because the Lok Sabha is the transmitting house and the Rajya Sabha holds the power to amend or reject a Finance Bill.
(d) Wrong: statements 2 and 3 correctly reflect Articles 109 and 108, so the answer cannot be none.
keyfact: Money Bill (Art. 109/110): Rajya Sabha can only recommend within 14 days and there is no joint sitting. Finance Bill (Art. 117) is treated like an ordinary bill, so the Rajya Sabha can amend or reject it and a joint sitting is possible.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: the statement wrongly says the Lok Sabha can amend or reject the Bill when it transmits it to the Rajya Sabha. It is the Rajya Sabha that can amend or reject a Finance Bill, since the Rajya Sabha has full powers over it, and the Lok Sabha is the transmitting house here.
2 — Correct: under Article 109 the Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations on a Money Bill within 14 days. It cannot amend or reject it, and the Lok Sabha may accept or reject the recommendations.

3 — Correct: a Money Bill has no joint sitting, because the Lok Sabha's view prevails. A Finance Bill, which is treated like an ordinary bill in this respect, can go to a joint sitting under Article 108 if the Houses disagree.
summary: The answer is (b): only two statements are correct. Statements 2 and 3 are correct, while statement 1 is incorrect. The Rajya Sabha has the same powers over an ordinary Finance Bill as over any ordinary bill (it can amend or reject it), but the Lok Sabha is not bound by what it does. The statement fails because it says the Lok Sabha 'can amend or reject' the Bill when transmitting it, when it is the Rajya Sabha that holds that power.

question: Consider the following statements : Once the Central Government notifies an area as a ‘Community Reserve’ 1. the Chief Wildlife Warden of the State becomes the _ governing authority of such forest hunting is not allowed in such area people of such area are allowed to collect non-timber forest produce 4. people of such area are allowed traditional agricultural practices How many of the above statements are correct?
subject: Economy
detail: Community Reserves were added by the Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2002, as a category of protected area (Chapter IV, Sections 36C and 36D). They are meant for community or private land where the owners and users wish to conserve wildlife and no government-owned habitat is involved. The declaration is made by the State Government, in consultation with the community or landholders, not by the Central Government. Management belongs to a Community Reserve Management Committee. It is the body responsible for conservation and for the management plan, and it works with the Chief Wildlife Warden's department but is not replaced by that officer. Because the area is a protected area under the Act, hunting of wild animals is prohibited (Section 9). The community's livelihood use, such as collecting non-timber forest produce, continues, because the land stays community or private land and there is no settlement or extinguishment of rights as in a sanctuary. Elimination logic: statement 1 is clearly wrong, because the committee, not the Chief Wildlife Warden, is the governing body. That rules out (c) and (d). Statements 2 and 3 are the safe, well-established ones, so (b) fits. The answer key treats the other statements as not all correct. Statement 4, on agriculture, is the one treated as incorrect here, because the Act does not guarantee traditional agricultural practices in the reserve.
explanations: (a) is wrong: two statements are correct, not one. Statements 2 and 3 are correct, and 1 and 4 are not.
(b) is right: exactly two statements, 2 and 3, are correct, and this matches the official answer.
(c) is wrong: statement 1 is incorrect because the management committee, not the Chief Wildlife Warden, governs the reserve. Statement 4 is also treated as incorrect, so three cannot be correct.
(d) is wrong: statements 1 and 4 are not correct, so all four cannot hold.
keyfact: Community Reserve: Sections 36C/36D of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (2002 amendment); declared by the State Government and managed by a Community Reserve Management Committee.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The governing body is the Community Reserve Management Committee, not the Chief Wildlife Warden. The declaration is also made by the State Government, not the Central Government.
2 — Correct: Community Reserves are protected areas under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, so hunting of wild animals is prohibited (Section 9).
3 — Correct: Local people keep their customary use of the area, including collecting non-timber forest produce.
4 — Incorrect: The Act does not guarantee traditional agricultural practices in the reserve. The key treats this statement as not correct.
summary: The answer is (b): only two statements are correct. A Community Reserve is declared under Section 36C of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, and the Chief Wildlife Warden does not become its governing authority. Hunting stays prohibited, and local people keep their customary access to forest produce.

question:
With reference to ‘Scheduled Areas’ in India, consider the following statements :
1. Within a State, the notification of an area as Scheduled Area takes place through an Order of the President.
2. The largest administrative unit forming the Scheduled Area is the District and the lowest is the cluster of villages in the Block.
3. The Chief Ministers of the concerned States are required to submit annual reports to the Union Home Ministry on the administration of Scheduled Areas in the States. How many of the above statements are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: Scheduled Areas are governed by the Fifth Schedule (Article 244(1)) of the Constitution, which covers the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in states other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram (those are under the Sixth Schedule). Under Paragraph 6 of the Fifth Schedule, the President may by order declare an area to be a Scheduled Area, and may also alter, increase, decrease or rescind it, in consultation with the Governor of the state concerned. The Scheduled Areas Order of 1950 and later orders (e.g. 1977 and subsequent state-specific ones) are examples. The criteria evolved from the Dhebar Commission (1960–61) and the Lokur Committee: preponderance of tribal population, compactness and reasonable size, a viable administrative unit such as a district, block or taluk, and economic backwardness. Hence the largest unit is the district and the smallest is a cluster of villages in a block. Under Paragraph 3, the Governor of each state having Scheduled Areas must submit a report annually, or whenever the President requires, to the President regarding administration of those areas. The Union's executive power extends to giving directions to the state on their administration. A Tribes Advisory Council is also set up under Paragraph 4. Elimination: since statement 3 names the wrong authority and the wrong recipient, 'all three' is out, and since 1 and 2 are right, 'one' and 'none' are out.
explanations: (a) is wrong: two statements, not just one, are correct, since statements 1 and 2 are both accurate.
(b) is right: statements 1 and 2 are correct and statement 3 is incorrect because the Governor reports to the President, so exactly two are correct.
(c) is wrong: statement 3 wrongly names the Chief Minister and the Home Ministry in place of the Governor and the President.
(d) is wrong: statements 1 and 2 are factually correct, so the count is not zero.
keyfact: Fifth Schedule: President declares Scheduled Areas (Para 6) after consulting the Governor, and the Governor reports annually to the President (Para 3); the Chief Minister has no such role.
statements: 1 — Correct: Under Paragraph 6(2) of the Fifth Schedule, the President declares, alters or rescinds Scheduled Areas by order, after consulting the state Governor.

2 — Correct: Scheduled Area designation follows administrative units, with the district as the largest unit and the cluster of villages in a block as the lowest, based on tribal preponderance, compactness and backwardness.
3 — Incorrect: Under Paragraph 3 of the Fifth Schedule, it is the Governor, not the Chief Minister, who reports annually to the President, not to the Union Home Ministry.
summary: The answer is (b): only two statements are correct. Statements 1 and 2 are correct, while statement 3 is wrong because the annual report on Scheduled Areas is submitted by the Governor to the President, not by the Chief Minister to the Home Ministry.

ocr: Consider the following statements : | Statement-I : fl The Supreme Court of India has held in some judgements that the = reservation policies made under Article 16(4) of the Constitution of India would be limited by Article 335 for maintenance of efficiency of administration. Statement-II : Article 335 of the Constitution of India defines the term ‘efficiency of administration’. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements? (a) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I (b) Both Statement-I and Statement
subject: Polity
detail: Article 16(4) empowers the State to make provisions for reservation in appointments or posts in favour of any backward class of citizens not adequately represented in State services. Article 335 says the claims of SCs and STs to services and posts shall be taken into consideration, consistently with the maintenance of efficiency of administration. In Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992) the Supreme Court upheld 27% OBC reservation, capped total reservation at 50% in general, excluded the creamy layer, and denied reservation in promotions. It also held that certain technical, specialised posts may be exempt from reservation, keeping efficiency in view. In M. Nagaraj (2006), the Court upheld the validity of the 77th, 81st, 82nd and 85th Amendments but required the State to show quantifiable data on backwardness and inadequacy of representation, and compliance with Article 335. The 82nd Amendment (2000) added a proviso to Article 335 allowing relaxation in qualifying marks and evaluation standards for SC/ST promotions. The Constitution never defines 'efficiency of administration'; its meaning has been shaped through judicial interpretation, for example in Indra Sawhney and in later cases such as Suraj Bhan Meena. Elimination logic: Statement-II is textually false, since Article 335 contains no definition, so options (a), (b) and (d) fall away and only (c) remains.
explanations: (a) Wrong: Statement-II is incorrect because Article 335 gives no definition of 'efficiency of administration', so it cannot explain Statement-I.
(b) Wrong: Statement-II is not correct, so the claim that both statements are correct fails, even though Statement-I is true.
(c) Right: Statement-I is correct, since the Court has balanced Article 16(4) reservations against Article 335, and Statement-II is incorrect because the Article does not define the term.
(d) Wrong: It reverses the truth values, as Statement-I is correct and Statement-II is incorrect.
keyfact: Article 335 requires SC/ST claims to be weighed consistently with 'efficiency of administration', but never defines the term; the Supreme Court has read Article 16(4) in light of it.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Supreme Court (Indra Sawhney, Nagaraj and others) has held that reservation under Article 16(4) must be consistent with Article 335, so efficiency of administration acts as a limiting consideration.

2 — Incorrect: Article 335 only requires that SC/ST claims be considered consistently with maintaining efficiency of administration. It does not define the term, and its content has been left to judicial interpretation.
summary: The answer is (c): Statement-I is correct and Statement-II is incorrect. The Supreme Court has held that reservation under Article 16(4) must be balanced against Article 335, which requires that the claims of SCs and STs be considered consistently with the maintenance of efficiency of administration. However, Article 335 does not define 'efficiency of administration'.

question: In which one of the following regions was Dhanyakataka, which flourished as a prominent Buddhist centre under the Mahasanghikas, located?
subject: Ancient History
detail: Dhanyakataka, also called Dhaññakata or Dharanikota, lay on the lower Krishna river in the Guntur region of ancient Andhra, close to Amaravati. It was the early capital of the Satavahanas in some traditions and a flourishing port and trade centre. After the Second Buddhist Council at Vaishali (c. 383 BCE), the Sangha split into Sthaviravadins and Mahasanghikas. The Mahasanghikas later divided into sub-sects such as the Chaitikas, Purvashailas (Pubbaseliyas) and Aparashailas (Aparaseliyas), which were centred in the Andhra country around Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda and Dhanyakataka. The Amaravati Mahachaitya (stupa) is a famous Andhra school monument built of white marble with sculpted panels. Nagarjunakonda, patronised by the Ikshvakus, was another major site. Elimination: Gandhara (Taxila, Peshawar) is associated with Sarvastivadins and Gandhara art; Kalinga is associated with Ashoka's war and Dhauli/Udayagiri; Magadha is the heartland of Rajagriha, Pataliputra and Bodh Gaya, linked to the early councils and Theravada-Sthavira tradition. So only Andhra fits Dhanyakataka.
explanations: Correct: Dhanyakataka (Dharanikota/Amaravati) lies on the Krishna river in Andhra and was a Mahasanghika centre.
Wrong: Gandhara in the north-west was known for Sarvastivada Buddhism, Kanishka's Fourth Council tradition and Greco-Buddhist art, not Dhanyakataka.
Wrong: Kalinga (Odisha) is known for Ashoka's conquest, Dhauli and Jaugada edicts, and Jain king Kharavela, not Dhanyakataka.
Wrong: Magadha was the political and early Buddhist heartland (Rajagriha, Pataliputra, Bodh Gaya) but Dhanyakataka was not there.
keyfact: Dhanyakataka (Amaravati/Dharanikota, Krishna valley) in Andhra was a Mahasanghika centre.
option_notes: Andhra: the region of the Krishna-Godavari delta and Deccan, ruled by Satavahanas and then Ikshvakus. It has Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Jaggayyapeta and Dharanikota. It was a major centre of Mahasanghika sub-schools (Chaitika, Purvashaila, Aparashaila) and of the Amaravati school of art, noted for white marble sculpture.

Gandhara: ancient region of north-west India and Pakistan (Peshawar, Taxila, Swat), a Mahajanapada. It was a centre of Sarvastivada Buddhism, the Kushana patronage under Kanishka, and Gandhara art that blended Greek and Indian styles, with Buddha images in schist.

Kalinga: ancient eastern region of coastal Odisha and north Andhra. Ashoka conquered it c. 261 BCE, and the war led to his conversion to Dhamma. It has the Dhauli and Jaugada rock edicts. King Kharavela of the Hathigumpha inscription ruled it in the 1st century BCE and favoured Jainism.

Magadha: the most powerful Mahajanapada, with capitals at Rajagriha and later Pataliputra, under the Haryankas, Shishunagas, Nandas and Mauryas. Buddha attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya there, and the First Council (Rajagriha) and Third Council (Pataliputra) were held there.
related: Mahasanghikas split from Sthaviravadins after the Second Buddhist Council at Vaishali.
Chaitika, Purvashaila and Aparashaila were Mahasanghika sub-sects in Andhra.
Amaravati stupa is in Guntur district, Andhra Pradesh, and the Amaravati school used white marble.
Nagarjunakonda was patronised by the Ikshvakus.
Sarvastivada flourished in Mathura, Kashmir and Gandhara.
Third Buddhist Council was held at Pataliputra under Ashoka.
Fourth Buddhist Council was held under Kanishka in Kashmir.
summary: The answer is (a) Andhra. Dhanyakataka (modern Amaravati/Dharanikota area on the Krishna river in Guntur district, Andhra Pradesh) was a major Mahasanghika centre, and the Mahasanghika-derived Chaitika, Purvashaila and Aparashaila schools flourished there.
topic_notes: Buddhist schools: After the Second Council at Vaishali (c. 383 BCE, under Kalasoka), a dispute over Vinaya rules split the Sangha into the orthodox Sthaviravadins (Theravada) and the liberal Mahasanghikas. The Mahasanghikas are regarded as precursors of Mahayana ideas, such as treating the Buddha as supramundane (lokottara). Their sub-sects include Ekavyavaharika, Lokottaravada, Bahusrutiya, Prajnaptivada, Chaitika, Purvashaila and Aparashaila. Southern sects were centred in Andhra, especially Dhanyakataka, Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda. The Sthaviravadins split into Sarvastivada (Mathura, Kashmir, Gandhara), Vatsiputriya, Mahishasaka, Dharmaguptaka and others. Four councils: First at Rajagriha (Ajatashatru, Mahakassapa), Second at Vaishali (Kalashoka), Third at Pataliputra (Ashoka, Moggaliputta Tissa), Fourth in Kashmir/Kundalvana (Kanishka, Vasumitra and Ashvaghosha). Andhra Buddhist sites: Amaravati stupa (Amaravati school of sculpture, Satavahana period), Nagarjunakonda (Ikshvaku, associated with Nagarjuna tradition), Salihundam, Bavikonda, Thotlakonda, Sankaram and Jaggayyapeta. Acharya Nagarjuna, who propounded Madhyamika/Shunyavada, is linked to Andhra. Dignaga and Dharmakirti were also associated with the south. Other art schools: Gandhara (Greco-Buddhist), Mathura (indigenous, red sandstone) and Amaravati (marble, narrative reliefs). Future questions could ask about Buddhist sects, councils, the Mahayana-Hinayana distinction, Buddhist caves and stupas such as Sanchi, Bharhut and Sarnath, and the Satavahana patronage of Buddhism.

question:
With reference to ancient India, consider the following statements :
1. The concept of Stupa is Buddhist in origin.
2. Stupa was generally a repository of relics.
3. Stupa was a votive and commemorative structure in Buddhist tradition. How many of the statements given above are correct? :
subject: Art & Culture
detail: A stupa is a mound-like or hemispherical structure. It began as a burial tumulus, and earthen funerary mounds (called chaityas or 'smashana' mounds in Vedic and later texts) existed before the Buddha. The Mahaparinibbana Sutta says the Buddha's relics were divided among eight claimants, who built stupas over them. Ashoka is said to have redistributed them into 84,000 stupas. Buddhism therefore did not invent the concept but made it central to its worship. Stupas hold relics (sarira) of the Buddha or monks, or objects they used, in a relic chamber (harmika/casket). They also serve as votive structures built to earn merit, and as commemorative ones marking events in the Buddha's life. Examples include Sanchi, Bharhut, Amaravati and Sarnath (Dhamekh). Elimination logic: statement 1 uses the absolute phrase 'Buddhist in origin', which is the trap. Statements 2 and 3 describe the standard function and tradition. So two are correct, which gives (b), and (c) is ruled out. Jainism and Hinduism also had stupa-like structures; Jain stupas are known from Mathura.
explanations: Wrong: 'Only one' would mean only one of the three is correct, but statements 2 and 3 are both correct.
Correct: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 1 is wrong because stupas, as burial mounds, existed before Buddhism.
Wrong: Statement 1 is not wholly true, since the stupa concept pre-dates Buddhism, so not all three can be correct.
Wrong: Statements 2 and 3 accurately describe Buddhist stupas, so 'none' cannot be right.
keyfact: The stupa is a pre-Buddhist burial mound form, but Buddhism made it a relic-holding, votive and commemorative monument.
option_notes: Only one: this would be the answer if just one statement held. It does not here, but it is a common trap for students who think only the relic function is valid. Remember that stupas are both relic repositories and commemorative or votive monuments.

Only two: the official answer. Statements 2 and 3 are correct and statement 1 is incorrect. This reflects the nuance that Buddhism adopted an existing funerary mound form and gave it religious and architectural elaboration, as at Sanchi, Bharhut and Amaravati, and Ashoka's 84,000 stupas spread the form.

All three: this would be right only if the stupa were originally Buddhist. Mounds for the dead are older, with Vedic references and megalithic burials, so this option is wrong. Remember that UPSC often tests absolute claims about 'origin'.

None: this would mean no statement is correct. That is wrong because relic enshrining and the votive and commemorative role are both standard features of Buddhist stupas, as in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta and Ashokan tradition.
related: Sanchi Stupa (Madhya Pradesh) was founded by Ashoka and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1989.
The Buddha's relics were divided into eight parts after his death at Kushinagar.
Ashoka is said to have built 84,000 stupas.
The Dhamekh stupa stands at Sarnath, where the Buddha gave his first sermon.
Amaravati stupa in Andhra Pradesh is associated with Satavahana patronage and rich sculpture.
The harmika is the square railing on the top of the dome, and the chhatra is the umbrella on its mast.
Chaityas are prayer halls with a stupa, while viharas are monastic residences.
Jain stupas have been found at Kankali Tila, Mathura.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The stupa was not originally Buddhist; burial mounds pre-date the Buddha and were adopted by Buddhism. Pre-Buddhist India had funerary mounds for chiefs and sages, mentioned in Vedic and later literature (smashana, 'chaitya'). The Buddha is said to have told Ananda that a stupa should be raised for a Chakravartin ruler, which suggests an existing royal practice. Buddhism gave the form religious meaning and spread it across Asia, producing pagodas in East Asia and chortens in Tibet. Jains also built stupas, as at Mathura (Kankali Tila). So 'Buddhist in origin' is wrong, though Buddhism is the tradition most associated with stupas.

2 — Correct: Stupas generally enshrined relics (sarira) of the Buddha, his disciples or revered monks. After the Buddha's death at Kushinagar (c. 483 BCE per the traditional view), his ashes were divided among eight claimants, including the Mallas, Shakyas and Magadha's Ajatashatru, and eight stupas were built. Ashoka is said to have opened them and distributed relics into 84,000 stupas. Relics were placed in caskets in a chamber within the dome (anda). Relic caskets were found at Piprahwa and Bhattiprolu, and Sanchi's Stupa 2 and 3 held relics of Sariputta and Mahamogallana. Some stupas held only objects the person had used, or sacred texts.

3 — Correct: In the Buddhist tradition stupas were commemorative, marking the Buddha's life events and holy places, and votive, built or donated to earn merit. Commemorative stupas mark the four great events at Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath and Kushinagar. Votive stupas, often small, were offered by donors, and inscriptions at Bharhut, Sanchi and Amaravati record gifts from kings, merchants, monks and nuns. Features include the anda (dome), harmika, chhatra (umbrella), vedika (railing), torana (gateway) and pradakshina-patha (circumambulation path). Worshippers circle it clockwise, and the Great Stupa at Sanchi is a UNESCO site from 1989.
summary: The answer is (b) Only two: statements 2 and 3 are correct, while statement 1 is incorrect. The stupa as a funerary burial mound predates Buddhism and existed in the Vedic and pre-Buddhist tradition, though Buddhism adopted and popularised it as a relic shrine and commemorative monument.
topic_notes: A stupa (Pali: thupa) is a solid, dome-shaped monument, usually containing relics. Its early form was the burial mound, and Buddhism made it the central object of worship. Eight original stupas were raised over the Buddha's relics. Ashoka (c. 268-232 BCE) is credited with spreading relics into 84,000 stupas, and the Ashokan core of Sanchi (Madhya Pradesh) dates from his time. Later stupas were enlarged under the Shungas, who added stone railings and gateways under the Satavahanas. Parts of a stupa are the anda (hemispherical dome), harmika (square railing on top), yasti (mast), chhatra (umbrella), medhi (drum or base), vedika (railing), torana (gateway) and pradakshina-patha. Major sites are Sanchi, Bharhut (Shunga period, now in Satna district), Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda (Andhra, Satavahana and Ikshvaku), Sarnath (Dhamekh), Piprahwa (Uttar Pradesh, possibly ancient Kapilavastu), Kesaria and Taxila's Dharmarajika. Stupas are classified as saririka (containing bodily relics), paribhogika (objects used by the Buddha), uddesika (commemorative) and votive. Chaitya halls are rock-cut halls of worship with a stupa at the end, such as Karla and Ajanta. Viharas are monasteries. Outside India, stupa forms developed into the pagoda (China and Japan), the chorten (Tibet) and Borobudur (Java) and Sri Lanka's dagoba. Jain stupas appear at Mathura. UPSC could ask next about stupa parts, sites, Buddhist councils and Ashokan edicts.

ocr: With reference to ancient South India, Korkai, Poompuhar and Muchiri were well known as (a) capital cities (b) ports (c) centres of iron-and-steel making (ad) shrines of Jain Tirthankaras [ P.T.O.
subject: Ancient History
detail: The question tests Sangam-age (c. 300 BCE-300 CE) geography and the maritime economy of early Tamilakam. Korkai on the Tamraparni river mouth was the Pandyan port famous for pearl fisheries. Poompuhar (Puhar, Kaveripattinam) was the Chola port at the Kaveri delta, described in Silappadikaram and Pattinappalai, with excavated wharves and warehouses. Muchiri (Muziris, near Kodungallur/Pattanam in Kerala) was the Chera port, a hub of the pepper-for-gold trade with Rome; the Peutinger Table and Periplus of the Erythraean Sea mention it, and the Muziris papyrus records cargo shipments. Elimination logic: the three capitals of the Sangam kingdoms were Madurai (Pandya), Uraiyur (Chola) and Vanji (Chera), so (a) fails. Iron-and-steel centres in the south are associated with Kodumanal, Adichanallur and Telangana's megalithic sites, not these three, so (c) fails. Jain Tirthankara shrines such as Shravanabelagola are in Karnataka, so (d) fails. The coastal, river-mouth locations of all three names point to ports.
explanations: Incorrect: the Sangam capitals were Madurai (Pandya), Uraiyur (Chola) and Vanji/Karur (Chera). Korkai, Poompuhar and Muchiri were primarily ports, though Poompuhar was sometimes a secondary Chola seat.
Correct: all three were major seaports. Korkai was a Pandya pearl port, Poompuhar a Chola emporium and Muchiri a Chera pepper port trading with Rome.
Incorrect: iron-and-steel making is linked to sites such as Kodumanal, Adichanallur, Mayiladumparai and Telangana's megalithic zones, not to these ports.
Incorrect: they were not Jain pilgrimage centres. Jain Tirthankara shrines are associated with places like Shravanabelagola, Madurai hills and Sittanavasal, and the three names are known for trade.
keyfact: Korkai (Pandya), Poompuhar (Chola) and Muchiri/Muziris (Chera) were Sangam-age ports, not capitals.
option_notes: Capital cities: the three Sangam kingdoms had capitals at Madurai (Pandya, with the Tamil Sangams), Uraiyur near Tiruchirappalli (Chola) and Vanji/Karur (Chera). Pandya ports were Korkai and Saliyur, Chola ports Puhar, Chera ports Muziris and Tondi. Kings such as Karikala (Chola), Nedunjeliyan (Pandya) and Senguttuvan (Chera) ruled from these centres. Capitals were political and administrative centres, unlike the ports named here.

Ports: ancient South Indian ports included Korkai (pearls, Pandya), Poompuhar/Kaveripattinam (Chola), Muziris (Chera, pepper), Tondi, Arikamedu (Virapatnam, Roman trading station near Puducherry), Naura, and Nelcynda. Exports were pepper, pearls, ivory, beryl, muslin and spices; imports were gold, wine, amphorae and coral. Roman gold coins found in the south confirm the trade. The Periplus describes these ports in the 1st century CE.

Centres of iron-and-steel making: South India had an Iron Age megalithic culture with sites like Adichanallur (Thoothukudi), Kodumanal (Erode, also beads and gems), Mayiladumparai and Hallur in Karnataka. Wootz steel from Telangana (Konasamudram) and Tamil regions was exported and later known as Damascus steel. Iron ploughshares aided agriculture. These were manufacturing sites and not the ports in the question.

Shrines of Jain Tirthankaras: Jainism reached the south through Bhadrabahu and Chandragupta Maurya traditions, with Shravanabelagola (Karnataka) housing the Gommateshwara/Bahubali statue. Tamil Nadu has Jain caves and Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions at Madurai (Samanamalai, Keezhavalavu) and Sittanavasal paintings. Tirthankaras number 24, with Rishabhanatha first and Mahavira last. These are religious sites and have no link to the three port names.
related: Muziris (Muchiri) was the Chera port, linked with the Roman pepper trade and the Muziris papyrus.
Korkai on the Tamraparni was the Pandya pearl-fishery port.
Poompuhar (Kaveripattinam) was the Chola port described in Silappadikaram and Pattinappalai.
Arikamedu near Puducherry was an Indo-Roman trading station.
Sangam capitals: Madurai (Pandya), Uraiyur (Chola), Vanji (Chera).
Silappadikaram was written by Ilango Adigal; Manimekalai by Sittalai Sattanar.
Kodumanal in Erode was an ancient bead and iron-working centre.
The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st century CE) describes ports of the Indian coast.
summary: The answer is (b) ports. Korkai, Poompuhar (Kaveripattinam) and Muchiri (Muziris) were famous coastal trading ports of ancient South India, linked to Indo-Roman and Southeast Asian maritime trade during the Sangam age.
topic_notes: The Sangam age (c. 300 BCE-300 CE) in Tamilakam saw the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas rule alongside chiefs such as the Velirs. Sangam literature includes Tolkappiyam, Ettuthokai, Pattuppattu, and the epics Silappadikaram (Ilango Adigal) and Manimekalai (Sittalai Sattanar). Capitals: Madurai (Pandya), Uraiyur (Chola), Vanji (Chera). Emblems: fish (Pandya), tiger (Chola), bow (Chera). Ports: Korkai (pearls), Poompuhar (Chola, also called Kaveripattinam), Muziris/Muchiri (Chera), Tondi, Arikamedu, Saliyur and Nelcynda. Indo-Roman trade flourished after the discovery of monsoon winds, traditionally credited to Hippalus in the 1st century CE. Exports were pepper (called yavanapriya), pearls, ivory, gems, textiles and spices; imports were gold, wine, glassware and coral. Archaeological evidence includes Arikamedu excavations, Pattanam (Kerala) digs, Roman coin hoards and Muziris papyrus. Trade guilds such as Manigramam and Ayyavole later also traded. Society had five tinai landscapes: kurinji, mullai, marutham, neithal and palai. Megalithic burials and iron use mark the earlier phase. The Sangam age declined with the Kalabhra period, followed by Pallavas and Pandyas. UPSC may ask about ports of the east and west coasts, Sangam literature authors, Roman trade evidence and the three Sangams at Madurai.

question: Which one of the following explains the practice of ‘Vattakirutal’ as mentioned in Sangam poems?
options: Learned persons assembling in royal courts to discuss religious and philosophical matters
Young girls keeping watch over agricultural fields and driving away birds and animals
A king defeated in a _ battle committing ritual suicide by starving himself to death
subject: Environment
detail: Vattakirutal literally means 'sitting facing the north' (vatakku = north, iruttal = sitting). In Sangam literature, especially the Purananuru and related puram poems, it describes a king, or sometimes a warrior or chieftain, who suffered defeat, a wound in the back, or public humiliation and chose to starve himself to death in a dedicated spot, in the open, facing north. This was an honour-bound act, akin to the later Jain sallekhana or the Hindu prayopavesa, but it was a martial and heroic code. The best-known case is the Chera king Cheraman Perumcheral Irumporai, who was captured by the Chola king and, humiliated, sat in vatakkiruttal; the Kovur Kizhar and Pisiraanthaiyar poems also describe such acts. Poets sometimes sat with the king in solidarity. Elimination: option (a) refers to the yavana or women bodyguards described in Tamil and Mauryan sources, not this term. Option (b) describes learned assemblies, linked to the Sangams themselves. Option (c) concerns the agricultural practice of 'kuravai' and 'kilikadival' (driving away parrots) in the Kurinji tinai, so it is a different custom.
explanations: Incorrect: Women bodyguards (the 'yavana' and women guards at royal courts) are mentioned in Sangam and Greek sources, but they have nothing to do with the term vattakirutal.
Incorrect: Learned assemblies refer to the Sangams (academies at Madurai) or royal courts with poets, not to vattakirutal, which is a death ritual.
Incorrect: Girls guarding millet fields and scaring away parrots is a theme in Kurinji-tinai poems (kilikadival), not vattakirutal.
Correct: Vattakirutal was the ritual fast unto death by a king, usually after defeat or disgrace, while sitting facing north, as described in the Purananuru.
keyfact: Vattakirutal = Sangam-era ritual fast to death by a defeated or disgraced king, sitting facing north.
option_notes: Women bodyguards: Sangam and early historical texts, including Megasthenes' account of Mauryan courts and Tamil poems, mention armed women attending kings. In Tamil Nadu 'yavanas' also served as palace guards. It reflects royal security arrangements and is a separate topic from the northward fasting custom. It is a plausible distractor but not related to vattakirutal.

Learned assemblies: Royal courts in Tamil country patronised poets (pulavar), bards (panar) and minstrels (viraliyar). The Sangams, held under Pandya patronage at Madurai, were gatherings of poets and scholars. Debates on religion and philosophy are associated more with later periods, including Buddhist and Jain monks, and with Pallava and Chola courts. This option confuses the term with the academies.

Girls guarding fields: In Sangam akam poetry the five tinais (Kurinji, Mullai, Marutham, Neithal, Palai) each have their own landscape and customs. Kurinji (hills) features millet fields guarded by young women who drive away parrots; this is a romantic setting for meetings between lovers. It is a poetic convention, not an act of vattakirutal.

Vattakirutal: A ritual starvation to death by a king facing north, observed in the puram tradition after military defeat, wounds on the back or public disgrace. The Chera king Kokkothai Marban and Cheraman Perumcheral Irumporai are linked with the practice in poems. It shows the high value placed on honour, valour (maram) and heroic death in early Tamilakam, and resembles later Jain sallekhana.
related: Vattakirutal: ritual fasting to death by a defeated king, facing north, in Sangam puram poetry.
Cheraman Perumcheral Irumporai is the Chera king associated with the practice.
Sangam poetry is classified into akam (love) and puram (war, kingship).
Five tinais: Kurinji, Mullai, Marutham, Neithal, Palai.
Karikala Chola won the Battle of Venni and built the Kallanai (Grand Anicut) according to tradition.
Silappadikaram was written by Ilango Adigal; Manimekalai by Sittalai Sattanar.
Hero-stones (nadukal) commemorated warriors who died in battle.
Jain sallekhana is a comparable fast unto death for religious reasons.
summary: The answer is (d). Vattakirutal (also called Vatakkiruttal or Vadakkiruttal) was the Sangam-era practice in which a defeated or dishonoured Tamil king sat facing north and fasted to death, choosing a ritual death over disgrace.
topic_notes: The Sangam age (roughly 3rd century BCE to 3rd century CE) is known from Tamil literature, Greek and Roman accounts and inscriptions. The three ruling dynasties were the Cheras (Vanji, west coast, emblem bow), Cholas (Uraiyur/Puhar, emblem tiger) and Pandyas (Madurai, emblem fish). Sangam literature includes Tolkappiyam (grammar), Ettuthokai (Eight Anthologies), Pattuppattu (Ten Idylls) and the epics Silappadikaram and Manimekalai. Poetry is classified as akam (love, inner life) and puram (war, kingship, public life). The five tinais are Kurinji (hills), Mullai (forest), Marutham (agricultural plains), Neithal (coast) and Palai (arid). Puram poetry also uses themes such as vetchi (cattle raid), vanji (invasion), ulinai (siege), tumbai (battle), vakai (victory) and kanchi (transience); the heroic custom of vattakirutal belongs to this world of honour. Heroic death was commemorated with hero-stones (nadukal). Society had tribal and clan features, with chiefs such as the Velir; the kings were patrons of bards and poets. Trade with Rome was significant, with ports at Muziris, Arikamedu and Puhar, and Roman coins found in many places. Other aspects UPSC may test: the three Sangams in tradition, the Karikala Chola and the Battle of Venni, Senguttuvan Chera and the Pattini cult, the Pandya king Nedunchezhiyan, and the Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions.

question:
Consider the following dynasties :
1. Hoysala
2. Gahadavala
3. Kakatiya
4. Yadava How many of the above dynasties established their kingdoms in early eighth century AD? :
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The question tests the chronology of post-Gupta regional powers. The early 8th century (c. 700-750 AD) saw the Chalukyas of Badami (Vikramaditya II), the Pallavas of Kanchi, the Karkota dynasty of Kashmir (Lalitaditya Muktapida), Yashovarman of Kannauj, and the Arab conquest of Sind (712 AD, Muhammad bin Qasim). The four dynasties listed belong to a later phase. The Hoysalas of Dorasamudra (Halebidu) emerged as feudatories of the Western Chalukyas and became independent under Vishnuvardhana in the early 12th century. The Gahadavalas (Rathores) of Kannauj and Varanasi were founded by Chandradeva around 1090 AD, after the Pratihara decline, and Jayachandra was defeated by Muhammad Ghori at Chandawar in 1194. The Kakatiyas of Warangal were Chalukya/Rashtrakuta feudatories who became sovereign under Prola II and Ganapati Deva in the 12th-13th centuries, with Rudramadevi ruling later. The Yadavas of Devagiri rose from the late 12th century under Bhillama V (c. 1187), with Ramachandra defeated by Alauddin Khalji in 1296. Since none was established in the early 8th century, the answer is none.
explanations: (a) Only one is wrong, because not even one of the four dynasties dates from the early 8th century.
(b) Only two is wrong, since none of the four fits the period, so no pair can qualify.
(c) Only three is wrong, since all four, not just three, belong to a much later period (c. 1000-1300 AD).
(d) None is correct, because the Hoysala, Gahadavala, Kakatiya and Yadava kingdoms were all established well after the early 8th century.
keyfact: Hoysala, Gahadavala (c. 1090), Kakatiya and Yadava (c. 1187) are all medieval (11th-13th century) powers, not early 8th century.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Hoysalas became independent only in the 11th-12th century (Vishnuvardhana), not the early 8th century.
2 — Incorrect: Gahadavalas were founded by Chandradeva c. 1090 AD at Kannauj.
3 — Incorrect: Kakatiyas rose as feudatories and became sovereign in the 12th-13th centuries.
4 — Incorrect: Yadavas of Devagiri were established in the late 12th century under Bhillama V.
summary: The answer is (d) None. All four dynasties, Hoysala, Gahadavala, Kakatiya and Yadava (of Devagiri), rose to prominence much later than the early 8th century, between roughly the late 10th and 12th centuries, mostly as successors or feudatories of the Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas and Pratiharas.

question:
With reference to ancient Indian History, , consider the following pairs : Literary work Author
1. ‘Devichandragupta : Bilhana
2. Hammira-Mahakavya : Nayachandra Suri
3. Milinda-panha : Nagarjuna
4. Nitivakyamrita : Somadeva Suri How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
subject: Ancient History
detail: The question tests the authorship of well-known Sanskrit and Pali works. Devichandraguptam is a Sanskrit play by Vishakhadatta, who also wrote Mudrarakshasa. Only fragments survive, and it deals with Ramagupta, Dhruvadevi and Chandragupta II. Bilhana was a Kashmiri poet at the Chalukya court of Vikramaditya VI, and he wrote Vikramankadevacharita and Chaurapanchashika. Hammira-Mahakavya was composed by the Jain scholar Nayachandra Suri in the 15th century. It glorifies the Chauhan ruler Hammira of Ranthambore, who fought Alauddin Khalji. Milinda-panha (Questions of Milinda) is a Pali Buddhist text recording a dialogue between the Indo-Greek king Menander (Milinda) and the monk Nagasena. Nagarjuna was a Mahayana philosopher who founded the Madhyamaka school and wrote the Mulamadhyamakakarika. Nitivakyamrita is a Sanskrit work on polity by the Digambara Jain monk Somadeva Suri, who also wrote Yashastilaka Champu. He lived in the Rashtrakuta period, in the 10th century. Elimination: once you know pairs 2 and 4 are correct and 1 and 3 are wrong, the answer is (b).
explanations: (a) is wrong because two pairs, not one, are correct: pairs 2 and 4.

(b) is correct because Hammira-Mahakavya (Nayachandra Suri) and Nitivakyamrita (Somadeva Suri) are right. Devichandragupta (Vishakhadatta) and Milinda-panha (Nagasena dialogue, no known author) are wrong.
(c) is wrong because it would require pair 1 or pair 3 to be correct, and neither is. Bilhana did not write Devichandragupta, and Nagarjuna did not write Milinda-panha.
(d) is wrong because pairs 1 and 3 are mismatched, so not all four are correct.
keyfact: Devichandragupta = Vishakhadatta; Milinda-panha = Menander and Nagasena; Hammira-Mahakavya = Nayachandra Suri; Nitivakyamrita = Somadeva Suri.
option_notes: Only one: this would mean a single correct pair. It is a distractor here. Many students confuse authors and know only one pair well. Remember that the correct pairs are Nayachandra Suri with Hammira-Mahakavya and Somadeva Suri with Nitivakyamrita, so the count is more than one. Such 'how many' questions need every pair checked individually, since there is no partial credit and a single error changes the answer.

Only two: this is the correct option. The two right pairs are Hammira-Mahakavya by Nayachandra Suri, a Jain poet who wrote on the Chauhan king of Ranthambore, and Nitivakyamrita by Somadeva Suri, a 10th-century Jain writer on polity under the Rashtrakutas. The wrong pairs are Devichandragupta, by Vishakhadatta, and Milinda-panha, a Pali dialogue with Nagasena and not a work of Nagarjuna.

Only three: this would need one of the two wrong pairs to be right. Bilhana is known for Vikramankadevacharita, a biography of the Chalukya king Vikramaditya VI, and for Chaurapanchashika. Nagarjuna was a Madhyamaka Buddhist philosopher, not the author of Milinda-panha. Since both are mismatched, three correct pairs is impossible. It is a trap for students who recognise only some authors' names.

All four: this would need every pair to be correct. It fails because Devichandragupta belongs to Vishakhadatta, the author of Mudrarakshasa, and Milinda-panha records the dialogue of Menander and Nagasena. Choosing it shows overconfidence in familiar-sounding names. UPSC often mixes real authors with the wrong works, so each pair must be checked on its own.
related: Vishakhadatta wrote Mudrarakshasa and Devichandraguptam.
Milinda-panha records the dialogue between Menander and the monk Nagasena.
Kalhana's Rajatarangini (12th century) is a chronicle of Kashmir kings.
Bilhana wrote Vikramankadevacharita on Vikramaditya VI of the Chalukyas of Kalyani.
Somadeva Suri also wrote Yashastilaka Champu (959 CE).
Jayanaka wrote Prithviraja Vijaya on Prithviraj Chauhan.
Kavirajamarga by Amoghavarsha is the earliest available Kannada work on poetics.
Sandhyakar Nandi's Ramacharita is about the Pala king Ramapala.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Devichandragupta (Devichandraguptam) was written by Vishakhadatta, not Bilhana. Vishakhadatta was a Sanskrit dramatist, probably of the Gupta or post-Gupta period, who also wrote Mudrarakshasa, a play on Chanakya and Chandragupta Maurya. Devichandraguptam survives only in fragments, quoted in later works such as the Natyadarpana and by Bhoja. It tells how the Gupta king Ramagupta, besieged by a Shaka ruler, agreed to hand over his queen Dhruvadevi, and how his brother Chandragupta II went disguised as the queen and killed the Shaka. Bilhana was a Kashmiri poet who wrote Vikramankadevacharita on the Chalukya king Vikramaditya VI.

2 — Correct: Hammira-Mahakavya was composed by the Jain scholar Nayachandra Suri, probably in the late 14th or 15th century. It is a Sanskrit epic poem in 14 cantos on the Chauhan (Chahamana) king Hammiradeva of Ranthambore, who sheltered Mongol rebels and resisted Alauddin Khalji. The siege ended in 1301 with Hammira's defeat, and the Rajput women performed jauhar. It is an important source for Chauhan history alongside Prithviraja Vijaya by Jayanaka. Nayachandra was associated with the Tomar court of Gwalior.

3 — Incorrect: Milinda-panha is a non-canonical Pali Buddhist text of uncertain authorship, dated around the 1st century BCE to 1st century CE. It records the dialogue between the Indo-Greek king Menander I (Milinda) of Sakala (Sialkot) and the Buddhist monk Nagasena. The questions concern the soul, rebirth, karma and nirvana. Nagarjuna was a different figure: a Mahayana philosopher of the 2nd century CE, associated with the Satavahana court and Nagarjunakonda, who founded the Madhyamaka (Shunyavada) school.

4 — Correct: Nitivakyamrita was written by Somadeva Suri, a Digambara Jain monk and scholar of the 10th century. He lived under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna III and the Chalukya feudatory Arikesari at Vemulavada. The work is a Sanskrit prose treatise on statecraft, politics and ethics, modelled on Kautilya's Arthashastra. It deals with the state, the king, ministers and diplomacy. Somadeva also wrote Yashastilaka Champu, a Jain prose-and-verse narrative composed in 959 CE, and his works are valued as sources on the social and political life of the period.
summary: The answer is (b): only two pairs are correctly matched. Pair 2 (Hammira-Mahakavya by Nayachandra Suri) and pair 4 (Nitivakyamrita by Somadeva Suri) are correct. Pair 1 is wrong because Devichandragupta was written by Vishakhadatta, not Bilhana, and pair 3 is wrong because the Milinda-panha is a Buddhist text with no known author, not a work of Nagarjuna.
topic_notes: This question belongs to ancient and early medieval Indian literature, where UPSC often asks for author-work matching. Key Sanskrit authors and works to remember: Kalidasa (Abhijnanashakuntalam, Meghaduta, Raghuvamsha, Kumarasambhava), Shudraka (Mricchakatika), Vishakhadatta (Mudrarakshasa, Devichandraguptam), Bhasa (Svapnavasavadatta), Banabhatta (Harshacharita, Kadambari), Bilhana (Vikramankadevacharita), Kalhana (Rajatarangini, 12th century, Kashmir), Jayadeva (Gita Govinda), Sandhyakar Nandi (Ramacharita), Jayanaka (Prithviraja Vijaya), Padmagupta (Navasahasankacharita), Hemachandra (Kumarapalacharita, Dvyashraya), Somadeva Suri (Nitivakyamrita, Yashastilaka), Nayachandra Suri (Hammira-Mahakavya), Amoghavarsha (Kavirajamarga, the earliest Kannada work), Pampa (Vikramarjunavijaya), Magha (Shishupalavadha), Bharavi (Kiratarjuniya), Dandin (Dashakumaracharita), Kshemendra and Somadeva Bhatta (Kathasaritsagara). Buddhist and Pali texts include Milinda-panha, Dipavamsa, Mahavamsa, the Jatakas and Buddhacharita by Ashvaghosha. Jain and philosophical works include Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka texts and Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakosha. Sangam literature includes Tolkappiyam, Silappadikaram (Ilango Adigal) and Manimekalai (Sattanar). Dharmashastra and polity texts include Arthashastra (Kautilya), Manusmriti and Kamandakiya Nitisara. Astronomy works include Aryabhatiya (Aryabhata, 499 CE) and Brihat Samhita (Varahamihira). Likely angles for the future are historical biographies as sources, plays about the Gupta period, and works linked to specific dynasties and patrons.

question: “Souls are not only the property~ of animal and plant life, but also of rocks, running water and many other natural objects not looked on as living by other religious sects.” The above statement reflects one of the core beliefs of which one of the following religious sects of ancient India?
subject: Environment
detail: Jainism classifies reality into jiva (soul/living) and ajiva (non-living). Jiva is found in beings with one to five senses. Ekendriya (one-sensed) beings include earth-bodied (prithvikaya, e.g. rocks, minerals), water-bodied (apkaya), fire-bodied (tejaskaya), air-bodied (vayukaya) and plant-bodied (vanaspatikaya) beings, all having the sense of touch. This is why Jain ethics demands extreme non-violence (ahimsa), the first of the Five Mahavratas: ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha and brahmacharya (the last added by Mahavira; Parshvanatha taught four). Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara (c. 6th century BCE), consolidated these ideas. The quoted statement, with its phrase 'not looked on as living by other religious sects', points to Jainism's distinctive extension of life to inanimate-seeming objects. Elimination: Buddhism accepts no permanent soul (anatta) and does not ascribe souls to rocks or water. Shaivism and Vaishnavism are theistic devotional traditions centred on Shiva and Vishnu; they do not hold that natural objects each possess souls as a core doctrine. Hence (b).
explanations: Incorrect: Buddhism denies a permanent self (anatta) and does not teach that rocks and water possess souls; its ahimsa is rooted in compassion and intention, not universal animism.
Correct: Jainism holds that jivas exist even in earth, water, fire, air and rocks (one-sensed beings), and the statement describes exactly this belief.
Incorrect: Shaivism is a theistic tradition devoted to Shiva; attributing souls to all natural objects is not its core belief.
Incorrect: Vaishnavism is a devotional tradition centred on Vishnu and his avatars; it does not teach souls in rocks and running water as a core tenet.
keyfact: Jainism attributes jiva (soul) even to rocks, water, fire and air, which is the basis of its strict ahimsa.
option_notes: Buddhism was founded by Siddhartha Gautama (Buddha, c. 563-483 BCE or thereabouts). Core teachings: Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path, Middle Way, anicca (impermanence), dukkha, and anatta (no permanent soul). Its canon is the Tripitaka in Pali (Vinaya, Sutta, Abhidhamma). Councils were held at Rajagriha, Vaishali, Pataliputra and Kashmir/Kundalvana. Schools: Theravada, Mahayana, Vajrayana. Ashoka patronised it after Kalinga.

Jainism's twenty-four Tirthankaras ended with Mahavira (born Vaishali region, c. 540 BCE, attained kevala jnana at Jrimbhikagrama). Rishabhanatha was the first and Parshvanatha the 23rd. Key ideas: anekantavada, syadvada, triratna (right faith, knowledge, conduct), jiva and ajiva, karma as subtle matter. Schism into Digambara and Svetambara; canon is the Agamas, compiled at Valabhi council (5th century CE). Patrons: Chandragupta Maurya, Kharavela, Ganga, Chalukya and Rashtrakuta rulers.

Shaivism is the tradition worshipping Shiva as the supreme god. Early evidence includes Pashupata sect (founded by Lakulisa), and later Kapalikas, Kashmir Shaivism and Shaiva Siddhanta. In Tamil Nadu, the 63 Nayanars composed the Tirumurai. Chola kings built great Shiva temples such as Brihadeshvara at Thanjavur. Virashaivism (Lingayatism) was founded in the 12th century Karnataka by Basavanna.

Vaishnavism worships Vishnu and his avatars (Rama, Krishna etc.). It grew from the Bhagavata cult of Vasudeva-Krishna, and its key texts include the Bhagavad Gita and Puranas. In Tamil Nadu, the twelve Alvars composed the Nalayira Divya Prabandham. Philosophers include Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), Madhva (Dvaita), Nimbarka and Vallabha. Gupta kings patronised it, and the Bhakti movement spread it widely.
related: Jainism has 24 Tirthankaras; Rishabhanatha first, Parshvanatha 23rd, Mahavira 24th.
Mahavira's emblem is the lion; Parshvanatha's is the serpent.
Five Mahavratas: ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha, brahmacharya.
Triratna: samyak darshana, samyak jnana, samyak charitra.
Digambara and Svetambara are the two major Jain sects.
Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela is a major Jain-related source in Odisha.
Gomateshwara (Bahubali) statue at Shravanabelagola was built under the Ganga minister Chavundaraya.
Buddhism rejects a permanent soul (anatta); Jainism affirms jiva in all elements.
summary: The answer is (b) Jainism. Jainism teaches universal animism (jiva): souls exist not only in humans, animals and plants but also in earth bodies, water, fire, air and rocks, which is why ahimsa is central to it.
topic_notes: The question tests the heterodox religious movements of 6th century BCE India and their philosophical distinctions. Jainism: Mahavira (Vardhamana), born to Siddhartha and Trishala, of the Jnatrika clan, left home at 30, attained kevala jnana after 12 years, and died at Pavapuri (c. 468 BCE by tradition). Core principles: five Mahavratas, three jewels (Triratna), anekantavada (many-sidedness of truth), syadvada, and nirgrantha (free from bonds). Jains reject a creator God and believe in karma and rebirth, with moksha through the shedding of karma. Jiva is found in all natural elements, so strict ahimsa is followed, including wearing a mouth cloth (muhapatti) and sweeping the path. Sallekhana is the ritual fast unto death. Digambara (sky-clad) followers of Bhadrabahu migrated south, while Svetambara (white-clad) followers stayed with Sthulabhadra; the first Jain council was at Pataliputra. Prakrit (Ardhamagadhi) was used for the teachings. Art and architecture: Dilwara temples (Mount Abu), Gomateshwara/Bahubali at Shravanabelagola, Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves in Odisha (Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription), and Palitana temples.
