The Toyota Mirai and Hyundai Nexo are well-known hydrogen fuel cell cars.
A plug-in hybrid (PHEV) has a larger battery that can be charged from an external source, unlike a regular hybrid.
India has set a target of net zero emissions by 2070.
statements: I — Correct: Full battery electric vehicles run only on stored electricity and an electric motor, with no ICE, so they are alternative powertrain vehicles. A BEV uses a lithium-ion battery pack (LFP or NMC chemistry), an inverter and a motor, and charges from the grid. It has zero tailpipe emissions, and regenerative braking recovers energy. Examples in India include the Tata Nexon EV, Tata Tiago EV and MG Windsor. Support comes from FAME-II, PM E-DRIVE, a reduced 5% GST on EVs, and PLI schemes for auto and Advanced Chemistry Cell batteries. India's national aim is 30% EV sales share by 2030.

II — Correct: Hydrogen fuel cell vehicles generate electricity on board from hydrogen in a fuel cell (usually a PEM fuel cell), and that electricity drives a motor. The only emission is water. Examples are the Toyota Mirai and Hyundai Nexo. Hydrogen is stored in high-pressure tanks, typically at 700 bar. India's National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023) targets 5 MMT of green hydrogen a year by 2030. Pilot hydrogen buses and trucks are running, for example with NTPC, Tata Motors and Ashok Leyland. Challenges are fuelling infrastructure, cost and the efficiency losses in producing hydrogen.

III — Correct: A fuel cell-electric hybrid combines a fuel cell stack with a battery or supercapacitor. The fuel cell supplies steady power, and the battery covers peak demand and stores energy from regenerative braking. This improves efficiency and fuel cell life. Most modern FCEVs are in effect such hybrids. It differs from a conventional hybrid (HEV) such as the Toyota Prius, which pairs an ICE with an electric motor. Both count as alternative powertrains, since the electric drive is either the main or a supplementary source of propulsion.
summary: The answer is (c) All the three. Battery electric vehicles, hydrogen fuel cell vehicles and fuel cell-electric hybrid vehicles all use powertrains other than a conventional petrol or diesel internal combustion engine, so all are alternative powertrain vehicles.
topic_notes: Powertrain means the set of components that generate power and deliver it to the wheels: engine or motor, transmission, drive shafts and differential. A conventional powertrain is an ICE on petrol or diesel. Alternative powertrains include: (1) BEV, with a battery and motor and zero tailpipe emissions; (2) HEV, a self-charging hybrid such as the Toyota Hybrid; (3) PHEV, a hybrid with a larger battery that can be plugged in; (4) FCEV, which runs on hydrogen through a fuel cell; and (5) alternative-fuel ICE vehicles running on CNG, LPG, ethanol, biodiesel or methanol. Indian policy: the National Electric Mobility Mission Plan 2020; FAME India (Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Hybrid and Electric Vehicles), with FAME-II running from 2019 with an outlay of Rs 10,000 crore; PM E-DRIVE (2024) with about Rs 10,900 crore, covering e-2W, e-3W, e-buses, e-trucks and charging infrastructure; the PLI scheme for Automobiles and Auto Components (Rs 25,938 crore) and the PLI ACC Battery scheme (Rs 18,100 crore, 50 GWh); the SPMEPCI scheme for EV manufacturing, with a reduced customs duty for investment of at least $500 million; the National Green Hydrogen Mission (Rs 19,744 crore); and the Scheme for Faster Adoption of E-buses. GST on EVs is 5%. Battery chemistries to know are Li-ion (NMC, LFP), sodium-ion and solid-state. Other points: the Bharat Charge standards, the battery swapping policy, the Battery Waste Management Rules 2022, and the global EV30@30 campaign. In terms of well-to-wheel emissions, green hydrogen from electrolysis powered by renewables is the cleanest, while grey hydrogen comes from natural gas.

question:
With reference to Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), consider the following statements :
I. All types of UAVs can do vertical landing. Il. All types of UAVs can do automated hovering. Ill. All types of UAVs can use battery only as a source of power supply. How many of the statements given above are correct?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: UAVs (drones) are classified by airframe: fixed-wing, rotary-wing (multirotor or helicopter), hybrid VTOL (vertical take-off and landing) and flapping-wing. Capability depends on the design. Rotary-wing drones can take off and land vertically and hover, because lift comes from rotors. Fixed-wing drones need forward airspeed to stay aloft. They usually take off by runway, catapult or hand launch, and they land by belly landing, parachute, net recovery or a runway. They cannot hover. Only hybrid VTOL designs combine both abilities. Power sources also differ: lithium-polymer or lithium-ion batteries on small drones, petrol or diesel engines on larger MALE/HALE drones (for example the Predator/MQ-9 Reaper uses a turboprop engine), hydrogen fuel cells, solar cells (high-altitude pseudo-satellites) and hybrid systems. India's Drone Rules 2021 classify drones by weight: nano (up to 250 g), micro (250 g to 2 kg), small (2 to 25 kg), medium (25 to 150 kg) and large (over 150 kg). Elimination logic: statements with 'all' or 'only' are risky in UPSC. A single counter-example, a fixed-wing or fuel-powered drone, falsifies each statement, so the answer is none.
explanations: (a) Only one — wrong, because none of the three statements is correct. Each one fails because of the word 'all'.
(b) Only two — wrong, because no pair of statements is correct either. Fixed-wing drones cannot hover or land vertically, and many drones do not run on battery alone.
(c) All three — wrong, because it would require every UAV type to land vertically, hover and run on batteries. Fixed-wing and fuel-powered drones are counter-examples.
(d) None — correct, because each statement is falsified by at least one UAV type. This matches the official answer.
keyfact: UAV capabilities depend on design: only rotary or VTOL types hover and land vertically, and power may be battery, fuel, solar or hybrid, so 'all UAVs' claims are false.
option_notes: Only one: this would be true if exactly one statement held universally. Here none does. The choice is a typical UPSC distractor for 'how many' questions, tempting students who recall that multirotors can hover or that small drones use batteries. Always test 'all' claims against the most extreme counter-example, such as a fixed-wing or fuel-powered military UAV. 'How many' questions give no partial credit.

Only two: this would need two statements to be universally true. A student might assume vertical landing and hovering go together because both belong to rotary-wing drones. They do not apply to fixed-wing or hybrid types in all phases. Multirotor features are not shared across all UAV types, so this is wrong. UAV classes are fixed-wing, multirotor, single-rotor helicopter, hybrid VTOL and flapping-wing.

All three: this would mean every UAV lands vertically, hovers and runs on batteries only. That ignores fixed-wing drones such as Rustom-II and MQ-9B SkyGuardian, which are fuel-driven and runway-based. India's Drone Rules 2021 cover all categories (nano to large), and the Drone Shakti and PLI schemes support the sector. It is a trap for students who think only of small quadcopters.

None: the correct and official answer. UAV capabilities depend on design. Fixed-wing drones need forward motion, land conventionally and cannot hover. Power sources include batteries, fuel engines, solar and hydrogen fuel cells. Remember the classification by airframe, weight (Drone Rules 2021) and role (MALE, HALE, tactical, micro). The word 'all' in a statement usually signals a false claim.
related: Drone Rules 2021 classify drones by weight: nano, micro, small, medium and large.
Digital Sky Platform shows green, yellow and red airspace zones for drones.
DGCA is India's civil aviation regulator and handles drone certification.
Namo Drone Didi scheme (2023) provides drones to women self-help groups for agriculture.
India signed a deal for 31 MQ-9B drones with the US in 2024.
Fixed-wing drones cannot hover, while multirotors can.
MALE means Medium Altitude Long Endurance and HALE means High Altitude Long Endurance.
PLI scheme for drones and drone components was approved in 2021.
statements: I — Incorrect: Only VTOL-capable drones (multirotors, helicopters, hybrid VTOL) land vertically; fixed-wing drones do not. Fixed-wing UAVs such as the Rustom-II, MQ-9B or Heron land on runways, or by parachute or net recovery. They rely on forward motion for lift. Vertical landing needs rotors or tilt-rotor or tail-sitter designs. Hybrid VTOL drones add rotors to a fixed-wing body so they can launch and land without a runway. Fixed-wing designs offer greater endurance and range, and multirotors offer manoeuvrability but shorter endurance. So the claim 'all types' fails.

II — Incorrect: Hovering means holding a fixed position in the air, which needs rotors that produce lift without forward speed. Multirotors and helicopter-type drones can hover, often with GPS and sensor-aided stabilisation (automated position hold). Fixed-wing drones must keep moving forward or they stall, so they cannot hover and can only loiter in circles. Hybrid VTOL drones can hover only in the vertical flight phase. Hovering is useful for photography, inspection, surveying and spraying, which is why multirotors dominate these uses.

III — Incorrect: Battery power is common, especially in small drones (lithium-polymer or lithium-ion), but it is not the only source. Larger military UAVs use internal combustion or turboprop engines (the MQ-9 Reaper uses a Honeywell TPE331 turboprop). Other options are hydrogen fuel cells, solar panels (for example Airbus Zephyr, a high-altitude pseudo-satellite), and hybrid gas-electric systems. Battery limits on endurance and payload push long-endurance drones toward fuel or solar power. India's Drone Rules 2021 do not restrict the power source.
summary: The answer is (d) None. Each statement uses the word 'all types of UAVs', and UAVs vary widely, so none of the three claims holds universally. Fixed-wing UAVs land conventionally and cannot hover, and many UAVs use fuel engines, hybrid systems or solar power instead of batteries alone.
topic_notes: UAVs (drones) are aircraft operated without a pilot on board, controlled remotely or autonomously. Classification by airframe: fixed-wing (long endurance, efficient, needs runway or launcher), rotary-wing (multirotor or helicopter; VTOL and hover), hybrid VTOL (combines both) and flapping-wing (bio-inspired). Classification by altitude and endurance: MALE (Medium Altitude Long Endurance, for example Heron, MQ-9B) and HALE (High Altitude Long Endurance, for example Global Hawk). Power sources: Li-Po batteries, internal combustion engines, turboprops, hydrogen fuel cells, solar and hybrid. Indian regulation: Drone Rules 2021 replaced the UAS Rules 2021 (March 2021). They were liberalised on 25 Aug 2021 and abolished many approvals, and the Digital Sky Platform handles registration and airspace maps (green, yellow, red zones). Weight categories: nano (up to 250 g), micro (250 g to 2 kg), small (2 to 25 kg), medium (25 to 150 kg) and large (over 150 kg). Schemes: PLI scheme for drones and components (2021, ₹120 crore), a ban on import of foreign drones (Feb 2022), Kisan Drones for agriculture, and Namo Drone Didi (2023) giving drones to women self-help groups. DGCA is the regulator; the Ministry of Civil Aviation oversees policy. Defence: India has the Rustom, Archer-NG, Heron, Nagastra loitering munitions, and has contracted 31 MQ-9B drones from the US (2024). Possible angles: counter-drone systems, swarm drones, the use of drones in conflicts such as Ukraine, and drone use in agriculture, disaster management and health delivery.

question:
In the context of electric vehicle batteries, consider the following elements :
I. Cobalt Il. Graphite
I. Lithium
IV. Nickel How many of the above usually make up battery cathodes?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: An EV lithium-ion cell has a cathode (positive electrode), an anode (negative electrode), an electrolyte and a separator. During discharge, lithium ions move from anode to cathode through the electrolyte. The cathode is a lithium metal oxide or phosphate. Common chemistries are NMC (lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide), NCA (lithium nickel cobalt aluminium oxide), LCO (lithium cobalt oxide), LFP (lithium iron phosphate) and LMO (lithium manganese oxide). Nickel gives high energy density, cobalt gives structural stability and longer life, and lithium is the charge-carrying ion in every chemistry. The anode is usually graphite (natural or synthetic), with silicon or lithium titanate as emerging or alternative options. Elimination logic: lithium is in every cathode, so (a) is out. Cobalt and nickel are both used in NMC and NCA, so (b) is out. Graphite is the anode, so it cannot be counted among the cathode elements, which rules out (d) and leaves (c). Note that LFP cathodes contain no nickel or cobalt, which is why the word 'usually' appears in the question.
explanations: (a) Wrong: Only one would be correct only if a single element were cathode material, but lithium, nickel and cobalt all are.
(b) Wrong: Two would leave out one of cobalt, nickel or lithium, yet all three occur in common cathodes such as NMC and NCA.
(c) Correct: Cobalt, lithium and nickel usually make up the cathode, while graphite forms the anode. That makes three.
(d) Wrong: Graphite is the anode material, so not all four are cathode components.
keyfact: In EV Li-ion batteries, lithium, nickel and cobalt (with manganese or aluminium) form the cathode, while graphite forms the anode.
option_notes: Only one: this would match a battery with a cathode of a single active metal. In practice the cathode is a lithium metal oxide or phosphate, which is a compound of lithium with at least one transition metal. Examples: LiFePO4 (LFP) has lithium and iron, and LiCoO2 has lithium and cobalt. A single-element cathode is not the usual EV design.

Only two: this would fit simpler chemistries such as LCO (lithium and cobalt) or LFP (lithium and iron). It does not fit NMC and NCA, the dominant EV cathodes, which combine lithium with nickel and cobalt, plus manganese or aluminium. LFP is growing quickly in India and China because it is cheaper and safer and contains no cobalt or nickel.

Only three: cobalt, lithium and nickel together describe NMC and NCA cathodes. NMC ratios such as 111, 523, 622 and 811 show nickel:manganese:cobalt. Higher nickel gives more energy but less thermal stability. Cobalt supports stability and cycle life. This is the official answer, because graphite is excluded as an anode.

All four: this is the trap that treats every battery material as a cathode material. Graphite is the standard anode, hosting lithium ions during charging. The cathode, anode, electrolyte (lithium salts such as LiPF6 in organic solvents) and separator are the four main parts of a cell. Knowing which part each material belongs to is the key skill tested.
related: Graphite is the usual anode material in Li-ion batteries.
LFP cathodes contain lithium, iron and phosphate, with no cobalt or nickel.
DR Congo produces roughly 70% of the world's cobalt.
Lithium Triangle: Argentina, Bolivia and Chile.
Indonesia is the world's largest nickel producer.
India's National Critical Mineral Mission was approved in January 2025.
KABIL is the joint venture of NALCO, HCL and MECL for overseas mineral assets.
Battery Waste Management Rules 2022 introduced Extended Producer Responsibility.
statements: I — Correct: Cobalt is a usual cathode component. Cobalt stabilises the layered oxide structure in LCO, NMC and NCA cathodes. About 70% of world cobalt comes from the Democratic Republic of Congo, and ethical sourcing and child-labour concerns are well documented. Cobalt is a by-product of copper and nickel mining. Producers are reducing cobalt content through high-nickel cathodes (NMC 811) and cobalt-free LFP. India has listed cobalt as a critical mineral.

II — Incorrect: Graphite is the usual anode material, not a cathode material. It stores lithium ions between its carbon layers when charging (intercalation). Both natural and synthetic graphite are used. China dominates graphite mining and anode processing. Graphite is on India's critical minerals list. The US and EU also classify it as critical. Silicon-graphite composite anodes are an emerging trend.

III — Correct: Lithium is in every Li-ion cathode, for example LiCoO2, LiFePO4 and NMC. Lithium ions shuttle between the electrodes. Major sources are the 'Lithium Triangle' (Argentina, Bolivia, Chile) and Australia's hard-rock spodumene. China leads in refining. India's first lithium inferences were at Reasi (Jammu and Kashmir) and Mandya (Karnataka). KABIL (Khanij Bidesh India Ltd) is acquiring overseas lithium assets.

IV — Correct: Nickel is a usual cathode component. High-nickel cathodes such as NMC 811 and NCA give high energy density and longer range. Indonesia is the largest nickel producer, followed by the Philippines and Russia. Class 1 (battery-grade) nickel is needed. Nickel is also used in stainless steel. It is on India's critical minerals list. Nickel-metal hydride batteries are an older, different technology.
summary: The answer is (c) Only three. Cobalt, lithium and nickel are the metals that usually make up the cathode of an EV lithium-ion battery (as in NMC, NCA and LCO chemistries). Graphite is the standard anode material, not the cathode.
topic_notes:
Lithium-ion batteries power most EVs. A cell has a cathode (positive), anode (negative), electrolyte and separator. On discharge, lithium ions move from anode to cathode and electrons flow through the external circuit. On charge the process reverses.

Cathode chemistries: NMC (nickel-manganese-cobalt) is widely used in cars. NCA (nickel-cobalt-aluminium) is used by Tesla in some models. LFP (lithium iron phosphate) is cheaper, safer and longer-lived but has lower energy density, and is rising in share. LCO is common in consumer electronics. LMO is also used in some applications.

Anode: graphite dominates. Silicon is an emerging additive, and lithium titanate (LTO) offers fast charging. Current collectors are aluminium for the cathode and copper for the anode.

Next-generation technologies: solid-state batteries, sodium-ion batteries (no lithium, cobalt or nickel), lithium-sulphur, and metal-air batteries.

Critical minerals: lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite, rare earths and others. India's 2023 critical minerals list has 30 minerals. The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Act 2023 allowed auctions of critical minerals blocks. The National Critical Mineral Mission was approved in January 2025. KABIL secures overseas assets, for example in Argentina's Catamarca. India is a member of the Minerals Security Partnership.

Schemes: FAME-II, PM E-DRIVE (2024), the PLI scheme for Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) batteries with 50 GWh capacity, and the PLI scheme for the automobile sector.

Supply concentration: China dominates refining of lithium, cobalt and graphite. DR Congo produces most cobalt. Indonesia leads nickel. Australia and Chile lead lithium production. Battery recycling rules in India are under the Battery Waste Management Rules 2022, which set Extended Producer Responsibility.

ocr: Consider the following : Cigarette butts I. Eyeglass lenses Il. Car tyres Ill. How many of them contain plastic? Only one (a) Only two (b) All the three (c) (a) None
subject: Environment
detail: The question tests awareness of hidden plastics in everyday items, a theme linked to microplastic pollution, the Plastic Waste Management Rules and the global plastics treaty negotiations. Plastics are synthetic or semi-synthetic polymers. Cigarette filters are made of cellulose acetate, a semi-synthetic thermoplastic derived from cellulose; they are non-biodegradable in practical terms, are among the most littered items worldwide, and shed microfibres. Eyeglass lenses are mostly organic polymer lenses: CR-39 (allyl diglycol carbonate), polycarbonate, Trivex and high-index plastics, which replaced heavier glass lenses. Car tyres are made from natural rubber plus synthetic rubbers such as styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR) and butadiene rubber, with carbon black and additives; tyre wear is one of the largest sources of primary microplastics in oceans and rivers. Elimination logic: once a student recognises that any one item contains plastic, (d) None is ruled out. Knowing that cigarette filters are plastic-based and tyres contain synthetic polymers rules out (a) and (b), leaving (c). The key lesson is that plastic is not only packaging; it is present in textiles, filters, lenses, tyres, cosmetics and paints.
explanations: (a) Only one is wrong because all three items contain plastic or plastic-type polymers, not just one.
(b) Only two is wrong because the third item also contains polymer plastics: cigarette filters, lenses and tyres all qualify.
(c) All the three is correct: cigarette butts (cellulose acetate), eyeglass lenses (CR-39 or polycarbonate) and car tyres (synthetic rubber and polymers) all contain plastic.
(d) None is wrong because every item listed contains plastic or a plastic-like polymer.
keyfact: Cigarette filters (cellulose acetate), spectacle lenses (CR-39 or polycarbonate) and tyres (synthetic rubber) all contain plastic polymers.
option_notes: Only one: this option would apply if just a single item contained plastic. It is a distractor for students who think of plastic only as bottles and bags. In reality, plastics are embedded in many everyday goods, including filters, optical lenses and automotive parts. Hidden plastics in such items contribute to microplastic pollution that UPSC often links to environment questions.

Only two: this is a distractor for students who identify two items, usually lenses and tyres or lenses and filters, but miss the third. Cellulose acetate in filters is the item most often missed because it looks like cotton. Tyres are often overlooked as plastic because they are called rubber, but they contain synthetic polymers.

All the three: this is the official answer. Cigarette filters (cellulose acetate), spectacle lenses (CR-39, polycarbonate) and tyres (synthetic rubber such as SBR and polybutadiene) all contain polymers classed as plastics or plastic-like materials. They are significant sources of microplastics and persistent pollution, and they matter in discussions of the plastics treaty and extended producer responsibility.

None: this would be correct only if none of the items had polymer content. It is a distractor for the view that plastic means only packaging. Glass lenses and natural rubber do exist, but most modern lenses are plastic and tyres are blended with synthetic polymers, so this option fails.
related: Cellulose acetate is the semi-synthetic polymer used in cigarette filters.
Microplastics are plastic particles smaller than 5 mm.
Tyre wear is one of the largest sources of primary microplastics.
CR-39 and polycarbonate are common plastic spectacle lens materials.
India banned identified single-use plastic items from 1 July 2022 under the Plastic Waste Management Rules.
Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) makes producers, importers and brand owners responsible for plastic waste.
UNEA-5.2 (2022) launched negotiations for a legally binding global plastics treaty.
World Environment Day 2018, themed 'Beat Plastic Pollution', was hosted by India.
statements: I — Correct: Cigarette filters are made of cellulose acetate, a plastic-type polymer. Cellulose acetate is a semi-synthetic thermoplastic made by acetylating cellulose from wood pulp or cotton. It was first developed in the late 1800s and commercialised in the 20th century for films, fibres and, from the 1950s, cigarette filters. Filters degrade very slowly, break into microfibres, and leach nicotine, heavy metals and other toxins. Cigarette butts are among the most common items found in beach clean-ups worldwide. Some countries and regions are considering bans or extended producer responsibility for filters.

II — Correct: Most modern eyeglass lenses are made of plastic polymers. The common materials are CR-39 (allyl diglycol carbonate, introduced in the 1940s), polycarbonate (impact-resistant, used in safety and children's glasses), Trivex and high-index plastics. They are lighter and safer than traditional glass, and they can be coated for UV protection and scratch resistance. Glass lenses are still used but are now a minority. Polycarbonate lenses are also used in sports eyewear and visors because of their high impact resistance.

III — Correct: Car tyres contain synthetic rubber polymers and are a major microplastic source. Tyres are made of natural rubber blended with synthetic rubbers such as styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR) and polybutadiene, plus carbon black, silica, steel or textile cords (often nylon or polyester) and chemical additives. Tyre-wear particles released during driving are among the largest sources of primary microplastics, and they carry additives such as 6PPD, which can form toxic 6PPD-quinone. Tyre dust reaches soil, rivers and oceans through road runoff.
summary: The answer is (c) All the three. Cigarette butts contain cellulose acetate (a plastic-like bioplastic polymer), most modern eyeglass lenses are made of plastics such as CR-39 or polycarbonate, and car tyres contain synthetic rubber (a polymer) and are a significant source of microplastics.
topic_notes: Plastics are polymers of repeating monomer units. Thermoplastics (polyethylene, PET, PVC, polypropylene, polystyrene) soften on heating and can be remoulded, while thermosets (Bakelite, epoxy) cannot. Semi-synthetic plastics such as cellulose acetate are made by modifying natural polymers. Microplastics are plastic particles under 5 mm, and nanoplastics are under 1 micrometre. Primary microplastics are released directly, for example from tyre wear, textile fibres and microbeads in cosmetics. Secondary microplastics come from the breakdown of larger plastic items. Hidden sources include synthetic clothing (polyester, nylon, acrylic), tea bags that are heat-sealed with polypropylene, chewing gum bases, paints, wet wipes, glitter and cigarette filters. Microplastics have been found in oceans, Himalayan snow, drinking water, human blood and placenta, and they carry adsorbed toxic chemicals. Indian policy: Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016, with amendments in 2018, 2021 and 2022, ban identified single-use plastic items from 1 July 2022, increased the minimum thickness of carry bags (75 to 120 microns), and introduced Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) guidelines for producers, importers and brand owners (PIBOs). India championed the UNEA-5.2 resolution of 2022 to negotiate a legally binding global plastics treaty through an Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee (INC). Other angles: biodegradable plastics such as PLA and PHA, bioplastics, the 'Beat Plastic Pollution' theme of World Environment Day 2018 hosted by India, recycling codes 1-7, and alternatives such as jute and bamboo.

ocr: Consider the following substances : Ethanol I Nitroglycerine Il. Ill. Urea Coal gasification technology can be used in the production of how many of them? Only one (a) Only two (b) All the three (c) (d) None
subject: Geography
detail: Coal gasification converts coal, through partial oxidation with steam and oxygen at high temperature and pressure, into synthesis gas (syngas), a mixture mainly of carbon monoxide and hydrogen. Syngas is a versatile chemical feedstock. It can be turned into methanol, dimethyl ether, synthetic natural gas, Fischer-Tropsch liquid fuels, and ethanol (by catalytic conversion or syngas fermentation). Hydrogen from syngas, combined with nitrogen, gives ammonia by the Haber-Bosch process, and ammonia reacts with CO2 (also a by-product of gasification) to give urea. This is why India's Ministry of Coal pushes coal gasification under its National Coal Gasification Mission, targeting 100 million tonnes of coal gasified by 2030, to reduce imports of methanol, ammonia and urea. Nitroglycerine, by contrast, is an explosive made by nitrating glycerol (glycerine, a by-product of fat/oil processing or biodiesel) with a mixture of concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids. It does not need syngas. Elimination logic: knowing that urea and ethanol are syngas-linked and nitroglycerine is not rules out (a), (c) and (d), leaving (b).
explanations: (a) Wrong: Two of the substances, ethanol and urea, can be made via coal gasification, so 'only one' undercounts.
(b) Correct: Ethanol and urea are syngas-based products; nitroglycerine is not, so exactly two.
(c) Wrong: Nitroglycerine comes from glycerol nitration, so not all three qualify.
(d) Wrong: Coal gasification is a recognised route to both ethanol and urea, so 'none' is incorrect.
keyfact: Coal gasification gives syngas (CO + H2), used for methanol, ammonia/urea, ethanol and synthetic fuels, but not nitroglycerine (glycerol + HNO3/H2SO4).
statements: I — Correct: Ethanol can be produced from coal-derived syngas by catalytic conversion or fermentation.
II — Incorrect: Nitroglycerine is made by nitrating glycerol with nitric and sulphuric acids, not from coal gasification.
III — Correct: Urea is made from ammonia (from syngas hydrogen) and CO2, both obtainable through coal gasification.
summary: The answer is (b) Only two. Coal gasification produces syngas (CO + H2), which can be converted into ethanol (via fermentation or catalytic synthesis) and into urea (via ammonia from the hydrogen in syngas plus CO2). Nitroglycerine is made by nitrating glycerol with nitric and sulphuric acids, and coal gasification is not used for it.

question: What is the common characteristic of the chemical substances generally known as CL-20, HMX and LLM-105, which are sometimes talked about in media? These are alternatives to hydro
options: fluorocarbon refrigerants These are explosives in military
weapons These are high-energy fuels for
cruise missiles These are fuels for rocket
subject: Science & Tech
detail: CL-20, HMX and LLM-105 belong to the class of 'energetic materials': nitramine and nitro-heterocyclic compounds that release large amounts of energy on detonation. The OCR'd question text is garbled. The stem seems to say these are alternatives to hydro-based refrigerants, and each option begins with a fragment of the next. Reading the options as 'explosives in military weapons', the official key (b) fits. HMX (octogen) is a widely used military high explosive, found in plastic-bonded explosives, shaped charges and warhead fills, and as an ingredient in solid rocket propellants. CL-20 (hexanitrohexaazaisowurtzitane) is a newer, denser and more powerful nitramine, about 14-20% more energetic than HMX, and is used in advanced munitions and propellants. LLM-105 (2,6-diamino-3,5-dinitropyrazine-1-oxide), developed at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, is a insensitive high explosive with performance near HMX but much safer handling. Elimination: refrigerants (a) are fluorocarbons or hydrofluorocarbons such as HFC-134a and have no link to nitramines. Cruise-missile fuel (c) is liquid hydrocarbon fuel such as JP-10. Rocket propulsion fuel (d) would involve things like hydrazine, kerosene or LOX/LH2. The shared feature is explosive use, so (b) is correct.
explanations: Wrong. Fluorocarbon refrigerants are CFCs, HCFCs and HFCs. CL-20, HMX and LLM-105 are nitrogen-rich, nitro-group explosives with no cooling role.
Correct. All three are high-energy explosive compounds used in military weapons, such as warheads, munitions and detonating charges.
Wrong. Cruise missiles run on hydrocarbon jet fuels such as JP-10. These three compounds are explosives, not fuels, though they may be in the warhead.

Wrong. Rocket propulsion uses propellants like hydrazine, kerosene, LH2 and ammonium perchlorate composites. HMX and CL-20 can be additives in solid propellants, but their defining character is as explosives, not as fuels.
keyfact: CL-20, HMX and LLM-105 are high-energy nitro/nitramine explosives used in military weapons, not refrigerants or fuels.
option_notes: Fluorocarbon refrigerants are halogenated carbon compounds. CFCs such as CFC-12 were phased out under the Montreal Protocol (1987) because they deplete ozone. HCFCs are transitional. HFCs such as HFC-134a do not harm ozone but are strong greenhouse gases, and the Kigali Amendment (2016) phases them down. India is to begin its phase-down in 2028. They are unrelated to explosives.

Military explosives are high-energy materials that detonate to produce a shock wave and gas. Common ones are TNT, RDX, HMX, PETN, CL-20 and LLM-105. They fill bombs, missile warheads, shells and mines. Modern work focuses on 'insensitive munitions', meaning high power with low accidental-detonation risk. This is the correct category for the three compounds in the question.

Cruise missiles are low-flying, air-breathing guided missiles. They use turbofan or turbojet engines on hydrocarbon fuels such as JP-10, and ramjets in some cases, as in BrahMos. India's examples are BrahMos (supersonic) and Nirbhay (subsonic). Their warheads hold explosives, but their fuels are not these compounds.

Rocket propulsion uses liquid propellants (kerosene/LOX, LH2/LOX, UDMH/N2O4, hydrazine) or solid propellants (ammonium perchlorate, aluminium powder and a HTPB binder). Cryogenic engines use LH2 and LOX. HMX or CL-20 appear only as energetic additives in some solid propellants, so they are not 'fuels' as such.
related: CL-20 is a polycyclic nitramine and one of the most powerful non-nuclear conventional explosives.
HMX is also called octogen, and its full name is cyclotetramethylene-tetranitramine.
RDX is also called cyclonite, and its full name is cyclotrimethylenetrinitramine.
HEMRL Pune is a DRDO lab working on high-energy materials.
The Kigali Amendment (2016) to the Montreal Protocol phases down HFCs.
BrahMos is a supersonic cruise missile developed by India and Russia.
Insensitive munitions are designed to resist accidental detonation.
LLM-105 was developed at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory.
summary: The answer is (b): CL-20, HMX and LLM-105 are high-energy explosive compounds used in military weapons (warheads, munitions, detonators and propellant formulations). They are energetic materials, not refrigerants or primarily rocket or cruise-missile fuels.
topic_notes: Energetic materials are substances that store chemical energy and release it rapidly. They fall into explosives (primary, secondary, tertiary), propellants and pyrotechnics. Primary explosives such as lead azide and mercury fulminate are sensitive and used in detonators. Secondary explosives such as TNT, RDX, HMX, PETN, CL-20 and LLM-105 are more stable and form the main charge. TNT has a detonation velocity of about 6,900 m/s. RDX (cyclonite) reaches about 8,750 m/s. HMX (octogen) is denser and has a higher melting point, with velocity about 9,100 m/s. CL-20, first synthesised in the 1980s at China Lake in the US, has the highest performance among them but is costly and sensitive. LLM-105, from Lawrence Livermore, is an insensitive high explosive with about 80-85% of the power of HMX. Plastic-bonded explosives (PBX) combine these with polymer binders. The common theme in recent news is insensitive munitions and the Indian push for indigenous production, through DRDO's High Energy Materials Research Laboratory (HEMRL), Pune, and the Explosives Research and Development Laboratory. India has reported indigenous work on CL-20 and HMX. UPSC may ask about the differences between explosives, propellants and fuels, the Montreal Protocol and Kigali Amendment, hypersonic or cruise missiles, or the Chemical Weapons Convention. Remember that nitramine explosives are not chemical weapons, since they work by blast and not by toxicity.

ocr: Consider the following statements : I. It is expected that Majorana 1 chip will enable quantum computing. Il. Majorana 1 chip has _ been introduced by Amazon Web Services (AWS). Ill. Deep learning is a subset of machine learning. Which of the statements given above are correct? (a) 1 and II only (b) 1 and III only (c) 1 and III only (a) 1, Il and Ill
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Majorana 1 was unveiled by Microsoft in February 2025 as the first quantum processing unit built on a 'topological core' architecture. It uses a new class of material called a topoconductor, made from indium arsenide and aluminium, to create and control Majorana zero modes (quasi-particles) that encode topological qubits. These qubits are expected to be more stable and less error-prone, and Microsoft says the design can scale to a million qubits on a single chip, which would make useful, fault-tolerant quantum computing possible. The claim is 'expected', which is why Statement I is correct. AWS has its own quantum chip, Ocelot (February 2025), which uses cat qubits for error correction. Google has Willow (December 2024). So Statement II confuses the company. On Statement III, the hierarchy is AI ⊃ machine learning ⊃ deep learning. Deep learning uses multi-layered artificial neural networks. Elimination logic: Statement II is wrong, so options (a), (b) and (d) are eliminated, leaving (c).
explanations: Wrong. It includes Statement II, which wrongly credits AWS with Majorana 1; the chip is Microsoft's. It also leaves out the correct Statement III.
Wrong. It includes Statement II, which is incorrect, and leaves out Statement I, which is correct.
Correct. Statements I and III are correct, and Statement II is incorrect because Majorana 1 is Microsoft's chip.
Wrong. It includes Statement II, which is factually incorrect because AWS's chip is Ocelot.
keyfact: Majorana 1 = Microsoft's topological quantum chip; AWS = Ocelot; Google = Willow; deep learning ⊂ machine learning.
related: Majorana 1 is Microsoft's topological quantum chip (Feb 2025).
AWS's quantum chip is Ocelot, which uses cat qubits.
Google's quantum chip is Willow (Dec 2024, 105 qubits).
National Quantum Mission: approved April 2023, outlay about ₹6,003 crore, 2023-31.
NQM has four T-Hubs: computing, communication, sensing and metrology, materials and devices.
AI ⊃ Machine Learning ⊃ Deep Learning ⊃ Generative AI.
2025 was declared the International Year of Quantum Science and Technology by the UN.
IndiaAI Mission was approved in March 2024 with an outlay of ₹10,372 crore.
statements: 1 — Correct: Majorana 1 is expected to enable scalable, fault-tolerant quantum computing. Microsoft announced it in February 2025 as the first quantum chip based on topological qubits. It uses a topoconductor (indium arsenide with aluminium) to host Majorana zero modes. The qubits are intended to be stable, with built-in error resistance. Microsoft claims it can scale to one million qubits on a palm-sized chip. It was developed partly with DARPA's US2QC programme support. The technology is still at an early stage and parts of the claim are debated by scientists.

2 — Incorrect: Majorana 1 was introduced by Microsoft, not Amazon Web Services. AWS's quantum chip is Ocelot, announced in February 2025, which uses cat qubits to reduce the cost of quantum error correction. Google's chip is Willow (December 2024, 105 qubits), and IBM has the Condor and Heron processors. The name Majorana comes from the Italian physicist Ettore Majorana, who predicted in 1937 particles that are their own antiparticles.

3 — Correct: Deep learning is a subset of machine learning, which is itself a subset of artificial intelligence. Deep learning uses multi-layered artificial neural networks (deep neural networks) to learn representations from large data. It powers image recognition, speech recognition, natural language processing and generative AI models such as large language models. Key architectures include CNNs, RNNs and Transformers. Pioneers include Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio, who received the 2018 Turing Award. Hinton also shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics.
summary: The answer is (c) I and III only. Majorana 1 is a quantum processor chip introduced by Microsoft (not Amazon Web Services) in February 2025, and it is expected to enable scalable quantum computing. Deep learning is indeed a subset of machine learning.
topic_notes: Quantum computing uses qubits, which exploit superposition (being in multiple states at once), entanglement (correlated states) and interference. Qubits are fragile and suffer decoherence and errors, so error correction is the central engineering challenge. Different hardware approaches include superconducting qubits (Google, IBM), trapped ions (IonQ, Quantinuum), photonic qubits, neutral atoms, cat qubits (AWS Ocelot) and topological qubits (Microsoft Majorana 1). Microsoft's topological approach uses Majorana zero modes in a topoconductor, aiming for hardware-level protection against noise. Key recent chips: Google Willow (Dec 2024) with 105 qubits, which showed error reduction as qubits scale; AWS Ocelot (Feb 2025); Microsoft Majorana 1 (Feb 2025). India's National Quantum Mission (NQM) was approved in April 2023 with an outlay of about ₹6,003 crore for 2023-31. It is run under the Department of Science and Technology and aims to build intermediate-scale quantum computers of 50-1000 physical qubits. It has four thematic hubs (T-Hubs): quantum computing, quantum communication, quantum sensing and metrology, and quantum materials and devices. Related concepts include quantum supremacy (advantage), quantum key distribution, post-quantum cryptography and the NIST standards. The AI hierarchy is: AI contains machine learning, which contains deep learning, which contains generative AI. Types of machine learning are supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning. Likely future angles: the IndiaAI Mission (₹10,372 crore, approved March 2024), large language models, and the Transformer architecture. Other angles are quantum communication in India (ISRO's free-space QKD demonstrations; DRDO-IIT Delhi), the 2025 International Year of Quantum Science and Technology (declared by the UN), and the physics Nobel for 2025 (macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits).

ocr: With reference to monoclonal antibodies, often mentioned in news, consider the following statements : I. They are man-made proteins. Il. They stimulate immunological function due to their ability to bind to specific antigens. Ill. They are used in treating viral infections like that of Nipah virus. Which of the statements given above are correct? (a) 1 and II only (b) 1 and III only (c) 1 and III only (da) 1, II and Ill
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Monoclonal antibodies are identical immunoglobulin (protein) molecules produced by a single clone of B-cells or hybridoma cells, so every molecule recognises the same epitope on one antigen. The technique was developed by Georges Köhler and César Milstein in 1975 (hybridoma technology), and they shared the 1984 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Early mAbs were murine (-omab), later ones chimeric (-ximab), humanised (-zumab) and fully human (-umab). Their binding to specific antigens can neutralise pathogens, tag cells for destruction by immune cells, block receptors or checkpoints (for example PD-1 inhibitors), and thereby modulate or stimulate immune function. Uses include cancer (trastuzumab, rituximab), autoimmune disease (adalimumab), COVID-19 (casirivimab-imdevimab) and Ebola (Inmazeb, Ebanga). For Nipah, the human mAb m102.4 was developed in the USA and sent to Kerala/India for compassionate use. Elimination logic: statement I is a basic definitional fact, and II and III are widely reported. Once you know any two of them are correct, only (d) can survive, because each of (a), (b) and (c) drops one statement.
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out statement III, which is correct because mAbs such as m102.4 are used against Nipah virus.
Wrong: it leaves out statement I, but mAbs are indeed man-made proteins.
Wrong: it leaves out statement II, but mAbs do stimulate immune function through specific antigen binding.
Correct: statements I, II and III are all accurate, so this is the official answer.
keyfact: mAbs are lab-made, single-clone antibody proteins that bind one specific antigen; they are used against cancers and viruses, including Nipah (m102.4).
option_notes: Option (a), 'I and II only', would mean mAbs are made-made and immune-stimulating but not used for viral infections. It is wrong. mAbs are in fact used against RSV, Ebola, COVID-19 and, on a compassionate basis, Nipah. They are lab-made proteins whose specificity lets them work as passive immunotherapy. UPSC often tests such partial combinations, so check each statement independently.

Option (b), 'II and III only', would mean that mAbs are not man-made proteins. That is wrong, because they are artificially produced by hybridoma or recombinant technology. Natural polyclonal antibodies come from many B-cell clones, whereas mAbs come from one clone. Their protein nature means they are usually given by injection or infusion rather than orally, since digestion would break them down.

Option (c), 'I and III only', would deny that mAbs stimulate immunological function by binding specific antigens. That is wrong. Binding specific antigens is the very basis of their immune action, whether by neutralisation, opsonisation, complement activation or checkpoint blockade. In cancer immunotherapy, mAbs such as pembrolizumab and nivolumab release T-cells to attack tumours.

Option (d), 'I, II and III', is the official answer. It reflects that mAbs are lab-made protein reagents or drugs, act through antigen-specific binding to modulate immunity, and have antiviral use, including for Nipah (m102.4). The related Nobel Prizes are 1984 (Köhler and Milstein) and 2018 (Allison and Honjo, checkpoint therapy).
related: Köhler and Milstein developed hybridoma technology in 1975 and won the 1984 Nobel Prize.
The first therapeutic mAb approved was muromonab-CD3 in 1986.
Nipah mAb m102.4 targets the viral G glycoprotein.
Nipah is carried by Pteropus fruit bats and is a Henipavirus.
Kerala reported Nipah outbreaks first in 2018, in Kozhikode.
Pembrolizumab and nivolumab are PD-1 checkpoint-inhibitor mAbs.
Trastuzumab targets HER2 in breast cancer.
The 2018 Chemistry Nobel recognised phage display, used to make human antibodies.
statements: 1 — Correct: mAbs are man-made (laboratory-produced) immunoglobulin proteins. They are made by hybridoma technology or recombinant DNA methods, in which a single B-cell clone is immortalised by fusion with myeloma cells. Every antibody is identical and targets one epitope. The technique was introduced by Köhler and Milstein in 1975, and the first therapeutic mAb, muromonab-CD3, was approved in 1986 to prevent transplant rejection. Modern mAbs are humanised or fully human, which lowers immunogenicity, and are produced in mammalian cell cultures such as CHO cells.

2 — Correct: a mAb binds specifically to its target antigen, and this action can enhance immune function. It can opsonise pathogens, activate complement, trigger antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, or block inhibitory checkpoints such as PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4 so that T-cells attack tumours. Checkpoint-inhibitor research won the 2018 Nobel Prize for James Allison and Tasuku Honjo. Specificity is the key feature of mAbs and the reason they are called targeted or 'magic bullet' therapy. The same principle underlies passive immunisation.

3 — Correct: mAbs are used against viral infections. For Nipah virus, the human mAb m102.4 targets the viral G glycoprotein and was supplied to India for compassionate use during Kerala outbreaks. Nipah is a zoonotic paramyxovirus carried by fruit bats (Pteropus), first identified in Malaysia in 1998-99, and Kerala has had outbreaks since 2018. Other antiviral mAbs include palivizumab (RSV), nirsevimab (RSV), Inmazeb and Ebanga (Ebola), and casirivimab-imdevimab (COVID-19). No licensed Nipah vaccine or drug exists yet.
summary: The answer is (d): all three statements are correct. Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) are laboratory-made proteins that bind to one specific antigen, which directs or boosts the immune response. They are also used against viral infections, including Nipah virus, where the mAb m102.4 has been used on a compassionate-use basis.
topic_notes: Monoclonal antibodies are antibodies, which are Y-shaped immunoglobulin proteins, made by identical immune cells that are clones of a single parent B-cell. Because they come from one clone, they recognise a single epitope. Hybridoma technology (Köhler and Milstein, 1975) fuses antibody-producing B-cells with immortal myeloma cells, producing hybridomas that grow indefinitely and secrete one antibody type. Later advances include phage display (Nobel 2018 in Chemistry for George Smith and Gregory Winter), which allows fully human mAbs, and recombinant production in CHO cells. Naming: -omab (mouse), -ximab (chimeric), -zumab (humanised), -umab (human). Applications: cancer (trastuzumab for HER2 breast cancer, rituximab for CD20 lymphoma, pembrolizumab and nivolumab as PD-1 inhibitors), autoimmune diseases (adalimumab and infliximab against TNF-alpha), asthma, migraine (CGRP mAbs), osteoporosis (denosumab) and infections (palivizumab for RSV; Ebola mAbs; COVID-19 mAbs; Nipah m102.4). Diagnostics use include pregnancy test kits, ELISA, immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry. Related terms: passive immunity (ready-made antibodies given, short-lived, versus active immunity from vaccines), antibody-drug conjugates (trastuzumab emtansine), and bispecific antibodies. Nipah virus: a Henipavirus in the Paramyxoviridae family, spread by Pteropus fruit bats, via contaminated date-palm sap or pigs, and by human contact; fatality is high (40-75%); outbreaks occurred in Malaysia, Singapore, Bangladesh, and in India in West Bengal (2001, 2007) and Kerala (2018 onwards). ICMR has been working on a Nipah mAb and vaccines. Limitations: high cost, injection-only delivery, immunogenicity, and viral escape mutations, as seen with COVID-19 variants.

question:
Consider the following statements :
I. No virus can survive in ocean waters. Il. No virus can infect bacteria. Ill. No virus can change the cellular transcriptional activity in host cells. How many of the statements given above are correct?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites. They are acellular, with a nucleic acid genome (DNA or RNA) inside a protein capsid, and some have a lipid envelope. They replicate only inside living host cells, using the host's machinery. Statement I is wrong because the oceans are the largest viral reservoir on Earth: roughly 10^7 viruses per mL of seawater, about 10^30 in total. Most are bacteriophages and viruses of phytoplankton. They drive nutrient cycling through the 'viral shunt', lysing 20-40% of marine bacteria daily, and they influence carbon cycling and climate. Statement II is wrong because bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria. Examples are T4, lambda and M13. Phage therapy is based on them. Statement III is wrong because viruses routinely alter host transcription. HIV's Tat protein boosts transcription, retroviruses integrate proviral DNA, influenza 'cap-snatches' host mRNA, and oncogenic viruses such as HPV (E6/E7) and EBV change host gene expression. Elimination logic: each statement uses the absolute word 'No', so a single counterexample falsifies it. Since all three fail, the answer is (d).
explanations: (a) Only one is wrong, because no statement is correct; each is contradicted by established virology.
(b) Only two is wrong, because even two correct statements are not possible here; all three absolute claims fail.
(c) All three is wrong, because the statements say 'No virus', which is false in each case: marine viruses, phages and transcription-altering viruses all exist.
(d) None is correct, because viruses are abundant in oceans, infect bacteria as phages, and modify host transcription.
keyfact: Viruses abound in oceans, phages infect bacteria, and many viruses reprogram host transcription, so none of the three 'No virus' claims is correct.
option_notes: Only one: this would mean exactly one of the statements is true. Here it is not the case. As a question format, the 'how many' type tests whether you can check each statement independently, and the 'one' option is a common distractor.

Only two: this would mean two statements are true. In this question none is true. 'How many correct' questions in UPSC often hinge on absolute words such as 'No', 'only' and 'all', which are usually wrong in biology.

All three: this would mean viruses cannot survive in the ocean, cannot infect bacteria and cannot alter host transcription. All of these are contradicted by evidence. It is the opposite of the real situation.

None: no statement is correct. This is the official answer. Viruses are the most abundant biological entities in the oceans, bacteriophages infect bacteria, and many viruses reprogram host gene expression and transcription.
related: Bacteriophages were discovered by Twort (1915) and d'Herelle (1917).
Marine viruses number about 10^30 and drive the 'viral shunt'.
Tobacco mosaic virus was the first virus discovered (Ivanovsky 1892).
Retroviruses such as HIV use reverse transcriptase to make DNA from RNA.
HPV E6 and E7 proteins inactivate p53 and Rb, leading to cervical cancer.
Viroids are naked circular RNA infecting plants (Diener, 1971).
CRISPR-Cas is a bacterial adaptive defence against phages.
Transduction is gene transfer between bacteria via phages.
statements: I — Incorrect: Viruses are abundant in the oceans and survive there in large numbers. Marine viruses number about 10^30 and are the most abundant biological entities in the sea. Most infect bacteria (phages), cyanobacteria and algae. Viral lysis releases dissolved organic matter in the 'viral shunt', which recycles nutrients and affects carbon export. Cyanophages infect Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus. Viral lysis can end algal blooms, for example Emiliania huxleyi blooms through EhV. Marine viromes have been surveyed by projects such as Tara Oceans, which found thousands of previously unknown viral populations.

II — Incorrect: Viruses that infect bacteria exist and are called bacteriophages (phages). They were discovered by Frederick Twort (1915) and Félix d'Herelle (1917), who coined the term. Phages attach to bacterial receptors and inject their genome. They then follow a lytic cycle, which kills the cell, or a lysogenic cycle, in which the prophage integrates into the host genome. Phages enable transduction, a form of horizontal gene transfer. They carry toxin genes, as in cholera and diphtheria. Phage therapy is being revived against antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Phage display and CRISPR research also use them.

III — Incorrect: Viruses commonly alter host-cell transcription. They hijack host RNA polymerase and transcription factors and shut off host gene expression. HIV Tat enhances viral transcription. Influenza virus uses cap-snatching from host pre-mRNA. Herpesviruses and poxviruses carry their own transcription machinery or modulators. HPV E6 and E7 inactivate p53 and Rb, which changes cell-cycle gene expression and can lead to cervical cancer. Retroviruses integrate as proviruses under host transcription control. Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from RNA, which is the basis of the central dogma exception noted by Temin and Baltimore.
summary: The answer is (d) None. All three statements are false: viruses are abundant in ocean waters, bacteriophages infect bacteria, and many viruses reprogram host-cell transcription.
topic_notes: Viruses are non-cellular, obligate intracellular parasites, typically 20-300 nm in size. They are classified by genome type (Baltimore classification, seven groups), host range (animal, plant, bacterial, archaeal, fungal) and morphology. Outside a host they are inert virions. Replication stages are attachment, entry, uncoating, synthesis, assembly and release. Bacteriophages follow lytic or lysogenic cycles, and transduction, either generalised or specialised, moves genes between bacteria. Marine virology: about 10^30 viruses in the oceans, the viral shunt, regulation of algal blooms, and control of bacterial populations. Viruses influence host transcription by shutting off host mRNA synthesis, using host RNA polymerase II, cap-snatching (influenza), integrating proviruses (retroviruses) and encoding oncoproteins (HPV E6/E7, SV40 large T antigen). Related ideas include viroids (naked RNA that infect plants, discovered by T.O. Diener, 1971), prions (infectious proteins), and giant viruses such as Mimivirus and Pandoravirus. Other angles UPSC may test: vaccines (live attenuated, inactivated, mRNA, viral vector), reverse transcriptase and the central dogma, CRISPR-Cas as a bacterial defence against phages, oncolytic viruses, zoonotic spillover (Nipah, SARS-CoV-2, H5N1), antivirals (acyclovir, remdesivir), the role of interferons, and the distinction between DNA and RNA viruses. Also remember that antibiotics do not work against viruses, and that the first virus discovered was tobacco mosaic virus (Ivanovsky 1892, Beijerinck 1898), with Stanley crystallising it in 1935.

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement I : Activated carbon is a good and an attractive tool to remove pollutants from effluent streams and to remediate contaminants from various industries.
Statement II : Activated carbon exhibits a large surface area and a strong potential for adsorbing heavy metals. Statement III : Activated carbon can be easily synthesized from environmental wastes with high carbon content. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement II and Statement III are correct and both of them explain Statement I
Both Statement II and Statement Il are correct but only one of them explains Statement I
Only one of the Statements II and Ill is correct and that explains Statement I
Neither Statement II nor Statement Ill is correct [ P.T.O
subject: Environment
detail: Activated carbon is carbon processed (by carbonisation followed by physical activation with steam or CO2, or chemical activation with agents such as H3PO4, KOH or ZnCl2) to develop an extensive network of micropores and mesopores. Its surface area typically ranges from about 500 to 1500 m2/g, sometimes more. This gives huge adsorption capacity, because adsorption is a surface phenomenon in which molecules stick to the solid surface. It removes organic pollutants, dyes, phenols, pesticides, odours, chlorine and heavy metals such as lead, mercury, cadmium, chromium and arsenic from water, air and industrial effluents. The feedstock can be coconut shells, rice husk, sawdust, bagasse, fruit stones, agricultural residues, tyres or coal, so production is cheap and also converts waste into a useful product. Statement II explains the effectiveness (a technical reason) and Statement III explains the attractiveness (an economic and environmental reason). Elimination: since both II and III are factually correct and both support I, options (b), (c) and (d) fail, because each denies either the correctness or the explanatory link of at least one statement.
explanations: Correct: Statement II (large surface area, strong heavy metal adsorption) and Statement III (easy, cheap synthesis from carbon-rich waste) are both true, and together they explain why activated carbon is a good and attractive remediation tool.
Wrong: this says only one of the two explains Statement I, but both do. Effectiveness comes from II and attractiveness (low cost, sustainability) from III.
Wrong: this says only one of II and III is correct, but both are factually correct.
Wrong: this says neither II nor III is correct, which is false because both are established facts about activated carbon.
keyfact: Activated carbon works because of its huge porous surface area (adsorption of heavy metals and organics), and it is attractive because it can be cheaply made from carbon-rich waste.
option_notes: Both II and III correct and both explain I: this is the right option here. It recognises that adsorption capacity (technical reason) and low-cost waste-based production (economic reason) jointly make activated carbon attractive for pollution control. Activated carbon is used in water treatment, air purification, solvent recovery and medicine, and is made from coconut shell, wood, coal and agricultural waste.

Both II and III correct but only one explains I: this is a plausible-looking distractor. UPSC uses such options to test whether you can judge the explanatory link. Here the link holds for both, because performance depends on surface area and wide adoption depends on cheap feedstock, so the 'only one explains' claim fails.

Only one of II and III is correct and it explains I: this would apply if one statement were factually false. Both statements are true, so it fails. In such 'statement-explanation' questions, first check each statement's factual accuracy, then check the explanatory relationship.

Neither II nor III is correct: this would mean activated carbon lacked high surface area and could not be made from waste, which is plainly wrong. Activated carbon surface area often exceeds 500 m2/g, and waste-derived carbons from rice husk and coconut shell are common in research and industry.
related: Adsorption is a surface phenomenon, while absorption occurs throughout the bulk of a material.
Activated carbon surface area can exceed 1000 m2/g.
Biochar is produced by pyrolysis of biomass and is used for soil amendment and carbon sequestration.
Common activating agents: steam, CO2, H3PO4, KOH and ZnCl2.
Coconut shell is a major raw material for activated carbon in India.
Heavy metals commonly removed: Pb, Hg, Cd, Cr and As.
The BET method measures specific surface area using nitrogen adsorption.
CPCB is the body that sets effluent standards in India.
statements: 1 — Correct: Activated carbon is widely used in effluent treatment and remediation. It is a form of carbon with a highly porous structure, used since ancient times (Egyptians used charcoal for medicine and Indians for water filtration). Modern industrial use began in the early 1900s. It is used in water purification, gas masks, air filters, sugar decolourisation, gold recovery, and medical treatment of poisoning. It is available as powdered (PAC), granular (GAC) and extruded forms. Spent carbon can be regenerated thermally.

2 — Correct: Activated carbon has a very large specific surface area and a porous structure with surface functional groups (carboxyl, hydroxyl) that bind heavy metal ions. Adsorption is a surface phenomenon, different from absorption. Pore sizes are classified by IUPAC as micropores (<2 nm), mesopores (2 to 50 nm) and macropores (>50 nm). It adsorbs metals like Pb, Cd, Hg, Cr(VI) and As, and the process depends on pH, contact time and temperature. Surface area is often measured by the BET method using nitrogen adsorption.

3 — Correct: Activated carbon can be made from low-cost, carbon-rich wastes such as coconut shell, rice husk, wood waste, bagasse, nut shells, fruit peels, sewage sludge and waste tyres. Preparation involves pyrolysis (carbonisation) at about 400 to 800 degrees C in limited oxygen, then activation by steam or CO2 at higher temperatures, or by chemicals such as KOH or H3PO4. This lowers cost, reduces waste disposal problems and supports a circular economy and waste-to-wealth goals. India is a major producer from coconut shells.
summary: The answer is (a). Activated carbon has a very large surface area and a strong capacity to adsorb heavy metals (Statement II), and it can be made cheaply from carbon-rich wastes (Statement III). Together these explain why it is a good and attractive tool for cleaning effluents and remediating industrial contaminants (Statement I).
topic_notes: Activated carbon (activated charcoal) is a highly porous carbonaceous adsorbent. Production has two steps: carbonisation (pyrolysis of the raw material in an oxygen-poor atmosphere) and activation (physical, using steam or CO2 at about 800 to 1000 degrees C; or chemical, using H3PO4, ZnCl2 or KOH at lower temperatures). Typical raw materials are coal, coconut shell, wood, peat, rice husk, bagasse, fruit stones and agricultural residues. Surface area is usually 500 to 1500 m2/g, and it is measured by the BET method. Adsorption works by physical forces (van der Waals) and sometimes chemical bonding (chemisorption). Forms are powdered (PAC), granular (GAC) and pelletised. Uses include drinking water purification (removal of taste, odour, chlorine, organics), industrial effluent treatment (dyes, phenols, heavy metals), air and gas purification, gas masks, solvent recovery, decolourising sugar, gold extraction (carbon-in-pulp), food and beverage processing, and emergency treatment of oral poisoning. Limitations: it is less effective for some small polar compounds, it saturates and needs regeneration (thermal, chemical) or disposal, and its performance depends on pH, temperature and contact time. Related concepts: adsorption versus absorption, biochar (made from biomass pyrolysis, used for soil improvement and carbon sequestration), bioremediation, phytoremediation, nanomaterials such as graphene and carbon nanotubes, ion exchange, reverse osmosis, and zeolites. Policy angles: waste-to-wealth, circular economy, Swachh Bharat, Namami Gange, effluent standards under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986, and the role of CPCB. UPSC often asks assertion-reason style questions on environmental technologies, so know both the mechanism and the use.

question:
With reference to the Indian polity, consider the following statements :
I. An Ordinance can amend any Central Act. Il. An Ordinance can abridge a Fundamental Right. Ill. An Ordinance can come into effect from a back date. Which of the statements given above are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: Article 123 empowers the President to promulgate Ordinances when Parliament is not in session (either House not in session, in fact) and he is satisfied that circumstances require immediate action. Article 123(2) says an Ordinance has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament, but only in respect of matters on which Parliament can legislate. It must be laid before Parliament and ceases to operate six weeks after Parliament reassembles, or earlier if both Houses disapprove it. Because it has the force of an Act, it can amend or repeal any Central Act, and it can be given retrospective effect, including in tax matters. Article 13(3)(a) defines 'law' to include an Ordinance, and Article 13(2) forbids the State from making any law that takes away or abridges Fundamental Rights. So an Ordinance cannot abridge a Fundamental Right, which makes statement II wrong. Elimination logic: II is false, so options (a), (b) and (d) all fall away, leaving (c). Also remember that an Ordinance cannot amend the Constitution. The Court in D.C. Wadhwa (1987) condemned the repeated re-promulgation of Ordinances as a fraud on the Constitution, and Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) held that the legislative necessity must be examined.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes II, which is incorrect, and leaves out III, which is correct.
(b) is wrong because it includes II, which is incorrect, and leaves out I, which is correct.
(c) is correct because I and III are right and II is wrong; an Ordinance is bound by Art. 13(2).
(d) is wrong because it includes statement II, but an Ordinance cannot abridge a Fundamental Right.
keyfact: An Ordinance (Art. 123) equals an Act in force, so it can amend Central Acts and operate retrospectively, but it is 'law' under Art. 13 and cannot abridge Fundamental Rights or amend the Constitution.
statements: I — Correct: An Ordinance has the same force as an Act of Parliament (Art. 123(2)), so it can amend or repeal any Central Act, subject to the limits on Parliament's own power.
II — Incorrect: 'Law' in Art. 13(3)(a) includes an Ordinance, and Art. 13(2) bars any law that takes away or abridges Fundamental Rights.
III — Correct: Like an Act, an Ordinance can have retrospective effect, since Parliament's legislative power includes making laws operate from a back date.
summary: The answer is (c): statements I and III are correct, and statement II is incorrect. An Ordinance under Article 123 has the same force and limits as an Act of Parliament, so it can amend Central Acts and can be made retrospective, but it cannot abridge Fundamental Rights because Article 13(2) bars any 'law' from doing so.

question:
Consider the following pairs : State Description
I. Arunachal : The capital is named after Pradesh a fort, and the State has two National Parks Il. Nagaland : The State came into existence on the basis of a Constitutional Amendment Act Il. Tripura : Initially a Part ‘C’ State, it became a centrally administered territory with the reorganization of States in 1956 and later attained the status of a full-fledged State How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
subject: Polity
detail: Pair I: Itanagar, the capital of Arunachal Pradesh, takes its name from the Ita Fort (brick fort, 14th-15th century). The State has two National Parks, Namdapha (Changlang district) and Mouling (Upper Siang district), so the description holds. Arunachal, formerly NEFA, became a Union Territory in 1972 and a State in 1987 via the 55th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1986. Pair II: Nagaland was formed as the 16th State by the State of Nagaland Act, 1962, enacted under the 13th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1962, which inserted Article 371A, giving special protection to Naga customary law, religious and social practices, and land ownership. It became a State on 1 December 1963. Pair III: Under the 1950 Constitution Tripura was a Part C State. The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 and the 7th Amendment made it a Union Territory, and the North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, 1971 made it a full State on 21 January 1972, together with Manipur and Meghalaya. Since all three descriptions are factually accurate, options (a), (b) and (d) are eliminated.
explanations: (a) Wrong: it implies only one pair is correct, but all three pairs are accurate.
(b) Wrong: it implies one pair is incorrect, but none is.
(c) Right: all three pairs are correctly matched, in line with the official answer.
(d) Wrong: it implies no pair is correct, which contradicts the facts for all three states.
keyfact: Nagaland: 13th Amendment 1962 (Art. 371A); Tripura: Part C, then UT 1956, then State 1972; Itanagar is named after Ita Fort.
statements: 1 — Correct: Itanagar is named after Ita Fort, and Arunachal Pradesh has two National Parks, Namdapha and Mouling.
2 — Correct: Nagaland was created by the 13th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1962 (Article 371A) and the State of Nagaland Act, 1962, and became a State in 1963.
3 — Correct: Tripura was a Part C State, became a Union Territory in 1956, and attained full statehood in 1972.
summary: The answer is (c): all three pairs are correctly matched. Itanagar is named after Ita Fort, Nagaland was created through the 13th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1962, and Tripura moved from Part C State to Union Territory (1956) to full statehood (1972).

question:
With reference to India, consider the following :
I. The Inter-State Council
II. The National Security Council Ill. Zonal Councils How many of the above’ were established as per the provisions of the Constitution of India?
subject: Polity
detail: The question tests the difference between constitutional bodies, statutory bodies and executive (non-statutory) bodies. Article 263 empowers the President to establish an Inter-State Council if it appears that the public interest would be served by one. It would investigate and discuss subjects of common interest between States, or between the Union and States, and make recommendations. The Council was actually set up in 1990 on the Sarkaria Commission's recommendation. Its constitutional source is Article 263, so it counts as established as per the Constitution's provisions. Zonal Councils (five originally: Northern, Central, Eastern, Western, Southern; the North-Eastern Council was created separately by the North Eastern Council Act, 1971) were set up under Part III of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. They are statutory, not constitutional. The National Security Council was constituted in 1998 by an executive resolution of the Government of India, with the Prime Minister as chair. It has no constitutional or statutory backing. Elimination: since Zonal Councils and the NSC are not constitutional, options (b) and (c) fail. Since the Inter-State Council is constitutional under Article 263, option (d) fails. This leaves (a).
explanations: Correct. Only the Inter-State Council (Article 263) is established under the Constitution, so exactly one of the three qualifies.
Wrong. Two cannot qualify, because Zonal Councils (statutory, 1956 Act) and the NSC (executive, 1998) lack a constitutional basis.
Wrong. All three would require the NSC and Zonal Councils to be constitutional, and they are not.
Wrong. The Inter-State Council is constitutional under Article 263, so at least one qualifies.
keyfact: Inter-State Council = Article 263 (constitutional); Zonal Councils = States Reorganisation Act 1956 (statutory); NSC = 1998 executive decision (non-statutory).
statements: 1 — Correct: The Inter-State Council is provided for under Article 263 of the Constitution, and the President may establish it. It was set up in 1990.
2 — Incorrect: The National Security Council was created in 1998 by an executive decision. It has no constitutional or statutory basis.
3 — Incorrect: Zonal Councils are statutory bodies set up by the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, not by the Constitution.
summary: The answer is (a) Only one. Of the three bodies, only the Inter-State Council has a basis in the Constitution (Article 263). The National Security Council was set up by an executive decision in 1998, and Zonal Councils were created by a statute, the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.

question:
Consider the following statements :
I. The Constitution of India explicitly mentions that in certain spheres the Governor of a State acts in his/her own discretion. Il. The President of India can, of his/her own, reserve a bill passed by a State Legislature for his/her consideration without it being forwarded by the Governor of the State concerned. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: Article 163(1) says the Governor acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers 'except in so far as he is by or under this Constitution required to exercise his functions or any of them in his discretion'. Express discretion appears in the Sixth Schedule (Para 9(2): the Governor of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram determines the share of royalty between the District Council and the State), and under Article 371-A, 371-H and similar special provisions (e.g., Nagaland law and order, Sikkim). Article 163(2) makes the Governor's decision on whether a matter falls within his discretion final. Under Article 200, the Governor may assent, withhold assent, return a non-money bill for reconsideration, or reserve a bill for the President. Article 201 then lets the President act only on a bill reserved by the Governor: assent, withhold assent, or direct its return. The Constitution gives the President no power to call up or reserve a State bill suo motu, unlike the Union's power to disallow State laws in other contexts. Hence Statement I is correct and II is incorrect, which eliminates (b), (c) and (d).
explanations: Correct: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, so 'I only' is right.
Wrong: Statement II is false because the President cannot reserve a State bill without the Governor forwarding it, and Statement I is true.
Wrong: Statement II is not correct, so both cannot be right.
Wrong: Statement I is correct, since the Constitution expressly mentions Governor's discretion.
keyfact: Governor's discretion is explicit in Art. 163(1) and the Sixth Schedule, but only the Governor can reserve a State bill for the President (Art. 200-201).
statements: 1 — Correct: Article 163(1) and provisions such as Sixth Schedule Para 9(2) and Articles 371-A and 371-H expressly provide for Governor's discretion.
2 — Incorrect: Under Articles 200-201, a bill reaches the President only when the Governor reserves it; the President has no power to reserve a State bill on his/her own.
summary: The answer is (a): only Statement I is correct. The Constitution explicitly provides for the Governor's discretion in certain spheres (e.g., Article 163(1) and the Sixth Schedule), but the President cannot reserve a State bill on his/her own, because reservation under Article 200 is initiated only by the Governor.

question: Consider the following pairs : Stated under Provision in the Constitution of India The Directive Separation of Judiciary Principles from the Executive in of the State the public services of Policy the State The FundaValuing and preserving Il. mental Duties of the rich heritage of our composite culture : The FundaProhibition of employIll. mental Rights ment of children below the age of 14 years in factories above pairs are How many of the correctly matched?
subject: Polity
detail: Each pair matches a provision to the part of the Constitution where it appears. Article 50 in Part IV (Directive Principles) directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State. Article 51A(f) in Part IVA (Fundamental Duties, added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976 on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation) makes it a duty of every citizen to value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture. Article 24 in Part III (Fundamental Rights, under the Right against Exploitation, Articles 23-24) prohibits employing children below 14 years in factories, mines or other hazardous employment. Note that Article 21A (free and compulsory education for ages 6-14, 86th Amendment 2002) and Article 45 (early childhood care) are separate provisions. The elimination logic is to verify each pair against its article number. Since all three are verifiable, 'None', 'Only one' and 'Only two' are all ruled out, leaving (d). If the official key really says (c), that would contradict the text above, so recheck the OCR of the question and the key.
explanations: (a) Only two: Wrong on the constitutional text, because no pair is mismatched, so the count cannot be two.
(b) Only one: Wrong, because all three pairs are correct, not just one.
(c) None: This is the key supplied with the question, but it conflicts with Articles 50, 51A(f) and 24, which make every pair correct. Verify against the official answer key.
(d) All the three: Correct on the constitutional text, since Article 50 (DPSP), Article 51A(f) (Duties) and Article 24 (Fundamental Rights) match the three pairs.
keyfact: Art. 50 = separation of judiciary from executive (DPSP); Art. 51A(f) = composite culture (Duty); Art. 24 = no child labour under 14 in factories/mines (FR).
statements: I — Correct: Article 50 (DPSP) provides for separation of the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
II — Correct: Article 51A(f) (Fundamental Duties) requires citizens to value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture.
